title: Spanish C2
description: The sixth and last step in Latin American Spanish, from C1 to CEFR level C2, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE C2 exam. Lessons cover the precise word among near-synonyms and confusable pairs, deliberate shifts of register, learned words and Latin phrases, the tenses as style, conditions and counterfactuals without si, relatives and the long sentence, formal prepositional phrases, figures of speech, the critical review and the vocabulary of style, narrative technique, reading between the lines of public language, and the specialized Spanish of law, medicine, finance and patents. A module on Spanish across the world covers dubbing and the pluricentric norm, Spain's Spanish, grammar and usage across the Americas, and language contact and change, and the last module practices writing from several sources, rewriting from notes, texts from data, oral mediation and the three tests of the DELE C2. Honors lessons add lexicography, place names, Old Spanish, hard cases of agreement, Golden Age theater, modernismo, medicine leaflets, notarial Spanish, Judeo-Spanish, Spanish in Equatorial Guinea and the Philippines, interpreting, and classics from the Lazarillo and Galdós to Lorca and Borges. About 620 new words build on the roughly 4,100 from Spanish A1 to C1, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's and other regions' usage taught for recognition. Conjugation drills keep all fifteen forms of the earlier courses, and a reading list suggests classics, podcasts, reference works and official exam material for this level. Unlocks when Spanish C1 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Ahumado, terroso, aterciopelado: the precise word
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 taught you to choose a register and the right collocation (C1 16: *cometer un error
garrafal*). C2 asks for something finer: of two words that both fit, which one says exactly what
you mean, about the thing and about yourself? A C2 writer controls that difference. This module
is about control of the word: this lesson takes near-synonyms, verbs of saying and words for
sensations; lesson 02 takes register, 03 confusable words and 04 learned words.

The theme is the *cata* (tasting) of three Mexican products judged by the senses: mezcal, coffee
and cacao.

## How near-synonyms differ

A **[[near-synonym]]** shares most of its meaning with another word but not all of it. Seven things
can separate two such words:

- **[[Denotation]]**, what the word refers to: *el aroma* is a pleasant smell; B2's *el sabor* is a
  taste.
- **[[Connotation]]**, the attitude or associations it carries: *esbelto* praises, *escuálido*
  worries.
- Register: *catar* belongs to professionals; A1's *probar* to everyone.
- **[[Collocation]]**, the words it habitually goes with: *esgrimir* takes *un arma* (a weapon) or
  *un argumento*, but *aducir* takes only reasons, never weapons.
- Region: in Mexico *flaco* is also an affectionate nickname (*¿Qué onda, flaca?*).
- Intensity: *molesto* (annoyed) → *enojado* (angry) → *furioso* (furious).
- Evaluation: *intenso* is usually praise in a tasting note; *agresivo* is a complaint.

A word that carries a negative judgment is *peyorativo* (pejorative): the suffix *-ucho* turns
*casa* into *casucha* (a hovel), and *-astro* turns *político* into *politicastro*.

### The substitution test

To check a choice, put each candidate in the same sentence and ask: does it change what we learn
about the thing, or about the speaker?

- *Es una mujer delgada.* — She is a slim woman. (a fact)
- *Es una mujer esbelta.* — She is a slender woman. (a fact plus admiration)
- *Es una mujer flaca.* — She is a thin woman. (plain, often informal, sometimes critical)
- *Es una mujer escuálida.* — She is a scrawny woman. (concern or contempt)

The thing hasn't changed; the speaker's attitude has. The same test separates B2's *terco* from
C1's *tenaz* and *perseverante* (persevering, C1's *la perseverancia*):

- *Es terco: no acepta que se equivocó.* — He's stubborn: he won't accept he was wrong.
- *Es tenaz: lleva diez años con el proyecto.* — She's tenacious: she has been on the project
  for ten years.

![A horizontal scale from praise on the left to criticism on the right. Four boxes sit on it: esbelto in green (praise), delgado in gray (neutral), flaco in light orange (plain, informal, can criticize) and escuálido in pale red (criticism). Below, a second row: tenaz and perseverante in green on the left, terco in pale red on the right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Verbs of saying, precisely

B2 13 taught *recalcar, puntualizar, insinuar* and *sostener*, and C1 added *objetar*. They
report what someone said. The verbs below also report how, why or in what mood. Each refines a
plain verb: *decir*, *afirmar* or A2's *comentar*.

| Verb | What it adds | Typical company |
|---|---|---|
| *aducir* | offers something as a reason, often one the writer doubts | *aducir razones, motivos, problemas de salud* |
| *esgrimir* | uses an argument as a weapon (literally, to wield a sword) | *esgrimir un argumento, un pretexto, el reglamento* |
| *argüir* | contends, argues that (formal) | *argüir que…* |
| *apostillar* | adds a short, pointed remark after someone else | in quotations: *—…, apostilló.* |
| *espetar* | says something blunt or rude, suddenly | *espetarle una pregunta a alguien* |
| *mascullar* | mutters between the teeth, often annoyed | *mascullar una disculpa, una maldición* |
| *balbucear* | stammers from nerves or surprise; babies babble | *balbucear una excusa* |
| *farfullar* | jabbers fast and unclearly | *farfullar una respuesta* |
| *refunfuñar* | grumbles, showing displeasure | often with no object: *refunfuñaba* |

Choosing among them is choosing a point of view. Compare three reports of the same words:

- *El proveedor dijo que hubo problemas de transporte.* — The supplier said there had been
  transport problems. (neutral)
- *El proveedor adujo problemas de transporte.* — The supplier cited transport problems. (a
  reason, perhaps an excuse)
- *El proveedor farfulló algo sobre el transporte.* — The supplier gabbled something about
  transport. (he sounded unconvincing)

The second and third are no longer neutral: the reporter has judged. That is fine in a chronicle
or a novel, and a fault in a news report or a set of minutes, where *dijo, afirmó* or *señaló* are
the honest choices.

## Words for sensations

Tasters need words that are both exact and shared. Most of them work on scales. A useful order
for a note is smell first (*en nariz*), then the mouth (*en boca*), then what remains (*el
regusto*, or *el final*).

| Sense | Words | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| smell | *el aroma; afrutado, ahumado, terroso, floral* | *afrutado* = like fruit; *terroso* = like damp earth |
| taste | *dulce* (sweet), *el amargor, la acidez* | in coffee *la acidez* is praise; in daily life *tengo acidez* is heartburn |
| texture | *astringente, aterciopelado, untuoso* | from dry and puckering to velvety to smooth and rich |
| after | *el regusto, persistente* (lingering) | *un regusto a madera* = an aftertaste of wood |
| age | *joven* (young), *reposado* (rested), *añejo* | categories of tequila and mezcal |

Intensity is graded with adverbs (*ligeramente ahumado, muy ahumado, intensamente ahumado*), and
evaluation with the adjective itself: *un amargor delicado* is praise, *un amargor agresivo* a
fault. *Untuoso* is a compliment for mezcal and an insult for a person (like English
"unctuous").

![A tasting wheel with three inner sectors, Aroma, Sabor and Textura en boca. The outer ring names ten descriptors with example smells or feelings: afrutado (plátano, piña, cítricos), ahumado (humo de leña, brasas), terroso (tierra mojada, hongos), herbal (pasto, hierbas); dulce (miel, panela), ácido (mandarina, limón), amargo (cacao, café oscuro); astringente (té fuerte, cáscara verde), aterciopelado (terciopelo, crema), untuoso (aceite, mantequilla).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Three tasting notes

Tasting notes use a nominal style (B2 18): few verbs, many nouns and adjectives.

> Café de altura, Chiapas. Aroma intenso a panela y frutos rojos. En boca, acidez brillante,
> cítrica, que recuerda a la mandarina; cuerpo medio y textura sedosa. Un leve amargor de cacao al
> final, sin rastro de astringencia. El regusto, dulce y limpio, dura varios segundos. Ideal para
> métodos de filtrado.

High-grown coffee, Chiapas. An intense aroma of raw cane sugar and red berries. In the mouth, a
bright, citrus acidity that recalls tangerine; medium body and a silky texture. A slight cacao
bitterness at the end, with no trace of astringency. The aftertaste, sweet and clean, lasts
several seconds. Ideal for filter methods.

> Cacao de Tabasco, 70 %. Aroma terroso, con notas de madera y tabaco. Amargor marcado pero
> equilibrado; ligera acidez de fruta seca. Astringente en el primer bocado, se vuelve
> aterciopelado al derretirse en el paladar. Regusto largo, con un toque de nuez tostada. Para
> quien busca un chocolate intenso, no dulce.

Tabasco cacao, 70%. An earthy aroma, with notes of wood and tobacco. A marked but balanced
bitterness; a slight dried-fruit acidity. Astringent at the first bite, it turns velvety as it
melts on the palate. A long aftertaste, with a touch of toasted nut. For anyone looking for an
intense chocolate, not a sweet one.

> Mezcal espadín joven, Oaxaca. Ahumado discreto, nada agresivo; en nariz, piña asada,
> cáscara de naranja y tierra húmeda. Entrada suave, cuerpo untuoso y un final ligeramente
> picante. Afrutado y terroso a la vez, con un regusto a hierbas que invita al segundo trago. Para
> tomar solo y despacio.

Young espadín mezcal, Oaxaca. A discreet smokiness, not at all aggressive; on the nose, roasted
pineapple, orange peel and damp earth. A smooth entry, a rich, oily body and a slightly spicy
finish. Fruity and earthy at once, with an herbal aftertaste that invites a second sip. To drink
neat and slowly.

## About mezcal

Mezcal is a *destilado de agave*, made from the cooked hearts of many species of agave
(*espadín* is the most widely grown; *tobalá* is a wild one), and the cooking in earth pits
gives many mezcales their smoky note, though not all are equally *ahumados*. Mexico protected
the name with a denomination of origin in 1994 (the IMPI's declaration of November 28, 1994);
its territory has been extended several times since, in 2018 for example to municipalities of
Aguascalientes, the Estado de México, Morelos and Puebla, and some extensions are still disputed.
The IMPI publishes the current list of states and municipalities, so check it before you name
them. Labels also carry age categories such as *joven*, *reposado* and *añejo*.

## Text: a tasting with a skeptic

> Mi tío Rodolfo y los nueve mezcales
>
> Mi tío Rodolfo es de Tequila, Jalisco, y nunca ha confiado en un destilado que no venga de su
> tierra. Cuando lo invité a una cata de mezcal en la colonia Roma, refunfuñó durante todo el
> trayecto: que si el tráfico, que si los precios, que si las modas de la capital.
>
> La catadora, una joven de Santiago Matatlán, nos sirvió nueve copitas en fila. Antes de probar
> nada, nos pidió que oliéramos. "El aroma les va a contar la mitad de la historia", explicó. El
> primero era un espadín joven: ahumado, sí, pero también afrutado, con algo de plátano maduro. Mi
> tío lo olió con desconfianza y masculló que olía a llanta quemada. La catadora sonrió y
> apostilló: "Pues a mí me recuerda la cocina de mi abuela".
>
> Con la segunda copita, un tobalá silvestre, la sala se quedó en silencio. Era terroso, casi
> mineral, y dejaba en el paladar un regusto a hierba mojada. Mi tío lo probó dos veces. Cuando la
> catadora le preguntó qué notaba, balbuceó algo sobre la tierra de su rancho y se calló,
> sorprendido de sí mismo.
>
> No se rindió tan fácil. Con la cuarta, un reposado de cuerpo untuoso, esgrimió su argumento
> favorito: el tequila tiene reglas desde hace décadas, y el mezcal, según él, es puro cuento. La
> catadora le explicó que el mezcal también tiene denominación de origen desde 1994 y una norma
> que fija sus categorías. Él arguyó que una norma no garantiza nada si nadie la hace cumplir. No
> le faltaba razón, y ella lo reconoció.
>
> El momento más tenso llegó con un ensamble de tres agaves, astringente al principio y
> aterciopelado al final. Un señor de la mesa de al lado, que llevaba una hora presumiendo de su
> paladar, le espetó a mi tío: "Usted no sabe tomar, nada más traga". Mi tío farfulló una
> respuesta que nadie entendió, se puso rojo y pidió agua.
>
> Al final, con un añejo de notas de cacao y un amargor delicado, mi tío aceptó que había "uno o
> dos que no están tan mal". Adujo que se parecían al tequila, aunque los dos sabíamos que no era
> cierto. Compró una botella del tobalá y, en el taxi, me pidió que no le contara nada a nadie en
> Tequila.

Summary. The narrator takes Uncle Rodolfo, a tequila loyalist from Tequila, Jalisco, to a mezcal
tasting in Mexico City; he grumbles all the way. The young taster from Santiago Matatlán asks
them to smell first. He mutters that the first mezcal smells of burnt tires; she adds a gentle
reply. A wild tobalá silences him: he stammers something about his ranch. With a rested mezcal he
wields his favorite argument, that mezcal has no real rules; she explains its denomination of
origin and standard, and he contends that rules mean nothing if no one enforces them, a fair
point she accepts. A know-it-all at the next table snaps an insult at him, and he jabbers a reply.
At the end he admits a couple are "not so bad", gives a weak reason, and buys a bottle in secret.

Glosses: *que si el tráfico, que si los precios* (complaining about this and that), *copitas*
(small glasses), *es puro cuento* (it's all hype), *hacer cumplir* (to enforce), *un ensamble*
(a blend of agaves), *presumir de* (to show off about), *nada más traga* (you just gulp it down).

Notice what the verbs do: *masculló, balbuceó, farfulló* show the uncle losing his footing;
*esgrimió* and *arguyó* show him fighting back; *adujo* tells us his last reason is an excuse.

## Checking a choice

When two words seem equal, check them. A good dictionary marks connotation and register (the
DLE writes *despect.* for derogatory and *coloq.* for colloquial), and a corpus shows which words
a candidate keeps company with and in which countries. Honors lesson 04h1 shows how.

## Pronunciation

- *argüir*: ar-GÜIR, two syllables; the two dots tell you to sound the *u*, like the *w* in
  English *Gwen*. *Arguyo* has no dots and three syllables: ar-GU-yo.
- *refunfuñar*: re-fun-fu-ÑAR, four syllables.
- *aterciopelado*: a-ter-cio-pe-LA-do, six syllables; *cio* is one syllable.
- *astringente*: as-trin-GEN-te, four syllables; *g* before *e* is the throat sound of *j*.
- *untuoso*: un-TUO-so, three syllables.

## Common mistakes

- False precision. A rare word is not a better word. *Aducir* for a plain report (*El
  director adujo que la reunión es a las diez*) sounds suspicious of the director.
- Judging by accident. *Masculló, espetó* and *refunfuñó* carry an opinion. In minutes or a
  news story, use *dijo, afirmó, señaló*.
- Calques from English. *Untuoso* praises a mezcal but not a waiter; *lívido* (lesson 03)
  means bruise-colored or very pale, not furious.
- Wrong company. *Esgrimir una razón* and *aducir una razón* both work, but only *esgrimir*
  takes *un arma*.

## Key points

- Near-synonyms differ in denotation, connotation, register, collocation, region, intensity and
  evaluation. Test a choice by substitution.
- *Aducir, esgrimir, argüir* report arguments; *apostillar, espetar* remarks; *mascullar,
  balbucear, farfullar, refunfuñar* manner. Most of them also judge.
- Tasting notes go from *nariz* to *boca* to *regusto*, grading intensity with adverbs and
  evaluation with adjectives.
- *Argüir* writes ü only before *i*: *argüimos* but *arguyo, arguyó*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Del parte al chisme: shifting register on purpose
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 01 put register on a scale and C1 02 taught Mexican colloquial speech; lesson 01 chose words
inside one register. This lesson moves a whole text from one register to another. At C2 you
rewrite for a new reader without losing a fact, and you notice when someone's shift of register
is a joke. One invented event, a collision on a Mexico City avenue, is told six times.

## One event, six texts

On Tuesday, March 3, 2026, at 8:40 a.m., a delivery van hit the car Mariana Solís was driving,
her mother's, and drove off. A motorcyclist behind her braked and fell.

### 1. The insurance report (specialized)

> REPORTE DE SINIESTRO 2026-03-0417. 03/03/2026, 08:40 h. Av. Insurgentes Sur, col. Del Valle,
> CDMX. Asegurada: Carmen Ruiz Ochoa, póliza AU-55821, cobertura amplia. Conductora: Mariana
> Solís Ruiz, ilesa. Vehículo tercero (camioneta de reparto, placas no identificadas) realiza
> cambio de carril sin precaución y colisiona con salpicadera delantera derecha y cofre; tercero
> se da a la fuga. Daños: abolladuras en salpicadera y cofre; carrocería sin daño estructural.
> Lesionados: un motociclista, leve. Se elabora croquis. Procede peritaje. Aplica deducible.

CLAIM REPORT 2026-03-0417. March 3, 2026, 8:40 a.m. Insurgentes Sur, Del Valle, Mexico City.
Policyholder: Carmen Ruiz Ochoa, policy AU-55821, comprehensive cover. Driver: Mariana Solís
Ruiz, unhurt. Third-party vehicle (delivery van, plates not identified) changes lanes without due
care and collides with the right front fender and the hood; third party flees. Damage: dents in
the fender and hood; no structural damage to the body. Injured: one motorcyclist, minor. Sketch
drawn up. Appraisal to follow. Deductible applies.

### 2. The police report (official)

> Siendo las 08:50 horas del día 3 de marzo de 2026, el suscrito, al realizar recorrido de
> vigilancia sobre avenida Insurgentes Sur, fue alertado de un hecho de tránsito. Al arribar, se
> observó un vehículo tipo sedán con daños en su parte frontal derecha y una motocicleta caída en
> el carril de baja velocidad. El conductor de esta, de 27 años, presentaba excoriaciones en el
> antebrazo y fue valorado por paramédicos en el lugar. Según testigos, el vehículo responsable
> se dio a la fuga con dirección al sur.

At 8:50 a.m. on March 3, 2026, the undersigned, while on patrol along Insurgentes Sur, was
alerted to a traffic incident. On arrival, a sedan with damage to its front right side was
observed, along with a motorcycle down in the slow lane. Its rider, aged 27, had abrasions on his
forearm and was examined by paramedics at the scene. According to witnesses, the vehicle
responsible fled southward.

### 3. The news brief (press)

> Choque en Insurgentes deja a un motociclista lesionado. Un motociclista resultó con lesiones
> leves la mañana de este martes en avenida Insurgentes Sur, a la altura de la colonia Del Valle.
> De acuerdo con testigos, una camioneta de reparto cambió de carril sin precaución, golpeó a un
> automóvil y se dio a la fuga. El motociclista cayó al frenar. La conductora del automóvil
> resultó ilesa.

Crash on Insurgentes leaves a motorcyclist injured. A motorcyclist suffered minor injuries on
Tuesday morning on Insurgentes Sur, near the Del Valle neighborhood. According to witnesses, a
delivery van changed lanes carelessly, hit a car and fled. The motorcyclist fell when he braked.
The car's driver was unhurt.

### 4. The radio host (spoken, public)

```dialogue
# Tráfico de las nueve
Locutor: Y ojo, que Insurgentes a la altura de la Del Valle sigue cargadita, ¿eh?, por un choque de hace rato. Una camioneta de reparto, nos cuentan, se cambió de carril así, sin poner direccional, le pegó a un carro y… ¿qué creen? Se dio a la fuga. Así, tal cual. Un muchacho en moto que venía atrás se fue al piso, pobre, pero ya lo revisaron y está bien. Así que si van para el sur, agarren por División del Norte. Paciencia, amigos.
= And watch out, Insurgentes near Del Valle is still pretty jammed, OK?, because of a crash a while ago. A delivery van, they tell us, switched lanes just like that, no turn signal, hit a car and… guess what? It took off. Just like that. A young guy on a motorbike behind went down, poor thing, but they've checked him over and he's fine. So if you're heading south, take División del Norte. Patience, friends.
```

### 5. The voice note (intimate)

```dialogue
# Nota de voz para Lupe
Mariana: Lupe, no sabes. Me chocaron con el carro de mi mamá. Estoy bien, ¿eh?, no me pasó nada. Pero una camioneta de reparto se me cerró, ¡pum!, me dio en la salpicadera y en el cofre, y el tipo se peló. Así nomás. Y un chavo en moto se cayó, pobrecito. Ya vino el ajustador, hizo su croquis y todo, pero voy a tener que pagar el deducible porque no hay a quién cobrarle. ¿Cómo le digo a mi mamá? Háblame.
= Lupe, you won't believe it. Someone hit me in Mom's car. I'm fine, OK?, nothing happened to me. But a delivery van cut in front of me, bam!, it hit the fender and the hood, and the guy beat it. Just like that. And a kid on a motorbike fell, poor thing. The adjuster came already, did his sketch and everything, but I'm going to have to pay the deductible because there's no one to charge. How do I tell Mom? Call me.
```

### 6. The comic retelling (a family meal)

```dialogue
# Domingo, en la sobremesa
Carmen: Y ahí estaba mi hija, ilesa, como dice el reporte, y mi carrito con la salpicadera hecha acordeón. Porque el señor de la camioneta, muy educado, se dio a la fuga, así lo escribió el policía, como en las películas. Y llega el ajustador, un muchachito de corbata: "Señora, el siniestro procede, pero aplica el deducible". ¡El siniestro! Como si me hubiera caído un meteorito. Yo nada más le dije: "Joven, lo siniestro es lo que me va a costar".
= And there was my daughter, unhurt, as the report says, and my poor little car with the fender like an accordion. Because the gentleman in the van, very polite, "fled the scene", that's how the policeman wrote it, like in the movies. And along comes the adjuster, a little guy in a tie: "Ma'am, the claim is valid, but the deductible applies." The claim! As if a meteorite had fallen on me. All I said was: "Young man, what's sinister is what it's going to cost me."
```

Glosses: *cargadita* (heavy, of traffic), *la direccional* (turn signal), *cerrarse* (to cut in),
*pelarse* (to beat it, Mexico, informal), *el chavo* (kid, Mexico).

![A ladder titled Un choque, seis registros, with six rungs between an arrow marked más formal at the top and más íntimo at the bottom. From top to bottom, each rung gives the version, its register and a sample: reporte de siniestro, especializado (Aplica deducible); informe policial, oficial (el suscrito, al arribar); nota periodística, prensa (resultó con lesiones leves); locutor de radio, oral público (¿qué creen? Se dio a la fuga); sobremesa, familiar (¡El siniestro!); nota de voz, íntimo (el tipo se peló). A curved arrow runs from the sobremesa rung up to the top rung, labeled cambio deliberado de registro.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## What moves from one version to the next

| | Report | Police | Press | Radio | Voice note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the van leaves | *se da a la fuga* | *se dio a la fuga* | *se dio a la fuga* | *se dio a la fuga* (quoted, amused) | *se peló* |
| the injury | *Lesionados: un motociclista, leve* | *excoriaciones en el antebrazo* | *lesiones leves* | *se fue al piso* | *se cayó, pobrecito* |
| people | roles: *asegurada, tercero* | roles and ages | roles | *un muchacho* | names, *mi mamá* |
| sentences | telegraphic: nominal phrases | long periods | short, full sentences | broken, with *¿eh?* | broken, with *¡pum!* |
| tense | present (*realiza, colisiona*) | past, impersonal *se observó* | past, *resultó* | past and present | past and present |

Five markers do most of the work: the words (*colisionar* for A2's *chocar*, the official *hecho
de tránsito* for *choque*); who is visible (roles and B2 14's impersonal *se observó*, or *yo, mi
mamá, el tipo*); nouns or verbs (B2 18's nominal style: *cambio de carril, peritaje*); sentence
shape (one long period, or fragments like *Así nomás*); and the marks of speech. *La oralidad*
shows in tags (*¿eh?*), sound words (*¡pum!*) and repetition, which written texts remove.

## Shifting on purpose

A **[[register shift]]** is a move from one register into another inside the same text. By
accident, it is a slip: a *coloquialismo* (colloquialism) such as *se peló* in a claim. On
purpose, it is a device. Carmen borrows the report's words (*ilesa, se dio a la fuga, el
siniestro*) and drops them into family talk. *La incongruencia*, the clash between the solemn
word and the setting, makes the joke, and her pun finishes it: *el siniestro* (the claim) and *lo
siniestro* (what's sinister).

The device works only when the reader sees the shift; it never belongs in a claim.

## *El parte*, *el reporte*, *el acta*

A1's *la parte* (part) has a masculine twin, *el parte*, an official report: *el parte médico*
(a medical bulletin); in Spain, the form drivers fill in after a crash. In Mexico the police write
*el informe policial* (the national standard form is the *Informe Policial Homologado*), the
adjuster opens *el reporte*, and a prosecutor's office draws up C1's *el acta* (official record).
Mexican criminal codes and the press call offenses through negligence *culposos* (*homicidio
culposo*); Spain's code says *por imprudencia*.

![A side view of a sedan with five parts labeled: el cofre over the engine at the front, el parabrisas, la salpicadera over the front wheel, la cajuela at the back, and una llanta. A dashed outline around the whole outer shell is labeled la carrocería, the whole exterior structure.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Slang, *argot* and *caló*

**[[Argot]]** is the vocabulary of a trade or group (*el argot de los ajustadores*), close to C1's
*la jerga*. *Caló* first means the Romani variety of the Spanish Gitanos, its usual sense in
Spain; in Mexico *el caló* is widely used for the slang of the street, which fiction uses to give
*el habla* of a neighborhood its sound. Learn both words for recognition only.

## A model rewrite: from voice note to statement

The insurer asks Mariana for a written statement. Here is the voice note rewritten for that
reader: the same events in a new register, plus details a statement needs (lane, speed, a
witness's photo).

> Asunto: Declaración sobre el siniestro 2026-03-0417 (póliza AU-55821)
>
> A quien corresponda:
>
> Por medio de la presente, yo, Mariana Solís Ruiz, conductora del vehículo asegurado a nombre de
> Carmen Ruiz Ochoa, declaro lo siguiente sobre el siniestro ocurrido el martes 3 de marzo de
> 2026, alrededor de las 8:40 horas, en avenida Insurgentes Sur, a la altura de la colonia Del
> Valle.
>
> Circulaba por el carril central a velocidad moderada cuando una camioneta de reparto blanca,
> que avanzaba por el carril derecho, cambió de carril sin encender la direccional y golpeó la
> salpicadera delantera derecha y el cofre de mi vehículo. Frené de inmediato. El conductor de la
> camioneta no se detuvo y se dio a la fuga hacia el sur. No pude ver las placas completas, pero
> un testigo tomó una fotografía parcial, que adjunto.
>
> Un motociclista que circulaba detrás de mí frenó para no impactarme, perdió el equilibrio y
> cayó. Tenía raspaduras en un brazo y fue atendido en el lugar por paramédicos. Yo resulté
> ilesa.
>
> El ajustador acudió al lugar, elaboró el croquis y me informó que, al no haberse identificado al
> tercero responsable, me corresponde pagar el deducible. Les solicito que me indiquen por escrito el
> monto y el procedimiento para la reparación.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Mariana Solís Ruiz

Summary: Mariana states who she is, whose car it is, and when and where; how the van hit the
fender and hood and fled; the witness's partial photo; the motorcyclist's fall; that she was
unhurt; and that the deductible applies. She asks for the amount and the procedure in writing.
Glosses: *a quien corresponda* (to whom it may concern), *impactar* (to hit, formal),
*al no haberse identificado* (since … has not been identified), *el monto* (the amount).

## Your turn: rewrite for another reader

Before you write, check:

- Who is the reader, what do they know, and what must they do after reading?
- Keep every fact; add none. A hedge in the source (*según testigos*) stays a hedge.
- Hold one register: one form of address, one level of vocabulary.
- Explain jargon the reader doesn't share; don't swap it for another hard word.
- Read it aloud as the reader would: does any word sound out of place?

```assignment
writing: es6-m1-w02-registro
```

## Pronunciation

- *siniestro*: si-NIES-tro, three syllables; *nie* is one.
- *carrocería*: ca-rro-ce-RÍ-a, five syllables; the accent splits *ía*.
- *incongruencia*: in-con-GRUEN-cia, four syllables.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing registers by accident: *El tercero se peló* in a claim, or *el siniestro* at
  dinner without meaning to be funny.
- Losing facts in a rewrite. Every version keeps the time, place, people and hedges.
- Inventing formality. *Se procedió a efectuar la realización del croquis* is padding; *Se
  elaboró el croquis* is enough.

## Key points

- Register moves on five markers: words, who is visible, nouns or verbs, sentence shape and the
  marks of speech.
- A register shift on purpose creates humor through incongruity; by accident it is a slip.
- *El parte* is an official report; in Mexico, *el informe policial*, the insurer's *reporte*
  and *el acta*.
- A rewrite keeps every fact and every hedge; only the register changes.

lessons.title: Infligir o infringir: confusable words and the editor's eye
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 03 taught the norm's grammar doubts (*dequeísmo, hubo / hubieron*), C1 21 spelling and
punctuation, and C1 12h2 false friends between English and Spanish. This lesson is about
meaning inside Spanish: words that look alike, and words whose careful-writing sense differs from
a frequent use. It also gives you the copy editor's vocabulary and the tact to correct someone.

The theme is a Mexican newspaper's corrections column, written by its readers' ombudsman (*la
defensora de los lectores*). The paper and its people are invented.

## Paronyms: words that look alike

A **[[paronym]]** (*el parónimo*) is a word so close to another in form that writers confuse them.
The eye slips; the meaning doesn't forgive.

| Pair | Means | Typical company |
|---|---|---|
| *infligir* / *infringir* | to inflict / to break (a rule) | *infligir un daño, una derrota* / *infringir una norma, la ley* |
| *absolver* / *absorber* | to acquit / to absorb | *absolver al acusado* / *absorber el agua* |
| *proveer* / *prever* (B2) | to supply / to foresee | *proveer de agua a la colonia* / *prever la escasez* |
| *el perjuicio* / *el prejuicio* (B2) | harm / prejudice | *daños y perjuicios* / *un prejuicio contra los jóvenes* |
| *expiar* / *espiar* | to atone for / to spy on | *expiar una culpa* / *espiar al vecino* |
| *la actitud* / *la aptitud* | attitude / aptitude | *una actitud positiva* / *aptitudes para la música* |

Memory hooks: you *infringe* (in*fr*ingir) a rule by *fr*acturing it; a *perjuicio* hurts
(*per-* as in *perder*), a *prejuicio* judges before (*pre-*). *Expiar* has the x of
*ex*culpar (to clear of blame). Some of these pairs also sound alike: in relaxed speech *x*
before a consonant is often said as *s*, so *expiar* and *espiar* can sound the same.

![A decision table titled ¿Cuál escribo? with ten rows in five color-coded pairs. Each row asks what you mean and gives the word: romper una norma, infringir; causar un daño o una derrota, infligir; declarar inocente, absolver; tomar un líquido, como una esponja, absorber; abastecer, proveer; ver con anticipación, prever; un daño, el perjuicio; una opinión sin fundamento, el prejuicio; pagar una culpa, expiar; observar en secreto, espiar.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Careful-writing senses

Some words have a sense careful writers keep and a frequent use that differs. Two rules for
C2: know what the dictionaries say, and never mark wrong a sense the DLE (*Diccionario de la
lengua española*) records.

| Word | What the dictionaries say | What is often heard | The safe choice |
|---|---|---|---|
| *adolecer de* | to suffer from a defect (DLE); the DPD calls "to lack" improper | *adolece de recursos* | *carece de recursos*; *adolece de imprecisiones* |
| *detentar* | to hold a power or office unlawfully (DLE) | for a lawful office | *ostentar* or *ocupar un cargo* |
| *álgido* | "very cold" and "critical, culminating" (DLE) | the culminating sense | both are correct |
| *lívido* | bruised, purplish; intensely pale (DLE) | "furious", from English | *pálido*, *amoratado* |
| *sendos* | one each (DPD) | "both", or "huge" | *sendos* only with one thing each |
| *bizarro* | brave, gallant (DLE); "bizarre" was rejected by the DPD (2005) as a calque, though the RAE is now reported to admit it | "weird" | *raro*, *extravagante* in formal writing |

Notes on the table:

- *Adolecer de* + a defect: *El informe adolece de imprecisiones* (The report suffers from
  inaccuracies). The Spanish dictionary of doubts, the DPD, calls *adolecer* for *carecer*
  improper; *Adolece de falta de…* isn't wrong, but *Carece de…* is clearer.
- *Detentar* vs *ostentar*: *La junta detentó el poder* (unlawfully) but *La rectora ostenta el
  cargo desde 2022* (lawfully, with honor). One nuance: the RAE's legal dictionary notes that
  legal Spanish uses *detentar* for possession, lawful or not. In the press, readers hear
  "usurped".
- *Álgido*: the Academy's dictionary added "culminating" in 1984 (as a 2021 newspaper column
  tells it), and it is now the usual sense. Don't "correct" it.
- *Sendos* (feminine *sendas*) is plural only: *Las dos ganadoras recibieron sendos diplomas*
  (one diploma each). A single winner can't receive *sendos* anything.
- *Ingente* (immense), *nimio* (trifling) and *prístino* (original, earliest; often also "pure,
  untouched", after English *pristine*, a sense the DLE may not record) are formal adjectives. *Nimio* reversed its meaning:
  in Latin *nimius* meant "excessive".

Using a word with a meaning it doesn't have is an **[[impropriety]]** (*la impropiedad*: *adolecer*
for *carecer*). An error of syntax (agreement, government, word order: *Hubieron quejas* for
*Hubo quejas*) is a **[[solecism]]** (*el solecismo*). Both differ from B2's *la errata* (a typo) and
from the slips everyone makes: *el lapsus* (a slip of the tongue or pen), *el desliz* (a small
slip-up) and *el gazapo* (a blooper that makes readers smile).

## The editor's checks

A copy editor (C1's *el corrector de estilo*) *coteja* (checks against the original) every
quotation, figure and name, *enmienda* (corrects) the text, and, when an error reaches print, the
paper publishes *una fe de erratas* (a correction). The worst fault is not an error but a
distortion: *tergiversar* is to twist someone's words, usually on purpose.

Correct a colleague with C1 04's tact: *Te sugiero cambiar "detenta" por "ocupa": "detentar"
sugiere que el cargo es ilegítimo.* (I'd suggest changing "detenta" to "ocupa": "detentar"
implies the office is illegitimate.) Give the reason and the dictionary, not a verdict. Here
the ombudsman talks to the sports editor about Monday's headline:

```dialogue
# En la redacción
Teresa: Julián, ¿tienes un minuto? Es por el título del lunes.
= Julián, do you have a minute? It's about Monday's headline.
Julián: Ya sé, ya sé: "infringe". Me lo han dicho cinco personas.
= I know, I know: "infringe". Five people have told me.
Teresa: No vengo a regañarte. A cualquiera se le va. Solo quería sugerirte que en la próxima junta repasemos los parónimos más frecuentes.
= I'm not here to scold you. It can slip past anyone. I just wanted to suggest we go over the most common paronyms at the next meeting.
Julián: Te lo agradezco. Aunque, entre nos, "le inflige una goleada" suena un poco rebuscado, ¿no?
= Thanks. Although, between us, "le inflige una goleada" sounds a bit stilted, doesn't it?
Teresa: Puede ser. Si te parece, ponemos "le propina una goleada": es igual de correcto y más natural en deportes.
= Maybe. If you like, we'll go with "le propina una goleada": it's just as correct and more natural in sports.
Julián: Mucho mejor. ¿Y lo de "sendas medallas"? Ese no fue mío, conste.
= Much better. And the "sendas medallas" thing? That one wasn't mine, for the record.
Teresa: Lo sé. Ya hablé con la reportera y lo tomó muy bien.
= I know. I've already talked to the reporter, and she took it very well.
```

Notice the moves: an opening that removes blame (*No vengo a regañarte*), a suggestion, not an
order (*quería sugerirte*), and an alternative when the correct word sounds stiff. A paronym fixed
is only half the job; the fixed sentence should also sound natural (*propinar una goleada*, to
hand out a heavy defeat).

![A typewritten proof of a sports story in the Diario del Altiplano with five marked errors and the corrections in red in the right margin. In the headline El Atlético Bajío le infringe una goleada al líder, infringe is struck through, with inflige in the margin. In El diputado Ramírez, que detenta la presidencia…, detenta is circled, with ocupa. In El club aún no conoce el presupesto, a caret marks the missing letter, with presupuesto. In Hubieron quejas por los boletos, Hubieron is underlined, with Hubo. In …el estadio adolece de recursos para crecer, adolece is circled, with carece.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: the ombudsman's column

> Cinco gazapos y una falsa alarma
>
> *Por Teresa Gálvez, defensora de los lectores*
>
> Esta semana recibí cuarenta y dos mensajes de lectores atentos. Casi todos señalaban errores
> reales; uno no. Los reviso en orden, porque cada uno enseña algo.
>
> El lunes, la sección de Deportes tituló: "El Atlético Bajío le infringe una goleada al líder".
> Un equipo no puede infringir una goleada, por la sencilla razón de que infringir es quebrantar
> una norma. Lo que se hace con una derrota, un castigo o un daño es infligirlos. Los dos verbos
> son parónimos: se parecen tanto que el ojo los confunde. El error se enmendó en la edición
> digital esa misma mañana.
>
> El martes, en Política, leímos que el diputado Ramírez "detenta la presidencia de la Comisión
> de Hacienda". Detentar significa, según el diccionario académico, retener y ejercer
> ilegítimamente un poder o un cargo. Nadie en esta redacción ha querido acusar al diputado de
> usurpación; el verbo adecuado era ostentar, o simplemente ocupar. Una precisión: en el lenguaje
> jurídico, detentar se usa también para la mera posesión, pero en una crónica política el lector
> entiende otra cosa.
>
> El miércoles, una nota sobre el presupuesto escolar afirmaba que "el programa adolece de
> recursos suficientes". Adolecer de significa padecer un defecto, no carecer de algo. Bastaba con
> escribir "el programa carece de recursos suficientes".
>
> El jueves, la reportera que cubrió la sequía escribió que el municipio "no previó de agua" a
> tres colonias. Quiso decir proveyó: proveer es abastecer; prever, anticipar. Lo curioso es que
> las dos ideas caben en la historia: el municipio no previó la escasez y, por eso, no proveyó
> de agua a esas colonias.
>
> El viernes, por último, una atleta potosina "ganó sendas medallas de oro". Sendos significa
> "uno para cada uno": dos ciclistas pueden recibir sendas medallas, una cada uno, pero una sola
> atleta no. Lo correcto era "dos medallas de oro".
>
> Ahora, la falsa alarma. Un lector nos reprochó haber escrito "el momento álgido de las
> negociaciones", porque, nos dijo, álgido significa "muy frío". Tiene razón a medias: ese es el
> sentido etimológico, pero el diccionario académico registra también el de "crítico o
> culminante", que hoy es el más frecuente. No hubo error, y así se lo hice saber, con gratitud
> por su atención.
>
> Corregir no es humillar a nadie. Un lapsus lo comete cualquiera; lo grave sería no reconocerlo.
> Por eso esta defensoría seguirá publicando cada domingo su fe de erratas. Escríbannos: sus
> correos nos hacen mejores.

Summary. The ombudsman reviews a week of readers' complaints. Monday: a sports headline used
*infringir* (to break a rule) for *infligir* (to inflict). Tuesday: a politics story said a
deputy *detenta* (holds unlawfully) a committee chair; *ostenta* or *ocupa* was meant, though
legal Spanish uses *detentar* for possession. Wednesday: *adolece de recursos* should have been
*carece de recursos*. Thursday: *previó* (foresaw) for *proveyó* (supplied). Friday: one athlete
can't win *sendas medallas*. Last, a false alarm: *álgido* for "culminating" is recorded by the
dictionary and was correct. She ends by saying that correcting isn't humiliating and invites
readers to write.

Glosses: *la goleada* (a rout, a heavy defeat in soccer), *quebrantar* (to break, formal),
*la usurpación* (usurpation), *la mera posesión* (mere possession), *a medias* (half), *así se lo
hice saber* (I told him so).

## Pronunciation

- *infligir*: in-fli-GIR, three syllables; *g* before *i* is the throat sound of *j*.
- *lívido*: LÍ-vi-do; *álgido*: ÁL-gi-do. Both stress the third syllable from the end, which
  always takes a written accent.
- *expiar*: ex-PIAR; *expío*: ex-PÍ-o, three syllables, the accent splitting *ío*.
- *prístino*: PRÍS-ti-no.

## Common mistakes

- Swapping the pair: *infringir un castigo*, *absorber al acusado*, *no previó de agua*.
- English senses: *lívido* for furious, *bizarro* for weird in a formal text.
- Sendos for "both": *Sendos equipos ganaron* means nothing; say *Ambos equipos ganaron*.
- Overcorrecting: marking *álgido* "culminating" as an error. Check the DLE before you
  correct; what it records isn't wrong, though careful writing may still prefer another word.
- Correcting without a reason. A bare *Está mal* wins no arguments; *El DLE define
  "detentar" como…* does.

## Key points

- Paronyms look alike but mean different things: *infligir / infringir, absolver / absorber,
  proveer / prever, perjuicio / prejuicio, expiar / espiar, actitud / aptitud*.
- *Adolecer de* is "to suffer from a defect"; *detentar* is "to hold unlawfully"; *sendos* is
  "one each".
- An impropriety is an error of meaning; a solecism, an error of syntax.
- Never mark wrong a sense the DLE records (*álgido* "culminating").
- Correct with the reason and the source, politely.

lessons.title: Motu proprio: learned words, Latin phrases and the names of species
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Formal Spanish leans on words borrowed from written Latin and Greek, and on Latin phrases that
educated writers drop into a sentence (*a priori, de facto, statu quo*). Using them precisely,
and spelling them as the RAE does now, is part of C2 control; misusing them (*de motu propio*) is
one of the most noticed slips. This lesson explains where these words come from, how to spot
them and how to use them, and ends with the Latin of biology. B2's *la etimología* (etymology) is the tool
throughout.

## Two kinds of Latin words

Spanish grew out of spoken Latin. Words that came down through centuries of speech changed with
it: they are **[[inherited words]]** (*las voces patrimoniales*). Later, scholars, lawyers and
priests borrowed words again from written Latin, lightly adapted: these are **[[learned words]]**
(*los cultismos*). When one Latin word gave both, the pair is a **[[doublet]]** (*el doblete*).

| Latin | Inherited word | Learned word |
|---|---|---|
| *clamare* | *llamar* (to call) | *clamar* (to cry out for: *clamar justicia*) |
| *integrum* | *entero* (whole) | *íntegro* (upright, complete) |
| *strictum* | *estrecho* (narrow) | *estricto* (strict) |
| *delicatum* | *delgado* (thin) | *delicado* (delicate) |
| *collocare* | *colgar* (to hang) | *colocar* (to place) |

The etymologies are the DLE's, as usually cited; check any you quote. Three clues mark a learned
word:

- It keeps Latin consonant clusters that speech simplified: *-ct-* in *estricto* (speech made it
  *-ch-*: *estrecho*), *cl-* in *clamar* (speech made it *ll-*: *llamar*).
- It keeps vowels that speech dropped: *delicado* has the *i* that *delgado* lost.
- It often keeps the Latin stress, three syllables from the end: *íntegro*, *el espécimen*.

The learned twin usually sounds more abstract or more formal. That is why it is useful in
register work (lesson 02): *una persona íntegra* is a moral judgment; *una pizza entera* is not.

![A word tree. At the top, the Latin verb stringere (apretar, atar: to tighten, to bind) and its participle strictus (apretado). A branch on the left, in orange, headed voces patrimoniales, leads to estreñir (de stringere) and estrecho (de strictus). A branch on the right, in blue, headed cultismos, leads to estricto (de strictus), restringir and restricción (re- + stringere) and astringente (ad- + stringere). A note at the bottom says astringente is the tasting word of lesson 01.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A **[[Latinism]]** (*el latinismo*) is any word, phrase or construction taken from Latin; a word
from Greek is *un helenismo*. Science builds new words from Greek and Latin roots (*la raíz*),
prefixes (*el prefijo*) and suffixes (*el sufijo*):

| Element | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *hiper-* / *hipo-* | over / under | *hipertensión, hipotermia* |
| *endo-* / *exo-* | inside / outside | *endoscopia, exoesqueleto* |
| *poli-* | many | *políglota, polisémico* |
| *-logía* | study of | *herpetología* (reptiles and amphibians) |
| *-grafía* | writing, description | *ortografía, biografía* |
| *-cracia* | power, government | *democracia, burocracia* |

## Latin phrases

Spanish writes a few Latin phrases as they are. They belong to formal writing, and each has a
plain Spanish alternative.

| Phrase | Meaning | Example | Plain alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| *a priori* | beforehand, before the evidence | *A priori, la idea parecía buena.* | *de antemano* |
| *de facto* | in fact, whatever the law says | *un monopolio de facto* | *de hecho* |
| *grosso modo* | roughly | *Grosso modo, la mitad aceptó.* | C1's *a grandes rasgos* |
| *in situ* | on site, in its place | *Lo estudiaron in situ.* | *en el lugar* |
| *motu proprio* | of one's own accord | *Renunció motu proprio.* | *por iniciativa propia* |
| *sui generis* | one of a kind | *un museo sui generis* | *peculiar* |
| *el statu quo* | the existing state of affairs | *mantener el statu quo* | *la situación actual* |
| *per capita* | per person | *el consumo per capita* | *por persona* |
| *sine qua non* | indispensable | *condición sine qua non* | B1's *imprescindible* |
| *el alter ego* | a second self | *el alter ego del autor* | *el doble* |

Translations: *A priori, la idea parecía buena* (At first sight the idea seemed good); *un
monopolio de facto* (a de facto monopoly); *Grosso modo, la mitad aceptó* (Roughly half
accepted); *Lo estudiaron in situ* (They studied it on site); *Renunció motu proprio* (He resigned
of his own accord); *un museo sui generis* (a one-of-a-kind museum); *mantener el statu quo* (to
keep the status quo); *el consumo per capita* (consumption per person); *condición sine qua non*
(an essential condition); *el alter ego del autor* (the author's alter ego).

The slips that careful readers notice, all three criticized in the RAE's works (the DPD, its
dictionary of doubts, and its grammar):

- *motu proprio*, not *de motu propio*: two *r*'s, no preposition;
- *grosso modo*, not *a grosso modo*;
- *statu quo*, not *status quo* (Spanish uses the Latin ablative form).

How to write them: the RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) treats Latin phrases as unadapted foreign
expressions, in italics (or in quotation marks) and without written accents: *per capita*. The
DPD (2005) had written *per cápita*, and much of the press still does, so you will see both. In
your own writing follow the *Ortografía*; don't mark the other spelling wrong in someone else's.

## The names of species

Biology names every species with two Latin words, a system called binomial nomenclature (*la
nomenclatura binomial*). The first word is the genus, written with a capital; the second is the
specific epithet (*el epíteto*, a word lesson 10 takes up), in lower case; both go in italics. The axolotl, B2's *el
ajolote*, is *Ambystoma mexicanum*: genus *Ambystoma*, epithet *mexicanum* (Mexican).

Epithets describe (*gracilis*, slender), name a place (*mexicanum*; *oaxacensis*, of Oaxaca) or
honor a person, an eponym use honors lesson 04h2 returns to: Latin adds *-i* for a man and *-ae*
for a woman. *La taxonomía*, the science of classifying, is the work of *el taxónomo* (*la taxónoma*);
plants are kept dry in *un herbario*; animals become *especímenes* in a scientific collection.
Mexico, in the words of CONABIO, its biodiversity commission, is *un país megadiverso*, one of a
select group of seventeen nations rich in animal and plant species (as quoted by a Mexican
government page that cites CONABIO, read November 17, 2026).

![A salamander drawn from above, slender, with a long tail and four short legs. Above it, its two-part Latin name: Pseudoeurycea, labeled género (genus), and zarateae, labeled epíteto específico (specific epithet). Small notes explain: pseudo-, falso, from Greek; zarateae, en honor de una mujer, Rosalía Zárate. Below the drawing: unos 4 cm, dorso color cobre, sin pulmones (about 4 cm, copper-colored back, no lungs), and especie ficticia (a fictional species).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: a press release

This press release is fictional: the species, the people and the institute are invented. Only
the genus *Pseudoeurycea* is real (lungless salamanders of Mexico and Guatemala).

> COMUNICADO DE PRENSA. Oaxaca de Juárez, Oax., 15 de septiembre de 2026
>
> Describen una nueva especie de salamandra en la Sierra Sur de Oaxaca
>
> Un equipo del Instituto de Investigaciones Biológicas de la Sierra Sur describió una nueva
> especie de salamandra, *Pseudoeurycea zarateae*, que habita en un bosque de niebla a unos 2600
> metros de altitud. El hallazgo confirma, una vez más, por qué México es considerado un país
> megadiverso.
>
> La nueva especie mide apenas cuatro centímetros, tiene el dorso color cobre y, como las demás
> salamandras de su familia, no tiene pulmones: respira a través de la piel. A priori, los
> investigadores pensaron que se trataba de una especie ya conocida. Sin embargo, al comparar los
> doce especímenes recolectados con los ejemplares de varias colecciones científicas, y tras
> someterlos a análisis genéticos, la taxónoma responsable, la doctora Elena Cruz Villalobos, concluyó que eran
> distintos.
>
> "Grosso modo, la diferencia genética es tan grande como la que separa a dos especies que nadie
> confundiría", explicó Cruz. "Y el trabajo in situ fue fundamental: sin observarlas en su
> hábitat, nunca habríamos notado su conducta nocturna".
>
> El nombre sigue las reglas de la nomenclatura zoológica. El género, *Pseudoeurycea*, une el
> prefijo griego *pseudo-*, "falso", al nombre de otro género de salamandras, *Eurycea*. El
> epíteto, *zarateae*, rinde homenaje a Rosalía Zárate, integrante de la comunidad que guio al
> equipo y que, motu proprio, había señalado años antes la presencia de "unas lagartijas
> raras" a los guardabosques. La terminación *-ae* indica, en latín, que se honra a una mujer.
>
> Para la comunidad, que de facto protege el bosque desde hace décadas, el reconocimiento tiene un
> sentido especial. El permiso de la asamblea comunitaria fue condición sine qua non para el
> estudio, y los resultados se presentaron primero en el pueblo, en español y en zapoteco.
>
> Las plantas del sitio se identificaron con ayuda del herbario de la universidad estatal. Los
> autores advierten que la especie podría estar amenazada por la tala y por los incendios, y
> recomiendan evaluar su estado de conservación cuanto antes. Ya en el siglo XIX, recuerda el
> estudio, naturalistas europeos recorrieron la región, pero esta salamandra, diminuta y
> nocturna, se les escapó.

Summary. A (fictional) institute has described a new salamander species, *Pseudoeurycea
zarateae*, from a cloud forest at about 2,600 meters in Oaxaca's Sierra Sur. It is four
centimeters long, copper-backed and lungless. The team first assumed it was a known species,
but comparisons with collection specimens and genetic tests showed otherwise; fieldwork revealed
that it is nocturnal. The genus name joins Greek *pseudo-* (false) to another genus, *Eurycea*;
the epithet honors a community member who guided the team and had reported the animals years
earlier. The community's permission was essential, and the results were presented first in the
village. The authors warn of logging and fires, and note that nineteenth-century naturalists
missed the species.

Glosses: *el bosque de niebla* (cloud forest), *el dorso* (back), *recolectar* (to collect),
*la lagartija* (lizard), *el guardabosques* (forest ranger), *la asamblea comunitaria* (community
assembly), *la tala* (logging), *diminuto* (tiny). *Guio* has no written accent (RAE, 2010).

## Pronunciation

- *el espécimen*: es-PÉ-ci-men; plural *los especímenes*: es-pe-CÍ-me-nes. Unusually, the stress
  moves one syllable in the plural (like *régimen / regímenes*), and the written accent with it.
- *el taxónomo*: ta-XÓ-no-mo; *x* is *ks*.
- *sui generis*: sui GE-ne-ris; *sui* is said as one syllable, like *swee*.
- *motu proprio*: MO-tu PRO-prio, with the second *r* clearly said.

## Common mistakes

- *De motu propio*, *a grosso modo*, *status quo*: the three most noticed slips.
- Latin as decoration. *Grosso modo* and *a priori* add nothing in a casual message; *más o
  menos* and *de entrada* do the job.
- Missing accents on Spanish learned words: *espécimen, especímenes, taxónomo, íntegro*.
  (Latin phrases, on the other hand, take none.)
- Capitals in species names: *Ambystoma mexicanum*, never *Ambystoma Mexicanum*.

## Key points

- Inherited words changed in speech (*llamar, entero, estrecho*); learned words were borrowed
  from writing (*clamar, íntegro, estricto*). Together they form doublets.
- Learned words keep Latin clusters, vowels and stress.
- Latin phrases go in italics without accents (*per capita*, *Ortografía* 2010); avoid *de motu
  propio, a grosso modo, status quo*.
- A species name is genus + specific epithet, both in italics, the genus capitalized.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Cómo trabaja un diccionario: lexicography and corpora
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 ended with advice: when two words seem equal, check them in a dictionary and a corpus.
This lesson shows how. You will see how three dictionaries a Mexican reader uses are made, how to
read an entry, how a corpus shows what a dictionary can't, and how to write a definition
yourself. *La lexicografía* is the craft of making dictionaries; *el lexicógrafo* (*la
lexicógrafa*) practices it.

## Three dictionaries

The DLE (*Diccionario de la lengua española*) is made by the Real Academia Española with the
other academies of the Spanish-speaking world (ASALE). Its 23rd edition appeared in 2014, as part
of the Academy's tricentenary celebrations (it was founded in 1713), and since then it has been
updated online in numbered versions: version 23.8 was presented in December 2024, and the entries read for this lesson (November 2026)
showed 23.8.1. The RAE has announced a printed 24th edition, planned for 2026; check whether it
has appeared. The DLE covers general Spanish and marks words and senses limited to a country.
Because the Academies make it, many readers treat it as the norm, but it records use: a sense in
the DLE is a sense people use, not a recommendation.

The DEM (*Diccionario del español de México*) is made at El Colegio de México by a team led by
the linguist Luis Fernando Lara, whose project began in 1973. It describes the Spanish used in
Mexico from 1921 on, all of it, not just what differs from Spain. Its first edition appeared in
2010, and a second, larger edition went online in 2020 (about 32,650 entries, according to a
newspaper report of that year). It is a descriptive dictionary: it reports how Mexicans
write and speak.

The *Diccionario de mexicanismos* of the Academia Mexicana de la Lengua (first published in
2010; check for later editions) takes the opposite approach: it lists only words and senses
particular to Mexico, compared with general Spanish.

Two related works: the DPD (*Diccionario panhispánico de dudas*) is openly normative (C1's
*normativo*): it gives advice on doubtful usage, as lessons 03 and 04 showed. *Un tesauro*
(a thesaurus) groups words by meaning; it suggests candidates but never tells you which one
fits.

## Reading an entry

![A simplified dictionary entry for the word cofre, written for this lesson in the style of a general dictionary. At the top, the headword cofre in bold, then its origin in parentheses, Del fr. coffre. Sense 1, marked m. for masculine, defines a box with a lid and a lock for keeping valuables. Sense 2, marked m. and Méx., defines the cover of a car's engine, followed by the example Abrió el cofre para revisar el motor in italics. Blue labels name the parts: lema, etimología, acepción (at the number 2), marca de uso (at Méx.) and ejemplo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every entry has the same parts:

- the **[[headword]]** (*el lema*): the form you look up. Spanish dictionaries file verbs under the
  infinitive and nouns and adjectives under the masculine singular, so *canté* and *cantaríamos*
  are found at *cantar*. Grouping forms under their headword is to *lematizar* (to lemmatize);
- the origin (*la etimología*), in parentheses;
- the senses (C1's *las acepciones*), numbered, each with its part of speech (*m., f., adj., tr.*);
- **[[usage labels]]** (*las marcas de uso*), abbreviations that limit a sense: by place (*Méx., Am.,
  Esp.*), by register (*coloq.* colloquial, *vulg.* vulgar), by attitude (*despect.* derogatory)
  or by time (*desus.*, *desusado*: obsolete);
- examples, in italics, which show the word in a sentence and often its collocations.

Read the labels before the definition. In the DLE, *adolecer* sense 1 carries *desus.*, so
don't use it that way; *detentar* sense 2 carries *Der.* (law), a technical sense.

## What a corpus adds

A **[[corpus]]** (*el corpus*, plural *los corpus*) is a large, searchable collection of real texts.
Where a dictionary gives one example, a corpus gives thousands, and with them two kinds of
evidence: *la frecuencia de uso* (how often a word appears, usually per million words) and
company (which words it appears with).

- CORPES XXI, the RAE's corpus of twenty-first-century Spanish, collects texts from 2001 on,
  from Spain and the Americas, written and oral (novels, news, blogs, social media, transcribed
  interviews). Each word is lemmatized and tagged, so a search can be filtered by country, region
  or topic. A 2021 RAE page described a version of a little over 333 million words; it is still
  growing.
- The Corpus del Español, built by Mark Davies at Brigham Young University, includes a
  collection of about two billion words of web pages from 21 Spanish-speaking countries,
  gathered in 2013–2014, according to its own site.

The main tool is the **[[concordance]]**: every occurrence of a word, one per line, with the word in
the center and its context on both sides. (C1's *la concordancia* meant grammatical agreement;
this is the word's second sense.) Reading down the column to the right of the word shows its
collocations at a glance.

A corpus filtered by country also shows region. Search A2's *platicar* (to chat) and its
near-synonym *charlar* country by country, and you can expect the familiar pattern to appear in
numbers: *platicar* far ahead in Mexico and Central America, *charlar* in Spain. Each *vocablo* (the lexicographer's
formal word for A1's *la palabra*) has a map as well as a meaning; a corpus draws it.

![A corpus concordance screen, with lines invented for this lesson. A search box at the top reads esgrimir (lema), all countries. Below, eight lines, each with the form of esgrimir highlighted in the middle: esgrimió el argumento, esgrimen razones, esgrimiendo un cuchillo, esgrimió el reglamento, esgrimir pretextos, esgrime la ley, esgrimieron datos, esgrimía una navaja. A note says the lines are illustrative, not real corpus data.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Writing a definition

Lexicographers define most nouns, verbs and adjectives by genus and difference: first a more
general word (*el género próximo*, the nearest genus), then what sets this word apart (*la
diferencia específica*). *El croquis* is *un dibujo* (genus) *rápido y esquemático* (difference).
Three rules:

- The definition must be able to replace the headword in a sentence: same part of speech, same
  construction.
- It mustn't be circular (*catar: acción de catar*).
- It mustn't use harder words than the headword.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: choosing with corpus evidence

A student writes *El asaltante adujo un cuchillo* and wonders whether *esgrimió* would be better.
A search for both lemmas gives, in invented, illustrative figures:

| | *aducir* | *esgrimir* |
|---|---|---|
| frequency (per million words) | 2.1 | 1.4 |
| most frequent objects | *razones, motivos, problemas, falta de* | *argumentos, razones, la ley, armas* |
| with weapons | almost never | often, literally |

Reading the concordances: *aducir* takes reasons and never weapons; *esgrimir* takes both,
literally and figuratively. So *esgrimió un cuchillo* is right, *adujo un cuchillo* is wrong, and
with *razones* both are possible, with the difference lesson 01 taught: *esgrimir* fights,
*aducir* offers (sometimes an excuse). The figures matter less than the company: frequency tells
you a word is common, not that it fits.

### Example 2: three definitions in dictionary style

The definitions below are written for this lesson.

- *catar* (tr.): *Probar con atención un alimento o una bebida para juzgar su sabor y su
  calidad.* Genus: *probar*; difference: *con atención… para juzgar*. It replaces the headword:
  *El experto cató el vino* → *probó con atención el vino para juzgar su sabor*. (To taste a food
  or drink attentively in order to judge its flavor and quality.)
- *el croquis* (m.): *Dibujo rápido y esquemático de un lugar, un objeto o una situación.*
  Genus: *dibujo*; difference: *rápido y esquemático*. (A quick, schematic drawing of a place,
  object or situation.)
- *refunfuñar* (intr.): *Quejarse en voz baja y de manera poco clara, mostrando disgusto.*
  Genus: *quejarse*; difference: *en voz baja… mostrando disgusto*. Not *decir cosas* (too
  general) and not *protestar* (too loud). (To complain under one's breath, unclearly, showing
  displeasure.)

Check each against the rules: no circularity, the same part of speech, words easier than the
headword. Then compare with a published dictionary: you'll find the same genus more often than
the same words.

### Example 3: reading the labels

Suppose a reader finds *nimio* in a dictionary with two senses: the first, "insignificant"; the
second, "excessive", marked *desus.* What can she conclude? That the usual meaning today is
"insignificant", and that the "excessive" sense, the Latin one, appears in old texts but not in
current writing. The label answered a question the definition alone couldn't.

## Pronunciation

- *lexicógrafo*: le-xi-CÓ-gra-fo; *x* is *ks*.
- *el corpus*: COR-pus, the same in the plural.
- *lematizar*: le-ma-ti-ZAR; *z* is said as *s*.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the DLE as a rulebook. It records use; a sense without a label is general, but
  that doesn't make it the best choice in every register.
- Using a thesaurus as a dictionary. A *tesauro* offers near-synonyms without telling you
  their connotation or company; check each in a dictionary and a corpus.
- Reading frequency as fitness. A frequent word can still be wrong for your sentence.
- Defining in circles: *el lexicógrafo: persona que hace lexicografía* tells a reader
  nothing new unless *lexicografía* is defined elsewhere.

## Key points

- The DLE records general Spanish, with country and usage labels; the DEM describes all Mexican
  Spanish; the *Diccionario de mexicanismos* lists what is particular to Mexico; the DPD advises.
- An entry: headword, origin, senses, usage labels, examples. Read the labels first.
- A corpus gives frequency and company; its concordance lines show collocations.
- Define by genus and difference, without circles, in a form that can replace the headword.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Los nombres de los lugares: toponymy and demonyms
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 04 traced words back to Latin and Greek. Place names keep even older layers: a Mexican
map holds Nahuatl, Spanish saints and the names of national heroes, and a Spanish map holds
Arabic. This lesson teaches you to read those layers, to write foreign place names as Spanish
does, and to choose the right name for a place's people in each register. B2 93 (Mexico's
languages) and A1's countries are assumed, not repeated.

Onomastics, in Spanish *la onomástica*, is the study of proper names: *los topónimos*
(place names, studied by *la toponimia*) and *los antropónimos* (personal names). In Spain
especially, *la onomástica* is also your name day, the feast of the saint you are named after.

## Nahuatl names: reading the endings

A **[[toponym]]** (*el topónimo*) often describes the place, and in central Mexico many describe it
in Nahuatl, B2's *el náhuatl*. A few endings recur. The meanings below are the ones scholars
usually give; for many individual names they disagree, and Spanish spelling has blurred some of
the original forms, so treat any single etymology as probable, not certain.

| Ending | Usual meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-tlan*, *-titlan* | place of, where there are many; near | *Mazatlán, Tepoztlán* |
| *-co*, *-c* | in, at the place of | *Acapulco, Chapultepec* (-c) |
| *-pan* | on, over | *Zapopan* |
| *-tepec* | at the hill (from *tepetl*, hill) | *Chapultepec, Tehuantepec* |
| *-apan* | in or by the water | (*a-* from *atl*, water) |

Endings tell you the kind of name; the first part tells you what the place was known for, often
an animal, a plant or a feature of the land.

![A chart titled Leer un topónimo náhuatl that splits three names into parts, each with its Nahuatl root and a Spanish meaning. Chapultepec: chapul- (chapolin, chapulín: grasshopper), tepe- (tepetl, cerro: hill) and -c (en: in), giving en el cerro del chapulín, on the grasshopper hill. Mazatlán: maza- (mazatl, venado: deer) and -tlan (lugar de: place of), giving lugar de venados. Acapulco: aca- (acatl, carrizo: reed), -pul (grande: large) and -co (lugar: place), giving lugar de los carrizos grandes. A note at the bottom says these are the meanings usually given and that specialists don't always agree.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Saints, heroes and the Spanish layer

The Spanish added a saint to many Indigenous names: *San Juan Teotihuacan*, *Santiago
Matatlán* (lesson 01's mezcal town). The saint is the town's
*patrono* (patron saint), and the church is dedicated to him or her: it stands *bajo la
advocación de* San Juan (*la advocación* is that dedication). The town's fiesta usually falls on
the patron's day.

Other names honor people. A name taken from a person is an *antropónimo* turned *topónimo*, and
the person is the place's eponym (*el epónimo*): Miguel Hidalgo for the state of Hidalgo,
José María Morelos for Morelos, Benito Juárez for Ciudad Juárez. *San Cristóbal de las Casas*
joins both kinds: a saint and Bartolomé de las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop.

Eponyms also hide in official names. Several Mexican states carry a hero in their official
names: *Coahuila de Zaragoza*, *Michoacán de Ocampo*, *Veracruz de Ignacio de la
Llave*. In everyday use only the first part survives.

A guide in Coyoacán, in the south of Mexico City, puts these layers together for a group of
visitors:

```dialogue
# Paseo por Coyoacán
Guía: Empecemos por el nombre. Coyoacán suele traducirse como "lugar de coyotes": la raíz es coyotl, coyote, y la terminación indica un lugar. No todos los especialistas están de acuerdo, pero es la lectura más aceptada.
= Let's start with the name. Coyoacán is usually translated as "place of coyotes": the root is coyotl, coyote, and the ending marks a place. Not all specialists agree, but it's the most accepted reading.
Guía: Ahora miren la plaza. Este es el Jardín Hidalgo, en honor del héroe de la Independencia, y aquel, el Jardín del Centenario, que recuerda el centenario de la Independencia, en 1910. Y al fondo, la parroquia de San Juan Bautista, el santo patrono de Coyoacán.
= Now look at the square. This is the Jardín Hidalgo, in honor of the hero of Independence, and that one is the Jardín del Centenario, which commemorates the centenary of Independence, in 1910. And at the far end, the parish church of Saint John the Baptist, Coyoacán's patron saint.
Visitante: O sea que en una sola plaza hay tres capas de nombres.
= So in a single square there are three layers of names.
Guía: Exacto: la náhuatl, la de los santos y la de los héroes.
= Exactly: the Nahuatl one, the saints' and the heroes'.
```

## Arabic names in Spain

Arabic was spoken in much of the Iberian Peninsula for centuries, and it left thousands of
words, *arabismos* (Arabic loanwords), many beginning with the article *al-*: *la almohada*
(pillow), *el algodón* (cotton). Place names kept it too, in the usual etymologies:

- *Guadalajara*, from *wādī al-ḥijāra*, "river (or valley) of stones". *Guad-* (from *wādī*,
  river) also begins *Guadalquivir*, "the great river". Mexico's Guadalajara took its name from
  the Spanish city, usually said to be the hometown of the conquistador who ordered its founding,
  Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán.
- *Medina*, from *madīna*, "city": *Medina del Campo*, *Medina-Sidonia*.
- *Alcalá*, from *al-qalʿa*, "the castle, the fortress": *Alcalá de Henares*, Cervantes's birthplace.

## Mexico, Oaxaca, Texas: the old x

The *x* of *México*, *Oaxaca* and *Texas* is an old Spanish spelling of a sound that became the
modern *j*. The spelling stayed in these names, and the RAE recommends writing *México* with *x*
and saying it with the *j* sound (*Méjico* is also recorded, but rare and old-fashioned). Other
Nahuatl names keep an *x* said as *sh* or *s* (*Xola, Xochimilco*): learn each as you meet it.

## Foreign places: exonyms

An **[[exonym]]** (*el exónimo*) is the name a language gives to a foreign place, different from the
local one: *Londres* (London), *Nueva York*, *Múnich*, *Pekín* (Beijing). Spanish keeps the
traditional exonyms where they are established. The RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) recommends *Pekín* as
the Spanish form; much of the press now also writes *Beijing*, so you will see both.
Where no Spanish form exists, Spanish uses the local name, adapted to Spanish spelling if it comes
from another alphabet.

## Demonyms

A **[[demonym]]** (*el gentilicio*) names a place's people. Spanish writes it in lower case, unlike
English: *los mexicanos*, *una tapatía*. Some are regular (*oaxaqueño, yucateco, poblano*); many
must simply be learned.

| Place | Demonym | Register and notes |
|---|---|---|
| Guadalajara | *tapatío* | standard in every register |
| Monterrey | *regiomontano*; *regio* | *regiomontano* is formal, from a Latin rendering of "royal mountain"; *regio* is colloquial |
| Mexico City | *capitalino*; *chilango* | *capitalino* is neutral; *chilango* is colloquial (below) |
| Puebla | *poblano* | standard |
| Veracruz | *veracruzano*; *jarocho* | *jarocho* is especially for the port city, and affectionate |
| Estado de México | *mexiquense* | standard; not the same as Mexico City |

*Chilango* has a history. Its origin is debated (a Maya word, a Nahuatl one and a Veracruz
nickname have all been proposed), and it began as a derogatory nickname for people from the
capital, recorded in Veracruz in the mid-twentieth century. Today many people from Mexico City
use it proudly, and the RAE records it as a colloquial word for someone from the city, without
the insult (as a UNAM report summarized in 2025). It is still colloquial: right for a chronicle
or a conversation, wrong for an official report. *Defeño*, from *D.F.* (*Distrito Federal*, the
city's official name until 2016), is fading.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: decoding three place names

- *Chapultepec*: *chapul(in)* (grasshopper) + *tepe(tl)* (hill) + *-c* (in): "on the grasshopper
  hill". The park's hill gives the name.
- *Mazatlán*: *maza(tl)* (deer) + *-tlan* (place of): "place of deer".
- *Acapulco*: *aca(tl)* (reed) + *-pul* (large) + *-co* (place): "place of the large reeds".

The method: find the ending, then the root; check the result in a toponymic dictionary, and
write "usually translated as" unless a source you trust is certain.

### Example 2: choosing demonyms for a formal text

A tourism office drafts a press release:

> *El fin de semana largo, los chilangos, los regios y los tapatíos llenaron los hoteles de la costa.*

Over the long weekend, the chilangos, the regios and the tapatíos filled the coast's hotels.

The sentence is lively but mixes two colloquial demonyms with a standard one. For an official
release:

> *Durante el fin de semana largo, visitantes de la Ciudad de México, Monterrey y Guadalajara
> llenaron los hoteles de la costa.*

Over the long weekend, visitors from Mexico City, Monterrey and Guadalajara filled the coast's
hotels.

Or, keeping the demonyms: *capitalinos, regiomontanos y tapatíos*. Naming the cities is the
safest choice for an international reader (lesson 17), who may not know any of the demonyms.

### Example 3: a foreign name

A student writes *Viajaremos a London y después a Beijing.* In Spanish prose, use the exonym where
one is established: *Viajaremos a Londres y después a Pekín* (or *Beijing*, now common in the
press). *London* in a Spanish sentence reads like an unedited English draft.

## Pronunciation

- *Chapultepec*: cha-pul-te-PEC, stress on the last syllable; *Mazatlán*: ma-za-TLÁN (in Mexico *tl*
  starts a syllable), with *z* said as *s*.
- *Teotihuacan*: te-o-ti-hua-CAN, five syllables; you will see it with and without an accent.
- *topónimo*: to-PÓ-ni-mo; *gentilicio*: gen-ti-LI-cio, four syllables.

## Common mistakes

- Capitalizing demonyms: *los Tapatíos* is English habit; Spanish writes *los tapatíos*.
- Using a colloquial demonym in formal writing: *chilango* and *regio* belong to
  conversation and chronicles.
- Confusing *mexiquense* with *capitalino*: the Estado de México and Mexico City are
  different entities.
- Presenting one etymology as certain: write *suele traducirse como* (is usually
  translated as).

## Key points

- Toponymy studies place names; onomastics, all proper names.
- Nahuatl endings (*-tlan, -co, -pan, -tepec*) help decode Mexican names; treat meanings as
  probable.
- Saints' names (*advocación, patrono*), eponyms (*Hidalgo*) and Arabic roots (*Guadalajara,
  Alcalá*) are other layers.
- Use established exonyms (*Londres, Pekín*).
- Demonyms are lower case and have registers: *capitalino* (neutral), *chilango* (colloquial).
