the lesson.

lessons.title: Aquella noche moría el comisario: tenses as style
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You already choose between the preterite and the imperfect (B2 01 compared Mexico and Spain) and
guess with the future and the conditional (*Habrá perdido el vuelo*, B2 08). At C2 the question
becomes "which tense gives the effect I want?" Novelists and journalists bend the tenses on
purpose: an imperfect where a preterite was expected, a present for events long past, a
conditional for what nobody has confirmed. This lesson names those choices.

## Mexican crime fiction in three names

Mexico has a long tradition of *novela policiaca* (the puzzle: crime, detective, solution) and of
*novela negra* (darker, where the city and *la impunidad* matter as much as the culprit).

- María Elvira Bermúdez (1916–1988), a lawyer, published *Diferentes razones tiene la
  muerte* in 1953: murders among the guests of a house in Coyoacán, solved by her amateur
  *sabueso* Armando H. Zozaya. A 2024 UNAM profile also credits her with María Elena Morán,
  which it calls the first woman detective in Latin American fiction.
- Rafael Bernal (1915–1972) published *El complot mongol* in 1969. Its *antihéroe*, the aging
  police gunman Filiberto García, has to uncover a plot against a visiting head of state in Mexico
  City's Chinatown; the book is often called the founding Mexican *novela negra*.
- Paco Ignacio Taibo II (born in Gijón, Spain, in 1949, raised in Mexico) began his series
  about Héctor Belascoarán Shayne, an engineer turned private detective, with *Días de combate*
  (1976). The series is known less for its *giros argumentales* than for its portrait of Mexico
  City.

The story below is original.

![A book jacket laid flat, with Spanish labels. On the left, the back cover (la contraportada): a block of text lines headed Sinopsis (la sinopsis) and a bar code. Between the covers, the spine. On the right, the dark blue front cover: a strip reading Novela negra across the top, the title La noche del comisario (el título) in large white letters, a pale silhouette of a man in a hat (el sombrero) beside a streetlamp, a large fingerprint (la huella dactilar) in the lower left corner, and a small round publisher's logo with the letter E (la editorial) at the bottom right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The narrative imperfect

The imperfect normally presents an event from inside, as ongoing or as background: its
**[[aspect]]** is imperfective (*La ciudad dormía* — The city was asleep). The preterite presents an
event as a whole, finished (*El comisario murió* — The police chief died).

In the **[[narrative imperfect]]** (*imperfecto narrativo*, also called *de ruptura* because it
breaks the expected pattern), a writer uses the imperfect for a single, completed event, almost
always pinned down by a time phrase:

- *Dos horas después, la policía detenía al sospechoso.* — Two hours later, the police arrested
  the suspect.
- *A las seis y diez, el monitor dejaba de sonar.* — At ten past six, the monitor stopped
  beeping.
- *Tras la redada, el comisario recibía una llamada.* — After the raid, the police chief got a
  call.

Both events are finished; a preterite (*detuvo, dejó*) is the plain choice. The imperfect holds
the camera on the moment, and in the press it often closes a sequence. The RAE's *Nueva
gramática* describes it as a feature of narrative and journalistic style (check the section). You
may use it in your narratives; it is never required, and a preterite is never wrong there.

Recognize the playful imperfect of games (*Yo era el detective y tú eras el
ladrón* — I'd be the detective and you'd be the thief) and the imperfect of dreams (*Soñé que
estaba en una estación y el tren no llegaba* — I dreamed I was in a station and the train didn't
come).

## The historical present

The **[[historical present]]** tells past events in the present to bring them close: *En 1969
Bernal publica su novela más famosa* — In 1969 Bernal publishes his most famous novel. In fiction, a narrator telling in the past switches to
the present at the key scene and the reader is suddenly in the room; switching back pushes the
scene away. The story below does both. Change the frame only at a scene break, for an effect.

## Guessing: the future and conditional of conjecture

B2 08 taught the **[[future of conjecture]]**: the future for a guess about now, the future perfect
for a guess about the recent past.

- *Serán las once.* — It must be about eleven.
- *Habrá salido por la puerta de atrás.* — He must have gone out the back door.

The conditional does the same one step back: a guess about a past moment.

- *Tendría unos setenta años.* — He must have been about seventy.
- *Habría sido el chofer.* — It must have been the driver (a guess about an earlier past).

Add the concessive future, which grants a point before *pero* (C1 04 used it to soften
criticism): *Será muy terco, pero no es tonto* — He may be very stubborn, but he isn't stupid.
In the first person it can be ironic: *Seré terco, pero…* And recognize the solemn future of
command of laws and scripture: *No matarás* — Thou shalt not kill.

## The conditional of rumor

Newspapers use the conditional for information they haven't confirmed: *El sospechoso habría
huido a otro estado* — The suspect has reportedly fled to another state. This 
**[[conditional of rumor]]** is frequent in the press of many countries. FundéuRAE counts it among common faults of
news writing, and newspaper style guides tell reporters to avoid it, because it passes on a claim
without saying who makes it (check FundéuRAE's current entry). The alternative is attribution:
*Según fuentes de la fiscalía, el sospechoso huyó a otro estado.* Read it as "reportedly"; in your
own news writing, attribute instead. (A guess inside a quotation, *"Habrá sido el chofer",
dijeron en la fiscalía*, is different: a conjecture credited to its source.)

## Tenses you will only read

B2 04h2 (an honors lesson) named these literary forms; in short:

- The **[[pretérito anterior]]**, *hube* + participle, after *apenas, en cuanto, cuando, no bien*:
  *Apenas hubo terminado la frase, cerró los ojos* — No sooner had he finished the sentence than he
  closed his eyes. Literary prose only; *En cuanto terminó la frase…* says the same.
- The literary *-ra* as a past: *el que fuera presidente del club* — the man who had been (once
  was) the club's president. Frequent in the press; *que fue* is the plain form.
- Spain's perfect for today's events, in a novel set in Madrid: *Esta mañana ha llegado el
  inspector* — The inspector arrived this morning. Mexican Spanish would say *llegó* (B2 01).

![A chart titled Tiempos y efectos with three columns: Form, Example, and Effect and use. Narrative imperfect: Dos horas después, la policía detenía al sospechoso; slows the frame, closes a sequence; news and fiction. Historical present: En 1969 Bernal publica su novela; brings events close; biography, key scenes. Future and conditional: Habrá salido. Tendría setenta años; a guess about now or then; used everywhere. Concessive future: Será terco, pero no es tonto; grants a point; argument. Conditional of rumor: El sospechoso habría huido; an unconfirmed report; press, advised against. Pretérito anterior: Apenas hubo terminado, se fue; no sooner had; literary only. The last two rows are shaded pink, and a key says pink means recognition only: read it, don't produce it.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: *Aquella noche moría el comisario*

An original noir opening told by a *narrador protagonista* (first-person narrator). Notice where
he switches into the present and back.

> Aquella noche moría el comisario Andrés Ibarra, y nadie en la colonia Guerrero parecía
> enterarse. Le decíamos así, comisario, por los años que pasó en la policía de Rosario, en
> Argentina, antes de volver a México; aquí nunca tuvo más rango que el de su terquedad. Yo era
> entonces reportero de nota roja, y él, mi mejor fuente.
>
> Me llamó pasadas las once. No me saludó, lo cual ya era una noticia. "El caso Orozco", dijo.
> "Ven antes de que me arrepienta."
>
> Llego al hospital a medianoche. El pasillo huele a cloro y a café recalentado; una enfermera me
> mira como se mira a un pariente que llega tarde. Ibarra está sentado en la cama, flaco como un
> perchero, con el periódico de la mañana doblado sobre las rodillas.
>
> "Dirás que soy un viejo necio", me dice. "Seré necio, pero no soy tonto. A Orozco no lo mató el
> chofer."
>
> Ocho años antes, el licenciado Ernesto Orozco había aparecido muerto en su despacho. La autopsia
> habló de un golpe en la nuca; los indicios, de una puerta forzada y de un chofer que
> desapareció esa misma tarde. "Habrá sido el chofer", dijeron en la fiscalía, y el caso se
> archivó sin juicio y sin culpable.
>
> "Había una huella dactilar en el vaso del escritorio", sigue Ibarra. "No inculpaba al chofer. La
> mandaron a cotejar y el resultado nunca volvió. Eso no es descuido: es encubrimiento."
>
> Le pregunto por qué no habló antes. Se ríe, y la risa se le vuelve tos.
>
> "Porque tenía una pensión, una hija y miedo. Ahora solo me queda lo tercero, y ya no me alcanza
> para callarme."
>
> Saca del periódico un sobre amarillo. Dentro hay una copia del informe del forense y una lista de
> nombres escrita a mano. El primero me hiela la sangre: es el de un empresario que hoy patrocina
> campañas contra la impunidad.
>
> "No lo publiques mañana", me pide. "Publícalo cuando lo hayas esclarecido. Un reportero sin
> pruebas es un soplón con credencial."
>
> Apenas hubo dicho la frase, cerró los ojos. Me quedé con él hasta que amaneció. A las seis y
> diez, el monitor dejaba de sonar. Afuera, la ciudad empezaba otro día como si nada; yo tenía un
> sobre, una lista y la sospecha de que la historia, como en las malas novelas policiacas, apenas
> empezaba.

**Summary.** A former crime reporter remembers the night Ibarra, an old policeman nicknamed "the
police chief" after his years in Argentina, called him to his deathbed. From the hospital scene
on, the story is in the present. Ibarra says a case closed eight years earlier was wrong: the
driver didn't kill the lawyer Orozco, and an unchecked fingerprint points to a cover-up. He hands
over the medical examiner's report and a list of names headed by a businessman who campaigns
against impunity, and asks the reporter to confirm before publishing. Past tenses return with his
death at dawn.

**Glosses.** *Aquella noche moría* — that night was dying, or died: the imperfect leaves both
readings open; *nunca tuvo más rango que el de su terquedad* — his only rank was his stubbornness;
*flaco como un perchero* — thin as a coat rack; *Seré necio, pero…* — I may be stubborn, but…
(concessive future); *cotejar* — to compare (a print); *la fiscalía* — the prosecutor's office; *una pensión* — a pension; *me hiela la sangre* — makes my blood run
cold; *Apenas hubo dicho* — no sooner had he said (pretérito anterior).

### The same events as a news brief

> Muere el expolicía Andrés Ibarra
>
> El expolicía Andrés Ibarra Solís, de 78 años, falleció la madrugada de este martes en un hospital
> de la colonia Guerrero. Ibarra ingresó el lunes por la noche con una insuficiencia respiratoria;
> a las 6:10, los médicos confirmaban su muerte. Conocido en el medio como "el comisario", Ibarra
> participó en las pesquisas del homicidio del abogado Ernesto Orozco, ocurrido en 2017 y
> archivado sin sentencia. Horas después del deceso, la fiscalía capitalina informaba que
> revisará el expediente a petición de la familia de Orozco. Le sobrevive una hija.

**Translation.** *Former policeman Andrés Ibarra dies.* Former policeman Andrés Ibarra Solís, 78,
died early this Tuesday in a hospital in the colonia Guerrero. Ibarra was admitted on Monday night
with respiratory failure; at 6:10 the doctors confirmed his death. Known in the field as "the
police chief," Ibarra took part in the inquiries into the homicide of the lawyer Ernesto Orozco,
which took place in 2017 and was closed without a ruling. Hours after his death, the city
prosecutor's office announced that it will review the file at the request of Orozco's family. He
is survived by a daughter.

Note the narrative imperfects *confirmaban, informaba*, and no conditional of rumor. (Ibarra and
Orozco are fictional.)

## Pronunciation

- *autopsia*: three syllables, au-TOP-sia, with *au* as in "ouch" and *sia* as one syllable.
- *homicidio*: o-mi-SI-dio, silent *h*; the *c* is an *s* sound in Latin America.
- *interrogatorio*: in-te-rro-ga-TO-rio, with a trilled *rr*.
- *hampa*: AM-pa, silent *h*, but still *el hampa*.

## Common mistakes

- Using the narrative imperfect without a time anchor: *La policía detenía al sospechoso*
  alone reads as a habit (the police used to arrest him). Give it its moment: *Dos horas
  después…*
- Writing the conditional of rumor in a news text: *El alcalde habría recibido sobornos*
  passes on an accusation without a source. Write *Según la denuncia, el alcalde recibió…*
- Reading the conditional of rumor as conjecture: in a newspaper, *El sospechoso habría huido*
  means "reportedly fled," not "must have fled."

## Key points

- The narrative imperfect presents a finished event, with a time phrase, for effect: allowed in
  your narratives, never required.
- The historical present brings past events close.
- The future and conditional, simple and compound, express conjecture; the concessive future
  grants a point before *pero*.
- The conditional of rumor marks unconfirmed news: recognize it, and attribute instead.
- The pretérito anterior and the literary *-ra* are for reading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Si la imprenta hubiera llegado tarde…: conditions and counterfactuals
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can already build conditions with *si* in every time (B2 04: *Si hubiera salido antes,
habría llegado*) and with connectors such as *a menos que, siempre y cuando, en el supuesto de
que* (B1 18, B2 12). Formal and literary Spanish often drops *si* altogether and lets an
infinitive, a gerund or a fixed phrase carry the condition. This lesson teaches those structures,
the mixed-time **[[counterfactual]]** (a past that didn't happen and a present that would be
different), and two fixed phrases with the future subjunctive. The theme is alternate history:
what if the printing press had reached New Spain late?

## Two halves of a condition

Grammars call the condition the **[[protasis]]** and the result the **[[apodosis]]**:

- *Si llueve* (protasis), *se suspende el partido* (apodosis). — If it rains, the game is called
  off.

Either half may come first. The terms help because the structures below change only the
protasis: the apodosis keeps the tenses you know.

## Conditions without *si*

An **[[implicit condition]]** is a protasis with no *si*. Spanish has several:

| Structure | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *de* + infinitive | *De seguir así, cerraremos en un año.* | If things go on like this, we'll close within a year. |
| *de* + compound infinitive | *De haberlo sabido, te habría avisado.* | Had I known, I would have told you. |
| *de* + infinitive + subject | *De haber ganado ellos, todo sería distinto.* | Had they won, everything would be different. |
| gerund | *Saliendo ahora, llegamos a tiempo.* | If we leave now, we'll be on time. |
| participle | *Bien mirado, el error tiene arreglo.* | Looked at carefully, the mistake can be fixed. |
| *con* + infinitive | *Con avisar bastaba.* | Just letting us know would have been enough. |
| *a poco que* + subjunctive | *A poco que estudies, apruebas.* | If you study even a little, you'll pass. |
| *de no ser por* + noun | *De no ser por ella, nos habríamos perdido.* | If it hadn't been for her, we would have got lost. |
| *como* + subjunctive | *Como no llegues a las ocho, nos vamos.* | If you're not here by eight, we're leaving. |

Notes on use:

- *De* + infinitive is the most useful in formal writing. The simple infinitive usually points to
  the present or future; the compound one (*de haber* + participle) to a past that didn't happen.
  Its subject, if different from the main clause's, goes after the infinitive: *De haber llegado
  la imprenta en 1600…* (Had the press arrived in 1600…).
- The gerund and the participle carry a condition only when the context makes it one:
  *Saliendo ahora* is "if we leave now," but *Salió corriendo* is just "he ran out." The
  participle is mostly in set phrases: *bien mirado, visto así, dicho de otro modo*.
- *Con* + infinitive means "just by": *Con que me avises basta* (*con que* + subjunctive: as
  long as you let me know, that's enough).
- *De no ser por* takes a noun. *De no ser que* + subjunctive means "unless" (*De no ser que
  llueva, vamos*); *de no ser porque* + indicative, "if it weren't for the fact that" (*De no ser
  porque llovió, habríamos ganado*).
- *Como* + subjunctive is a warning or a threat. With the indicative, *como* means "since":
  *Como no llegaste, nos fuimos* (Since you didn't come, we left).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a condition structure
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question, is the condition a warning or threat to the listener? If yes, use como plus subjunctive. If no, is the text formal or written? If no, use si, the everyday choice. If yes, does the condition refer to a past that did not happen? If yes, use de haber plus participle, or si plus pluperfect subjunctive. If no, is it a minimal condition, even a little? If yes, use a poco que plus subjunctive. If no, is it an exception, but for something? If yes, use de no ser por plus noun. If no, use de plus infinitive, or si.
  Q1{"A warning or a threat?"} -- yes --> C1["como + subjunctive"]
  Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Formal or written text?"}
  Q2 -- no --> C2["si: the everyday choice"]
  Q2 -- yes --> Q3{"A past that didn't happen?"}
  Q3 -- yes --> C3["de haber + participle, or si + pluperfect subjunctive"]
  Q3 -- no --> Q4{"A minimal condition: even a little?"}
  Q4 -- yes --> C4["a poco que + subjunctive"]
  Q4 -- no --> Q5{"An exception: but for something?"}
  Q5 -- yes --> C5["de no ser por + noun"]
  Q5 -- no --> C6["de + infinitive, or si"]
```

## Counterfactuals across times

A counterfactual imagines what didn't happen. B2 04 taught the mixed types: a past protasis with a present apodosis, or the reverse.

- *Si no hubiera llegado la imprenta, hoy leeríamos menos.* — If the press hadn't arrived, we
  would read less today.
- *Si fuera más prudente, no habría firmado.* — If he were more careful (in general), he wouldn't
  have signed (then).

In the apodosis of a past counterfactual, *habría* and the *-ra* form are both standard: *Si lo
hubiera sabido, habría venido / hubiera venido*. The *-se* form (*hubiese venido*) also occurs;
it is accepted, never required. *Pudiera* and *debiera* also soften a statement like a
conditional: *Debieras descansar* (You ought to rest; *deberías* is the everyday form); *Pudiera ser
un error* (It might be a mistake).

## Two phrases with the future subjunctive

The **[[future subjunctive]]** (*fuere, hubiere, tuviere*) has disappeared from speech. Learn two fixed
phrases for production:

- *Sea como fuere, el libro salió.* — Be that as it may, the book came out.
- *Sea cual fuere el resultado, lo publicaremos.* — Whatever the result, we'll publish it. With a
  plural noun: *sean cuales fueren los resultados*.

The everyday forms are *sea como sea* and *sea cual sea*. In older laws and contracts you'll read
other future subjunctives (*El que causare un daño…* — Whoever causes damage…); lesson 13 returns
to them. Read them as present subjunctives.

## Thinking counterfactually

A good *ucronía* (alternate history) changes one fact and follows its consequences with
discipline. Three questions test it. Is the change plausible: could it have happened (*¿es
plausible?*)? What depended on *la contingencia*, the things that might not have happened, and
what was *ineluctable*? Where is the *bifurcación*, the fork after which *el devenir* (the course
of events) splits? The more steps from the fork, the more *especulativo* the claim, and the more
the writer should hedge (*cabe suponer, es probable que*).

The vocabulary of the genre, in use:

- *Un encuentro fortuito en Sevilla lo trastocó todo.* — A chance meeting in Seville upended
  everything.
- *El proyecto pudo malograrse; lo que acaeció después no era inexorable.* — The project could
  have come to nothing; what happened next was not inexorable.
- *Si hubiera sobrevenido una epidemia, el taller habría cerrado.* — Had an epidemic struck, the
  workshop would have closed.
- *Es una conjetura, un caso hipotético: el razonamiento contrafáctico no prueba nada, pero
  ilumina.* — It's a conjecture, a hypothetical case: counterfactual reasoning proves nothing, but
  it sheds light.
- Many alternate histories turn on *una derrota* (a defeat), *una alianza* (an alliance) or *una
  sublevación* (an uprising) that went the other way, and imagine another *hegemonía*
  (dominance), a lost *soberanía* (sovereignty) or a territory never *anexado* (annexed). A novel
  may even offer *un desenlace alternativo* (an alternative ending).

![A timeline that forks. A single line on the left, labeled 1539: la imprenta llega a la Ciudad de México, runs to a point marked Bifurcación. From there a solid upper branch, labeled Historia real, passes three marks: cartillas y vocabularios impresos, libros en varias lenguas, periódicos en el siglo XVIII. A dashed lower branch, labeled Ucronía: la imprenta llega en 1600, passes three marks: copias a mano, menos libros en lenguas indígenas, una cultura del manuscrito.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: *Si la imprenta hubiera llegado tarde*

An original essay, followed by two shorter premises.

> En 1539, un impresor italiano al servicio de la casa sevillana de Juan Cromberger instaló en la
> Ciudad de México el primer taller de imprenta del continente. Se llamaba Juan Pablos. Supongamos,
> como ejercicio, que el barco que traía la prensa se hubiera hundido, y que la imprenta no hubiera
> llegado a la Nueva España sino hacia 1600.
>
> De haber sucedido así, los primeros sesenta años del virreinato se habrían escrito a mano. No es
> un detalle técnico. La imprenta no solo multiplica los textos: los fija. Un copista se cansa, se
> distrae, corrige lo que no entiende; una prensa repite el mismo error mil veces, pero también el
> mismo acierto. Sin ella, cada cartilla para aprender a leer habría sido distinta, y cada
> vocabulario de una lengua indígena, un objeto casi único.
>
> Cabe suponer, además, que se habría impreso menos en náhuatl y en otras lenguas de la tierra. En
> la historia real, las primeras prensas publicaron doctrinas, gramáticas y vocabularios en
> varias lenguas. En nuestra ucronía, a falta de imprenta, esos textos habrían circulado en pocas
> copias, y a poco que se hubiera perdido alguna, se habría perdido con ella una manera de
> escribir una lengua.
>
> ¿Es plausible el supuesto? Lo es, porque nada en la llegada de la imprenta fue ineluctable:
> dependía de un contrato, de un barco y de la salud de un hombre. La historia está hecha de
> contingencias de este tipo. Pero conviene no exagerar. Si la prensa hubiera llegado en 1600, hoy
> no leeríamos de otra manera; lo que cambiaría es lo que tendríamos para leer. Muchos documentos
> que hoy citan los historiadores no existirían, y el devenir de algunas lenguas se contaría con
> más silencios.
>
> Sea como fuere, el ejercicio sirve para algo: nos obliga a ver como frágil lo que damos por
> hecho. De no ser por un taller pequeño, en una casa de esquina, nuestra memoria escrita del siglo
> XVI sería mucho más pobre.
>
> *Primera premisa.* ¿Y si el cacao nunca hubiera salido de Mesoamérica? De haberse quedado el cacao
> en estas tierras, Europa no conocería el chocolate, y hoy lo probaríamos solo los que vivimos
> donde crece.
>
> *Segunda premisa.* ¿Y si nunca se hubieran desecado los lagos de la cuenca de México? La capital
> sería hoy, quizá, una ciudad de canales, y nadie hablaría de hundimientos.

**Summary.** The essay recalls that in 1539 Juan Pablos, an Italian printer working for the
Seville firm of Juan Cromberger, set up the continent's first press in Mexico City, and imagines
it arriving around 1600 instead. The first sixty years would have been handwritten: texts would
vary from copy to copy, and fewer would have been printed in Nahuatl and other languages, so a
single lost copy could take a way of writing a language with it. The premise is plausible, since
the press depended on chance, but the writer warns against exaggerating: we would read the same
way, with less to read. The two short premises imagine cacao never leaving Mesoamerica and the
lakes never drained.

**Glosses.** *Supongamos, como ejercicio* — let's suppose, as an exercise; *De haber sucedido
así* — had it happened that way; *los fija* — fixes them (makes them stable); *un copista* — a copyist (scribe); *el mismo acierto* —
the same correct reading; *Cabe suponer* — one may suppose; *a poco que se hubiera perdido
alguna* — if even one had been lost; *lo que damos por hecho* — what we take for granted; *hoy lo
probaríamos solo los que vivimos donde crece* — today only those of us who live where it grows
would taste it.

The facts in the first sentence come from historical accounts of the press (its house in Mexico
City now belongs to UAM); the rest is speculation, and the essay says so with *supongamos, cabe
suponer, quizá*.

## Pronunciation

- *ucronía, hegemonía*: the stress falls on the *í*, which is a separate syllable: u-cro-NÍ-a,
  e-ge-mo-NÍ-a.
- *acaecer*: four syllables, a-ca-e-CER; keep *a* and *e* apart.
- *contingencia*: con-tin-JEN-sia; *g* before *e* is the Spanish *j* sound.

## Common mistakes

- *Si habría sabido…*: the conditional never goes in a *si* protasis. *Si hubiera sabido* or *De
  haberlo sabido*.
- Leaving the time unclear: *De saberlo, te habría avisado* is common and understood as past, but
  in writing *De haberlo sabido* leaves no doubt about a past that didn't happen.
- Reading *Como no llegaste* as a threat: with the indicative, *como* gives a reason (since).
- *Sea cual fuere los resultados*: *cual* and *ser* agree with a plural noun: *sean cuales fueren
  los resultados*.
- Overclaiming in counterfactual arguments: "would certainly have" is rarely defensible. Hedge
  the later steps.

## Key points

- The protasis is the condition, the apodosis the result.
- Formal Spanish expresses conditions without *si*: *de* + infinitive (compound for the past),
  the gerund, set participles, *con* + infinitive, *a poco que, de no ser por, como* +
  subjunctive.
- Mixed counterfactuals pair a past protasis with a present apodosis; *habría* and *hubiera* are
  both standard in the result.
- *Sea como fuere* and *sea cual fuere* are fixed phrases with the future subjunctive.
- A good counterfactual changes one fact, checks its plausibility and hedges each step.

lessons.title: La ciudad que se hunde: relatives and the long sentence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Formal Spanish likes long sentences: a main clause carrying relatives, asides and qualifications,
held together by commas and semicolons. A C2 reader unpacks them quickly; a C2 writer builds them
without losing the reader, and knows when to cut. This lesson goes beyond B2 09, which taught
*cuyo*, to the relatives of formal prose, the comma that changes a relative's meaning, and the
long sentence itself. C1 21 taught the punctuation marks; here you see them at work. The theme is
Mexico City's sinking ground.

## Relatives after a preposition

After a preposition, Spanish uses an article with *que*, or *el cual*, or *quien* for people:

- *el pozo del que sacan el agua* — the well they draw the water from
- *la norma conforme a la cual se otorgan los permisos* — the rule under which permits are granted
- *la falla geológica sobre la cual se abrió la grieta* — the geological fault along which the
  crack opened
- *los técnicos con quienes hablamos* — the technicians we talked to

*El que* and *el cual* are often interchangeable. Prefer *el cual*:

- after long or compound prepositions: *según la cual, junto al cual, a través del cual, debajo
  de la cual*;
- when the relative sits far from its noun, because its gender and number point back clearly:
  *la grieta del muro norte de la iglesia, la cual apareció en 2019…* (the crack, not the wall or
  the church, appeared).

Without a preposition, a restrictive clause takes plain *que*: *el pozo que perforaron* (not *el
pozo el cual perforaron*). In a nonrestrictive clause, *el cual* without a preposition is possible
but stiff: *La presa, la cual se construyó en 1950, …*; *que* is the usual choice.

## *Lo que, lo cual*: pointing to a whole clause

When the antecedent is a whole idea, use *lo que* or *lo cual*:

- *El suelo cede, lo cual agrieta los muros.* — The ground gives way, which cracks the walls.
- *Se bombea más de lo que se recarga, por lo que el nivel baja.* — More is pumped than is
  recharged, so the level drops.

*Lo cual* is a little more formal and is common after a preposition: *a raíz de lo cual, con lo
cual, por lo cual*: *Se desecó el lago, a raíz de lo cual la arcilla quedó expuesta* (The lake
was drained, as a result of which the clay was exposed).

## *Cuyo* in formal writing

*Cuyo* links a possessor to the thing possessed and agrees with the thing possessed:

- *una colonia cuyas calles se hunden* — a neighborhood whose streets are sinking
- *el edificio cuya cimentación falló* — the building whose foundations failed

In speech, many people say *una colonia que sus calles se hunden*. The DPD (2nd edition,
provisional, *cuyo*, consulted November 2026) rejects this *que su* construction for careful
language and suggests *cuyo, del que, del cual* or, informally, a verb of possession (*una
colonia que tiene calles hundidas*). It is very frequent in speech across the Spanish-speaking
world; in your writing, use *cuyo*.

## Where: *donde, en el que, en que, adonde*

*Donde* refers to a place: *la zona donde más se bombea* (where most is pumped). *En el que* and
*en que* work for places and also for times and situations: *el año en que se secó el pozo*.
*Adonde* (C1 21) marks a destination: *la planta adonde llega el agua*.

## Restrictive or nonrestrictive

A **[[restrictive relative clause]]** picks out which ones you mean; a 
**[[nonrestrictive relative clause]]** adds information about all of them. The commas make the difference:

- *Los vecinos que protestaron recibieron respuesta.* — The residents who protested got an answer
  (only those).
- *Los vecinos, que protestaron, recibieron respuesta.* — The residents, who protested, got an
  answer (all of them protested).

After a noun, *quien* without a preposition appears only in nonrestrictive clauses: *los vecinos, quienes
protestaron, …*, never *los vecinos quienes protestaron*. A name or a unique thing takes the
nonrestrictive comma: *el Gran Canal, que cruza el oriente de la ciudad, …*

## The long sentence and the parenthetical

In grammar and rhetoric a **[[period]]** (*el período* or *el periodo*) is a long sentence whose
clauses form one unit of sense. Its building blocks are the main clause, subordinate clauses and
the **[[parenthetical]]** (*el inciso*): an aside that interrupts the sentence and could be lifted
out without breaking it.

![A tree diagram of one long sentence, printed at the top: La arcilla del antiguo lago, que guarda agua como una esponja, se compacta —según los geólogos— cuando se extrae agua del acuífero, del cual depende la ciudad. Below it, a box for the main clause, La arcilla del antiguo lago se compacta. Three arrows lead down from it: from la arcilla to a nonrestrictive relative between commas, que guarda agua como una esponja; from the verb to a parenthetical (inciso) between dashes, según los geólogos; and at the end to a clause of time, cuando se extrae agua del acuífero. From that box an arrow labeled from el acuífero leads to a relative after a preposition, after a comma, del cual depende la ciudad. A key reads: commas, a nonrestrictive relative; dashes, a stronger aside; one main verb, se compacta.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) describes the marks for asides as a scale of separation (check the
sections on the comma, the dash and the parenthesis):

- commas for asides closely tied to the sentence: *La arcilla, que guarda agua, se compacta.*
- dashes (*rayas*) for a stronger interruption: *La arcilla —según los geólogos— se compacta.*
- parentheses for information outside the line of thought: dates, figures, sources.
- the semicolon to separate long parts that already contain commas: *El primer pozo,
  perforado en 1950, se secó; el segundo, más profundo, todavía funciona.*

One rule doesn't bend with length: no single comma between the subject and its verb, however long
the subject is (*Los edificios construidos sobre la antigua zona lacustre del oriente se
inclinan*, with no comma before *se inclinan*). A comma there is correct only as one of a pair
around an aside (or after *etc.*).

When to split? Cut a period when the reader has to hold two open clauses at once, when two
asides sit side by side, or when a relative's antecedent is more than a line away. Long sentences
are a resource, not a goal.

To unpack one, find the main verb and its subject first, then bracket every aside, then link
each relative to its antecedent.

## Reading: *La ciudad que se hunde*

An original popular-science article. Its paragraphs are built of long periods on purpose.

> La Ciudad de México, cuyo centro ocupa el sitio de la antigua Tenochtitlan, levantada sobre un
> islote en un sistema de lagos, se asienta hoy, en buena parte, sobre la arcilla que esos lagos dejaron al
> desaparecer: un material blando, formado por sedimentos finos, que guarda agua como una esponja.
>
> La desecación de los lagos fue obra humana. Desde la época virreinal, y durante siglos, se buscó
> sacar el agua de la cuenca para proteger a la ciudad de las inundaciones; obras como el Gran Canal del Desagüe,
> abierto hacia 1900, forman parte de una historia en la que el agua fue, antes que un recurso, una
> amenaza.
>
> El problema empieza bajo esa capa. Debajo de la arcilla se encuentra el acuífero del cual se
> extrae buena parte del agua que consume la ciudad, y cuyo nivel —el manto freático— ha bajado con
> la sobreexplotación del último siglo. Cuando el agua sale de los poros de la arcilla, sus
> partículas se acomodan y ocupan menos espacio, lo cual hace que el suelo descienda; y, como la
> arcilla compactada no recupera su volumen, el hundimiento es, en la práctica, irreversible.
>
> La velocidad varía de una zona a otra. Según la Secretaría de Gestión Integral de Riesgos y
> Protección Civil de la ciudad, que mide el fenómeno comparando imágenes de un año a otro, en
> partes de Iztapalapa, de Gustavo A. Madero y del Centro el suelo baja hasta 40 centímetros al
> año, mientras que en otras zonas lo hace a un ritmo de 10 a 12 centímetros (datos difundidos en
> junio de 2024).
>
> Que el suelo se hunda de manera desigual —y no de forma pareja, como un elevador— es lo que causa
> los daños. Los edificios cuya cimentación descansa sobre capas de distinto espesor sufren un
> asentamiento diferencial y se inclinan; los muros se agrietan; las tuberías se rompen, con lo cual se pierde agua; y los colectores,
> que necesitan una pendiente para que el agua corra, la pierden poco a poco. A veces, donde un
> tubo roto ha lavado la tierra, se abre un socavón en plena calle.
>
> Hay, sin embargo, una parte de la cuenca en la que el agua todavía entra al subsuelo: los bosques
> y suelos volcánicos del sur, a través de los cuales la lluvia se infiltra y contribuye a la
> recarga del acuífero. Mientras tanto, en los meses de estiaje, cuando bajan las presas y los
> embalses que abastecen a la ciudad desde fuera de la cuenca, muchas colonias reciben el agua por
> tandeo.

**Summary.** The city, whose center occupies the site of Tenochtitlan, built on an island in a
lake system, stands largely on the clay the lakes left behind, a soft material that holds water
like a sponge. The lakes were drained on purpose, over centuries, against floods. Below the clay lies the aquifer that supplies much of the city's water; a century of
pumping has lowered the water table. As water leaves the clay, it compacts, and the ground sinks
for good.
The city's civil protection office reported in June 2024 rates of up to 40 cm a year in parts of
Iztapalapa, Gustavo A. Madero and the Centro, and 10 to 12 cm elsewhere. Uneven sinking causes
the damage: tilting buildings, cracks, broken pipes, sewers losing their slope, the occasional
sinkhole. In the south, forests and volcanic soils still let rain recharge the aquifer; in the
dry season, as reservoirs outside the basin drop, many neighborhoods get water by turns.

**Glosses.** *se asienta* — stands, is built on; *al desaparecer* — when they disappeared; *del
cual se extrae* — from which is drawn; *se acomodan* — settle into place; *asentamiento diferencial* — differential (uneven) settling; *de manera desigual* —
unevenly; *como un elevador* — like an elevator (all at once); *pendiente* — slope; *se infiltra*
— seeps in.

### One paragraph, rewritten in short sentences

> El problema empieza bajo la arcilla. Ahí está el acuífero. De él sale buena parte del agua de la
> ciudad. El bombeo ha hecho bajar el manto freático. Cuando el agua sale de la arcilla, sus
> partículas se acomodan. El suelo desciende. La arcilla compactada no recupera su volumen. Por
> eso el hundimiento es irreversible.

**Translation.** The problem begins beneath the clay. That's where the aquifer is. Much of the
city's water comes from it. Pumping has lowered the water table. When the water leaves the clay,
its particles settle. The ground sinks. Compacted clay doesn't recover its volume. That's why the
subsidence is irreversible.

The short version is easier to follow, but it loses the links (*del cual, lo cual, y, como*) that
showed cause and consequence, and it reads like a list. A good expository paragraph usually mixes
the two: one long period for the mechanism, a short sentence for the conclusion.

![A cross-section of the ground under a city street, with Spanish labels. On the street stand an upright building, a tilting building with a crack in its wall (la grieta) and a small pump house. Under the street lies a thick brown layer of layered clay (la arcilla). Below it, a blue layer of porous rock full of water (el acuífero), crossed by a dashed line that marks the top of the water (el manto freático). A pipe runs from the pump house down through the clay into the blue layer (el pozo). A bracket on the left spans both layers (el subsuelo).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *acuífero*: a-CUÍ-fe-ro, four syllables; the stress is on the *í*.
- *freático*: fre-Á-ti-co, four syllables; *e* and *a* stay apart.
- *desagüe*: de-SA-güe; the *ü* is pronounced, like the *w* in "way".
- *estiaje*: es-TIA-je, three syllables.

## Common mistakes

- *Los vecinos quienes protestaron…*: *quien* without a preposition needs the nonrestrictive comma.
- *el pozo el cual perforaron*: without a preposition, a restrictive clause takes *que*.
- *cuyo* agreeing with the possessor: *la colonia cuyo calles* is wrong; *cuyas calles* agrees
  with *calles*.
- A comma between a long subject and its verb.
- Dropping the commas around a nonrestrictive clause, or adding them to a restrictive one: the
  meaning changes.
- Stacking asides until the main verb comes three lines later. Split the sentence.

## Key points

- After a preposition: *el que, el cual, quien*; prefer *el cual* after long prepositions and far
  from the antecedent.
- *Lo que, lo cual* refer to a whole clause.
- *Cuyo* agrees with the thing possessed; *que su* is frequent in speech and avoided in careful
  writing.
- Commas mark a nonrestrictive clause and change the meaning.
- A period holds clauses and asides together: commas, dashes and parentheses separate asides by
  degree, a semicolon separates long parts. Split when the reader would get lost.

lessons.title: En pos de la monarca: prepositional phrases and government
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Formal reports in Spanish lean on fixed phrases that work like prepositions: *en virtud de, a
efectos de, sin perjuicio de*. C1 taught some of them (*en aras de, so pena de, con miras a, en
el marco de*), and B2 taught *a raíz de*. This lesson adds seventeen more, with their register and
their plain equivalents, looks at four phrases the norm guides argue about, and practices the
prepositions that formal verbs require. The theme is the monarch butterfly's winter in the
forests of Michoacán and the State of Mexico.

## What a prepositional phrase is

A **[[prepositional phrase]]** (*locución prepositiva*) is a fixed group of words, usually ending in
a preposition, that works as a single preposition: *a la luz de los datos* means "considering the
data," and you can't change its parts (*a la luz de* is fixed, not *en la luz de*). Most are
formal; each has a plainer equivalent that is never wrong. The skill at C2 is choosing the one
that fits the register, without stacking three in one sentence.

## Seventeen formal phrases

| Phrase | Plain equivalent | Example | Translation |
|---|---|---|---|
| *merced a* | *gracias a* | *merced a la vigilancia comunitaria* | thanks to community patrols |
| *a tenor de* | *según, de acuerdo con* | *a tenor de lo dispuesto en el reglamento* | in accordance with the regulations |
| *de cara a* | *pensando en* | *de cara a la próxima temporada* | looking ahead to next season |
| *en pos de* | *en busca de, detrás de* | *en pos de un clima templado* | in pursuit of a mild climate |
| *en virtud de* | *por, debido a* | *en virtud del decreto* | under the decree |
| *a efectos de* | *para* | *a efectos de este informe* | for the purposes of this report |
| *en detrimento de* | *perjudicando a* | *en detrimento del bosque* | to the detriment of the forest |
| *a expensas de* | *a costa de* | *a expensas de los vecinos* | at the neighbors' expense |
| *en lo tocante a* | *en cuanto a* | *en lo tocante a la tala* | as regards logging |
| *a instancias de* | *a petición de* | *a instancias de la comunidad* | at the community's request |
| *al amparo de* | *protegido por* | *al amparo de los oyameles* | sheltered by the firs |
| *a la zaga (de)* | *detrás (de)* | *ir a la zaga de otras regiones* | to lag behind other regions |
| *so pretexto de* | *con la excusa de* | *so pretexto de limpiar el terreno* | on the pretext of clearing the land |
| *en vísperas de* | *justo antes de* | *en vísperas de la migración* | on the eve of the migration |
| *a la luz de* | *considerando* | *a la luz de los nuevos datos* | in light of the new data |
| *a falta de* | *sin* | *a falta de datos fiables* | for lack of reliable data |
| *sin perjuicio de* | *sin afectar* | *sin perjuicio de otras sanciones* | without prejudice to other penalties |

Points to watch:

- *Merced a* introduces a cause that helped; for a harmful cause, *debido a* or *a causa de*.
- *A expensas de* is someone's cost (*creció a expensas de los vecinos*), or who pays (*vive a
  expensas de sus padres*). *En detrimento de* is harm to a thing or a value.
- *A la zaga* works as an adverb: *ir a la zaga*, *quedarse a la zaga de*. *No irle a la zaga a
  alguien* means to be just as good as them.
- *Sin perjuicio de* means "without affecting" another rule or action. It doesn't mean
  "although": *sin perjuicio de que* + subjunctive keeps the same sense (without ruling out that).
- *So* is an old preposition (under) that survives only in *so pretexto de, so pena de* and a few
  more.
- *A efectos de* has the variant *para efectos de*, frequent in Mexico.

![A three-column chart titled Del registro formal al llano. The left column, Jurídico y administrativo, lists en virtud de, a tenor de, sin perjuicio de, a efectos de and a instancias de. The middle column, Informe formal, lists a la luz de, en lo tocante a, de cara a, en detrimento de, a expensas de and a falta de. The right column, Lengua general, lists por, según, sin afectar, para, a petición de, considerando, en cuanto a, pensando en, perjudicando a, a costa de and sin. Arrows run from left to right, and a note at the bottom says the right-hand forms are never wrong.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Phrases the norm guides argue about

- *En base a*. The DPD (2nd edition, provisional, *base*, consulted November 2026) advises
  against it: its prepositions don't fit the image, and it may be a calque of Italian *in base a*.
  It is very frequent, in Mexico too, above all in administrative and legal writing. The DPD
  recommends *sobre la base de* or *a base de*; *con base en*, more frequent in the Americas than
  in Spain, is not faulted on linguistic grounds, though careful style prefers the other two. In
  your formal writing: *sobre la base de los datos*, *con base en los datos*.
- *A nivel de*. Keep it for real levels (*a nivel del mar*, *a nivel nacional* is widely
  accepted). For "as regards," write *en cuanto a* or *en el ámbito de* (check the DPD's
  *nivel*).
- *Bajo el punto de vista*. The usual form is *desde el punto de vista* (from the point of view;
  check the DPD's *punto*).
- *De acuerdo a*. The DPD's 2005 edition, as a university language service summarizes it,
  accepts it and notes that it is the more common form in the Americas; *de acuerdo con* is
  preferred in careful use, and only *con* is used for agreeing with someone (*estoy de acuerdo con
  la bióloga*).

None of the four is starred in this course's questions. They are choices of register, and the
careful form is never wrong.

## Government: the preposition a verb takes

**[[Government]]** (*régimen*) is the preposition, or the construction, that a verb or adjective
requires. C1 15 taught *carecer de, optar por*. Formal reports add these:

- *consistir en*: *El conteo consiste en medir la superficie ocupada.* — The count consists of
  measuring the occupied area. (Not *consistir de*, a pattern modeled on English "consist of.")
- *incidir en*: *La tala incide en la temperatura del bosque.* — Logging affects the forest's
  temperature.
- *redundar en*: *La vigilancia redunda en beneficio de todos.* — Patrols benefit everyone.
- *abogar por*: *Las comunidades abogan por un corredor biológico.* — The communities are
  calling for a wildlife corridor.
- *propender a*: *Las mariposas propenden a agruparse cuando baja la temperatura.* — The
  butterflies tend to cluster when the temperature drops.

*Informar*: in the Americas, *informar que* is the usual construction (*La CONANP informó que…*);
in Spain, *informar de que* is more usual. Both are considered correct (check the DPD's
*informar*). Use *informar que* in Mexican writing and don't mark *de que* wrong.

## The route south

```map
base: world
title: La ruta del este de la mariposa monarca (simplificada)
view: 52, -110 to 15, -70
point: Sur de Canadá | 45.5, -78.0
point: Grandes Llanuras | 37.0, -97.0
point: Texas | 30.5, -98.5
point: Santuarios de Michoacán y el Estado de México | 19.6, -100.3
route: Migración de otoño | 45.5, -78.0; 40.0, -90.0; 37.0, -97.0; 30.5, -98.5; 25.0, -100.5; 19.6, -100.3
caption: Simplified. The eastern population flies south each fall across a broad front, from southern Canada and the eastern United States, and gathers in the oyamel forests of central Mexico; the line shows the general direction, not one path.
```

## Reading: a report on the wintering season

An original report written in the style of a technical summary for a community committee. The
figures are from the CONANP and WWF México announcements cited in it; the committee is invented.

> Informe de la temporada de hibernación 2024–2025
>
> En virtud del acuerdo firmado con los ejidos de la zona, este comité presenta un resumen de la
> temporada. A efectos de este informe, se entiende por colonia un conjunto de árboles ocupados
> por mariposas monarca, cuya extensión se mide en hectáreas de bosque y no en número de
> individuos.
>
> La Reserva de la Biosfera Mariposa Monarca, inscrita en la Lista del Patrimonio Mundial de la
> UNESCO en 2008, protege unas 56 mil hectáreas de bosque en los límites de Michoacán y el Estado
> de México. Al amparo de los oyameles, en bosques que rondan los 3 mil metros de altitud, las
> mariposas pasan el invierno agrupadas en racimos, en pos de un clima frío pero estable que les
> permite ahorrar energía.
>
> Según los resultados que la CONANP y WWF México dieron a conocer en marzo de 2025, las mariposas
> ocuparon esta temporada 1.79 hectáreas, repartidas en ocho colonias: tres en Michoacán y cinco
> en el Estado de México. La cifra casi duplica la de la temporada anterior, cuando se registraron
> 0.9 hectáreas, una de las superficies más bajas desde que comenzó el monitoreo. A la luz de estos
> datos, y sin perjuicio de lo que muestren las próximas temporadas, cabe hablar de una
> recuperación; una sola temporada, sin embargo, no permite hablar de tendencia.
>
> En lo tocante a las amenazas, el comité señala tres. La tala ilegal, que avanza en detrimento
> de la zona de amortiguamiento, a veces so pretexto de sanear el bosque. La pérdida de
> algodoncillo, planta de la que dependen las orugas, en las zonas de reproducción. Y el clima extremo,
> que incide en la supervivencia de las crisálidas y de los adultos.
>
> Merced a la vigilancia comunitaria, los recorridos de este año se ampliaron, aunque la zona sur
> sigue a la zaga en número de guardabosques. A falta de un financiamiento estable, el comité
> propone, de cara a la próxima temporada, que el monitoreo se haga a instancias de las propias
> comunidades y no a expensas de ellas, y aboga por un corredor biológico que una los santuarios.
>
> En vísperas de la llegada de las primeras mariposas, a finales de octubre, se reforzarán los
> recorridos a tenor de lo acordado en la asamblea.

**Summary.** Under an agreement with the local ejidos, the committee summarizes the season, and
defines a colony by the hectares of forest it occupies. The reserve, on UNESCO's World Heritage
List since 2008, protects about 56,000 hectares on the border of Michoacán and the State of
Mexico, where the butterflies cluster in the oyamel forests. CONANP and WWF México reported 1.79
hectares in eight colonies, almost double the previous season's 0.9, but one season isn't a
trend. Three threats: illegal logging, loss of milkweed in the breeding areas, and extreme
weather. The committee asks for monitoring at the communities' own request, not at their expense, and
a corridor between sanctuaries.

**Glosses.** *zona de amortiguamiento* — buffer zone; *sanear el bosque* — to clear diseased trees
(literally, to make the forest healthy); *racimos* — clusters; *recorridos* — patrols;
*guardabosques* — forest rangers; *la asamblea* — the ejido's assembly.

The report follows Mexican usage for numbers: a decimal point (*1.79*), which the RAE's
*Ortografía* (2010) recommends while still accepting the comma, and *56 mil* for thousands. Count
the phrases: the report uses all seventeen, which no real report would do. One or two per
paragraph is a good dose.

## Pronunciation

- *vísperas*: VÍS-pe-ras, stress on the first syllable.
- *crisálida*: cri-SÁ-li-da.
- *oyamel*: o-ya-MEL, stress on the last syllable.
- *algodoncillo*: al-go-don-SI-yo; *ll* sounds like *y*.

## Common mistakes

- *En la luz de los datos*: the phrase is fixed: *a la luz de*.
- Using *merced a* for a harm: *merced a la sequía* sounds ironic. Use *debido a la sequía*.
- *Consistir de*: the verb takes *en*.
- Reading *sin perjuicio de* as "despite": it means "without affecting."
- Stacking phrases (*En virtud de lo cual, a efectos de…, sin perjuicio de…*): one per sentence
  is plenty.
- Marking *en base a* or *de acuerdo a* wrong in someone else's text: they are frequent and, in
  the second case, accepted. Recommend the careful form instead.

## Key points

- A prepositional phrase works as one preposition and can't be changed inside.
- The seventeen phrases are formal; each has a plain equivalent that is never wrong.
- *En base a* is advised against by the DPD; *sobre la base de* and *con base en* are the safe
  choices. *De acuerdo a* is accepted; *de acuerdo con* is preferred.
- Learn verbs with their preposition: *consistir en, incidir en, redundar en, abogar por,
  propender a*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Leer el español antiguo: from the Cantar to the eighteenth century
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05 showed tenses you only read, and lesson 06 a future subjunctive that survives in two
phrases. Go back far enough and those forms were ordinary. This honors lesson is a reader's guide
to **[[Old Spanish]]**: the Castilian of the Middle Ages, written in spellings that look wrong until
you know what they stood for. You'll meet the first texts, the people who copied them, the
letters and abbreviations of manuscripts (**[[paleography]]**), and a method for reading a passage
line by line. C1 90 (an honors lesson) read the Spanish of 1605; this lesson goes further back
and stops before it.

A rule for the whole lesson: every old-style passage here is the writer's own imitation, made up
to show the forms. Nothing is quoted from a real text.

## From Latin to *romance*

For centuries people in the Iberian kingdoms spoke a Latin that had changed so much it was a new
language, but they wrote in Latin. That spoken language was called *romance*, the "Roman" way of
speaking, as opposed to Latin. Writing in *romance* began in glosses and notes, spread to legal
documents, and by the thirteenth century was the language of history and law in Castile.
Scholars use *el castellano antiguo* (Old Spanish) for the language up to about the end of the
fifteenth century; the dividing lines are conventions, not dates when anything changed overnight.

## The *jarchas*

The *jarchas* (kharjas) are short closing verses of a kind of poem, the *moaxaja* (muwashshah),
written in al-Andalus in Arabic or Hebrew. Some close with lines in a Romance language mixed with
Arabic words, put in the mouth of a girl speaking of her love. The scholar Samuel Miklos Stern
drew wide attention to them in 1948. Since then they have been argued about: they are written in
Arabic or Hebrew letters, usually without vowels, so each reading is a reconstruction, and
scholars disagree about how much of each one is Romance and what they show about early lyric
poetry. Read any claim that they are "the first poems in Spanish" as one position in that
debate.

## The *cantar de gesta* and the *Cantar de mio Cid*

A *cantar de gesta* is an epic poem about the deeds (*gestas*) of a hero, made to be recited.
Its performers were *juglares*, professional entertainers who recited, sang and played in squares
and halls. The poems use long lines in two halves, grouped by assonance (the same vowels at the
end of each line), with set formulas that helped both memory and listener.

The *Cantar de mio Cid* is the one Castilian epic that survives almost whole. In outline: Rodrigo
Díaz, a knight who lived in the eleventh century, is sent into exile by his king, wins lands
and wealth fighting his way to Valencia, sees his daughters married to two noblemen who mistreat
them, and wins back his honor before the royal court. The facts about the text are a lesson in
themselves:

- It survives in a single manuscript, now in the Biblioteca Nacional de España, with its first
  page and two others missing; about 3,730 lines remain.
- At its end, a note (the colophon) names a Per Abbat as the one who wrote it, with a date that
  corresponds to 1207. Many scholars think the note was copied from an earlier manuscript, and the
  copy we have is usually dated to the fourteenth century.
- When the poem was composed is still debated: Ramón Menéndez Pidal argued for about 1140, and
  many later scholars place it nearer 1200. Who composed it, one poet or a tradition, is debated
  too.

So "Per Abbat wrote the *Cantar* in 1207" says more than the evidence does. Say instead that the
only manuscript carries a note naming Per Abbat and a date of 1207.

## Alfonso X and Castilian prose

Alfonso X of Castile, called *el Sabio* (1221–1284, king from 1252), gathered teams of scholars and
*copistas* who produced histories (the *Estoria de España*, the *General estoria*), a great legal
code (the *Siete Partidas*), and works of astronomy, many of them in Castilian rather than Latin.
Historians credit his court with giving Castilian prose its first steady written form; the
spellings his scriptorium used are often taken as the reference for Old Spanish.

## Old spellings and what they stood for

Old Spanish wasn't badly spelled. Its *grafías* (written forms) stood for sounds that modern
Spanish has lost.

| Old form | Modern form | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| *fazer, fijo, fablar* | *hacer, hijo, hablar* | Latin *f-* became an aspirated sound, then silent; the spelling *h-* came later |
| *plaça, coraçón* | *plaza, corazón* | *ç* (c with a *cedilla*) was a "ts" sound; *z* was a "dz" sound |
| *passar* / *casa* | *pasar* / *casa* | between vowels, *ss* was a voiceless *s*, single *s* a voiced one (like English *z*) |
| *dixo, xabón* | *dijo, jabón* | *x* was like English "sh"; it later became the *j* sound |
| *cantades, tenedes* | *cantáis, tenéis* | the second-person plural ending before it lost its *d* |
| *anno* or *año* with a tilde | *año* | *nn*, often abbreviated with a tilde over one *n*: the origin of *ñ* |
| *si vinieres* | *si vienes* | the future subjunctive, ordinary in conditions and laws |
| *maguer que* | *aunque* | an old concessive conjunction |
| *asaz* | *muy, bastante* | "very, quite"; today archaic or mock-solemn |

Most of these sound distinctions disappeared between the fifteenth and the seventeenth century,
and the RAE's spelling rules of the eighteenth century removed the *ç* and the *ss* (check the
editions and years). The table's
examples are illustrations of the spellings, not quotations.

Some forms trick a modern reader: *vos* was a polite form of address (closer to today's *usted*
than to *tú*); the imperfect often ends in *-ie* (*tenie* for *tenía*); object pronouns attach
to the verb (*dixol* for *le dijo*); and the future could be split around a pronoun (*dar lo
he*, "I will give it").

## Copyists and the manuscript page

Until printing, every copy was made by hand, and every *copista* left traces. The commonest slip
is the eye-skip: the copyist's eye jumps from one word to the same word further down, and the
lines in between vanish. Others "correct" what they don't understand, or modernize spellings
without meaning to. That's why modern editions of a medieval work differ, and why a *critical
edition* compares every surviving copy.

Paleography (*la paleografía*) is the study of old handwriting: how letters were shaped, how they were joined and
abbreviated, and how to date a hand. A first-time reader of a medieval page meets: no accents;
*u* and *v*, *i* and *j* used for either sound; a long *s* (ſ) inside words; words run together or
split oddly; and abbreviations, above all a line or tilde over a letter for a missing *n* or *m*,
and *q* with a mark for *que*.

![An imitation of a medieval manuscript page, drawn for this lesson. A cream page with a large red capital E at the top left, then eight lines of brown text: n aquel año (with the tilde drawn over the n) mando el rey fazer una puente sobre el rio, ca las aguas eran asaz grandes e los omnes non podien passar. E mando que ningun mercader non pagasse portadgo en la plaça. E dixo: qualquier que este mandado quebrantare, peche cient maravedis. Six numbered circles mark, and a key on the right names: 1 la mayúscula (the red E), 2 la tilde (abreviatura) over the n, 3 la f inicial of fazer, 4 la doble s of passar, 5 la cedilla of plaça, 6 la x of dixo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## How to read an old passage

1. Read it aloud. Many words you don't recognize on the page you'll recognize by ear.
2. Make the regular swaps: *f-* to *h-*, *ç* to *z* or *c*, *ss* to *s*, *x* to *j*, *u/v* and
   *i/j* as needed, *nn* to *ñ*.
3. Find the verb and its ending: *-ades/-edes* is *vosotros* or a polite *vos*; *-ie* is an
   imperfect; *-re* is often a future subjunctive.
4. Watch the little words: *e* (and), *ca* (because), *non* (no), *fasta* (until), *maguer*
   (although).
5. Check meaning, not just form: a familiar-looking word may have changed sense.
6. Write your modern version, then compare it with a good edition's notes.

### Example 1: a chronicle in imitation

The writer's own imitation of thirteenth-century chronicle prose, not a real passage. As in
modern editions, the quotation marks and colon are added; the old spellings are kept.

> En aquel anno mando el rey fazer una puente sobre el rio, ca las aguas eran asaz grandes e los
> omnes non podien passar. E mando que ningun mercader non pagasse portadgo en la plaça fasta que
> la obra fuesse acabada. E dixo: «Qualquier que este mandado quebrantare, peche cient
> maravedis».

Line by line:

- *En aquel anno mando el rey fazer una puente* — *Aquel año el rey mandó hacer un puente*: *nn*
  is *ñ*, *f-* is *h-*, no written accents, and *puente* was often feminine.
- *ca las aguas eran asaz grandes e los omnes non podien passar* — *porque las aguas estaban muy
  crecidas y la gente no podía pasar*: *ca* is "because," *asaz* "very," *omnes* "men, people,"
  *-ie* an imperfect, *ss* a voiceless *s*.
- *E mando que ningun mercader non pagasse portadgo en la plaça* — *Y mandó que ningún mercader
  pagara peaje en la plaza*: *pagasse* is the *-se* imperfect subjunctive with *ss*; *portadgo* (the
  later *portazgo*) was a toll; *ningún… non* is a double negative, normal then.
- *fasta que la obra fuesse acabada* — *hasta que la obra estuviera terminada*.
- *Qualquier que este mandado quebrantare, peche cient maravedis* — *Quien desobedezca esta
  orden, que pague cien maravedís*: *quebrantare* is a future subjunctive, *peche* a subjunctive
  of *pechar* (to pay a fine), and the *maravedí* a coin.

**Modern English.** That year the king had a bridge built over the river, because the waters were
very high and people couldn't cross. And he ordered that no merchant should pay toll in the square
until the work was finished. And he said: "Whoever breaks this order shall pay a hundred
maravedís."

### Example 2: a minstrel's opening in imitation

The writer's own imitation of epic verse, not a real passage. Each line ends on the stressed
vowel *a*: that is the assonance.

> Oid, sennores, lo que vos quiero contar:
>
> de un ferrero pobre que morava cerca del mar.
>
> Fazie buenas espadas, mas non las podie levar;
>
> dixo a su muger: «Que faremos, por caridad?»
>
> Respuso la duenna, que era de buen pensar:
>
> «Si vos a la feria fueredes, alguno las querra comprar».

Line by line:

- *Oid, sennores* — *Oíd, señores*: the opening call of a *juglar* to the audience; *nn* is *ñ*.
- *de un ferrero pobre que morava* — *de un herrero pobre que vivía*: *f-* for *h-*; *morar* (to
  dwell) is now literary.
- *Fazie buenas espadas, mas non las podie levar* — *Hacía buenas espadas, pero no podía
  llevarlas*: two *-ie* imperfects; *levar* is the old *llevar*; *mas* is "but."
- *dixo a su muger* — *le dijo a su mujer*: *x* and *g* where modern Spanish has *j*.
- *Respuso la duenna, que era de buen pensar* — *Le respondió la señora, que era sensata*: *duenna*
  (modern *dueña*) meant a lady.
- *Si vos a la feria fueredes* — *Si vas a la feria*: a future subjunctive with the old *-edes*
  ending, which went with *vos* for one person or several; here the wife addresses her husband
  with a respectful *vos*.

**Modern English.** Hear, my lords, what I want to tell you: of a poor blacksmith who lived near
the sea. He made good swords, but couldn't take them to market; he said to his wife, "What shall
we do, for pity's sake?" The lady, who was wise, replied: "If you go to the fair, someone will
want to buy them."

## Common mistakes

- Reading old *x* as "ks": in *dixo* it was a "sh" sound on its way to *j*.
- Treating *vos* as informal: in medieval texts it is respectful or plural.
- Taking every *-re* for a misprint: *quebrantare, fueredes* are future subjunctives.
- Calling old spelling "wrong": it recorded sounds that modern Spanish no longer has.
- Stating the date 1207 as the date of the *Cantar*: it is the date in the manuscript's note.
- Reading a modernized edition as if it were the manuscript: editors change spelling and
  punctuation, and they should tell you how.

## Key points

- Old Spanish spellings stood for real sounds: *f-*, *ç*, *ss*, *x* tell you how the language
  sounded.
- The *Cantar de mio Cid* survives in one manuscript with a note naming Per Abbat and the date
  1207; its date of composition is debated.
- The *jarchas* are Romance closing verses in Arabic or Hebrew poems, read through
  reconstruction and debate.
- Alfonso X's court gave Castilian prose a steady written form.
- Read aloud, make the regular swaps, find the verb, watch the little words, and check meanings.

lessons.title: Honors: La mayoría votó o votaron: hard cases of agreement
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 07 built long sentences; the longer the sentence, the easier it is to lose track of what
agrees with what. This honors lesson covers the cases where even careful writers hesitate:
collective nouns, *la mayoría de* + a plural, *ser* with a plural predicate, *uno de los que*,
compound subjects, nouns with one gender for both sexes or two genders for one thing, feminine job
titles, and *se venden casas*. In several of them two answers are correct, and the skill is
knowing which one a careful reader expects. (*Hubo / hubieron*, C1 03, is not repeated here: the
standard is *hubo problemas*.)

## The basic rule, and the head

**[[Agreement]]** (*concordancia*) is the matching of forms: the verb agrees with its subject in
person and number, and articles and adjectives agree with their noun in gender and number. In a
long subject, the verb agrees with its *núcleo*, the head noun, not with the noun nearest the verb:

- *El informe de los peritos sobre las grietas llegó ayer.* — The experts' report on the cracks
  arrived yesterday. (The head is *informe*; *peritos* and *grietas* are inside phrases.)

Most agreement errors in long sentences are a verb agreeing with the wrong noun. Find the head
first.

## Collective nouns

A **[[collective noun]]** (*un sustantivo colectivo*) is singular in form and names a group: *la gente, el público, la familia,
el comité, el equipo*. Its verb is singular: *La gente llegó tarde* (People arrived late), *El
comité decidió aplazar la votación* (The committee decided to postpone the vote).

Speakers often switch to the plural when the group is thought of as its members, especially in a
following clause: *La gente llegó tarde y se quejaron del calor*. This agreement by meaning, not
form, is called **[[syllepsis]]** (*la silepsis*). The DPD's 2005 edition (*concordancia*, §4.7)
accepts the plural when it belongs to a later clause with an unstated subject, and rejects it when
only an aside separates subject and verb: *La gente, cansada de esperar, se fue* (not *se
fueron*). In careful writing, keep collectives singular within their clause.

## *La mayoría de* + plural, and similar

With a quantity word followed by *de* and a plural noun (*la mayoría de, la mitad de, un grupo
de, una veintena de, el 40 % de*), the verb can agree with either noun:

- *La mayoría de los vecinos votó a favor.* / *La mayoría de los vecinos votaron a favor.* — Most
  of the residents voted in favor.

The DPD (2005, §4.8) accepts both and notes that the plural is more frequent. It adds a limit worth
learning: when the verb has a predicate adjective or noun, only the plural is normal: *La
mayoría de los vecinos están molestos* (Most of the residents are annoyed), not *está molesta*.
Without a determiner, *infinidad de, cantidad de, multitud de* take the plural: *Acudieron
infinidad de personas.*

Choose one agreement and keep it through the paragraph.

## *Ser* with a plural predicate

When the subject of *ser* is a neuter word (*lo que, esto, eso, todo*) and the predicate is a
plural noun, the verb agrees with the predicate, *el atributo*:

- *Lo que necesito son vacaciones.* — What I need is a vacation.
- *Todo eso son excusas.* — All that is excuses.

With a noun subject, both orders and both agreements occur (*El problema son las lluvias* is
common), but the plural is the usual choice when the plural noun is the information.

## *Uno de los que*

- *Es uno de los que más saben.* / *Es uno de los que más sabe.* — He's one of those who know
  the most.

The DPD (2005, §4.11) calls the plural the more grammatical, since the subject of *saben* is *los
que*, and accepts the singular too. Use the plural in writing; don't mark the singular wrong.

## Compound subjects

A *sujeto compuesto* joins two or more nouns. With *y*, the verb is plural (*El director y la
secretaria firmaron*), unless the two form one idea or one person (*La compra y venta de terrenos
está regulada*: buying-and-selling as one activity). With *o*, the verb is singular if only one
can be true (*Juan o Pedro será el presidente*) and either number if the choice excludes nothing
(*Ana o Luisa pueden ayudarte*, also *puede*). With *tanto… como*, plural (*Tanto el alcalde como
la gobernadora asistieron*).

## Gender: one form for both, two genders for one

An **[[epicene noun]]** (*un epiceno*) has one grammatical gender for beings of either sex: *la persona, la víctima,
el personaje, la criatura*, and animal names such as *la jirafa* (*la jirafa macho*). Agreement
follows the noun, not the person: *La víctima, un hombre de 40 años, fue trasladada al hospital*.

A few nouns are used with either gender for the same thing; grammars call them *sustantivos
ambiguos*. *El mar* is the general form, and *la mar* is typical of sailors, poetry and set
phrases (*alta mar, hacerse a la mar*); *el azúcar* is usual, often with a feminine adjective
(*el azúcar morena*). The DPD describes both (check its entries *mar* and *azúcar*). *El bebé*
is often given as an epicene, and it is one in Spain (*un bebé* for a girl), but in much of the
Americas it is used with both genders (*el bebé, la bebé*), as the *Nueva gramática* records.

Job titles: the DLE records feminine forms such as *la jueza, la presidenta, la médica, la
ministra* (as of its online edition; check). *La juez* and *la presidente* are also heard. This is
*la feminización* of titles: the feminine *marca de género* (*-a*) replaces a masculine *-o*
(*médico, médica*) or is added after a consonant (*juez, jueza*). Use the form the person, the institution or the publication uses;
in an open choice, the forms the DLE records are safe.

## *Se venden casas*

In the passive with *se*, the noun is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: *Se
venden casas* (Houses for sale), *Se rentan departamentos*. *Se vende casas* is frequent on signs
and in speech in many countries, but norm guides treat it as nonstandard; don't use it in writing.

With people introduced by *a*, the construction is impersonal, and the verb stays singular: *Se
busca a los responsables* (They are looking for those responsible). Here the singular is the
standard form.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing verb agreement
  accDescr: A decision chart. First, find the head of the subject. Is it a collective noun such as gente or comité? If yes, use the singular in its own clause. If no, is it a quantity word with de and a plural, such as la mayoría de los vecinos? If yes, does the verb have a predicate adjective or noun? If yes, plural. If no, singular or plural, keep one choice. If the head is not a quantity word, is the subject neuter, lo que or esto, with ser and a plural predicate? If yes, the verb agrees with the plural predicate. If no, is it passive se with a noun? If yes, agree with the noun, se venden casas. If no, agree with the head.
  A["Find the head of the subject"] --> B{"A collective noun?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Singular in its own clause"]
  B -- no --> D{"Quantity word + de + plural?"}
  D -- yes --> E{"Predicate adjective or noun?"}
  E -- yes --> F["Plural"]
  E -- no --> G["Singular or plural: keep one"]
  D -- no --> H{"Neuter subject + ser + plural noun?"}
  H -- yes --> I["Agree with the predicate"]
  H -- no --> J{"Passive se + noun?"}
  J -- yes --> K["Agree with the noun: se venden casas"]
  J -- no --> L["Agree with the head"]
```

### Example 1: four news sentences

Choose the agreement a careful copy editor would choose, and say why.

1. *La mayoría de los encuestados ___ (considerar) que el servicio empeoró.* Both *considera* and
   *consideran* are correct; the plural is more frequent. Keep it through the article.
2. *La mayoría de los encuestados ___ (estar) insatisfechos.* Only *están*: the verb has a
   predicate adjective, and the adjective is plural.
3. *El público, que llenaba el auditorio, ___ (aplaudir) de pie.* *Aplaudió*: a collective with
   only an aside before its verb stays singular.
4. *Lo que preocupa a los vecinos ___ (ser) las grietas.* *Son*: a neuter subject with a plural
   predicate.

**Translation.** (1) Most of those surveyed think the service got worse. (2) Most of those
surveyed are dissatisfied. (3) The audience, which filled the auditorium, gave a standing ovation.
(4) What worries the residents is the cracks.

### Example 2: correcting a report

A draft from a neighborhood committee, with five *discordancias* (agreement mismatches):

> La revisión de las viviendas mostraron daños graves. La mayoría de las familias está
> preocupada, y la gente, después de la asamblea, firmaron una carta. Se reparará los muros del
> lado norte. La víctima del derrumbe, un señor de 70 años, fue atendido en el lugar.

Corrected:

> La revisión de las viviendas mostró daños graves. La mayoría de las familias están
> preocupadas, y la gente, después de la asamblea, firmó una carta. Se repararán los muros del
> lado norte. La víctima del derrumbe, un señor de 70 años, fue atendida en el lugar.

The reasons: *revisión* is the head (singular); *la mayoría de las familias* with a predicate
adjective takes the plural; *la gente* with only an aside before the verb stays singular; passive
*se* agrees with *los muros*; *la víctima* is an epicene, and the participle agrees with the noun.

**Translation.** The inspection of the homes showed serious damage. Most of the families are worried, and after
the meeting the people signed a letter. The walls on the north side will be repaired. The victim
of the collapse, a man of 70, was treated at the scene.

## Common mistakes

- Making the verb agree with the nearest noun: *El informe de los peritos llegaron*. Find the head.
- *La mayoría de los asistentes está contenta*: with a predicate adjective, use the plural.
- *La gente, al ver el humo, salieron*: an aside isn't a new clause; keep *salió*.
- *Se vende departamentos* in a written ad: *se venden*.
- *Se buscan a los culpables*: with *a* + people, the verb is singular (*se busca*).
- Making an epicene agree with the person: *la víctima… fue trasladado*. Agree with *víctima*.
- Marking *la mayoría de los socios votaron* or *uno de los que sabe* wrong: both are accepted.

## Key points

- Find the head of the subject; the verb agrees with it.
- Collective nouns take a singular verb in their own clause; a plural by meaning (syllepsis) is
  accepted only in a later clause.
- *La mayoría de* + plural takes either number, but only the plural with a predicate adjective or
  noun.
- A neuter subject with *ser* and a plural predicate takes the plural: *Lo que necesito son
  vacaciones*.
- Epicene nouns keep their gender whatever the person's sex; a few nouns take either gender.
- *Se venden casas* is the standard; *se busca a los responsables* stays singular.
