lessons.title: El discurso del premio: figures of speech beyond C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 gave you the grammar of formal prose. This module turns to style: how a writer
chooses and arranges words for effect. It starts with the oldest toolbox there is, the
**[[figures of speech]]** (*las figuras retóricas*): patterns of meaning, order and sound that make
words stick.

C1 12h1 (an honors lesson) named four of them; the table below re-teaches them. This lesson adds
about a dozen more, says what each does and when it becomes too much, and takes apart an original
acceptance speech so that you can both name a figure and write one on purpose.

## The four you may know

| Figure | Spanish | What it does | Original example |
|---|---|---|---|
| hyperbole | *la hipérbole* | exaggerates on purpose | *Te esperé una eternidad.* — I waited an eternity for you. |
| anaphora | *la anáfora* | repeats the start of phrases | *Por los que leen, por los que escriben, por los que esperan.* — For those who read, those who write, those who wait. |
| antithesis | *la antítesis* | sets opposites side by side | *Llegamos con dudas y nos vamos con planes.* — We came with doubts and leave with plans. |
| rhetorical question | *la pregunta retórica* | asks without wanting an answer | *¿Quién no ha dudado alguna vez?* — Who hasn't doubted at some point? |

**[[Hyperbole]]**, **[[anaphora]]**, **[[antithesis]]** and the **[[rhetorical question]]** are the speech
figures par excellence: the ear can follow them without rereading.

## Tropes: when a word changes its meaning

A **[[trope]]** (*el tropo*) uses a word in a sense that isn't its own. Metaphor (*la metáfora*) is
the famous one, built on resemblance: *Esta escuela fue nuestro puerto* (This school was our
harbor). Two other tropes work by closeness instead.

- **[[Metonymy]]** (*la metonimia*) names a thing by something closely linked to it: the author for
  the work, the place for the institution, the container for its contents. *Leí a Rulfo en la
  prepa* (I read Rulfo in high school: his books). *Palacio Nacional anunció un nuevo plan*
  (The National Palace announced a new plan: the building for the presidency). *Se tomó dos
  tazas* (She drank two cups: what was in them).
- **[[Synecdoche]]** (*la sinécdoque*) is the part for the whole, or the whole for the part. *Hay seis
  bocas que alimentar* (There are six mouths to feed: six people). *México ganó el partido*
  (Mexico won the game: the national team, a part of the country).

Many manuals treat synecdoche as a kind of metonymy. A quick test: if you can say "X is a part of
Y", it's synecdoche; if the link is place, author or container, metonymy.

## Contradictions that make sense

- **[[Oxymoron]]** (*el oxímoron*) joins two words whose meanings clash, inside one phrase: *una
  calma impaciente* (an impatient calm), *un silencio que grita* (a silence that shouts).
- **[[Paradox]]** (*la paradoja*) is a whole statement that seems to contradict itself but hides a
  truth: *Para encontrar tu voz, primero hay que callar mucho tiempo* (To find your voice, you
  first have to keep quiet for a long time).
- Antithesis, by contrast, opposes two ideas without claiming they are the same thing.

## Figures of order

- **[[Chiasmus]]** (*el quiasmo*) repeats two elements in reverse order, A B / B A: *No cambié mi
  pueblo; mi pueblo me cambió a mí* (I didn't change my town; my town changed me). It's the
  figure of the memorable closing line.
- **[[Hyperbaton]]** (*el hipérbaton*) breaks the expected word order. Spanish word order is free
  (module 2 used it constantly), so ordinary fronting is not hyperbaton; the term is for an
  order that a reader feels as marked, usually in verse or solemn prose: *De la ciudad las luces se
  apagaban* (The lights of the city were going out: *de la ciudad* is pulled away from its
  noun, *las luces*).
- **[[Gradation]]** (*la gradación*; C1 12h1's "enumeration and climax") arranges a series in rising
  (or falling) steps: *Primero fue
  una libreta; luego, un cuento; después, una novela; al final, una vida* (First it was a
  notebook; then a story; then a novel; in the end, a life).

## Figures of linking

- **[[Polysyndeton]]** (*el polisíndeton*) repeats the conjunction: *Escribí en cocinas y en
  camiones y en salas de espera y en hoteles baratos* (I wrote in kitchens and on buses and in
  waiting rooms and in cheap hotels). The effect is slow and cumulative.
- **[[Asyndeton]]** (*el asíndeton*) removes the conjunctions: *Escribí cansada, enojada, enferma,
  feliz* (I wrote tired, angry, sick, happy). The effect is speed and urgency.
- **[[Zeugma]]** (*el zeugma*) lets one word serve several phrases and be understood in the rest.
  The plain kind leaves out a repeated verb: *Él pidió café; ella, té* (He ordered coffee; she,
  tea). The witty kind gives the shared verb two senses: *Mi abuela contaba historias; mi madre,
  el dinero* (*contar* is "tell" in the first clause and "count" in the second), or *Aquel año
  perdí el miedo y el autobús de las seis* (That year I lost my fear and the six o'clock bus).
  English calls the witty kind zeugma or syllepsis.

## Sound and voice

- **[[Alliteration]]** (*la aliteración*) repeats a sound in nearby words, usually a consonant:
  *la lluvia lenta y limpia del lunes* (Monday's slow, clean rain). In prose, a little goes a
  long way.
- **[[Prosopopoeia]]** (*la prosopopeya*), or personification, gives human traits or a voice to
  things and ideas: *Las palabras me esperaban en la mesa de la cocina* (The words were waiting
  for me on the kitchen table).
- The **[[rhetorical apostrophe]]** (*el apóstrofe*) turns away from the audience to address
  someone absent or dead, or something that can't answer: *Y a ti, abuela, que no sabías leer…*
  (And to you, grandmother, who couldn't read…). Don't confuse it with *el apóstrofo*, the
  apostrophe mark (').

## The parts of a formal speech

C1 12h1 (an honors lesson) divided a speech into four classical parts; at C2 you need the two
ends by name. The opening, *el exordio*, wins goodwill, often with modesty or a small story. The
closing, *la peroración*, sums up and moves; the strongest figure usually goes there.

Praise has its own words. *El elogio* is praise of any kind; *el panegírico* is praise with no
reservations, often used ironically. *Una semblanza* is a short biographical sketch, read before
a prize is handed over. A *laudatorio* tone is full of praise. *Una alocución* is a short formal
address by an authority: *el rector pronunció una alocución de bienvenida* (the university
president gave a welcoming address).

When is it too much? One strong figure per paragraph carries weight; a figure in every sentence
reads as parody, a style lesson 10 calls *ampuloso* (bombastic).

## Prizes and their ceremonies

The best-known prize for literature in Spanish is the Premio Cervantes, awarded each year by
Spain's Ministry of Culture for a whole body of work. It's presented on April 23, the
anniversary of Cervantes's death as usually given, in the *paraninfo* (great hall) of the
Universidad de Alcalá, in Cervantes's birthplace, by the King of Spain. Seven Mexican
writers have received it: Octavio Paz (1981), Carlos Fuentes (1987), Sergio Pitol (2005), José
Emilio Pacheco (2009), Elena Poniatowska (2013), Fernando del Paso (2015) and Gonzalo Celorio
(2025). Their *discursos de aceptación* are published: read one and
name the figures yourself.

![A university great hall during a prize ceremony. On a raised platform at the front stands the prizewinner at a lectern, speaking. Beside her, at a long table on the same platform, sit three members of the jury. Below the platform, rows of seated people in the audience face her. A banner on the back wall reads Paraninfo. Labels name la galardonada, el atril, el jurado, el estrado and el público.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture: *el galardonado* or *la galardonada* (the prizewinner; *el laureado* is more
formal) speaks from *el atril* (the lectern) on *el estrado* (the raised platform), beside *el
jurado* (the jury), facing *el público*.

## The speech

> *Discurso de aceptación de Rosaura Ibarra, Premio Iberoamericano de Narrativa Tomás Ojeda
> (texto original; la autora y el premio son ficticios)*
>
> Señora rectora, miembros del jurado, queridos colegas, amigas y amigos:
>
> Me piden que hable, y yo, que llevo cuarenta años escribiendo precisamente para no tener que
> hablar, acepto el encargo con el miedo de quien sube a un escenario sin libreto. Perdonen,
> pues, si leo.
>
> Vengo de un pueblo de la sierra donde no había biblioteca, pero había abuelas. En mi casa había
> seis bocas que alimentar y un solo radio, que nos traía el mundo hasta que mi madre lo apagaba
> a las nueve. Leí a Rulfo a los catorce años, en una edición prestada que, lo confieso ante
> ustedes, todavía no he devuelto.
>
> De aquel pueblo aprendí dos cosas. La primera, que se puede esperar con una calma impaciente:
> esperar el camión, la lluvia, la carta que no llega. La segunda, que para encontrar tu voz
> primero hay que callar mucho tiempo. Mi abuela contaba historias; mi madre, el dinero. Las dos
> me enseñaron a medir las palabras.
>
> Aquel año en que me fui a la ciudad perdí el miedo y el autobús de las seis, y gané, a cambio,
> una costumbre: escribir. Escribí en cocinas y en camiones y en salas de espera y en hoteles
> baratos. Escribí cansada, enojada, enferma, feliz. Primero fue una libreta; luego, un cuento;
> después, una novela; al final, una vida.
>
> Las palabras me esperaban cada noche en la mesa de la cocina, pacientes, como perros fieles. Y
> de la sierra la lluvia lenta y limpia me enseñó, más que ningún maestro, el ritmo de mis
> frases.
>
> ¿Para qué sirve un premio? ¿Para que escribamos mejor? ¿Para que nos lean más? No lo sé.
> Sé, en cambio, a quién pertenece este. Es de las abuelas que contaron sin saber escribir; es de
> las maestras rurales que prestaban libros sin pedirlos de vuelta; es de los lectores que me
> siguieron cuando nadie sabía mi nombre. La literatura no cambió a mi pueblo; mi pueblo cambió
> mi literatura.
>
> Y a ti, abuela Chayo, que no sabías leer y me enseñaste a contar: este premio, que hoy recibo
> en un paraninfo que nunca imaginaste, también es tuyo.
>
> Muchas gracias.

Summary: (1–2) The author greets the audience: she has written for forty years so as not to have
to speak, so she will read. (3) She grew up in a mountain town with no library, six people to feed
and one radio, and read Rulfo in a borrowed copy she never returned. (4) The town taught her to wait
and to keep quiet; her storytelling grandmother and money-counting mother taught her to weigh words. (5) In the city she
wrote everywhere, in every mood, from a notebook to a life's work. (6) Words waited for her; the
rain taught her rhythm. (7) This prize belongs to grandmothers, rural teachers and readers. (8) She
dedicates it to her grandmother.

(*el encargo* — the task; *el libreto* — the script; *a cambio* — in return; *prestar* — to lend;
*pedirlos de vuelta* — to ask for them back; *el radio* — the radio set, masculine in Mexico; Chayo
is a Mexican nickname for Rosario.)

## Worked example: the speech figure by figure

| Part | Passage | Figure | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| exordio (1–2) | *escribiendo para no tener que hablar* | paradox, gentle irony | modesty: she wins goodwill |
| narración (3–6) | *seis bocas que alimentar* | synecdoche | the family seen as hunger |
| | *Leí a Rulfo* | metonymy | the author for his books |
| (4) | *una calma impaciente* | oxymoron | the tension of waiting |
| | *para encontrar tu voz… callar* | paradox | the lesson of the town |
| | *mi abuela contaba historias; mi madre, el dinero* | zeugma (and wordplay on *contar*) | two women, one verb |
| (5) | *perdí el miedo y el autobús* | zeugma | humor before the turn |
| | *y en camiones y en salas… y en hoteles* | polysyndeton | years that never ended |
| | *cansada, enojada, enferma, feliz* | asyndeton | speed; every mood |
| | *una libreta… un cuento… una novela… una vida* | gradation | a career in one line |
| (6) | *las palabras me esperaban* | prosopopoeia (with a simile) | words as companions |
| | *de la sierra la lluvia lenta y limpia* | hyperbaton, alliteration | the rain's sound and rhythm |
| peroración (7–8) | *¿Para qué sirve un premio?* | rhetorical questions | she refuses easy answers |
| | *es de las abuelas…; es de las maestras…; es de los lectores…* | anaphora | the thanks as a list that grows |
| | *no cambió a mi pueblo; mi pueblo cambió…* | chiasmus, antithesis | the memorable line |
| | *Y a ti, abuela Chayo* | rhetorical apostrophe | the emotional close |

Notice the order: humor and small figures first, the heavy ones (anaphora, chiasmus,
apostrophe) saved for the *peroración*. After the crowded fifth paragraph comes a short, quiet one:
a rest before the close.

## Worked example: adding a figure on purpose

A flat sentence: *Agradezco al jurado y a mi editorial.* (I thank the jury and my publisher.)

- With anaphora: *Gracias al jurado, que leyó con paciencia; gracias a mi editorial, que esperó
  sin prisa.* (Thanks to the jury, who read patiently; thanks to my publisher, who waited without
  hurrying me.)
- With chiasmus: *Este jurado premió mi libro; ojalá mi libro no defraude a este jurado.* (This
  jury rewarded my book; I hope my book doesn't let this jury down.)

Anaphora suits thanks in the middle of a speech; chiasmus, a closing line.

## Pronunciation

- *Hipérbaton*: four syllables, *i-PÉR-ba-ton*; the *h* is silent.
- *Oxímoron*: four syllables, *ok-SÍ-mo-ron*; the *x* is *ks*.
- *Polisíndeton*: five syllables, *po-li-SÍN-de-ton*; *asíndeton*: four, *a-SÍN-de-ton*.
- *Sinécdoque*: four syllables, *si-NÉK-do-ke*.
- *Prosopopeya*: five syllables, *pro-so-po-PE-ya*.
- *Quiasmo*: two syllables, *KIAS-mo*; *peroración*: four, *pe-ro-ra-SIÓN*.

## Common mistakes

- *El apóstrofo* for the figure: that's the punctuation mark. The figure is *el apóstrofe*.
- Calling any repetition anaphora: it must be at the start of successive phrases. A word
  repeated at the end is something else (epistrophe), and plain repetition is just repetition.
- Hyperbaton for normal Spanish order: *Ayer llegó mi hermana* is ordinary, not a figure.
- Mixing up oxymoron and paradox: two clashing words in one phrase vs a whole statement.

## Key points

- Tropes change a word's meaning: metaphor (resemblance), metonymy (closeness), synecdoche (part
  and whole).
- Contradiction: oxymoron (one phrase), paradox (a statement). Order: chiasmus, hyperbaton,
  gradation. Linking: polysyndeton (slow), asyndeton (fast), zeugma (one word, several phrases).
  Sound and voice: alliteration, prosopopoeia, apostrophe.
- A speech opens with an *exordio* and closes with a *peroración*; the heaviest figures belong at
  the close.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Una prosa depurada: the critical review and the vocabulary of style
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 gave you the figures a writer uses; this lesson gives you the words to judge how well
they're used. A review (B1's *la reseña*) at C2 does more than say "I liked it": it places the
work, describes what it attempts, weighs how well it succeeds with evidence, and gives a verdict a
reader can trust. C2 programs list reviews and critical assessments among the texts a C2 user writes, and
Mexico's cultural pages are full of them: the weekly supplements of national dailies (*La Jornada Semanal*, for one) and
monthly magazines such as *Letras Libres* and *Nexos*.

You'll learn the evaluative adjectives with their exact weight, how adjective position changes
meaning, how to soften a criticism without losing it, and the method of the
**[[textual commentary]]**. Then you'll read three original reviews and write your own.

## The review as a genre

![A review's structure as six stacked boxes joined by arrows. 1, Ficha: title, author, publisher or venue, year. 2, Presentación: what the work is and its context. 3, Descripción: what it attempts, without spoilers. 4, Valoración: strengths and weaknesses, each with evidence. 5, Comparación: with earlier work or similar works. 6, Veredicto: for whom, and why. Arrows lead from each box to the next. A side bar marks boxes 1 to 3 as describing and boxes 4 to 6 as judging.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A review moves from describing to judging, ending in *el veredicto* (the verdict, a lesson 05
word). The first half is information; the second is argument, and every judgment needs a piece
of evidence: a scene, a line of dialogue described in your own words, a choice in the staging. Without evidence, *magistral* is just a loud word.

The register is neutral to formal, with room for one striking image. *El reseñista* (the
reviewer) usually writes in the third person (*la novela propone…*), may use the first person
for the verdict (*no conozco otro libro que…*), and never retells the ending.

## Evaluative words and their weight

![A chart titled Pesar las palabras de una reseña. First, a quality scale shaded from red to green with an arrow from fracaso to maestría: soporífero and anodino at the failure end, then fallido, then desigual and con altibajos in the middle, then logrado and, at the mastery end, magistral. Second, a style panel in two boxes: contención (elogio) with sobrio, pulcro and depurado; exceso (crítica) with recargado, efectista, ampuloso and pretencioso. Two more boxes: esfuerzos e intenciones with encomiable and loable; material gastado with manido, trillado and el lugar común.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two scales are at work. One measures quality, from *fallido* (failed) to *logrado* (well
executed) and *magistral* (masterly); *desigual* (uneven) and *con altibajos* (with ups and downs)
are the honest middle. The other measures ornament: *sobrio* (restrained), *pulcro*
(immaculate) and *depurado* (polished, refined) praise economy; *recargado* (overdone),
*ampuloso* (bombastic), *efectista* (flashy, going for effect) and *pretencioso* criticize excess.
A work can be *sobrio* and *fallido*, or *recargado* and still *logrado*: keep the scales apart.

The fine distinctions that matter:

- *Encomiable* and *loable* (worthy of praise) usually praise an effort or intention, so they often come before a *pero*:
  *La intención es loable; el resultado, menos* (The intention is laudable; the result, less so).
  *Logrado* praises the result itself.
- *Manido* (hackneyed) and *trillado* (trite) both describe worn-out material. *Manido* suits an
  image or phrase handled too often (*una metáfora manida*); *trillado* suits a path or plot
  everyone has walked (*un argumento trillado*). *El lugar común* (a platitude, stock idea) is
  the noun, close to *el tópico* (stock idea) and *el cliché*, both B2 honors words.
- *Anodino* (bland) has no flavor; *soporífero* (soporific) puts you to sleep. The second is
  stronger and more personal.
- *Efectista* (flashy) is for effects with nothing behind them; B2's *ostentoso* (showy) is for
  a display of wealth or luxury.
- *La verosimilitud* (plausibility) is whether a story is believable on its own terms; a fantasy
  novel can be *verosímil* (believable) and a realist one *inverosímil* (implausible).

The nouns of style go with them: *la sobriedad* (restraint), the B2 honors word *la prosa*
(prose), the C1 honors word *la cadencia* (cadence), and A2's *la factura* in a new sense: not an
invoice but the craftsmanship of a work, *una novela de factura impecable* (a novel of flawless
craftsmanship).

## Adjective position and the epithet

Most Spanish adjectives follow the noun and distinguish it from others: *la casa blanca* (the
white house, not the blue one). An adjective before the noun often states a quality the noun
already has, for emphasis or tone: *la blanca nieve* (the white snow). That adjective is an
**[[epithet]]** (*el epíteto*), a mark of literary or solemn style. One epithet adds color; three in a
sentence make prose *recargada*.

A few adjectives change their meaning with position. A1 08 showed *una gran ciudad* (a great
city) beside *una ciudad grande* (a big city); here are the others a reviewer needs:

| Before the noun | After the noun |
|---|---|
| *un pobre hombre* — a poor (pitiable) man | *un hombre pobre* — a poor (penniless) man |
| *cierto rumor* — a certain rumor | *un rumor cierto* — a true rumor |
| *un simple comentario* — a mere comment | *un comentario simple* — a simple (plain) comment |
| *un viejo amigo* — an old (long-standing) friend | *un amigo viejo* — an elderly friend |
| *un nuevo libro* — a new (another) book | *un libro nuevo* — a (brand-)new book |
| *pura casualidad* — sheer chance | *agua pura* — pure water |
| *el mero hecho* — the mere fact | (rare after the noun) |

In colloquial Mexican Spanish *mero* has other uses as well (*el mero día*, the very day): keep
them out of a review.

## Criticizing with nuance

C1 04 taught softened criticism and C1 09 concession; reviews use both constantly, because a
judgment that admits strengths is more credible.

- Concede, then judge: *Si bien la trama es previsible, los diálogos están muy logrados* (Although
  the plot is predictable, the dialogues are very well done). *Con todo, la novela se sostiene*
  (Even so, the novel holds up).
- Mitigate: *Se echa de menos una segunda mitad más ágil* (One misses a brisker second half). *Se
  le podría reprochar cierta prisa en el desenlace* (One could fault it for a certain haste in the
  ending). *No es una obra fallida, pero sí desigual* (It's not a failed work, but it is uneven).

Avoid false precision: *el 80 % del libro es excelente* sounds measured but isn't evidence.

## Stylistics and the textual commentary

**[[Stylistics]]** (*la estilística*) studies how form creates meaning: why this word, this order,
this rhythm. Its classic exercise is the **[[textual commentary]]** (*el comentario de texto*),
standard in schools and universities, especially in Spain. It has four steps:

1. Theme: what the text is about, in one sentence.
2. Structure: its parts and how they connect.
3. Form: register, syntax, figures (lesson 09) and vocabulary.
4. Assessment: what the form does for the content, and how well.

A review is a commentary for the general public: less technical, but built on the same
observation.

## Three reviews

> *Tres reseñas (textos originales; las obras son ficticias)*
>
> *1. Los años del granizo, de Julia Arredondo (novela).* Arredondo vuelve al pueblo minero de
> su primer libro, pero esta vez lo cuenta desde la mirada de una niña de nueve años que no
> entiende lo que ve: la huelga, el silencio de su padre, las visitas nocturnas de unos hombres
> armados. La apuesta es arriesgada y está muy lograda. La prosa, sobria y depurada, deja que el
> lector complete lo que la niña calla, y los pocos adjetivos que hay pesan. Si bien el último
> capítulo se apresura y resuelve en diez páginas lo que había sembrado en doscientas, la novela
> confirma a Arredondo como una de las voces más pulcras de su generación. Una lectura
> imprescindible.
>
> *2. Mudanza, en el Foro Las Arcadas (teatro).* La puesta en escena de Mudanza, primera obra
> de una dramaturga joven, tiene momentos magistrales y otros francamente soporíferos. La actriz
> protagonista sostiene la primera hora con una sobriedad admirable: una mujer que empaca su casa
> y, caja por caja, su matrimonio. Luego el director llena el escenario de humo, música en vivo y
> proyecciones, y la obra se vuelve recargada y efectista, como si no confiara en su propio
> texto. Es loable que una compañía independiente se arriesgue con una autora nueva; con todo, el
> resultado es desigual. Vale la pena por el primer acto y por una interpretación que merece un
> montaje más sencillo.
>
> *3. Agua y memoria, en el Museo Ramírez Garza (exposición).* La curaduría promete «repensar
> nuestra relación con el agua», un lugar común que el recorrido nunca supera. Las ochenta piezas
> se suceden sin un hilo claro, mezclando épocas y técnicas sin explicar por qué, y las cédulas,
> ampulosas y pretenciosas, intentan decir lo que las obras no logran. La museografía, en cambio,
> es pulcra, y hay dos fotografías encomiables en la última sala, dedicadas a los pozos de una
> comunidad de la sierra. Lo demás es anodino. Es un esfuerzo fallido, aunque la idea merecía
> mejor suerte y una selección más rigurosa.

Summary: (1) A novel told through a nine-year-old girl in a mining town; restrained, polished prose
lets the reader fill the silences; the rushed last chapter is the one flaw; essential reading. (2)
A new play: the lead actress is restrained and masterly for an hour, then the director's smoke and
projections make it overdone and flashy; laudable risk, uneven result. (3) An exhibition built on a
platitude, with no thread and pretentious labels; neat display and two commendable photographs,
but bland and failed overall.

(*la mirada* — gaze, eyes; *la huelga* — the strike; *sembrar* — to sow; *apresurarse* — to rush; *imprescindible* —
essential; *empacar* — to pack (Mexico); *el montaje* — the production; *en vivo* — live; *el acto* — act; *la interpretación* —
performance; *la museografía* — the display
design, a lesson 22 word; *el recorrido* — the route through an
exhibition; *la cédula* — the wall label beside a museum piece, a Mexican museum term taught in
lesson 22; *el hilo* — thread.)

Notice how each verdict is earned: the first review praises and names one flaw; the second
separates the actress from the director; the third finds the only strength before condemning the
rest. All three concede something.

## Your turn: a graded review

The model below reviews an invented book for a magazine's culture section, in 217 words.

> *Mapa de una ausencia, de Tomás Leyva.* Leyva, conocido por sus crónicas de viaje, debuta en
> la novela con la historia de un hijo que recorre el norte del país siguiendo las cartas de un
> padre al que no conoció. El planteamiento no es nuevo: la búsqueda del padre es casi un género
> en las letras mexicanas. Lo que distingue a esta novela es su factura. Leyva escribe con una
> prosa sobria, sin adjetivos de más, y alterna los capítulos del viaje con las cartas, cuyo tono
> ampuloso y anticuado retrata al padre mejor que cualquier descripción.
>
> El libro no está exento de altibajos. La trama secundaria de la hermana, que promete mucho en
> los primeros capítulos, se diluye sin explicación, y algunas escenas en carretera repiten
> imágenes un tanto manidas: el desierto infinito, el motel solitario. Se le podría reprochar,
> además, un desenlace demasiado limpio para una historia tan llena de dudas.
>
> Con todo, Mapa de una ausencia es un debut logrado. Quien haya leído las crónicas de Leyva
> reconocerá su ojo para el detalle; quien no, encontrará una novela breve, honesta y bien
> construida sobre lo que heredamos sin saberlo. No es una obra magistral, pero sí una de las
> primeras novelas más encomiables del año, y anuncia a un autor al que conviene seguir.

Summary: Leyva, a travel writer, debuts as a novelist with a son tracing his unknown father's
letters across northern Mexico. The premise isn't new, but the craftsmanship is: restrained prose
alternates with the father's pompous letters. Weaknesses: a vanishing subplot, some hackneyed road
images, a too-tidy ending. Verdict: a successful, commendable debut. (*debutar* — to debut; *no
estar exento de* — not to be free of; *diluirse* — to fade away; *heredar* — to inherit; *la trama secundaria* — the subplot, a lesson 11 word.)

Checklist before you write: a *ficha* in the first line; one paragraph of description, no ending
given away; at least two strengths and two weaknesses, each with evidence; one concession (*si
bien, con todo*); a verdict that says for whom; no adjective used without a reason.

```assignment
writing: es6-m3-w10-resena
```

## Pronunciation

- *Soporífero*: five syllables, *so-po-RÍ-fe-ro*.
- *Encomiable*: four syllables, *en-ko-MIA-ble*; *mia* is one syllable.
- *Verosimilitud*: six syllables, *ve-ro-si-mi-li-TUD*.
- *Epíteto*: four syllables, *e-PÍ-te-to*.

## Common mistakes

- Praise without evidence: *magistral* needs a scene, a choice, a detail.
- *Loable* or *encomiable* as the whole verdict on a result: they mostly praise the effort; for a result that works, say *logrado*.
- *Un amigo viejo* for a long-standing friend: say *un viejo amigo*.
- Retelling the ending: a review describes the premise, not the outcome.
- Stacking epithets (*la tenue y dorada luz de la callada tarde*): that's the *recargado* style you
  would criticize.

## Key points

- A review: *ficha*, presentation, description, assessment with evidence, comparison, verdict.
- Quality: *fallido → desigual → logrado → magistral*; ornament: *sobrio, depurado, pulcro* vs
  *recargado, ampuloso, efectista, pretencioso*; efforts: *loable, encomiable*; worn material:
  *manido, trillado, el lugar común*.
- An adjective before the noun can be an epithet or change meaning (*un pobre hombre, cierto
  rumor, un simple comentario, un viejo amigo*).
- *La factura* also means craftsmanship.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Quién cuenta y desde dónde: narrative technique
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 judged a novel from outside; this lesson opens the machine. Two questions decide almost
everything in a story: who tells it, and through whose eyes we see it. Spanish has precise terms
for both, and one technique, free indirect style, that depends on the tenses module 2 taught
(the imperfect and the conditional, lesson 05). You'll learn to name what a writer is doing and
to do it yourself: retelling one scene from two points of view.

## Who tells: the narrator

The **[[narrator]]** (B1's *el narrador*) is the voice that tells, never simply the author.

- *El narrador omnisciente* (omniscient narrator) knows every mind, moves freely in time and can
  comment: *Nadie en la casa sabía que aquella sería su última cena juntos* (No one in the house
  knew that it would be their last dinner together).
- *El narrador testigo* (witness narrator) speaks in the first person from beside the main
  character: a brother, a neighbor, a friend. He knows only what he saw or was told.
- The protagonist narrator tells his or her own story in the first person.
- The second person (*tú*) addresses the protagonist, or the reader, as if from outside:
  *Abres la puerta y ya sabes que algo cambió* (You open the door and you already know something
  has changed).

*La voz narrativa* (the narrative voice) is the sum of these choices: person, tone, distance,
reliability.

## Who sees: focalization

**[[Focalization]]** (*la focalización*) is the point of view from which events are perceived. It
can differ from the voice: a third-person narrator can tell everything through the eyes of one
child, so that we see only what she sees. *El punto de vista* (point of view) is the everyday
term. Critics often distinguish three kinds: zero (the omniscient view, no limit), internal
(through one character) and external (only what a camera would record, no minds).

## Distance: from the narrator's voice to the character's mind

![A horizontal scale of narrative distance from far, at left, to near, at right, with five steps. Narrator's summary: Ana pasó la tarde ordenando los libros. Indirect speech: Pensó que nunca terminaría. Free indirect style: ¿Cuándo iba a terminar? Mañana vendría el camión. Direct speech: «Nunca voy a terminar», pensó. Interior monologue: nunca voy a terminar, cien cajas, y el camión mañana. An arrow under the scale says that the narrator's control shrinks and the character's voice grows from left to right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At one end, the narrator summarizes. At the other, the **[[interior monologue]]** (*el monólogo
interior*, which C1 92, an honors lesson, met) gives the character's thoughts directly, in the
present, often without full sentences or punctuation. In between sits the technique that defines
the modern novel.

## Free indirect style

**[[Free indirect style]]** (*el estilo indirecto libre*) gives a character's thoughts in the
narrator's voice, without a verb of thinking. Compare:

- Indirect: *Ana pensó que el camión llegaría al día siguiente.* (Ana thought that the truck
  would arrive the next day.)
- Free indirect: *El camión llegaría mañana. ¡Y ella todavía con cien cajas!* (The truck would
  arrive tomorrow. And her still with a hundred boxes!)

How Spanish marks it:

1. Tenses of the narrator's past: the imperfect and the conditional (*llegaría*), not the
   present and future the character would use.
2. Deixis from the character's here and now: *mañana, ahora, aquí* with past tenses (*El camión
   llegaría mañana*), which a strict narrator would turn into *al día siguiente, entonces, allí*.
3. Exclamations, questions and colloquial words in the character's style, with no *pensó* or
   *se preguntó*: *¿Y si su hermano no venía?*

Free indirect style lets a writer stay ironic and close at the same time: the words are the
narrator's, the feelings the character's. In reading, watch for it whenever a third-person text
suddenly asks questions nobody speaks.

## Time and structure

- **[[Analepsis]]** (*la analepsis*) is a flashback, a jump to the past; **[[prolepsis]]** (*la
  prolepsis*) is a flash-forward, often to announce an ending: *Años más tarde, vendería la
  casa* (Years later, she would sell the house). A story that starts *in medias res*
  begins in the middle of the action and explains later.
- A story is *lineal* (linear) when it follows the order of events. *La temporalidad* is how a
  text handles time in general.
- A **[[frame story]]** (*el relato marco*) contains another: a conversation in which someone tells
  a tale.
- **[[Metafiction]]** (*la metaficción*) is fiction that talks about its own writing; **[[intertextuality]]**
  (*la intertextualidad*) is a text's dialogue with other texts, by allusion, parody or
  rewriting.
- **[[Polyphony]]** (*la polifonía*) is many voices with none in charge; its form is *la novela
  coral* (the ensemble novel). *La autoficción* (autofiction) mixes the author's life with
  invention, and *el desdoblamiento* is the splitting of a narrator into two (*yo* and *ella*).

Other terms of the trade: *la caracterización* (characterization), *el antagonista*, *el
arquetipo* (archetype), *la alegoría* (allegory), *el leitmotiv* (a recurring motif), *la trama
secundaria* (subplot), *el clímax* (climax), *la novela corta* (novella) and *el lector
implícito*, the reader a text seems to expect.

## Twenty-first-century Mexican fiction

Five writers show these techniques at work; plots are given in a line, and the books are not
quoted.

- Valeria Luiselli, *Los ingrávidos* (2011): a young mother in Mexico City writes a novel about a
  Mexican poet in 1920s New York, and the two voices begin to bleed into each other: metafiction
  and *desdoblamiento*.
- Guadalupe Nettel, *El cuerpo en que nací* (2011), a first-person account close to autofiction,
  and *Después del invierno* (2014, Premio Herralde), whose chapters alternate between two
  first-person narrators.
- Yuri Herrera, *Señales que precederán al fin del mundo* (2009): a short novel about a young
  woman's journey north to find her brother, often read as an allegory of a descent to the
  underworld.
- Fernanda Melchor, *Temporada de huracanes* (2017; its English
  translation was shortlisted for the 2020 International Booker Prize): a violent story, here
  noted only for its technique, chapters of a single unbroken paragraph, most of them centered
  on a different character, a true *novela coral*.
- Emiliano Monge, *Las tierras arrasadas* (2015): a hard subject as well, which reviewers have
  described as a polyphonic novel in which narration and other voices interweave.

## One scene, two ways

> *Texto original*
>
> *A. Narrador omnisciente*
>
> Ana pasó la tarde del sábado ordenando los libros de su padre, muerto tres semanas antes. El
> departamento de la colonia Narvarte, donde la familia había vivido cuarenta años, olía todavía
> a tabaco y a papel húmedo. Ana no sabía que su hermano Julián, a cuatrocientos kilómetros,
> había decidido no venir; tampoco sabía que entre los libros la esperaba una carta. Trabajaba
> despacio, con la meticulosidad de quien posterga una despedida, y separaba en dos montones lo
> que regalaría y lo que no se atrevía a regalar. A las seis abrió un tomo de poesía que su padre
> nunca le había prestado y encontró un sobre con su nombre. Lo dejó sobre la mesa sin abrirlo.
> Afuera empezaba a llover, y en el edificio de enfrente una vecina, la señora Cruz, la observaba
> desde la ventana, como había observado durante treinta años las idas y venidas de aquella
> familia. Ana tardaría todavía dos días en leer la carta, y cuando por fin lo hiciera entendería
> por qué su padre nunca le había prestado ese libro.
>
> *B. Estilo indirecto libre*
>
> Otra caja, y otra. ¿Cuántos libros podía tener un hombre? Su padre había leído todo eso, o lo
> había comprado para no leerlo, que era otra manera de quererlo. Y el olor: tabaco, papel
> húmedo, cuarenta años de Narvarte metidos en cada página. El camión llegaría mañana a las ocho
> y Julián, claro, no contestaba. Siempre lo mismo con Julián. Ahora le tocaba a ella, como le
> había tocado todo: el hospital, los papeles, la funeraria. Este para la biblioteca de la
> escuela, este no, este tampoco. Abrió el libro de poemas, ese que su padre nunca le había
> querido prestar, ¡ni siquiera cuando estuvo enferma!, y de entre las páginas cayó un sobre. Su
> nombre, con aquella letra inclinada. No, ahora no. Lo puso en la mesa, boca abajo, y siguió con
> la caja siguiente, aunque las manos ya no le obedecían del todo. Afuera llovía. Seguro la
> señora Cruz estaba en su ventana, como siempre, contando cajas. Que contara. Mañana, cuando se
> llevaran todo, ya no habría nada que ver.

Summary: (A) The omniscient narrator reports that Ana spent Saturday sorting her late father's
books; he tells us what she can't know (her brother won't come; a letter is waiting), describes the
neighbor watching her, and jumps ahead (a prolepsis: she will read the letter two days later and
understand). (B) The same afternoon in free indirect style: Ana's questions and complaints about her
brother, an exclamation, *mañana* and *ahora* with past tenses, the letter she won't open yet, and
her irritation at the neighbor, all without a single *pensó*. (*la colonia Narvarte* — a Mexico City neighborhood; *el montón* — pile; *el tomo* — volume;
*postergar* — to put off; *la funeraria* — the funeral home; *las idas y
venidas* — the comings and goings; *le tocaba a ella* — it was her turn, it fell to her; *boca
abajo* — face down; *que contara* — let her count.)

## Worked example: analyzing the two versions

- Voice: both are third person, but A's narrator knows Julián's decision and the future; B's
  knows only what Ana knows.
- Focalization: A is zero (the narrator also sees through the neighbor's window); B is internal,
  through Ana.
- Time: A uses a prolepsis (*tardaría todavía dos días*); B stays in the present moment and its
  *mañana*.
- Marks of free indirect style in B: questions (*¿Cuántos libros…?*), an exclamation (*¡ni
  siquiera…!*), colloquial *claro* and *seguro*, deixis (*mañana, ahora*) with the imperfect and
  conditional (*llegaría*), the subjunctive *que contara* in Ana's voice.

## Worked example: retelling from another point of view

As the witness, the neighbor, in the first person and the preterite: *Esa tarde vi a la hija de
don Rafael ir y venir con cajas. A las seis se quedó quieta, con algo en la mano, y luego lo puso
en la mesa sin abrirlo. Llovía. A su hermano no lo vi ni en el velorio.* (That afternoon I saw don
Rafael's daughter going back and forth with boxes. At six she stood still with something in her
hand, then put it on the table without opening it. It was raining. Her brother I didn't see even
at the wake.) The witness can't know what the envelope is: her
limits are the technique.

## Pronunciation

- *Omnisciente*: four syllables, *om-ni-SIEN-te*; the *sc* sounds like one *s* in Latin America.
- *Analepsis, prolepsis*: four and three syllables, *a-na-LEP-sis, pro-LEP-sis*.
- *Focalización*: five syllables, *fo-ka-li-sa-SIÓN*.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the narrator as the author: say *el narrador afirma*, not *la autora afirma*, unless
  you mean her own opinion.
- Free indirect style in the present (*El camión llega mañana*, inside a past narration): keep the
  imperfect and the conditional.
- Calling every first-person novel autofiction: autofiction mixes the real author's life with
  invention on purpose.
- Confusing voice and focalization: the first is who speaks, the second who sees.

## Key points

- Narrator (omniscient, witness, protagonist, second person) and focalization (zero, internal,
  external) are separate choices.
- Distance runs from the narrator's summary to the interior monologue; free indirect style sits in
  the middle, marked by the imperfect and conditional, shifted deixis and verbless questions and
  exclamations.
- Time: analepsis, prolepsis, *in medias res*; structure: frame story, metafiction,
  intertextuality, polyphony.

lessons.title: Leer entre líneas: framing, implicature and the language of power
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09–11 looked at language that wants to be noticed: figures, style, narrative technique.
This lesson looks at language that prefers not to be: the official statement, the press release,
the campaign speech. Its tools are quieter than a metaphor, but a C2 reader sees them: a word
chosen to frame an issue, an assumption slipped in as fact, an agent who vanishes. You'll learn
a method for **[[critical discourse analysis]]** and practice the C2 skill that follows from it:
rewriting a framed text neutrally.

## Framing

**[[Framing]]** (*el encuadre*) is the choice of words that decides how an issue is seen before any
argument is made. The same measure can be *una reforma* or *un recorte* (a cut), *un ajuste* or
*un aumento* (an increase), *una actualización tarifaria* (a rate update) or *una subida de
tarifas* (a rate hike). B2's *el planteamiento* (approach) is broader; *el encuadre* is the frame
itself.

A frame often comes with a story about who is good and who is to blame: in current public
language, *la narrativa* (*el gobierno intenta imponer su narrativa*). That sense is recent,
often attributed to the influence of English "narrative", and its status is debated (check
the DLE and FundéuRAE before calling it standard); *el relato* and *el discurso* are safe
alternatives. Its older meaning, fiction as a genre (*la narrativa mexicana actual*), is
uncontroversial.

C1's *la consigna* (a task brief, lesson 23) has another sense here: a slogan, a short phrase
repeated by a movement or a government, *Agua para todos, cuentas claras*.

## What is assumed and what is implied

A **[[presupposition]]** is what a sentence takes for granted (C1 08h1, an honors lesson, used the
term). *Seguiremos mejorando el servicio* (We'll keep improving the service) assumes it
has been improving; *Ya no habrá cortes* (There will be no more cuts) admits there were some.
Verbs like *seguir, volver a, dejar de* and phrases like *una vez más* carry presuppositions; so do
*el hecho de que* and definite descriptions (*la crisis heredada*: what crisis?).

An **[[implicature]]** (*la implicatura*) is what a sentence suggests without saying, which a
listener infers because a speaker is assumed to be relevant and informative (the philosopher Paul
Grice described this in the 1960s and 1970s). *Algunos funcionarios cumplieron* (Some officials
complied) implies that others didn't. *Este gobierno no esconde la realidad* implies that others
did. Implicature is deniable, which is why it's useful: *el sobreentendido* (the unspoken
assumption), *la insinuación* (insinuation) and *el subtexto* (subtext) all live here.

## Vagueness, evasion and hidden agents

- Vague quantifiers: *hasta un 30 %* (up to 30%: perhaps much less, perhaps for very few),
  *más de, alrededor de, la mayoría de los hogares*. *La vaguedad* (vagueness) is not always
  dishonest, but it always needs a question.
- Evasion: to *eludir* (dodge) a question is to answer with *evasivas* (evasive answers), often a
  change of subject or an answer to a different question.
- Hidden agents: the agentless passive and *se* (B2 14) and the nominal style (B2 18) can remove
  whoever decided. *Se tomó la decisión de actualizar las tarifas* (The decision was made to
  update the rates): who decided? *La regularización de las tomas* (the regularization of water
  connections): who will do what to whom?
- Euphemism (C1 04): *reordenamiento del suministro* (reorganization of supply) for water by
  turns, what Mexican Spanish calls *el tandeo* (lesson 07).

## The vocabulary of spin

- To make bad news look better: *maquillar las cifras* (to dress up the figures), *edulcorar*
  (to sugarcoat). Twisting someone's words is *la tergiversación* (distortion).
- To attack the speaker instead of the argument: *descalificar* (to disparage) *al adversario*
  (the opponent); *las descalificaciones personales* are personal attacks. Blaming a weaker group
  makes it *el chivo expiatorio* (the scapegoat).
- To divide: *polarizar* (to polarize) a debate, *la polarización*; *demagógico* promises what
  can't be delivered; *la propaganda* presents persuasion as information.
- *El doble discurso* (double-talk) says one thing and does another, or says two things to two
  audiences. *La opacidad* (opacity) is the opposite of transparency. *El posicionamiento*
  (stance), very frequent in Mexican public language, is an official position.
- *La ambivalencia* is a word or stance that can be read two ways. *El lenguaje políticamente
  correcto* (politically correct language) is itself a contested frame: for some it means
  respectful language, for others a censorship; describe it, don't take sides in a summary.

## A method: who did what?

![A chart titled ¿Quién hizo qué? with four columns. ¿Quién actúa? (named, hidden, blamed), with the example se tomó la decisión, a hidden agent. ¿Qué se da por hecho? (presuppositions), with seguir garantizando un servicio de calidad. ¿Qué se insinúa? (implicatures), with a diferencia de otros: earlier governments lied? ¿Qué falta? (figures, dates, alternatives), with hasta un 18 %, no figure for a typical home. A line at the bottom says to judge the frame next: which words could be replaced by neutral ones.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**[[Critical discourse analysis]]** (*el análisis del discurso*, in its critical form) asks four
questions of any public text:

1. Who acts? Who is named as doing good, who is hidden, who is blamed?
2. What is assumed? List the presuppositions.
3. What is implied? List the implicatures.
4. What is left out? Figures, dates, costs, alternatives, the other side.

Then judge the frame: which words could be replaced by neutral ones?

## The statement

> *Comunicado (texto original; el municipio y el organismo son ficticios)*
>
> *Agua para todos, cuentas claras: actualización tarifaria 2027*
>
> Con el firme compromiso de seguir garantizando un servicio de agua de calidad, el Organismo
> Operador de Agua de Santa Lucía de los Llanos informa a la ciudadanía que, tras un análisis
> responsable, se tomó la decisión de actualizar las tarifas a partir del 1 de enero de 2027.
>
> Durante años, el consumo irresponsable de algunos usuarios y la falta de pago de otros han
> puesto en riesgo la viabilidad del sistema. Este gobierno, a diferencia de otros, no esconde la
> realidad: la red tiene más de cuarenta años y pierde agua en cada colonia. Hoy, cuatro de cada
> diez litros se pierden antes de llegar a los hogares.
>
> El ajuste será, en promedio, de hasta un 18 %. La mayoría de los hogares prácticamente no notará
> la diferencia, y se reforzarán los apoyos a los sectores más vulnerables. Los recursos se
> destinarán a la modernización de la red, a la regularización de las tomas y a un
> reordenamiento del suministro en las zonas con mayor demanda.
>
> Para facilitar la transición, se pondrá en marcha un programa de regularización con descuentos
> de hasta el 50 % en recargos para quienes se pongan al corriente antes del 31 de marzo.
> Asimismo, en las próximas semanas se instalarán módulos de atención en las principales
> colonias, donde personal capacitado resolverá cualquier duda. Estas acciones forman parte de
> una estrategia integral que coloca a Santa Lucía entre los municipios más modernos de la región.
>
> Lamentamos que ciertos actores políticos hayan preferido la desinformación y el alarmismo, en
> lugar de sumarse a una tarea que es de todos. Quienes hoy critican son los mismos que durante
> décadas dejaron crecer el problema. La ciudadanía sabrá distinguir entre quienes trabajan y
> quienes solo hablan.
>
> El Organismo reitera su vocación de transparencia y su cercanía con la gente. Cuidar el agua no
> es una opción: es una responsabilidad compartida. Agua para todos, cuentas claras.

Summary: The water utility of an invented municipality announces a "rate update" from January 1,
2027, to "keep guaranteeing" good service. It blames some users' waste and nonpayment and
says, unlike others, it hides nothing: the network is old and leaks. The "adjustment" will average
"up to 18%"; most homes "will hardly notice"; support for vulnerable groups "will be reinforced";
the money goes to modernization, regularizing connections and "reorganizing supply". Late payers
who catch up get discounts on surcharges, and help desks will open; the utility calls this a
modern, "comprehensive strategy". It attacks
critics as alarmist and as the cause of the problem, and closes with its slogan. (*la ciudadanía*
— the public, the citizens; *la toma* — a water connection (Mexico); *los recargos* — late-payment surcharges; *ponerse al corriente* — to catch up on
payments; *el módulo de atención* — help desk; *sumarse a* — to join; *la
cercanía* — closeness; *la desinformación* — disinformation; *la vocación* — commitment.)

## Worked example: analyzing the statement

- Who acts? The utility acts only in good things (*informa, reitera*); the decision has no agent
  (*se tomó la decisión*); blame falls on *algunos usuarios* (a scapegoat), *otros* governments and
  *ciertos actores políticos*, all unnamed.
- Assumed: that the service is now of quality (*seguir garantizando*); that an analysis took
  place (*tras un análisis responsable*), though none is published.
- Implied: *a diferencia de otros* implies earlier governments lied; *la ciudadanía sabrá
  distinguir* implies critics only talk. That last paragraph disparages and polarizes.
- Left out: the source of the *cuatro de cada diez litros*, the rate for an average home, how many homes pay *hasta un 18 %*, what *apoyos* and
  for whom, what *reordenamiento del suministro* means (water by turns?), and when the network
  will be fixed.
- Frame words: *actualización, ajuste* (for *aumento*); *reordenamiento* (euphemism);
  *desinformación, alarmismo* (labels, not arguments).

## Worked example: a neutral rewrite

> *El Organismo Operador de Agua de Santa Lucía de los Llanos aumentará las tarifas a partir del 1
> de enero de 2027. Describe el aumento como «en promedio, de hasta un 18 %», sin indicar cuánto
> pagará un hogar típico. Según el organismo, el aumento se debe a las pérdidas de una red de más
> de cuarenta años, al consumo excesivo y a la falta de pago. El dinero se usará para renovar la
> red, regularizar las tomas y reorganizar el suministro en las zonas de mayor demanda, sin
> precisar si esto implicará cortes por turnos. El organismo dijo que reforzará los apoyos a los
> sectores más vulnerables, sin detallarlos, y acusó a «ciertos actores políticos», a quienes no
> nombró, de desinformar.*

Translation: The water utility of Santa Lucía de los Llanos will raise its rates from January 1,
2027. It describes the increase as "on average, up to 18%", without saying how much a typical home
will pay. According to the utility, the increase is due to losses in a network over forty years
old, excessive consumption and nonpayment. The money will be used to renew the network, regularize
connections and reorganize supply in the areas of highest demand, without specifying whether this
will mean cuts by turns. The utility said it will reinforce support for the most vulnerable
groups, without details, and accused "certain political actors", whom it didn't name, of spreading
disinformation.

What changed: the agent is named and acts (*aumentará*); *ajuste* became *aumento*; the
utility's claims are attributed (*según el organismo*) and its unclear figure is quoted, not
fixed: *en promedio* and *hasta* pull in different directions (an average and a maximum), so the
rewrite reports the wording instead of choosing one. Every gap is stated, not filled, and the
attack on critics is reported in one neutral clause. A summary of a framed text keeps the source's
claims and hedges, adds none, and keeps your opinion out.

## Pronunciation

- *Implicatura*: five syllables, *im-pli-ka-TU-ra*.
- *Demagógico*: five syllables, *de-ma-GÓ-hi-ko*.
- *Tergiversación*: five syllables, *ter-hi-ber-sa-SIÓN*.

## Common mistakes

- Calling every vague text a lie: vagueness can be honest caution. Ask, then judge.
- Replacing one frame with another: *un tarifazo brutal* is as framed as *una actualización*.
  Neutral is *un aumento de tarifas*, with the figure as the source gives it.
- Adding hedges or claims the source didn't make when you summarize it.
- Using *narrativa* for every argument: *relato* or *discurso* are safer in formal writing.

## Key points

- Framing chooses the words (*ajuste / aumento*) before the argument.
- Presuppositions are taken for granted (*seguir, volver a, dejar de*); implicatures are suggested
  and deniable (*algunos, a diferencia de otros*).
- Watch for hidden agents (*se tomó la decisión*), nominalizations, vague quantifiers (*hasta*),
  euphemisms, scapegoats and attacks on the speaker.
- Analyze with four questions: who acts, what is assumed, what is implied, what is left out. A
  neutral rewrite names the agent, states the figure and attributes the claims.

lessons.title: Honors: La comedia del Siglo de Oro: Lope, Calderón and Ruiz de Alarcón
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 asked who tells a story; theater has no narrator, only voices on a stage. This honors
lesson goes back to the seventeenth century, when Spanish theater was mass entertainment: three
playwrights, their stock characters, their playhouses, and an original
scene in modern Spanish that imitates the old conventions. Nothing below quotes a real play:
plots are retold in this lesson's own words, and the scene and verses are the writer's own.

## The Golden Age and the comedia nueva

The **[[Golden Age]]** (*el Siglo de Oro*) is the great period of Spanish literature and art, roughly
from the early sixteenth century to the late seventeenth; its end is often placed at Calderón's
death in 1681. Cervantes, Góngora, Quevedo and, in New Spain, Sor Juana belong to it.

Its theater had a formula, the **[[comedia nueva]]** (the new comedy), associated above all with
Félix Lope de Vega (1562–1635), who wrote hundreds of plays (how many is disputed). In 1609 he
published a verse treatise, the *Arte nuevo de hacer comedias en este tiempo*, which defended,
half ironically, what audiences liked over what classical rules required. In this lesson's
words, the formula was:

- Three acts, called *jornadas* (not B1's *jornada laboral*), instead of the classical five.
- Tragic and comic mixed.
- Many meters in one play, each fitted to a situation: Lope advised, for example, the *décima*
  for complaints, the *romance* (ballad meter, lesson 08h1's word) for telling past events, and eight-syllable quatrains for love.
- Plots of love and *la honra* (honor), the theme Lope said moved audiences most, with the
  outcome kept for the last scene.

## The stock characters

- *El galán* (leading man) and *la dama* (the lady) fall in love against an obstacle.
- *El gracioso* (comic servant) is the galán's servant: hungry, cowardly, sharp-tongued, the
  voice of common sense who mocks his master's lofty passions. *La graciosa*, the lady's maid,
  is his match.
- *El barba*, an old man named for the actor's beard, guards the family's honor; a king or a
  nobleman often settles the conflict at the end.

*La honra* is not virtue but reputation: what others say about you. A family's honor depended on
its women's conduct, so a rumor could be as dangerous as a crime. Honor plots run from the comic
to the terrible (Calderón's honor tragedies, such as *El médico de su honra*). *El enredo* (the
tangle, a plot of mix-ups: letters, cloaks, darkness, mistaken identities) is the other engine;
from its favorite props come the *comedias de capa y espada* (cloak-and-sword plays).

## The playhouse: the corral de comedias

![A plan, seen from above, of a generic seventeenth-century corral de comedias. At the top, el escenario (the stage) with the vestuario (dressing room) behind it. In front of the stage, el patio, a large open yard with standing spectators. Along both sides of the yard, las gradas (tiered benches), and on the outer walls rows of latticed boxes, los aposentos. At the bottom, opposite the stage, la cazuela, the women's gallery.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Plays were performed in the afternoon, by daylight, in *corrales de comedias* (open-air
playhouses): courtyards between houses, with a stage at one end. The men standing in *el patio*
(the yard), the *mosqueteros*, were the noisiest public. Along the sides rose *las gradas*
(tiered benches); above them, noble families rented *los aposentos* (boxes, often latticed).
Opposite the stage, *la cazuela* was the women's gallery. Madrid's two great corrales, de la Cruz
and del Príncipe, are long gone (the Teatro Español stands where the Príncipe was). The best
preserved is in Almagro (Ciudad Real): rediscovered around 1950 and opened in 1954, it hosts a
festival of classical theater every July. The picture is a generic plan, not Almagro's.

An afternoon at the corral was a whole program: a short *loa* (prologue), the play, *entremeses*
(comic one-act interludes) between the acts, often better loved than the play, and a closing
dance.

## Calderón: La vida es sueño and the auto sacramental

Pedro Calderón de la Barca (1600–1681), the great playwright of the next generation, is more
philosophical and more tightly built than Lope. *La vida es sueño* (Life Is a Dream), first
printed in 1636, is his best-known play. In this lesson's retelling: a king of Poland, warned by
the stars that his son will be a tyrant, keeps the prince locked in a tower. Years later he tests
the prophecy: the drugged prince wakes up in the palace as heir, behaves violently, and is drugged
again and told it was a dream. Freed by rebels, no longer sure what is real, he chooses to act
well anyway. The play's questions are *el libre albedrío* (free will) against fate, and *el
desengaño* (disillusionment), seeing that worldly glory is appearance, a central idea of the
Baroque. Its *soliloquios* (soliloquies), spoken by the prince alone on stage, are among the most
memorized passages in Spanish.

Calderón was also the master of the **[[auto sacramental]]** (sacramental play): a one-act religious
allegory performed for the feast of Corpus Christi, with abstract figures (the World, Grace,
Beauty) as characters. In *El gran teatro del mundo*, the world is a stage where each person
plays a role handed out by God. The autos were banned in 1765.

## Ruiz de Alarcón: a Mexican in Madrid

Juan Ruiz de Alarcón was born in New Spain around 1581, in Taxco or Mexico City (sources differ;
Britannica gives Taxco), studied in Mexico and Salamanca, and settled in Madrid. He wrote about
twenty-five plays, published in 1628 and 1634, held a post in the Council of the Indies from
1626, and died in Madrid in 1639. Rivals, Lope among them, mocked his hunched back; his plays are
more moral than Lope's, each built around one flaw of character.

*La verdad sospechosa* (The Suspicious Truth), retold: don García, newly arrived in Madrid, lies
for pleasure. He falls for a lady but mixes up her name with her friend's, each lie forces a
bigger one, and in the end nobody believes him even when he tells the truth: he must marry the
woman he didn't want. Pierre Corneille adapted it in French as *Le Menteur* (1644).

## An original scene

> *Escena original en español moderno, escrita para esta lección; imita las convenciones de la
> comedia, no copia ninguna obra. Madrid, una calle de noche.*
>
> *(Sale don Félix, embozado en su capa, y Tomillo, su criado, con una linterna.)*
>
> TOMILLO. Señor, es medianoche, hace frío y yo no he cenado. Tres buenas razones para irnos
> a casa.
>
> DON FÉLIX. Calla y apaga esa luz. Ella dijo que se asomaría a la reja cuando su hermano
> durmiera.
>
> TOMILLO. ¿Y si su hermano no duerme? Los hermanos de las damas nunca duermen, señor. Es lo
> único que hacen bien.
>
> DON FÉLIX. El amor no mide peligros, Tomillo; los cuenta como victorias.
>
> TOMILLO. Por eso mido yo, que no estoy enamorado más que de un buen guisado.
>
> *(Se abre la ventana tras la reja. Aparece doña Clara.)*
>
> DOÑA CLARA. ¿Don Félix?
>
> DON FÉLIX. Aquí estoy, Clara, aunque la noche entera me sobra si me falta tu voz.
>
> TOMILLO. *(Aparte.)* Ya empezó. Ahora hablará una hora y yo me moriré de hambre en verso.
>
> DOÑA CLARA. No hay tiempo. Mi hermano sabe que alguien ronda la casa. Esta tarde encontró
> en el patio un guante que no es suyo.
>
> TOMILLO. *(Aparte.)* El guante que perdí yo. Mejor no digo nada.
>
> DOÑA CLARA. Si te descubre aquí, mi honra queda en boca de toda la calle, y la tuya en la
> punta de su espada. Vete y vuelve mañana por la iglesia, a la hora de misa.
>
> DON FÉLIX. ¿Irme sin saber si me quieres?
>
> DOÑA CLARA. ¿Te parece poca prueba que me asome a una reja a medianoche?
>
> LUCÍA. *(Dentro, a doña Clara.)* Señora, que se despierta don Gonzalo.
>
> TOMILLO. ¿Es Lucía? Lucía, luz de la cocina, ¿no te sobró un pedazo de pan?
>
> LUCÍA. Para ti, ni las migas. Tu amo promete estrellas y tú pides pan: no sé cuál de los dos
> me cansa más.
>
> TOMILLO. El de las estrellas, que no se comen.
>
> DOÑA CLARA. Félix, prométeme que no harás ninguna locura.
>
> DON FÉLIX. Te prometo lo que quieras, menos olvidarte.
>
> *(Ruido dentro. Se cierra la ventana.)*
>
> TOMILLO. Señor, ese ruido tiene bigote y espada.
>
> *(Sale don Gonzalo, hermano de Clara, también embozado.)*
>
> DON GONZALO. ¿Quién va? ¿Quién busca esta casa a estas horas?
>
> DON FÉLIX. Un caballero que pasaba.
>
> DON GONZALO. Los caballeros que pasan no se detienen bajo una reja. Diga su nombre.
>
> TOMILLO. *(A don Gonzalo.)* Yo me llamo Tomillo, señor, y no he visto nada, ni a nadie,
> ni sé dónde estoy.
>
> DON GONZALO. No hablo con criados, y menos con criados que hablan tanto.
>
> TOMILLO. Pues es una lástima, porque somos los únicos que decimos la verdad.
>
> DON FÉLIX. Mi nombre no importa. Si ofendí esta casa, aquí está mi espada para responder.
>
> DON GONZALO. No será esta noche. Un escándalo a la puerta deshonra más que una herida. Mañana,
> al amanecer, junto al puente. Y si no viene, sabré quién es por el guante que dejó.
>
> *(Vase don Gonzalo.)*
>
> TOMILLO. El guante, señor, es mío. Así que, si alguien tiene que morir mañana, propongo que
> sea usted, que al menos está enamorado.
>
> DON FÉLIX. *(Solo, mientras Tomillo se aleja.)* ¡Qué extraña ley la del honor! Gonzalo
> quiere matarme para que nadie hable de su hermana, y si me mata, toda la ciudad hablará. Yo la
> quiero y no puedo decir su nombre; él la guarda y no puede decirle la verdad. Mañana iré al
> puente, porque un caballero no falta a una cita con la muerte. Pero antes iré a misa, porque
> tampoco falta a una cita con su dama. Y que el cielo decida cuál de las dos llega primero.

Summary: Night in a Madrid street. Don Félix waits under Clara's window with his servant Tomillo,
who complains of cold and hunger. Clara warns that her brother has found a stranger's glove
(Tomillo, aside, admits it was his) and sends Félix away; her maid Lucía refuses Tomillo even a
crumb. Her brother don Gonzalo arrives; Félix won't give his name. To avoid a scandal at his door,
Gonzalo challenges him to a duel at dawn and says the glove will identify him. Tomillo suggests
Félix be the one to die, since he at least is in love. Alone, Félix reflects on the strange law of
honor and decides to keep both appointments, the duel and the mass. (*embozado* — face hidden in
his cloak; *la reja* — the window grille; *asomarse* — to appear at a window; *el guisado* — stew;
*las migas* — crumbs; *rondar* — to hang around (a house, a lady); *aparte* — an aside, for the
audience only; *vase* — old stage direction, "exits".)

## Worked example 1: the conventions in the scene

- Characters: *galán* (Félix), *dama* (Clara), *gracioso* (Tomillo) and *graciosa* (Lucía), and a
  brother as guardian of honor, the role an old *barba* often plays.
- *Enredo*: the glove is the typical small object that drives the plot; only the audience knows
  whose it is, thanks to an *aparte*.
- *Honra*: Clara fears gossip (*en boca de toda la calle*) more than violence, and Gonzalo avoids
  a fight at his door for the same reason: the paradox Félix names at the end.
- The *gracioso* lowers every high moment: love becomes hunger (*moriré de hambre en verso*),
  stars become bread, and he claims that servants alone tell the truth.
- Félix closes with a short *soliloquio* built on antithesis (lesson 09): *yo la quiero y no
  puedo decir su nombre; él la guarda y no puede decirle la verdad*.

In a real comedia the scene would be in verse. Here, for comparison, is an eight-syllable
quatrain rhymed *abba* (a *redondilla*), the writer's own imitation, which Félix might speak as
he waits:

> *Si el frío me vuelve hielo,*
> *me abriga tu voz lejana,*
> *que más que la luz temprana*
> *me alumbra en este desvelo.*

(If the cold turns me to ice, your distant voice warms me; more than the early light, it lights
my sleepless night.) Count with synalepha (B1 90 explained it): *me‿a-bri-ga*, *lum-bra‿en* join vowels across words, so
each line has eight syllables.

## Worked example 2: the gracioso and the modern sidekick

- Same as a modern film's comic sidekick: he speaks for common sense, deflates the hero and is
  more afraid than brave; his jokes about food remind us of the body behind the ideals.
- Different: the *gracioso* belongs to a fixed social order (he is a servant, and his insolence is
  licensed by the genre); the modern sidekick is usually a friend and an equal. And the *gracioso*
  often parodies his master's plot: when the galán courts the lady, he courts her maid.

## Common mistakes

- *Comedia* as "comedy" only: in the Golden Age *comedia* meant any full-length play, including
  tragic ones.
- *Honra* and *honor* as exact synonyms: in these plays *la honra* is public reputation; *el
  honor* is often the inner quality or the abstract value.
- Treating the *auto sacramental* as a comedia: it's a one-act allegory with abstract characters.
- Calling Ruiz de Alarcón simply Spanish: born in New Spain, he is claimed by both literatures.

## Key points

- *La comedia nueva*: three *jornadas*, mixed tragedy and comedy, many meters, honor and *enredo*;
  Lope's *Arte nuevo* (1609).
- Stock characters: *galán, dama, gracioso, barba*. The *corral*: *patio, gradas, aposentos,
  cazuela, escenario*.
- Calderón: *La vida es sueño* (printed 1636), free will and *desengaño*; the *auto sacramental*.
- Ruiz de Alarcón, born in New Spain: *La verdad sospechosa*, the liar trapped by his lies.
