lessons.title: Honors: El modernismo: Darío, Martí and Gutiérrez Nájera
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 gave you the vocabulary of style; this honors lesson applies it to the movement that
made style itself the subject. Between about 1880 and 1915, a generation of poets and chroniclers
from Cuba, Mexico, Nicaragua and Colombia renewed the Spanish language more deeply than anyone
since the Golden Age (lesson 12h1). It's often described as the first literary movement born in
Spanish America to change the literature of Spain. You'll learn what the movement was, its main writers,
its images and its verse, then read an original essay about it and practice describing a poem's
technique.

As everywhere in this course, no poem is quoted, not even one line. Poems are described in this
lesson's own words, and the short examples of technique are the writer's own prose, labeled as
such. Read the poems themselves in any good anthology: all are in the public domain.

## A false friend: modernismo is not modernism

**[[Modernismo]]** (*el modernismo*) is the Hispanic movement of the late nineteenth century. English
"modernism" (Joyce, Eliot, Woolf) is something later, closer to what Spanish calls the
*vanguardias* (avant-gardes, the C1 honors word *la vanguardia*). In English, call the movement
*modernismo* and its writers *modernistas*.

It sits between two moments: after Romanticism, whose emotion it kept but whose loose form it
rejected, and before the avant-gardes of the 1920s, which broke the forms it had perfected. Its
models were French: the Parnassians' cult of perfect, sculpted form and the Symbolists' music and
suggestion (*el simbolismo*).

## The writers

- José Martí (Cuba, 1853–1895): *Ismaelillo* (1882), poems for his son; *Versos sencillos* (1891),
  short poems in eight-syllable quatrains; and the essay *Nuestra América* (1891). He wrote much of
  his work in exile in New York and died fighting for Cuba's independence.
- Manuel Gutiérrez Nájera (Mexico City, 1859–1895): poet and *cronista* who signed many pieces as
  El Duque Job; *Cuentos frágiles* (1883); and in 1894, with Carlos Díaz Dufoo, the *Revista
  Azul*, the magazine of Mexican modernismo, which outlived him by more than a year.
- Rubén Darío (Nicaragua, 1867–1916), the movement's center: *Azul…* (Valparaíso, 1888), stories
  and poems; *Prosas profanas* (Buenos Aires, 1896), its most ornate book; *Cantos de vida y
  esperanza* (Madrid, 1905), graver and more American after Spain's defeat in 1898.
- José Asunción Silva (Colombia, 1865–1896), the movement's most melancholy voice, known for
  experiments with rhythm.
- Amado Nervo (Tepic, 1870–1919), Mexican poet and diplomat, from the *Revista Moderna* (founded
  in 1898) to a late, more spiritual poetry.

![A timeline of modernismo from 1880 to 1920. 1882, Martí, Ismaelillo. 1883, Gutiérrez Nájera, Cuentos frágiles. 1888, Darío, Azul…. 1891, Martí, Versos sencillos. 1894, Revista Azul founded in Mexico City. 1895, deaths of Martí and Gutiérrez Nájera. 1896, Darío, Prosas profanas. 1898, Spain loses its last American colonies; Revista Moderna founded in Mexico. 1905, Darío, Cantos de vida y esperanza. 1916, death of Darío. A green band, explained in a note on the chart, marks the movement's peak, about 1880 to 1915.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Images and techniques

- *El cisne* (the swan): the movement's emblem of beauty, grace and art for its own sake; later
  poets attacked it for exactly that.
- *El exotismo* (exoticism): Versailles, ancient Greece, Japan and China, princesses and
  pagodas, places far from the poets' own cities.
- *La musicalidad* (musicality): rhythm, repetition and sound mattered as much as meaning.
- *La sinestesia* (synesthesia, C1 05): one sense described in terms of another, colors that
  sound, notes that shine. The writer's own example, in prose: *un azul que suena a campana
  lejana* (a blue that sounds like a distant bell).
- Precious objects: gold, ivory, pearls, marble. Critics called the excess *preciosismo*
  (preciosity), and the poets compared their craft to *la orfebrería* (goldsmithing).
- New words: rare, learned and foreign words, used for their sound and color.

The verse changed too. The **[[alexandrine]]** (*el alejandrino*), a fourteen-syllable line split
into two halves of seven, had been rare in Spanish since the Middle Ages (some
Romantics tried it); the modernistas made it
their signature line. They also revived and invented other lengths and mixed them freely, a step
toward the **[[free verse]]** (*el verso libre*) of the avant-gardes: lines with no fixed meter or
rhyme. For counting syllables, B1 90 (an honors lesson) has the method.

## An original essay

> *Ensayo original*
>
> *El modernismo, o el día en que América enseñó a escribir a España*
>
> Hacia 1880, la poesía en español parecía agotada. El Romanticismo había dejado una lengua
> sentimental y repetitiva, y los poetas de ambos lados del Atlántico escribían versos que sonaban
> igual. En apenas una generación, un grupo de escritores hispanoamericanos cambió esa situación
> para siempre. No formaron una escuela ni firmaron un manifiesto: compartían revistas, cartas y
> una idea, la de que la belleza de la forma era también una manera de pensar.
>
> Sus maestros fueron franceses. De los parnasianos tomaron el culto de la forma perfecta, el
> verso trabajado como una joya; de los simbolistas, la música y la sugerencia, la convicción de
> que un poema debe evocar más que explicar. Pero lo que hicieron con esas lecciones fue nuevo.
> Llenaron sus versos de cisnes, princesas y jardines de Versalles, de pagodas y dioses griegos;
> mezclaron los sentidos y buscaron palabras raras por su sonido. Los críticos los acusaron de
> preciosismo, de escribir para nadie, de imitar a París desde Managua o desde la Ciudad de
> México. No siempre se equivocaban.
>
> Sin embargo, reducir el modernismo a un salón lleno de adornos es leerlo a medias. Detrás del
> exotismo había una forma de rebeldía: en sociedades que medían todo por su utilidad, estos
> escritores defendían el arte como un valor en sí mismo. Muchos vivían del periodismo, y en sus
> crónicas retrataron con agudeza las ciudades modernas que crecían a su alrededor. Gutiérrez
> Nájera llevó a la prensa mexicana una prosa ligera y elegante que todavía se lee con gusto;
> Martí, desde Nueva York, explicó a los lectores de América Latina la vida de una metrópoli que
> admiraba y temía.
>
> Martí y Darío suelen presentarse como los dos polos del movimiento. Martí buscó la sencillez:
> versos breves, palabras comunes, una sinceridad casi desnuda puesta al servicio de una ética y
> de una causa política. Darío buscó la riqueza: el alejandrino, la mitología, la música de las
> palabras llevada hasta el límite. Pero la oposición es menos clara de lo que parece. Martí
> podía ser deslumbrante en su prosa, y Darío, en su madurez, escribió poemas graves sobre la
> muerte, la fe y el destino de los pueblos hispánicos, sobre todo después de 1898, cuando España
> perdió sus últimas colonias en América y Estados Unidos se convirtió en la potencia del
> continente.
>
> En México, el movimiento tuvo casa propia. La Revista Azul, fundada en 1894, reunió a poetas
> jóvenes y tradujo a los franceses; pocos años después, la Revista Moderna continuó esa labor.
> Amado Nervo pasó por ambas etapas: empezó con una poesía de imágenes refinadas y terminó
> escribiendo versos cada vez más despojados, casi oraciones. Su trayectoria resume la del
> movimiento entero: del brillo de la superficie a la búsqueda de una voz más íntima.
>
> La influencia del modernismo cruzó el océano en dirección contraria a la habitual. Cuando Darío
> viajó a España, los jóvenes poetas españoles lo recibieron como a un maestro, y varios de ellos
> reconocieron después su deuda con él. Por primera vez, la renovación de la lengua literaria no
> llegaba de Madrid a las antiguas colonias, sino de las antiguas colonias a Madrid.
>
> El movimiento se agotó hacia 1915, víctima de su propio éxito: sus cisnes y sus princesas se
> volvieron fórmulas, y una nueva generación pidió dejar de lado los adornos para mirar la vida
> cotidiana. Las vanguardias de los años veinte romperían después la métrica que los modernistas
> habían perfeccionado. Pero esa ruptura solo fue posible porque antes alguien había demostrado
> que el verso en español podía sonar de otra manera. Leídos hoy, los modernistas no son una
> colección de piezas de orfebrería, sino los escritores que enseñaron a la lengua a escucharse a
> sí misma.

Summary: (1) Around 1880, poetry in Spanish seemed worn out; within a generation, Spanish American
writers changed it, sharing magazines and the idea that beautiful form was a way of thinking. (2)
They learned perfect form from the Parnassians and suggestion from the Symbolists, filled their
verse with swans and pagodas, and were accused, not always wrongly, of preciosity. (3) But their
exoticism was a rebellion against a utilitarian society, and their journalism portrayed the new
cities: Gutiérrez Nájera's light prose in Mexico, Martí's chronicles of New York. (4) Martí sought
simplicity and Darío richness, but the contrast blurs: Martí's prose dazzles, and the mature Darío
wrote grave poems, especially after 1898. (5) In Mexico, the *Revista Azul* and then the *Revista Moderna*
gave it a home; Nervo moved from refined images to bare, prayer-like verse. (6) Its influence
crossed to Spain, reversing the usual direction. (7) It exhausted itself around 1915, but made possible the avant-gardes'
break. (*agotado* — exhausted, worn out; *la agudeza* — sharpness, wit; *deslumbrante* —
dazzling; *la potencia* — a power, a great power; *la deuda* — debt; *despojado* — stripped bare.)

## Worked example 1: describing a poem's technique from a summary

Here is a summary, in this lesson's own words, of a famous poem in *Prosas profanas*, Darío's
"Sonatina": a young princess sits sad and silent in a luxurious palace, indifferent to her
jewels, her garden and her court, dreaming of a distant prince who will come to free her.

How to describe its technique without quoting it:

1. Meter: alexandrines, each split into two halves of seven syllables, which gives the poem a
   slow, swaying rhythm, like a lullaby.
2. Sound: repetitions and internal echoes make it musical; the poem is famous for being read
   aloud.
3. Images: luxury and exotic far-off kingdoms, the catalog of precious things the princess no
   longer wants: *exotismo* and *preciosismo* in one.
4. Meaning: under the decoration, a theme of longing and confinement, which some readers take as a
   portrait of the artist's own dream of an ideal.

A sentence for a commentary: *El poema combina la musicalidad del alejandrino con un catálogo de
objetos preciosos para retratar el tedio de una princesa que sueña con una liberación ideal* (The
poem combines the musicality of the alexandrine with a catalog of precious objects to portray the
tedium of a princess who dreams of an ideal deliverance).

## Worked example 2: Darío and Martí side by side

| | Darío (*Prosas profanas*) | Martí (*Versos sencillos*) |
|---|---|---|
| Line | long lines, often alexandrines | short eight-syllable lines in quatrains |
| Words | rare, learned, musical | everyday, plain |
| World | mythology, Versailles, the Orient | nature, friendship, the homeland |
| Aim | beauty and suggestion | sincerity and an ethical voice |

Two sentences in the two manners, both the writer's own prose imitations:

- In Darío's manner: *Sobre el estanque de nácar dormía un cisne, y el crepúsculo, violín de oro, le
  tocaba su última nota.* (On the mother-of-pearl pond a swan slept, and the dusk, a golden
  violin, played it its last note.) Exotic color, synesthesia, a metaphor of music.
- In Martí's manner: *Quiero decir la verdad con pocas palabras y no pedirle nada a quien no
  tiene nada.* (I want to tell the truth in few words and ask nothing of anyone who has nothing.)
  Plain words, two short clauses, a moral wish.

## Pronunciation

- *Alejandrino*: five syllables, *a-le-han-DRI-no*.
- *Preciosismo*: four syllables, *pre-sio-SIS-mo*; *cio* is one syllable.
- *Orfebrería*: five syllables, *or-fe-bre-RÍ-a*; the *í* breaks the vowel pair.

## Common mistakes

- Translating *modernismo* as "modernism": say *modernismo* (or "Spanish American modernism"
  with a note).
- Treating it as only decoration: the essay's point is that form was also a stance.
- Counting the Spanish alexandrine like the French one: Spanish counts fourteen syllables (seven
  plus seven), the French tradition twelve, because the two languages count line endings
  differently.
- Quoting a famous first line in a commentary as decoration: describe it instead, and quote only
  what your argument needs, from an edition you cite.

## Key points

- *El modernismo* (about 1880–1915): Spanish America renews the language and influences Spain.
- Martí, Gutiérrez Nájera, Darío, Silva, Nervo; *Azul…* (1888), *Versos sencillos* (1891), the
  *Revista Azul* (1894), *Prosas profanas* (1896), *Cantos de vida y esperanza* (1905).
- Its marks: the swan, exoticism, musicality, synesthesia, preciosity, the alexandrine, a step
  toward free verse.

lessons.title: Se concede el amparo: reading a Mexican judgment
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module is about **[[specialized language]]**: the Spanish of law, medicine, finance and
technology, where a word can have a precise meaning fixed by a law, a standard or a profession.
At C2 you read a specialized text for what it decides and why, and explain it to someone who
isn't a specialist. B2 12h1 (an honors lesson) showed how a Mexican regulation is laid out, and C1 04h1 (another honors lesson) taught
plain-language rewriting. This lesson reads a court ruling, the genre that ties a law to a real
person's case, and then rewrites one for the person it affects.

A note before we start: this lesson explains how legal texts work. It is not legal advice, and
the case in it is invented.

## Terms, not just words

A **[[term]]** (*un término*, a technical term) is a word whose meaning a field fixes. Some of the
terms of a courtroom, beside the everyday words you know:

| Term | In law | Beside |
|---|---|---|
| *el fallo* | the final ruling, the part that decides | B2's *la sentencia*; outside law, a fault (*un fallo técnico*) |
| *el juzgador / la juzgadora* | whoever judges (formal, gender-neutral) | B1's *el juez* |
| *el juzgado* | a lower court of first instance; also its building | B2's *el tribunal*, the general word |
| *la instancia* | a level of court (*en primera instancia*) | also a stage, or a written petition |
| *el demandado / la demandada* | the defendant in a civil suit | B2's *la demanda*; B2's *el acusado* in a criminal case |
| *el litigio, litigar* | a lawsuit; to take part in one | *el litigante / la litigante*: any party or lawyer who litigates |
| *el agravio* | a grievance: each specific way an appellant says a court wronged them | everyday "offense" |

*Litigó durante diez años contra la constructora.* — She litigated against the construction
company for ten years.

## The amparo, in depth

B2 taught *el amparo* as "legal protection". In Mexico the **[[amparo]]** (*el juicio de amparo*) is a
federal lawsuit in which a person asks the federal courts to protect their constitutional rights
against an act of authority: an arrest, a closure order, a law, a ruling.

**Origins.** Historians usually trace it to the constitution of Yucatán of 1841, drafted mainly
by Manuel Crescencio Rejón, and to the federal *Acta de Reformas* of 1847, where Mariano Otero's
proposal brought it to national level; the 1857 and 1917 constitutions kept it, and today
articles 103 and 107 of the Constitution and the Ley de Amparo govern it.

**The parties.** The Ley de Amparo (article 5, in the text current in November 2026) names four:

| Party | Who it is |
|---|---|
| *el quejoso / la quejosa* | the complainant, who asks for protection |
| *la autoridad responsable* | the authority whose act is challenged |
| *el tercero interesado* | a third party with an interest in the act standing (in a lawsuit, the other side) |
| *el Ministerio Público Federal* | the federal prosecution service, which may take part in every amparo |

*El quejoso* is the legal role, not a "complainer". The other key terms:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *el acto reclamado* | the challenged act |
| *la suspensión* | a stay: the act is stopped while the case goes on, so the complainant isn't harmed first |
| *sobreseer, el sobreseimiento* | to dismiss the case without deciding the merits (the act doesn't exist, or a bar applies); the dismissal |
| *improcedente* | inadmissible: the law doesn't allow the action (not "improper") |
| *inconstitucional* | contrary to the Constitution |
| *la potestad* | the legal power to act |
| *el debido proceso* | due process |

Whether an authority had *la potestad* to act, and whether it respected *el debido proceso*, are
the questions an amparo asks most often.

**[[Case law]]** (*la jurisprudencia*) is the body of court decisions that bind other
courts. Careful: English "jurisprudence" usually means legal theory, while Spanish
*jurisprudencia* is binding case law. In Mexico a criterion is published as *una tesis*: here
B2's *la tesis* is not a dissertation but a short, numbered statement of a court's
interpretation. Not every *tesis* binds;
it becomes *jurisprudencia* only under the conditions the Ley de Amparo sets, which have
changed with reforms (a 2021 reform let some Supreme Court rulings bind directly as
*precedentes*). Check the current text before citing a rule. *El precedente* in general is a past decision relied on as a
guide.

**Who decides.** A justice of Mexico's Supreme Court (*la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la
Nación*) is *un ministro* or *una ministra*, not a government minister.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The path of an indirect amparo (simplified)
  accDescr: A simplified flowchart. An act of authority affects a right. The affected person files an amparo claim and becomes the complainant. If the court doesn't admit it, the claim is rejected. If it does, the court can grant a stay. The responsible authority sends its report, a constitutional hearing is held, and the ruling grants the amparo, denies it, or dismisses the case. Any of these can be appealed by review before a collegiate court.
  A["Un acto de autoridad afecta un derecho"] --> B["La persona presenta la demanda de amparo: es la quejosa"]
  B --> C{"¿Se admite la demanda?"}
  C -- no --> D["Se desecha"]
  C -- sí --> E["Suspensión: el juzgado puede detener el acto mientras dura el juicio"]
  E --> F["Informe de la autoridad responsable"]
  F --> G["Audiencia constitucional"]
  G --> H{"Sentencia"}
  H --> I["Se concede el amparo"]
  H --> J["Se niega el amparo"]
  H --> K["Se sobresee en el juicio"]
  I --> L["Recurso de revisión ante un tribunal colegiado"]
  J --> L
  K --> L
```

This is the indirect amparo, filed before a *juzgado de distrito*; the direct amparo, against
final judgments, goes to a higher court. Many steps are left out.

**Background: criminal cases.** An amparo can arise from any field, criminal law included. A
constitutional reform published on June 18, 2008, gave Mexico an accusatory, oral criminal
system, with eight years to put it in place; the deadline, June 18, 2016, is when it applied
across the country. Since then an investigation is kept in *la carpeta de investigación*
(investigation file), which replaced the older *averiguación previa*. The prosecution service
is *el ministerio público* (capitalized for the institution), and the offices that house it
are now usually called *fiscalías* (prosecutor's offices); B2's *el fiscal* is the person.

## How a ruling is built

![A diagram of a ruling's layout, top to bottom. A heading box gives the court, the case number and the parties. Below it, a short line reads VISTOS, para resolver. Then three large blocks: RESULTANDO, labeled what happened in the case; CONSIDERANDO, labeled the court's reasons and legal grounds; then the line Por lo expuesto y fundado, se resuelve; and RESUELVE, labeled the decision, in numbered points. At the bottom, Notifíquese and two signature lines.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After a heading (*el encabezado*: court, case number, parties), a traditional Mexican ruling
opens with *Vistos, para resolver, los autos…* ("having seen the case file, in order to
decide…"), then has three parts:

- *resultandos*: the history of the case, each paragraph starting *PRIMERO, SEGUNDO…*
- *considerandos*: the reasoning, one numbered section per question. Each section is *un
  considerando*; the word is usually plural, *los considerandos*.
- *puntos resolutivos*: the decision, also numbered. Mexican lawyers shorten this to *los
  resolutivos*: *Lea primero los resolutivos* (Read the operative points first).

Many recent rulings, including the Supreme Court's, use plainer headings (*antecedentes,
estudio de fondo, decisión*), but the logic is the same.

**Reading strategy.** Read the *resolutivos* first, then the *considerandos* that support them;
skim the *resultandos*.

## Legal formulas and style

A **[[legal formula]]** is a fixed expression a legal genre requires or expects. You recognize them
as wholes:

| Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *el suscrito / la suscrita* | the undersigned |
| *en lo sucesivo* | hereinafter |
| *en términos de* | under (a law or article) |
| *por lo expuesto y fundado, se resuelve* | for the reasons and on the grounds stated, it is resolved |
| *fundar y motivar* | to state the legal grounds and the reasons |
| *la Justicia de la Unión ampara y protege a…* | the federal courts grant protection to… |
| *notifíquese* | let it be notified |

*Fundar y motivar* comes from article 16 of the Constitution, which requires a written act of a
competent authority that states its legal basis and its reasons. To *fundar* is to cite the
exact rules that apply; to *motivar* is to explain why this case fits them. *La orden no está
debidamente fundada ni motivada* (The order doesn't properly state its grounds or its reasons) is
a finding you'll often meet in amparo rulings.

Style: the institution speaks, so rulings use the passive with *se* (*se admitió la demanda*),
the impersonal (*procede sobreseer*), nouns for actions and long periods. Older statutes keep the
future subjunctive (*el que causare un daño…*, whoever causes damage; B2 12h1): read it as a
present subjunctive, never write it.

## Reading a ruling

The text below is invented. Read the *resolutivos* first.

> **Juzgado Primero de Distrito (ficticio). Juicio de amparo indirecto 512/2026**
>
> Quejosa: Lucía Ramírez Ocampo. Autoridades responsables: Presidente Municipal y Director de
> Reglamentos del Municipio de San Isidro del Monte.
>
> VISTOS, para resolver, los autos del juicio de amparo 512/2026, y
>
> RESULTANDO:
>
> PRIMERO. Por escrito presentado el 9 de febrero de 2026, Lucía Ramírez Ocampo, por propio
> derecho, solicitó el amparo y protección de la Justicia Federal contra la orden de clausura de
> su panadería, ubicada en la calle Morelos 41, y contra su ejecución, actos que atribuyó a las
> autoridades señaladas al rubro.
>
> SEGUNDO. Se admitió la demanda y se concedió la suspensión para el efecto de que el
> establecimiento no fuera clausurado mientras se resolvía el juicio. Seguidos los trámites de
> ley, se celebró la audiencia constitucional.
>
> CONSIDERANDO:
>
> PRIMERO. Este juzgado es competente para conocer del presente juicio en términos de los
> artículos 103 y 107 de la Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos.
>
> SEGUNDO. El Presidente Municipal, al rendir su informe, negó la existencia del acto reclamado,
> sin que la quejosa aportara prueba alguna en contrario. Por tanto, procede sobreseer en el
> juicio respecto de dicha autoridad.
>
> TERCERO. El Director de Reglamentos, en cambio, reconoció haber emitido la orden, y alegó que
> el juicio es improcedente porque la quejosa debió agotar antes un recurso ante el propio
> municipio. No le asiste la razón: la orden no expresa fundamento legal alguno, y en ese supuesto
> la ley no obliga a agotar los recursos ordinarios antes de acudir al amparo.
>
> CUARTO. Es fundado el argumento de la quejosa. Todo acto de molestia debe constar por escrito,
> provenir de autoridad competente y estar fundado y motivado. La orden reclamada, sin embargo, se
> limita a mencionar "irregularidades en el funcionamiento", sin precisar cuáles ni en qué
> disposición se apoya. Ello impide a la quejosa defenderse y vulnera su derecho al debido
> proceso. Este criterio es acorde con la jurisprudencia y los precedentes de los tribunales
> federales en la materia.
>
> QUINTO. Lo anterior no significa que la orden sea inconstitucional por su contenido, ni que la
> autoridad carezca de potestad para verificar los establecimientos comerciales. El amparo se
> concede para el efecto de que la autoridad deje sin efectos la orden y, si lo estima procedente,
> emita una nueva, debidamente fundada y motivada.
>
> Por lo expuesto y fundado, se resuelve:
>
> PRIMERO. Se sobresee en el juicio respecto del acto atribuido al Presidente Municipal.
>
> SEGUNDO. La Justicia de la Unión ampara y protege a Lucía Ramírez Ocampo contra el acto del
> Director de Reglamentos, para los efectos precisados en el considerando quinto.
>
> Notifíquese personalmente.

**Summary in English.** A baker, Lucía Ramírez, filed an amparo against a municipal order to
close her bakery. The court admitted the case and granted a stay so the bakery stayed open. It
dismissed the case against the mayor, who denied giving the order (she offered no proof
otherwise). Against the director of regulations, who admitted the order, it rejected his
inadmissibility argument and found the order unlawful because it cited no legal basis and gave no
concrete reasons, which left her unable to defend herself. The ruling stresses that the
municipality may still inspect businesses and may issue a new, properly grounded order. Decision:
case dismissed as to the mayor; amparo granted as to the director.

**Glosses.** *Por propio derecho* = on her own behalf; *al rubro* = in the heading; *seguidos los
trámites de ley* = once the legal steps were completed; *rendir su informe* = to submit its
report; *no le asiste la razón* = he is not right; *agotar un recurso* = to exhaust a remedy;
*el acto de molestia* = an act that interferes with someone's rights; *para el efecto de que* = so
that (the ruling's specific effect).

## Explaining the ruling to the complainant

C1 04h1's method applies: the decision first, the reader's words, and every limit the court
set.

> Estimada señora Ramírez:
>
> Le explico lo que decidió la jueza en su caso. En lo principal, le dio la razón. La orden para
> cerrar su panadería no decía qué ley se aplicaba ni qué problema concreto había, y la
> Constitución exige que toda orden de una autoridad explique ambas cosas, para que la persona
> pueda defenderse. Por eso la orden quedará sin efecto.
>
> Sobre el presidente municipal, la jueza no estudió el fondo: él dijo que no había dado la
> orden, y no pudimos demostrar lo contrario.
>
> Esto no significa que el municipio ya no pueda revisar su negocio. Puede dar una nueva orden,
> pero tendrá que explicar bien sus razones. El municipio también puede impugnar la decisión; si
> lo hace, le avisaré de inmediato.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Lic. Andrés Gil Montaño

Dear Ms. Ramírez: Let me explain what the judge decided in your case. On the main point, she
ruled in your favor. The order to close your bakery didn't say which law applied or what the
specific problem was, and the Constitution requires every order from an authority to explain
both, so that the person can defend herself. That's why the order will be void. As for the mayor,
the judge didn't look at the substance: he said he hadn't given the order, and we couldn't prove
otherwise. This doesn't mean the municipality can no longer inspect your business. It can issue a
new order, but it will have to explain its reasons properly. The municipality can also challenge
the decision; if it does, I'll let you know right away. Sincerely, Andrés Gil Montaño, attorney.

The letter turns *se sobresee* into what it means for her, keeps the court's limit and adds no
promise.

## Pronunciation

- *sobreseer*: four syllables, *so-bre-se-ER*; both *e*'s are pronounced. *Sobreseimiento*: five,
  *so-bre-sei-MIEN-to*.
- *jurisprudencia*: *ju-ris-pru-DEN-sia* (with seseo, *c* = *s*).
- *improcedente*: *im-pro-se-DEN-te*; *litigio*: *li-TI-hio*, three syllables.

## Common mistakes

- **False friends**: *jurisprudencia* (case law), *el ministro* (a justice), *improcedente*
  (inadmissible).
- **Mixing parties**: a civil suit has *el demandado*; an amparo has *la autoridad responsable*.
- **Dropping the court's limits**: "she won, the bakery can never be closed" changes the ruling.
- **Formulas in ordinary prose**: *en lo sucesivo* and *el suscrito* don't belong in a letter to
  a client.
- **Producing the future subjunctive**: recognize *causare*; write *cause*.

## Key points

- Specialized texts use terms whose meaning the field fixes; check them, don't guess from
  English.
- The amparo protects constitutional rights against acts of authority; its parties are the
  *quejoso*, the *autoridad responsable*, the *tercero interesado* and the *Ministerio Público
  Federal*.
- A ruling has *resultandos* (facts), *considerandos* (reasons) and *resolutivos* (decision):
  read the decision first.
- *Fundar y motivar*: every act of authority must state its legal basis and its reasons.
- A plain explanation keeps the decision, its reasons and its limits.

lessons.title: Cuadro clínico: from the clinical record to the patient
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 read a ruling and explained it to the person it affected. This lesson does the same
with medicine: it reads the notes doctors write for each other, then turns one into an
explanation for the patient. B2 gave you the everyday words of health (*el diagnóstico, el
tratamiento, la recaída*) and C1 the words of public health (*la incidencia, la prevalencia*).
Here you meet the record itself: its sections, its Greek and Latin terms, its clipped style and
its careful hedges.

The patient and the notes in this lesson are invented. Nothing here is medical advice: if you
have a question about your own health, ask a health professional.

## The clinical record

The **[[clinical record]]** is the set of documents a health service keeps on each patient. In
Mexico it is *el expediente clínico*, and a federal standard, NOM-004-SSA3-2012, sets what it
must contain and that it be kept for at least five years. Spain says *la historia clínica*,
which in Mexico usually names one part of the record, the first full history. The main sections:

| Section | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| *ficha de identificación* | name, age, sex, occupation, record number |
| *anamnesis* (in Mexico also *el interrogatorio*) | *antecedentes heredofamiliares* (family history), *antecedentes personales patológicos y no patológicos*, *padecimiento actual* (present illness) |
| *exploración física* | vital signs, weight and height, what the examination finds |
| *estudios* | lab results, imaging |
| *diagnóstico, diagnóstico diferencial* | the conclusion, and the alternatives still being weighed |
| *plan* or *indicaciones* | treatment, tests ordered, follow-up |

*La anamnesis* is the history the patient tells. Here C1's *el antecedente* (background) has its
medical sense: a past condition or a relative's illness that matters now. *Antecedente de
infarto en el padre* means the father had a heart attack. *El padecimiento* is the condition the
patient has, a Mexican favorite in records (*padecimiento actual*); it comes from *padecer* (to
suffer from), which isn't an earlier word: *padece diabetes desde hace ocho años*.

Each later visit adds *una nota de evolución* (a progress note). When a patient leaves the
hospital, the record closes with a summary of the stay; many Spanish-speaking countries call it
*la epicrisis*, while Mexican hospitals usually say *la nota de egreso* or *el resumen clínico*.

![A one-page clinical record laid out as a form. A header strip reads Expediente clínico with a record number. Below it, six labeled boxes from top to bottom: Ficha de identificación, Anamnesis, Exploración física, Estudios, Diagnóstico and Plan. A narrower box at the bottom right reads Nota de evolución, with a date.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Greek and Latin at work

Medical Spanish builds terms from Greek and Latin parts, as lesson 04 showed for learned words
in general. Knowing a dozen pieces lets you decode hundreds of terms:

| Piece | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-itis* | inflammation | *gastritis, artritis* |
| *-algia* | pain | *neuralgia, mialgia* |
| *-emia* | in the blood | *anemia, glucemia* |
| *hiper- / hipo-* | above / below normal | *hipertensión, hipoglucemia* |
| *-logía* | study of | *etiología, epidemiología* |
| *a-* | without | *asintomático* |
| *co-* | together | *comorbilidad* |

So *la etiología* is the cause of a disease (*de etiología desconocida*, of unknown cause); *la
sintomatología* is the symptoms as a whole; *la epidemiología* studies how diseases spread in
populations; *la comorbilidad* is another disease present at the same time; *la cronicidad* is
the quality of being chronic (B2's *crónico*); *la hipertensión* is high blood pressure. A
patient with no symptoms is *asintomático* (*asintomática*).

A tumor is *benigno* (it doesn't invade other tissue) or *maligno* (it can invade and spread). A
malignant tumor's spread to another organ is *la metástasis*, plural *las metástasis*. To tell
them apart, doctors take *una biopsia*, a small sample of tissue. After treatment, a disease may
go into *remisión* (remission), and it may leave *secuelas* (lasting aftereffects, usually
plural).

## The style of a note

Doctors write for colleagues and in a hurry, so a clinical note is telegraphic:

- **No subject, few articles:** *Femenina de 58 años. Acude por tos.* (A 58-year-old woman. She
  comes in for a cough.)
- **Reporting verbs** for what the patient says: *refiere* (reports), *niega* (denies: *niega
  fiebre*, she reports no fever), *acude por* (comes in for).
- **Nouns for events:** *inicio de tos hace seis semanas* (onset of cough six weeks ago).
- **Impersonal *se*** for what the team does: *se solicita hemograma* (a blood count is ordered).
  In Mexico the blood count is also *la biometría hemática*.
- **Abbreviations:** *TA* (blood pressure), *FC* (heart rate), *IMC* (body-mass index).

## Hedged diagnosis

A diagnosis is often a probability, and the record says so precisely:

| Hedge | Strength |
|---|---|
| *compatible con* | the findings fit, without proving it |
| *probable, probablemente* | likely |
| *sugestivo de* | points toward |
| *a descartar* | still to be ruled out (*descartar* = to rule out) |
| *diagnóstico diferencial* | the list of alternatives |

*Cuadro clínico* is the clinical picture, all the signs and symptoms together: *un cuadro
compatible con gastritis*.

## A progress note

> **Hospital General (ficticio). Consulta externa de Medicina Interna. Nota de evolución**
>
> 12 de octubre de 2026, 10:40 h
>
> **Ficha de identificación.** Rosalba Ortega Ruiz, femenina de 58 años, contadora, originaria y
> residente de Puebla.
>
> **Antecedentes heredofamiliares.** Madre con hipertensión arterial sistémica; padre finado por
> infarto agudo de miocardio a los 66 años.
>
> **Antecedentes personales patológicos.** Diabetes tipo 2 de ocho años de evolución, en
> tratamiento con hipoglucemiante oral. Linfoma de Hodgkin a los 34 años, tratado con
> quimioterapia; en remisión completa desde hace 24 años, sin secuelas aparentes. Niega alergias
> y tabaquismo.
>
> **Padecimiento actual.** Acude a control de hipertensión arterial diagnosticada hace tres meses
> en un tamizaje de su centro de trabajo, cuando estaba asintomática. Se inició tratamiento
> antihipertensivo en la consulta previa. Refiere tos seca, persistente, de seis semanas de
> evolución, de predominio nocturno, que inició dos semanas después de comenzar el fármaco. Niega fiebre,
> disnea y otra sintomatología respiratoria. Refiere cefalea occipital ocasional, leve. Refiere
> también una lesión pigmentada en el antebrazo derecho que ha crecido en el último año.
>
> **Exploración física.** TA 148/92 mmHg, FC 78 lpm, temperatura 36.5 °C. Peso 74 kg, talla
> 1.60 m, IMC 28.9. Consciente, orientada. Campos pulmonares bien ventilados. Ruidos cardiacos
> rítmicos, sin soplos. En antebrazo derecho, lesión pigmentada de 7 mm, de bordes irregulares.
>
> **Estudios.** Hemograma dentro de parámetros normales. Glucosa en ayuno 132 mg/dL.
>
> **Impresión diagnóstica.**
> 1. Hipertensión arterial sistémica en descontrol. Comorbilidad: diabetes tipo 2. Otros
> factores de riesgo cardiovascular: sobrepeso, antecedente familiar.
> 2. Tos seca, probablemente secundaria a efecto adverso del antihipertensivo. Diagnóstico
> diferencial: infección respiratoria, enfermedad por reflujo, poco probables por el cuadro
> clínico.
> 3. Lesión pigmentada de etiología a determinar; a descartar lesión maligna.
>
> **Plan.** Se suspende el antihipertensivo actual y se sustituye por uno de otro grupo. Se
> solicita interconsulta a Dermatología para valoración y, en su caso, biopsia. Registro
> domiciliario de la presión arterial. Se explica el plan a la paciente y se resuelven sus dudas.
> Cita de control en cuatro semanas.
>
> Dra. Mariana Celis Duarte, Medicina Interna

**Summary in English.** A progress note on a 58-year-old accountant. Her mother had high blood
pressure; her father died of a heart attack. She has had type 2 diabetes for eight years and had
lymphoma at 34, in complete remission. Her high blood pressure, found at a workplace screening
three months ago, is not yet controlled. A dry cough began two weeks after the new drug, which is
probably the cause; she also has mild headaches and a growing dark spot on her arm. Plan: switch
drugs, refer her to dermatology (possibly for a biopsy), home blood-pressure readings, and a
follow-up in four weeks.

**Glosses.** *Finado* = deceased; *de ocho años de evolución* = for eight years; *el
hipoglucemiante* = a glucose-lowering drug; *de predominio nocturno* = mostly at night; *la
disnea* = shortness of breath; *la cefalea* = headache; *lpm* = beats per minute; *en
descontrol* = uncontrolled; *el efecto adverso* = an adverse (side) effect, also B2's *el efecto
secundario*; *la interconsulta* = a referral to another specialty; *en su caso* = if needed.

## From the record to the patient

The note is accurate but closed to the patient. The rewrite keeps every fact and every hedge
and changes everything else: *usted*, everyday words (*la presión* for *la tensión arterial*, *la
mancha* for *la lesión pigmentada*), one idea per sentence, what happens next, and an
invitation to ask. It doesn't reassure beyond the evidence: the note says *a descartar*, so the
letter says "we don't know yet". In a consultation the same goes for informed consent
(*el consentimiento informado*): the patient agrees to a procedure only after understanding
what it is, its risks and its alternatives.

> Estimada señora Ortega:
>
> Le resumo lo que platicamos el 12 de octubre. Su presión sigue más alta de lo que buscamos, y
> como usted tiene diabetes, nos importa mucho controlarla.
>
> La tos probablemente se debe al medicamento para la presión: a algunas personas les pasa. Por
> eso lo cambiamos por otro. Si la tos no mejora, buscaremos otras causas.
>
> La mancha del brazo todavía no sabemos qué es. La va a revisar el servicio de Dermatología y,
> si lo considera necesario, tomará una pequeña muestra para analizarla.
>
> Anote su presión en casa, como le expliqué, y tráigame las notas en cuatro semanas. Si tiene
> cualquier duda, llámeme.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Dra. Mariana Celis Duarte

Dear Ms. Ortega: Here's a summary of what we talked about on October 12. Your blood pressure is
still higher than we're aiming for, and since you have diabetes, controlling it matters a lot.
The cough is probably due to the blood-pressure medicine: it happens to some people. That's why
we switched it for another one. If the cough doesn't get better, we'll look for other causes. We
don't know yet what the spot on your arm is. The dermatology department will examine it and, if
it thinks it necessary, take a small sample to analyze. Write down your blood pressure at home, as I
explained, and bring me the notes in four weeks. If you have any questions, call me. Sincerely,
Dr. Mariana Celis Duarte.

## Screening and public health

Rosalba's diagnosis came from *el tamizaje*, screening people who have no symptoms. *Tamizaje*
is usual in Mexico and parts of Latin America; Spain says *el cribado*. High blood pressure is a
classic case for it, because it is often silent and is a major *factor de riesgo* for heart and
kidney disease. The World Health Organization's fact sheet on hypertension (dated September 25,
2025) gives its definition as a reading of 140/90 mmHg or more measured on two different days,
and estimates that in 2024 about 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 had hypertension, 44% of them
without knowing it. That is the language of *la epidemiología*: figures with their population,
their year and their source.

## Pronunciation

- *anamnesis*: *a-nam-NE-sis*; *epicrisis*: *e-pi-CRI-sis*; *metástasis*: *me-TAS-ta-sis*. All
  three keep the same form in the plural.
- *etiología*: five syllables, *e-tio-lo-HÍ-a*; *hemograma*: *e-mo-GRA-ma* (silent *h*).

## Common mistakes

- **Calques**: *el expediente clínico* (not *el récord médico*); *la tensión arterial* or *la
  presión arterial*, never *la presión de sangre* in a record.
- **Losing the hedge**: *probablemente secundaria a* is not *causada por*. A patient letter that
  says "the medicine caused your cough" claims more than the note.
- **Record style in the letter**: *Femenina de 58 años* is for colleagues; to the patient, full
  sentences and *usted*.
- **Over-reading terms**: in a record, *la sintomatología* is the patient's symptoms as a whole, not a field of study.

## Key points

- *El expediente clínico* has a fixed structure: identification, history, examination, studies,
  diagnosis, plan, and progress notes.
- Greek and Latin pieces (*-itis, -algia, -emia, hiper-, hipo-*) decode most terms.
- Notes are telegraphic and hedged: *refiere, niega, compatible con, probable, a descartar*.
- A letter to a patient keeps every fact and every hedge and adds no reassurance the record
  doesn't support.

lessons.title: La Junta de Gobierno decidió…: central-bank and financial Spanish
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 20h2 (an honors lesson) read economic news and a short central-bank statement, and turned
the statement into three plain sentences: *los puntos base* (basis points; 25 = a quarter of a
percentage point), *la inflación subyacente* (core inflation), *sesgado al alza* (tilted upward).
This lesson goes to the source documents: the full monetary-policy statement, the signals about
the future that markets read word by word, and a company's financial statements. The skill is
the same as in lessons 13 and 14: read a specialized text for exactly what it says, then report
it without adding or losing anything, hedges above all.

Figures in this lesson are invented or dated. Nothing here is investment advice.

## Mexico's central bank in its own terms

The Banco de México (Banxico) has been autonomous since April 1994. Its law gives it a
priority objective, *procurar la estabilidad del poder adquisitivo de la moneda nacional*: to
keep the national currency's purchasing power stable. That is its mandate (*el mandato*). In
practice it pursues an inflation target of 3%, with a variability range of one percentage point
either way. Decisions are taken by *la Junta de Gobierno* (the governing board), five members: a
governor and four deputy governors. Its main instrument is *la tasa objetivo* (the target
rate) for overnight interbank lending, and the whole set of decisions about rates and money is
*la política monetaria* (monetary policy). (Sources and dates in this course's notes; check
banxico.org.mx for current figures, which this lesson doesn't give.)

## The anatomy of a statement

Central-bank statements follow a fixed order, so you can read them quickly:

| Part | Typical language |
|---|---|
| decision and vote | *La Junta de Gobierno decidió por unanimidad / por mayoría mantener (reducir, incrementar) la tasa objetivo en 25 puntos base* |
| external context | *la desaceleración de la economía mundial; un entorno de elevada volatilidad* |
| domestic activity | *la economía se expandió a un ritmo moderado; persiste holgura* |
| inflation | *la inflación general; la inflación subyacente; las expectativas de inflación* |
| balance of risks | *el balance de riesgos se mantiene sesgado al alza / a la baja / equilibrado* |
| guidance | *Hacia delante, la Junta evaluará…* |

*El balance de riesgos* weighs what could push inflation up against what could pull it down.
*La holgura* is slack: spare capacity in the economy (idle workers, unused plants), which
holds prices down. *Las expectativas de inflación* are what businesses and analysts expect
inflation to be. A policy that keeps rates high to cool demand is *restrictiva*: *una postura
monetaria restrictiva* (a tight monetary stance).

## Forward guidance

**[[Forward guidance]]** is what a central bank says about its future decisions. Markets read every
word, because a small change in a phrase moves rates and the exchange rate. The press calls a
bank that worries most about inflation a hawk and one that worries most about growth a dove
(*halcón* and *paloma* are used in Spanish too). The same scale, in phrases:

![A vertical scale from más flexible (paloma) at the top to más restrictivo (halcón) at the bottom, with five statement phrases in order. Prevé continuar con el ciclo de recortes. Evaluará la pertinencia de reanudar los recortes. Mantendrá la tasa sin cambios por un periodo prolongado. No se descarta un ajuste adicional al alza. Será necesario incrementar la tasa. A note at the bottom says the scale is illustrative and that the context of each statement matters.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The scale is illustrative: "hold for a long time" is a hawkish signal after a series of cuts,
and the same phrase could read differently in another cycle.

## Hedges, and how to keep them

Forward guidance is hedged on purpose. These are the main devices:

| Device | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *se prevé / se anticipa que* | *Se prevé que la inflación converja (convergerá) a su meta en 2027.* | it is expected: both moods occur after *se prevé que* |
| modal conditional | *podría, sería necesario* | possibility, not commitment |
| condition without *si* | *De materializarse estos riesgos…* | should these risks materialize (lesson 06 covers these conditions) |
| *no se descarta* | *No se descarta un ajuste adicional.* | it isn't ruled out |
| *en función de* | *en función de la evolución de los datos* | depending on |

The reporter's rule: **the verb must keep the strength.** *El banco prevé* is not *el banco
asegura*; *evaluará la pertinencia de recortar* is not *recortará*; *no se descarta* is not
*planea*. A report that upgrades a hedge into a promise is wrong, even if every number is right.

## A statement

> **Banco Central de la República de Altamar (ficticio). Comunicado de política monetaria**
>
> Ciudad de Altamar, 5 de noviembre de 2026
>
> La Junta de Gobierno decidió, por mayoría, mantener la tasa objetivo en 7.25 %. Dos miembros
> votaron por reducirla en 25 puntos base.
>
> **Entorno externo.** La actividad económica mundial continúa mostrando una desaceleración, en
> un contexto de elevada volatilidad en los mercados financieros. Los diferenciales de los bonos
> gubernamentales de las economías emergentes se ampliaron ligeramente. Una de las principales
> calificadoras modificó la perspectiva de la deuda soberana del país de estable a negativa, sin
> cambiar su calificación.
>
> **Actividad interna.** La economía nacional se expandió a un ritmo moderado en el tercer
> trimestre. Se estima que persiste cierta holgura, en particular en el mercado laboral.
>
> **Inflación.** La inflación general anual disminuyó de 4.6 % en septiembre a 4.3 % en octubre.
> La inflación subyacente, que excluye los componentes más volátiles, se ubicó en 4.5 % y ha
> mostrado una mayor resistencia a bajar, sobre todo en los servicios. Las expectativas de
> inflación para los próximos doce meses se mantienen por encima de la meta de 3 %; las de largo
> plazo permanecen estables. La moneda nacional registró una depreciación de 2 % frente al dólar
> en el periodo, lo que podría presionar los precios de las mercancías importadas.
>
> **Balance de riesgos.** La Junta considera que el balance de riesgos para la trayectoria
> prevista de la inflación se mantiene sesgado al alza. Entre los riesgos al alza destacan una
> depreciación adicional de la moneda y presiones de costos en los servicios; a la baja, una
> desaceleración de la actividad más pronunciada de lo previsto.
>
> **Decisión y perspectivas.** Con base en lo anterior, la Junta decidió mantener una postura
> monetaria restrictiva. Se prevé que la inflación converja a su meta en el segundo semestre de
> 2027. Hacia delante, la Junta evaluará la pertinencia de reanudar los recortes, en función de la
> evolución de la inflación subyacente. De materializarse los riesgos al alza, no se descartaría
> mantener la tasa sin cambios por un periodo más prolongado. La Junta reitera su compromiso con
> su mandato prioritario: procurar la estabilidad del poder adquisitivo de la moneda nacional.

**Summary in English.** By a majority, the board held its target rate at 7.25%; two members
voted for a quarter-point cut. Abroad, growth is slowing and markets are volatile; emerging-market
bond spreads widened a little, and a rating agency moved the country's outlook to negative
without changing the rating. At home, growth was moderate and some slack remains. Headline
inflation fell to 4.3%, but core inflation (4.5%) is slow to fall; expectations stay above the
3% target, and the currency's 2% depreciation could push up import prices. Risks are tilted
upward. The board keeps a tight stance, expects inflation to reach target in the second half of
2027, will consider resuming cuts depending on core inflation, and might hold longer if upside
risks materialize.

**Glosses.** *Se ampliaron* = widened; *la deuda soberana* = sovereign (government) debt; *se
ubicó en* = stood at (common in Latin American financial writing); *la trayectoria prevista* = the expected path;
*hacia delante* = going forward; *evaluará la pertinencia de* = will assess whether it is
appropriate to; *reanudar* = to resume.

## Reporting it with every hedge

> **Altamar deja su tasa en 7.25%; dos miembros de la Junta pedían un recorte**
>
> El Banco Central de Altamar mantuvo este jueves su tasa objetivo en 7.25%, en una decisión
> dividida: dos integrantes de la Junta de Gobierno votaron por reducirla en un cuarto de punto.
>
> La institución informó que la inflación bajó a 4.3% en octubre, aunque la subyacente, de 4.5%,
> se resiste a ceder. Prevé que la inflación alcance la meta de 3% en el segundo semestre de 2027.
>
> Sobre sus próximos pasos, el banco indicó que evaluará si reanuda los recortes según la
> evolución de la inflación subyacente, y advirtió que, si se materializan riesgos como una mayor
> depreciación de la moneda, podría mantener la tasa sin cambios por más tiempo.

Altamar leaves its rate at 7.25%; two board members wanted a cut. The Central Bank of Altamar
held its target rate at 7.25% on Thursday in a split decision: two members of the governing board
voted to cut it by a quarter point. The institution said inflation fell to 4.3% in October,
although core inflation, at 4.5%, is slow to give way. It expects inflation to reach the 3% target
in the second half of 2027. On its next steps, the bank said it will assess whether to resume
cuts depending on how core inflation evolves, and warned that if risks such as a further
depreciation of the currency materialize, it could hold the rate for longer.

The report imitates a Mexican newspaper, which usually writes *7.25%* with no space; the
statement follows the RAE's *7.25 %*. Every hedge survives: *prevé, evaluará si, podría*. The
report even turns *no se descartaría* into *podría*, the same strength in plainer words.

## Reading a balance sheet

A company's financial statements (*los estados financieros*; one is *un estado financiero*)
include the balance sheet, *el balance general*, which lists what the company owns and how it is
financed on one date:

![A balance sheet for a fictional company, Cerámicas del Bajío, in millions of pesos. The left column, Activo, lists Activo circulante (cash 30, accounts receivable 50, inventories 40, subtotal 120) and Activo no circulante (machinery and equipment 180, real estate 100, subtotal 280), with Total activo 400. The right column lists Pasivo (suppliers 40, short-term loans 30, bonds issued 150, total 220) and Capital contable (share capital 100, retained earnings 80, total 180), with Total pasivo más capital 400.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *El activo* (assets): what it owns. *El pasivo* (liabilities): what it owes. *El capital
  contable* (equity, the usual Mexican term; also *el patrimonio*): what belongs to the owners.
  Assets always equal liabilities plus equity.
- *La liquidez* (liquidity) is the ability to pay short-term debts: here current assets of 120
  against short-term liabilities of 70, about 1.7 to 1.
- *La solvencia* (solvency) is the ability to meet all obligations in the long run.
- *El apalancamiento* (leverage) is the use of debt to finance the business: here liabilities
  of 220 against equity of 180, about 1.2 to 1. *El endeudamiento* is borrowing, or the level of
  debt.
- *El dividendo* is the share of profits paid to shareholders (C1's *el accionista*).
- *Un bono* is a bond, a debt security (not B2's *la complicidad*, a bond between people). A
  *calificadora* (credit rating agency; in full *agencia calificadora*) rates it, and gives an
  outlook, *una perspectiva*: *estable, positiva, negativa*. *El diferencial* is the spread, the
  gap between two interest rates.

A currency loses value through *la depreciación* and gains it through *la apreciación*; in
accounting, *la depreciación* is also the loss of value of a machine over time. *La volatilidad*
is how sharply a price swings.

The annual report (*el informe anual*) wraps the statements in prose: the year's results, the
risks, the outlook. Its language mixes the statement's hedges with the optimism of a company
talking about itself, so read its verbs as carefully as a central bank's.

## Pronunciation

- *apalancamiento*: *a-pa-lan-ka-MIEN-to*; *endeudamiento*: *en-deu-da-MIEN-to* (*deu* is one
  syllable).
- *subyacente*: *sub-ya-SEN-te*; the *b* closes the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

- ***Un billón* is a trillion** (a million millions); English "billion" is *mil millones*.
- **Points and percent**: a rise from 4.3% to 4.6% is *0.3 puntos porcentuales* (30 basis
  points), not "0.3%".
- **Upgrading hedges**: *prevé* is not *asegura*; *no se descarta* is not *planea*.
- **Calques**: *actual* means current, not "actual"; liabilities are *el pasivo*, not *las
  responsabilidades*.

## Key points

- A statement runs: decision and vote, context, inflation, balance of risks, guidance.
- Forward guidance signals future decisions; small changes in wording matter.
- Report hedges at their own strength: *prevé, podría, evaluará, no se descarta, de
  materializarse*.
- On the balance sheet, assets equal liabilities plus equity; liquidity is short-term, solvency
  long-term, leverage the weight of debt.
