lessons.title: Un semestre en Salamanca: reading and hearing Spain's Spanish
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 said that Spain's educated norm is one standard among several. This lesson is about
understanding it, and the colloquial Spanish around it, well enough to study or work in Spain.
Everything here is for recognition: you'll read and hear it, and you keep writing Mexican
Spanish. A2 05 named Spain's *le vi*, B2 01 compared the past tenses of Mexico and Spain, and C1
04h2 (an honors lesson) described Spain's sounds, such as the *th* of *distinción* in *gracias*.
Here the focus is grammar and words.

A note on listening: this lesson's listening questions use a voice set to Spain's Spanish
(es-ES), but device voices vary and none reproduces real regional speech. Spanish radio,
podcasts and television are the real practice.

## *Vosotros* in every tense

In most of Spain, *vosotros* is the familiar "you all" and *ustedes* the formal one (in the
Canary Islands and western Andalusia *ustedes* is used for both). You will never need to produce
these forms, but you must recognize them at once:

| Tense | *hablar* | *comer* | *vivir* |
|---|---|---|---|
| present | *habláis* | *coméis* | *vivís* |
| preterite | *hablasteis* | *comisteis* | *vivisteis* |
| imperfect | *hablabais* | *comíais* | *vivíais* |
| future / conditional | *hablaréis / hablaríais* | *comeréis / comeríais* | *viviréis / viviríais* |
| present / imperfect subjunctive | *habléis / hablarais* | *comáis / comierais* | *viváis / vivierais* |
| perfect | *habéis hablado* | *habéis comido* | *habéis vivido* |
| command | *hablad* | *comed* | *vivid* |

The pronouns are *os* (*os veo*, I'll see you all) and *vuestro* (*vuestra casa*). A reflexive
command drops the *-d*: *sentaos* (sit down), *callaos* (be quiet). In speech you'll often hear
the infinitive as the command, *¡Sentaros!*, which the RAE's grammar treats as colloquial, not as
the written norm.

## Leísmo: *le vi* for a man

A2 05 showed that much of Spain, especially the center and north, says *le* where Mexico says
*lo* for a man as a direct object: *A Juan le vi ayer* (I saw Juan yesterday). This is
**[[leísmo]]** (*el leísmo*, lesson 19's word). The RAE's reference works accept it for one male
person, so it appears in Spain's careful writing too; the use of *le* for things (*el libro le
compré*) and for women is not accepted. Mexican writing keeps *lo*, and so do you. When you read *le
conocí* or *les vi* in a Spanish text, read "him" or "them".

## Today's events in the perfect

B2 01 showed that most of Spain uses the perfect for events of today: *Esta mañana he salido
temprano* (I left early this morning), where Mexico says *salí*. In Spain the perfect marks the
time frame "today, this week, this year"; the preterite marks a finished time before it (*Ayer
salí temprano*). You'll meet this in every Spanish e-mail. Read *he salido* as a simple past.

## *A por*: going to fetch something

In Spain *ir a por* means "to go and get": *Voy a por pan* (I'm going for bread); *Bajo a por el
periódico* (I'm going down for the paper). Mexico says *voy por pan*. The RAE's works describe
*a por* as typical of Spain, where it alternates with *por* alone, and as odd to speakers in the
Americas, who use only *por*; FundéuRAE, which bases its advice on them, sees no reason to censure
it. Recognize it; you don't need it.

## Spain's colloquial words

The words below are labeled "Spain" because that is where they are usual; some are heard
elsewhere too. The online DLE marks *currar* and *flipar* "*coloq. Esp.*" but gives *molar* no
country mark. All of them are informal unless the table says otherwise.

| Word | Meaning | Mexican equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| *currar*, *el curro* | to work (hard); job, work | *chambear*, B1's *la chamba* |
| *flipar* | to be amazed, to freak out: *¡Flipo!* | C1's *alucinar* |
| *molar* | to be cool, to like: *Me mola tu chaqueta* | *me late*, *está padre* |
| *el chaval*, *la chavala* | kid, youngster | *el chavo*, *la chava* |
| *majo*, *maja* | nice, likable | *buena onda* |
| *cutre* | tacky, shabby (one form for both genders) | *chafa*, *de mala calidad* |
| *la pasta* | money ("dough") | C1's *la lana* |
| *el chollo* | bargain, great deal | *una ganga* |
| *la peña* | group of friends, crowd | C1's *la palomilla* |
| *el enchufe* | connections, pull: *entró por enchufe* | *las palancas* |
| *¡venga!* | come on!, OK!, go on! | C1's *¡ándale!* |

B1 24h1 (an honors lesson) taught *¡vale!* (OK!) and *guay* (cool), and A1 words have Spanish
senses too: *el tío* (uncle) is also "guy" (*un tío muy majo*), and *el puente* (bridge) is a long
weekend made by a holiday next to a weekend, often with a working day taken off between them, a
sense Mexico uses as well (*el puente de septiembre*).

Going out and the city:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *la tasca* | a simple tavern, a bar |
| *la caña* | a small draft beer (*cane, reed* in general Spanish) |
| *el tapeo* | going round bars for tapas: *ir de tapeo* |
| *el bocadillo* | a sandwich in a baguette; in Mexico a *bocadillo* is often a small snack |
| *el chiringuito* | a beach bar or stall |
| *el botellón* | a street drinking party of young people |
| *la movida* | a cultural scene; *la Movida madrileña*, Madrid's countercultural scene, usually dated from the late 1970s to the mid-1980s |
| *castizo* | traditional, authentically Spanish (often of Madrid) |
| *el atasco* | traffic jam (Mexico *el embotellamiento*, A2's *el tráfico*) |
| *el grifo* | faucet (Mexico A1's *la llave*, whose first sense is "key") |

University and work, for words a C2 user writes about Spain:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *el colegio mayor* | a university residence hall with its own activities |
| *el máster* | a postgraduate master's program (Mexico A2's *la maestría*); plural *másteres* or *másters*, both accepted in the DPD's 2024 second edition as Excélsior reported it |
| *las oposiciones* | competitive exams for civil-service and public teaching posts: *preparar unas oposiciones* |

![A street in Salamanca. On the left, a small bar with the sign EL RINCÓN; on the ledge of its open window, a beer tap, a small glass of beer and a long sandwich on a plate. On the building on the right, above stone arches, a poster with a palm tree, the sea, a small beach bar and the word ¡VERANO! Labels name la tasca, el grifo, la caña, el bocadillo and el chiringuito.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One more word needs care. Spain's *coger* means "to take, to catch" (*coger el tren*). Lesson 17
explained why you use *tomar* or *agarrar* in Mexico; in Spain you'll hear *coger* constantly, and
it is perfectly polite there.

## Switching variety: what each side adjusts

![A chart with two columns, Spain and Mexico, and nine rows: vosotros / ustedes; le vi / lo vi (a man); esta mañana he salido / esta mañana salí; voy a por pan / voy por pan; el curro / la chamba; la pasta / la lana; el grifo / la llave; el atasco / el tráfico; el ordenador / la computadora.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A Mexican in Spain is understood everywhere; the adjustments are about comfort, not correctness.
Mexican *ahorita* often puzzles Spaniards (Spain says *ahora mismo*), *¿Mande?* for "pardon?" sounds odd
(Spain says *¿Perdona?* or *¿Cómo?*), and *el carro* is understood but sounds American. A Spaniard
in Mexico learns to drop *coger* and *vosotros*. At C2, switching variety means two things: write
your own standard consistently, and understand the other one without effort.

## Text: an e-mail exchange

Mariana, a Mexican student in Salamanca, writes to Álvaro, a friend from Madrid. Each writes in
their own variety. (The University of Salamanca dates its founding to 1218 and celebrated its
eighth centenary in 2018.)

> **Asunto: ¡Ya estoy en Salamanca!**
>
> Hola, Álvaro:
>
> Ya llevo dos semanas aquí y todavía no me acostumbro a que la gente cene a las diez. Vivo en un
> colegio mayor cerca de la Plaza Mayor; es como una residencia de estudiantes, pero con
> actividades y hasta equipo de futbol. Mis compañeras son muy buena onda, aunque a veces no les
> entiendo nada. Una me preguntó si el sábado me apuntaba "al tapeo" y le dije que sí sin saber qué
> era: resulta que es ir de bar en bar pidiendo una caña y algo de comer. Fuimos a una tasca
> chiquita donde el mesero (aquí dicen "camarero") nos regaló las tapas.
>
> Lo que más me sorprende es cómo hablan: todos usan "vosotros" y una chava me preguntó si había
> ido "a por" el pan. Por cierto, la llave del baño gotea y aquí nadie entiende "llave": dicen
> "grifo". El máster empieza en serio el lunes. ¿Cuándo vienes? Te invito un bocadillo, que aquí es
> como una torta en pan largo.
>
> Un abrazo,
> Mariana

> **Asunto: RE: ¡Ya estoy en Salamanca!**
>
> ¡Hola, Mariana!
>
> Esta mañana he leído tu correo en el metro, de camino al curro, y me he reído yo solo. ¡Qué majas
> tus compañeras! Lo del tapeo me mola: cuando salgáis de tapas, pedid una tortilla de patatas en
> cualquier tasca: es de lo más castizo.
>
> Yo estoy currando un montón. Mi jefe entró por enchufe (su padre conoce al director) y mi
> hermano prepara unas oposiciones a profesor, así que en casa nadie tiene tiempo ni pasta. Y sí,
> aquí "vamos a por el pan"; ya sé que tú dirías "voy por el pan".
>
> En el puente de diciembre voy a verte. A tu primo Jorge le vi ayer y le dije que se viniera: es
> un chaval muy majo. Un consejo: los bares cutres cerca de la universidad a veces son los mejores.
> Si ves un chollo de piso para el verano, avísame. En agosto me voy con la peña a Cádiz; hay un
> chiringuito donde ponen unos bocadillos de calamares que flipas.
>
> Te dejo, que a esta hora siempre hay atasco. ¡Venga, un beso!
>
> Álvaro

**Summary.** Mariana has been in Salamanca two weeks: she lives in a residence hall, has gone
tapas-hopping with friendly classmates, and is surprised by *vosotros*, *a por* and *grifo* for
her *llave*; her master's starts on Monday and she invites Álvaro for a sandwich. Álvaro read her
e-mail on the subway to work and laughed. He recommends the potato omelet at any traditional bar, is
working hard, mentions his boss who got the job through connections and his brother's
civil-service exams, plans to visit on the December long weekend, saw her cousin, praises cheap
bars, asks her to look out for a cheap apartment, and is going to a beach bar in Cádiz in August.

**Glosses.** *Me apuntaba* = I was in, I'd join; *me he reído yo solo* = I laughed out loud on my
own (Spain's perfect for today); *salgáis, pedid* = *vosotros* subjunctive and command; *de lo
más castizo* = as traditional as it gets; *que flipas* = amazing (literally, "that you freak
out"); *el piso* = apartment (Spain); *te dejo, que…* = I'll leave you, because…

## Pronunciation

- *chaval*: cha-VAL, stress on the last syllable.
- *botellón*: bo-te-LLÓN; *chiringuito*: chi-rin-GUI-to, the *u* silent.
- *máster*: MÁS-ter, plural *másteres*, MÁS-te-res.
- In Madrid you'll hear *-ado* as *-ao* (*cansao*) and *vosotros* forms like *habéis* with a
  strong final *s*.

## Common mistakes

- **Taking leísmo as a mistake.** *Le vi* for a man is accepted in Spain; recognize it, but write
  *lo*.
- **Reading Spain's perfect as "have done".** *Esta mañana he salido* is just "I left this
  morning".
- **Producing Spain's slang in Mexico.** *Currar* or *molar* in a Mexican e-mail sounds borrowed.
- **Taking *el bocadillo* as Mexican.** In Spain it's a sandwich; in Mexico, often a snack.
- **Writing *¡Sentaros!*** The written command is *sentaos*, and you won't need it anyway.

## Key points

- Spain's familiar plural is *vosotros*, with forms in every tense: recognize them, never drill
  them.
- Leísmo of a male person (*le vi*) is accepted in Spain; Mexico and this course write *lo*.
- Spain uses the perfect for today's events and *a por* for "to go and get".
- Spain's colloquial words (*currar, molar, majo, la pasta, el chollo*) are for recognition.
- *El colegio mayor, el máster, las oposiciones* name Spanish institutions; you may write them
  about Spain.
- At C2, switching variety means writing your standard consistently and understanding the other
  without effort.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Al tiro, ahorita, ahoritita: grammar and usage across the Americas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 18 was Spain. This lesson covers the rest of the Americas: the grammar a C2 listener meets
in Caribbean, Andean, Chilean and Rioplatense Spanish, the systems of address, the leísmo family,
and words from a dozen countries. As in lesson 18, it's all for recognition: you'll understand
it and keep writing the Mexican standard. C1 04h2 (an honors lesson) covered the sounds of these
regions and B1 24h1 (honors) some everyday words, so this lesson is about grammar and new words.
The listening questions ask your device for a Chilean or Argentine voice, but device voices vary
and none reproduces real regional speech; that is on each country's radio and podcasts.

## The Caribbean: the overt subject and questions without inversion

In Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and coastal Venezuela and Colombia, speakers use
subject pronouns far more than Mexicans do. Linguists call this the **[[overt subject]]** (*el sujeto
explícito*): *Yo creo que yo voy mañana* (I think I'll go tomorrow), where Mexico says *Creo que
voy*. One reason often given is that Caribbean speakers weaken final *s*, so *tú* makes clear who
*habla(s)* refers to; take that as a common explanation, not a proven cause.

Two patterns follow:

- **Questions without inversion**: *¿Qué tú quieres?* (What do you want?), *¿Dónde tú vives?*
  The standard elsewhere is *¿Qué quieres (tú)?*
- **A subject before an infinitive**: *Me lo explicó para yo entenderlo* (She explained it so I'd
  understand), where the standard has *para que yo lo entendiera*. It's also heard elsewhere in
  informal speech.

In the Caribbean, Venezuela and the Canary Islands you'll also hear *más nada, más nunca, más
nadie* for *nada más, nunca más, nadie más*: *No dijo más nada* (He said nothing else).

## The Andes: *dice*, double possessives and *dame pasando*

In the Andean highlands of Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia:

- **Reportative *dice***: a *dice* at the end of a sentence marks what you heard, not what you
  saw: *Mañana va a llover, dice* (It's going to rain tomorrow, they say). Researchers often link
  it to Quechua, which marks hearsay with a suffix on the verb.
- **Double possessives**: *su casa de Juan* (Juan's house), where the standard says *la casa de
  Juan*; also *de Juan su casa*.
- ***Dar* + gerund**: in Ecuador, *Dame pasando la sal* (Pass me the salt, would you?) is a
  softened request. Studies describe it as typical of Ecuadorian Spanish and discuss whether it
  comes from contact with Kichwa; that is debated.
- ***Nomás***, C1's Mexican word, is also Andean: *Pase nomás* (Come right in).

## Three systems of address

Each pronoun of address is *una forma de tratamiento* (a form of address), and B2 24h1 (an honors
lesson) taught the names of the systems. **[[Tuteo]]** (*el tuteo*) is the use of *tú*
for one person you're close to, as in Mexico. **[[Voseo]]** (*el voseo*) is *vos* in that role.
**[[Ustedeo]]** (*el ustedeo*) is *usted* even with family and friends, as many speakers do in parts of
Colombia and Costa Rica (*Mi amor, ¿usted ya comió?*).

Voseo has its own verb forms. A review:

| | Río de la Plata | Chile (verbal voseo, informal) | Mexico (tuteo) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *hablar* | *vos hablás* | *tú hablái(s)* | *tú hablas* |
| *comer* | *vos comés* | *tú comís* | *tú comes* |
| *ser* | *vos sos* | *tú erís* | *tú eres* |
| *estar* | *vos estás* | *¿Cómo estái(s)?* | *¿Cómo estás?* |
| command | *¡Hablá! ¡Comé! ¡Vení!* | standard *tú* commands | *¡Habla! ¡Come! ¡Ven!* |

Chile is the odd case: informal Chilean Spanish keeps the pronoun *tú* (or drops it) and uses
voseo verb endings (*¿Cachái?*, Do you get it?). Educated Chilean writing uses the standard *tú*
forms.

```map
base: world
title: Address systems in informal speech (simplified)
view: 33, -118 to -56, -34
region: Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica | Voseo common in everyday speech
region: Chile | Verbal voseo with tú (informal)
region: Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, Venezuela | Voseo in some regions
region: Mexico, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Peru, Panama | Tuteo usual
point: Ciudad de México | 19.43, -99.13 | Tuteo usual
caption: A simplification of common descriptions: countries are shaded as wholes, but address systems change by region, age and situation. Mexico's state of Chiapas has voseo, Colombia mixes voseo, tuteo and ustedeo by region, and Venezuela's voseo is mainly in Zulia. Usted is used everywhere for formal address.
```

## Leísmo, laísmo and loísmo

Lesson 18 introduced **[[leísmo]]** (*el leísmo*): *le* as a direct object for a person, accepted in
Spain for one man. Its relatives are **[[laísmo]]** (*el laísmo*), *la* as an indirect object for a
woman (*La dije que viniera* for *Le dije que viniera*, I told her to come), and **[[loísmo]]** (*el
loísmo*), *lo* as an indirect object (*Lo di un regalo* for *Le di un regalo*).

| Feature | Where (simplified) | Status |
|---|---|---|
| leísmo of a male person | the center and north of Spain; also described in Paraguay and Andean Ecuador, where studies link it to contact with Guarani and Kichwa | accepted for one man; not for women or things |
| laísmo | the center of Spain (Madrid, much of Castile) | not accepted by the norm |
| loísmo | rarer: parts of rural central Spain | not accepted by the norm, and stigmatized |

In the Americas, laísmo and loísmo are rare. The Mexican standard, *lo / la* for direct objects
and *le* for indirect ones, is the one you write.

## Indigenous languages and Spanish

Contact with Indigenous languages left grammar and words. *El quechuismo* (a Quechua loanword)
is everywhere in Andean Spanish: *la cancha* (field, court), *el choclo* (ear of corn), A1's *la
papa*, *la pampa*, *el cóndor*, and *la guagua* (baby, in the Andes; *la guagua* "bus", from B1 24h1 (an honors lesson), is
Caribbean). From Tupi-Guarani languages come *el jaguar* and *el ñandú* (rhea).

Two constitutions give these languages official status. Paraguay's (1992, art. 140) makes Spanish
and *el guaraní* (Guarani) its official languages, and most Paraguayans speak both. Peru's (1993,
art. 48) makes Quechua, Aymara and other Indigenous languages official "where they predominate",
beside Spanish. Bolivia's 2009 constitution also lists many Indigenous languages as official.

## Words across the Americas

| Word | Meaning | Where it's usual | Mexico |
|---|---|---|---|
| *al tiro* | right away | Chile | C1's *luego luego* |
| *cachar* | to get, to understand: *¿Cachái?* | Chile (in Mexico *cachar* is "to catch" a ball) | *entender* |
| *fome* | boring (one form for both genders) | Chile | A1's *aburrido* |
| *pololear*, *el pololo / la polola* | to go steady; boyfriend, girlfriend | Chile | *andar con*, *el novio* |
| *la chompa* | sweater (probably from English *jumper*) | the Andes | A1's *el suéter* |
| *el choclo* | ear of corn | South America | *el elote* |
| *el chamo, la chama* | kid, youngster | Venezuela | *el chavo* |
| *el pana, la pana* | buddy | Venezuela, the Caribbean | B1's *el cuate* |
| *la vaina* | thing, stuff (informal; also "pod") | Venezuela, Colombia, the Caribbean | *la cosa* |
| *la buseta* | small bus | Colombia, Venezuela | *el microbús* |
| *el bondi* | bus | the Río de la Plata (informal) | *el camión* |

People and places: *el porteño / la porteña* (from Buenos Aires), *el limeño / la limeña* (from
Lima), *el canario / la canaria* (from the Canary Islands, also "canary"). *El gallego* is a
Galician, or the Galician language, but in much of Latin America (Argentina, Uruguay, Cuba) it is
also, colloquially, any Spaniard, because so many emigrants came from Galicia. Words of one country
are *el chilenismo, el argentinismo, el colombianismo*, like lesson 17's *el mexicanismo*.

![A chart in Spanish with eight features in rows and five regions in columns: Caribe, Andes, Chile, Río de la Plata, México. Dots mark the frequent overt subject, ¿Qué tú quieres? and más nada for the Caribbean; dice (what was heard) and su casa de Juan for the Andes; voseo verb forms for Chile (marked verbal) and the Río de la Plata; leísmo of person for the Andes (marked en parte, in part); and tuteo for the Caribbean, the Andes (marked Perú) and Mexico. A note says the chart is simplified and every feature also varies within each region.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Asking for clarification politely

You won't know every word, and asking is normal. Useful ways to ask:

- *Perdona, ¿qué quiere decir "fome"?* (Sorry, what does … mean?)
- *¿Cómo le dicen ustedes a…?* (What do you call …?)
- *No te entendí bien, ¿me lo repites?* (I didn't quite get you, can you say it again?)
- *¿"Al tiro" es como "ahorita"?* (Is … like …?)

Mexican *ahorita* is itself a good example: it can mean "right now" or "in a while", and
*ahoritita* (with a double diminutive) is "this very minute". A Chilean colleague may need that
explained.

## Text: a video call

A remote team plans a product launch: Paola (Mexico City, the coordinator), Catalina (Santiago),
Renzo (Lima), Andreína (Caracas) and Martín (Buenos Aires). Each speaks their own variety.

```dialogue
# Reunión semanal del equipo
Paola: Buenos días a todos. Bueno, buenas tardes para algunos. ¿Me escuchan? Ahorita comparto la pantalla.
Catalina: Te escuchamos perfecto, Paola. Oye, antes de empezar, ¿cachái que mañana es feriado acá? Si necesitan algo de mí, pídanmelo hoy y lo hago al tiro.
Paola: Perdona, Catalina, ¿"al tiro" es como nuestro "ahorita"?
Catalina: Más rápido que tu ahorita, te lo aseguro. Al tiro es ya, en este momento.
Martín: Che, ¿y vos sabés si llegaron los diseños? Yo los esperé toda la mañana y nada.
Andreína: Chamo, los mandé anoche. ¿Qué tú quieres que haga si el correo no los entrega? Esa vaina siempre falla. Te los paso por el chat y más nada.
Renzo: En Cusco, dice, también están sin internet desde ayer. Me escribió la coordinadora de allá; su laptop de ella no prende.
Paola: Uy. Renzo, ¿puedes hablar con ella y me cuentas? Ahora, la presentación del lanzamiento. Catalina, ¿cómo vas con el video?
Catalina: Bien, aunque el primer guion me quedó súper fome. Mi pololo lo vio y se quedó dormido. Lo estoy cambiando.
Andreína: ¡Qué cómico! Si quieres te paso a mi pana Daniel, que edita videos. Mi abuelo, que era canario, decía que todo se arregla con un buen amigo.
Martín: Yo puedo revisar los textos. Pero ojo, que acá en Buenos Aires vamos a tener que adaptar varias cosas. Lo que ustedes llaman "camión" para nosotros es el bondi, y el gallego del bar de abajo, que en realidad es de Madrid, ya me preguntó qué es una "chamba".
Renzo: Y en Lima nadie dice "elote", Paola. Si el anuncio sale con una foto de mazorcas, pongan "choclo" o mejor nada.
Paola: Buen punto. Por eso pensamos en un texto neutro para toda la región y versiones locales para las redes. ¿Les parece?
Catalina: Me parece bien. Cuando tengas la versión neutra, mándamela y la reviso.
Andreína: Dale. Yo mando las fotos de nuevo, y esta vez por la nube.
Martín: Perfecto. ¿Nos vemos el jueves a la misma hora?
Paola: El jueves. Y Renzo, abrígate, que en Lima dicen que ya hace frío.
Renzo: Ya me puse la chompa. ¡Hasta el jueves!
```

**Summary.** Paola opens the meeting. Catalina warns that tomorrow is a holiday in Chile and
offers to do anything today "al tiro", which she explains is faster than Paola's *ahorita*.
Martín asks whether the designs arrived; Andreína says she sent them last night, blames the
e-mail and will resend them in the chat. Renzo reports that the Cusco office has no internet and
its coordinator's laptop won't turn on. Catalina is rewriting a video script her boyfriend found
boring; Andreína offers a video-editor friend. Martín and Renzo warn that words like *camión,
chamba* and *elote* need local versions, and Paola proposes one neutral text plus local versions
for social media. They agree to meet on Thursday.

**Glosses.** *El feriado* = public holiday (South America; Mexico *el día festivo*); *pídanmelo* =
ask me for it; *¿Qué tú quieres que haga?* = what do you want me to do? (Caribbean word order);
*su laptop de ella* = her laptop (Andean double possessive); *no prende* = won't turn on; *¡Qué
cómico!* = how funny!; *dale* = OK, sure (Río de la Plata, Venezuela and elsewhere); *la mazorca*
= ear of corn (general); *abrígate* = wrap up warm.

## Pronunciation

- *guaraní*: gua-ra-NÍ, stress on the last syllable; plural *guaraníes*.
- *porteño*: por-TE-ño; *limeño*: li-ME-ño.
- *la buseta*: bu-SE-ta; *el bondi*: BON-di.
- Chilean *¿cachái?*: ca-CHÁI, two syllables, with a falling diphthong.

## Common mistakes

- **Calling regional grammar "wrong".** *¿Qué tú quieres?* and *su casa de Juan* are regional
  patterns, not errors; laísmo and loísmo are the ones the norm rejects.
- **Mixing systems in writing.** Writing *vos tenés* in a Mexican text, or *tú sabís*, sounds like
  a costume. Write *tú tienes* and recognize the rest.
- **Trusting a word's "Latin American" label.** *Al tiro, fome, pololo* are Chilean; *el bondi*
  is Argentine and Uruguayan. Few words are truly continent-wide.
- **Assuming *el gallego* always means a Galician.** In Buenos Aires it may mean any Spaniard.
- **Forgetting that *usted* is universal.** In formal contexts *usted* works everywhere.

## Key points

- The Caribbean favors the overt subject, questions like *¿Qué tú quieres?*, *para yo* +
  infinitive and *más nada*.
- The Andes use reportative *dice*, double possessives and, in Ecuador, *dame pasando*.
- Tuteo, voseo and ustedeo coexist; Chile mixes *tú* with voseo verb endings.
- Leísmo of a male person is accepted; laísmo and loísmo are not.
- Guarani is official in Paraguay (1992) and Quechua where it predominates in Peru (1993).
- The regional words of this lesson are for recognition; ask about the ones you don't know.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El español que viene: contact, change and the debates about usage
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 17–19 described Spanish as it is spoken now. This lesson asks how it changes: through
contact with other languages, through new words and lost ones, and through public debates about
how it should be used. The C2 skill is describing a linguistic situation neutrally and presenting
a debate fairly: who says what, since when, on what grounds, without taking sides unless you are
asked to.

## Spanish in the United States

A **[[heritage speaker]]** (*el hablante de herencia*, *la hablante de herencia*) grew up hearing
Spanish at home but was schooled mainly in English; Spanish is their *lengua de herencia* (heritage
language). Heritage speakers often understand and speak with native ease but write less
confidently, and their Spanish is a variety of its own, not "broken" Spanish. The Census Bureau's
surveys count more than 40 million people aged five and over who speak Spanish at home, and the
United States has its own academy, the Academia Norteamericana de la Lengua Española.

**[[Code-switching]]** (C1 20h1, an honors lesson, named it *el cambio de código*) is moving between
two languages in one conversation: *Te llamo después, I'm driving*. Research describes it as a
skilled practice with its own rules (speakers switch at clause boundaries, rarely in the middle of
a word), not as a sign of weak Spanish. It is different from the calque (C1's *el calco*), a
phrase translated word for word: *llamar para atrás* (to call back) for *devolver la llamada*,
*aplicar para un trabajo* for *solicitar un trabajo*. *El espanglish* (Spanglish) names both, often
loosely; the DLE spells it *espanglish* (as of its online edition: check), and *spanglish* is also
written.

## Contact, substrate and borrowing

**[[Language contact]]** (*el contacto de lenguas*) is what happens when two languages are used by
the same people. Its traces come in three kinds:

- ***El préstamo léxico*** (lexical borrowing, a loanword): a word taken from another language, as
  Mexican Spanish took *el elote, el cuate, el papalote* (kite) and *el tianguis* (street market)
  from Nahuatl. A2's *el préstamo* is a loan of money; this is its linguistic sense.
- **[[Substrate]]** (*el sustrato*): an earlier language whose speakers shifted to Spanish and left
  traces in it. Nahuatl is a substrate of Mexican Spanish, Quechua of Andean Spanish; how much of
  their grammar survives is debated, and loanwords are the clearest trace.
- ***La convergencia*** (convergence): two languages in long contact growing alike, as Andean
  Spanish and Quechua have in some structures (lesson 19's reportative *dice*).

```timeline

event: 1490s | Taíno and other Caribbean languages: canoa, huracán, maíz | The Americas

event: 20th century | English: el fútbol, el líder, el clic | Modern languages
caption: Dates are when each language's influence was strongest, not when every word entered; English influence continues today, and English words reached Spanish through both Spain and the Americas.
```

## Shift, vitality and diglossia

**[[Language shift]]** (*el desplazamiento lingüístico*) is a community moving from one language to
another over generations. Its engine is *la transmisión intergeneracional* (intergenerational
transmission): when parents stop speaking a language to their children, it loses *vitalidad*
(vitality) within a lifetime. A common pattern among immigrants is the three-generation shift: the
first generation is *monolingüe* (monolingual) in Spanish, the second bilingual, the third often
monolingual in English. *La asimilación* (assimilation) speeds it; *la lealtad lingüística*
(language loyalty), the value a group gives its language, slows it.

![A diagram of three generations of one family. The grandmother speaks Spanish only. Her daughter speaks Spanish and English. The grandson speaks English with a little Spanish. An arrow labeled desplazamiento lingüístico (language shift) runs from the first generation to the third.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A language's vitality is measured by *el censo lingüístico* (language census) and surveys. Mexico's
2020 census (INEGI) counted about 7.4 million people aged three and over who speak an Indigenous
language. **[[Diglossia]]** (*la diglosia*), a term the linguist Charles Ferguson made famous in 1959,
is a situation in which two varieties or languages have separate roles: one for school, law and
writing, the other for home. Paraguay, with Spanish and Guarani, is the usual Spanish-speaking
example, although Guarani's official status since 1992 has changed that division.

## Change in progress

Language changes in every *comunidad de habla* (speech community). Speakers *acuñan* (coin) new
words (*tuitear, la posverdad*), and others *caen en desuso* (fall out of use) until *el desuso*
(disuse) leaves them in old books. *El cambio lingüístico* (language change) shows in grammar too:
the DPD's second edition, presented in November 2024, accepts both *másteres* and *másters*,
and both plurals for many recent loanwords ending in a consonant, as Excélsior reported. *La planificación lingüística* (language
planning) and *la política lingüística* (language policy) are the deliberate side: academies set
spelling, governments decide which languages are official (Mexico's 2003 Ley General de Derechos
Lingüísticos de los Pueblos Indígenas recognizes Indigenous languages as national languages beside
Spanish), and schools decide what is taught.

## The inclusive-language debate, described

**[[Inclusive language]]** (*el lenguaje inclusivo*) is wording meant to make women and, for some,
nonbinary people visible. Three options are discussed:

| Option | Example | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **[[generic masculine]]** (*el masculino genérico*) | *los estudiantes* for a mixed group | the RAE's grammar treats it as inclusive; standard |
| *el desdoblamiento de género* (gender doubling) | *los estudiantes y las estudiantes*, *mexicanas y mexicanos* | standard; frequent in Mexican public speech |
| collective or neutral wording | *el alumnado, la ciudadanía, quienes estudian* | standard |
| forms in *-e*, *-x*, *@* | *les estudiantes*, *todxs* | not accepted by the RAE |

The positions, with dates. The RAE approved a report by Ignacio Bosque on linguistic sexism in
2012, which defended the generic masculine and criticized guides that recommend systematic
doubling. In 2020 the RAE answered a request from the Spanish government's vice-president with a
report concluding that the Constitution's wording, generic masculine included, needs no
grammatical change, though it suggested updating some terms. On the other side, many public bodies
and universities publish guides recommending doubling and neutral wording; in Mexico, the
national women's institute (INMUJERES) has published a manual of nonsexist communication. Forms
in *-e* are used by some groups, especially young people, as a deliberate choice.

What formal writing usually expects: no official DELE rule on this was found, so don't assume one.
The generic masculine, doubling and neutral wording are all standard; forms in *-e* are not. Choose
one approach and use it consistently, and when you report the debate, attribute each position to
its source.

## Text: a round table

A radio round table (invented) on the future of Spanish. The speaker figures are the Instituto
Cervantes' *El español en el mundo 2025*, as Euronews reported them (October 28, 2025).

```dialogue
# El español que viene
Moderadora: Bienvenidos. Según el informe *El español en el mundo 2025* del Instituto Cervantes, hay más de 635 millones de hablantes, y los nativos superan por primera vez los 500 millones. ¿Qué nos dicen esas cifras?
Dra. Ruiz: Que el español crece, pero no de manera uniforme. En Estados Unidos, por ejemplo, muchos jóvenes son hablantes de herencia: entienden todo y hablan con soltura, pero escriben poco en español. Si la escuela no los apoya, la tercera generación suele pasarse al inglés.
Moderadora: ¿Y el espanglish? ¿Es una amenaza?
Dra. Ruiz: Yo no lo veo así. El cambio de código es una habilidad de bilingües, no una deficiencia. Lo que sí preocupa es la falta de transmisión intergeneracional.
Mtro. Quispe: Ese mismo problema lo vivimos en los Andes, pero al revés. Allí el quechua es la lengua que pierde hablantes frente al español. Hay familias en las que los abuelos son monolingües en quechua y los nietos solo hablan español. Las leyes lo reconocen como oficial, pero la lealtad lingüística no se decreta.
Moderadora: Usted habla de desplazamiento lingüístico.
Mtro. Quispe: Exacto. Y a la vez el español andino lleva siglos de contacto con el quechua: hay préstamos léxicos y, para algunos colegas, también rasgos de sustrato en la gramática. Ese punto todavía se discute.
Moderadora: Licenciada Montes, usted trabaja en planificación lingüística. ¿Quién decide cómo hablamos?
Lic. Montes: Nadie del todo. Las academias describen y recomiendan, los gobiernos fijan políticas lingüísticas y las comunidades de habla hacen lo que quieren. Las palabras se acuñan en la calle y en las redes; el diccionario llega después.
Moderadora: ¿Y el lenguaje inclusivo?
Lic. Montes: Es el debate más vivo. La RAE sostiene que el masculino genérico incluye a todos; muchas instituciones recomiendan el desdoblamiento de género o fórmulas como "la ciudadanía". En los textos que edito pedimos coherencia: el autor elige una opción y la mantiene. Las formas en -e no forman parte de la norma, aunque hay quien las usa a propósito.
Dra. Ruiz: Yo añadiría que muchas formas caen en desuso sin que nadie lo decida. El cambio lingüístico no se puede planificar del todo.
Moderadora: Una última pregunta: ¿qué español viene?
Mtro. Quispe: Uno con más acentos, no con menos.
```

**Summary.** The moderator cites the Instituto Cervantes' 2025 figures: over 635 million speakers,
over 500 million native. Dr. Ruiz says growth is uneven: in the US, heritage speakers speak well
but write little, and without school support the third generation shifts to English; she sees
code-switching as a bilingual skill and worries instead about intergenerational transmission. Mr.
Quispe describes the reverse in the Andes, where Quechua loses speakers to Spanish despite its
legal status; Andean Spanish has Quechua loanwords and, some argue, substrate features, a point
still debated. Ms. Montes, a language planner, says academies describe, governments set policy and
communities decide; on inclusive language she summarizes both positions and asks her authors for
consistency. Ruiz adds that change can't be fully planned; Quispe predicts more accents, not
fewer.

**Glosses.** *Con soltura* = fluently; *pasarse al inglés* = to switch to
English; *al revés* = the other way round; *no se decreta* = can't be decreed; *nadie del todo* =
nobody entirely; *hay quien las usa a propósito* = some people use them on purpose.

## Pronunciation

- *diglosia*: di-GLO-sia, three syllables (*-sia* is one).
- *monolingüe*: mo-no-LIN-güe; the dieresis makes the *u* sound: *-gwe*.
- *sustrato*: sus-TRA-to; *convergencia*: con-ver-GEN-cia.
- *espanglish*: es-PAN-glish, stress on the second syllable.

## Common mistakes

- **Judging instead of describing.** "Spanglish is bad Spanish" is an opinion. A C2 description
  says who uses it, where and how researchers describe it.
- **Unattributed positions.** "Inclusive language is incorrect" or "the generic masculine excludes
  women" should be "the RAE holds that…" or "many guides recommend…".
- **Calling every Nahuatl word a substrate.** A loanword is borrowing; substrate is the deeper
  trace a language leaves when its speakers shift.
- **Inventing rules.** No official DELE rule on inclusive language was found; don't cite one.
- **Mixing approaches.** *Los alumnos y las alumnas … todos ellos* switches system mid-sentence.

## Key points

- Heritage speakers, code-switching and calques are features of Spanish in the US, described
  without judgment.
- Contact leaves loanwords, substrate traces and convergence.
- Shift happens when transmission between generations stops; diglossia gives languages separate
  roles.
- New words are coined and old ones fall out of use; academies, governments and schools plan
  language, but communities decide.
- In the inclusive-language debate, report each position with its source and date; in your own
  writing, choose a standard option and keep it.

lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 listed the academies of Spanish, and lesson 20 described how languages shift and lose
vitality. This lesson follows one variety that left Spain more than five centuries ago and kept
developing on its own: **[[Judeo-Spanish]]** (*el judeoespañol*), the language of the Sephardic Jews.
It is for recognition and cultural knowledge. Every Judeo-Spanish word below comes from a named
source (listed in the notes); the Spanish example sentences are original.

## 1492 and the diaspora

Medieval Spain had large Jewish communities. A self-governing Jewish or Muslim community was an
*aljama* (*la aljama*), and the Jewish quarter of a town was *la judería*; Toledo, Girona and
Córdoba still keep theirs. The word *sefardí* (Sephardic; plural *sefardíes*, also *sefardís*)
comes from *Sefarad*, the Hebrew name for the Iberian Peninsula.

On March 31, 1492, the Catholic Monarchs signed in Granada *el edicto* (the edict) that ordered
the Jews of their kingdoms to convert or leave within months. Those who converted, and their
descendants, were called *conversos* (*el converso*, *la conversa*), and many lived under the
Inquisition's suspicion. Those who refused chose *la expulsión* (expulsion) and exile, and Portugal
ordered its own expulsion a few years later. Historians' estimates of how many left vary widely.

The refugees spread in a *diáspora* (*la diáspora*). Many settled in the Ottoman Empire, whose
sultan welcomed them: Thessaloniki, Istanbul, Izmir and, later, Sarajevo became Sephardic centers.
Others crossed to North Africa, where the Judeo-Spanish of northern Morocco, rich in Arabic words,
is called *la haquitía* (Haketia; also spelled *jaquetía*, *haquetía*).

```map

view: 47, -10 to 30, 32

route: To Istanbul | 40.64, 22.94; 41.01, 28.98 | Routes to the east
route: To North Africa | 36.72, -4.42; 35.57, -5.37 | Routes to North Africa
point: Sevilla | 37.39, -5.98 | Spain
point: Toledo | 39.86, -4.02 | Spain
point: Thessaloniki | 40.64, 22.94 | Ottoman centers
point: Istanbul | 41.01, 28.98 | Ottoman centers
point: Izmir | 38.42, 27.14 | Ottoman centers
point: Sarajevo | 43.86, 18.41 | Ottoman centers
point: Tetuán | 35.57, -5.37 | Haketia (northern Morocco)
point: Tánger | 35.76, -5.83 | Haketia (northern Morocco)
caption: The routes are schematic: people left by many ports, often in stages and by way of Portugal or Italy. In the twentieth century, emigration and the Holocaust scattered the communities again, to the Americas (Mexico among them), France and Israel.
```

## What Judeo-Spanish keeps and what it adds

Cut off from Spain, Judeo-Spanish didn't follow the changes of the sixteenth and seventeenth
centuries, and it took words from its neighbors. The English Wikipedia article on the language
(read through a mirror on November 17, 2026) and SpanishDict's guide to Ladino give these
examples:

| Judeo-Spanish | Modern Spanish | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| *fijo*, *favlar* | *hijo*, *hablar* | the old *f-* that later became a silent *h* |
| *baxo* (with an *sh* sound) | *bajo* | an older *sh* sound, before Spanish *j* |
| *muestro* | *nuestro* | *nue-* → *mue-*, as in some dialects |
| *kaza*, *sivdad*, *syelo* | *casa, ciudad, cielo* | a spelling that writes sounds as they are said |
| *kantika* | *canción* | a different word for "song" |

The loanwords show where the speakers lived. From Turkish: *araba* (carriage), *musafir* (guest)
and the suffix *-dji* for trades (*halvadjí*, a seller of sweets). From Hebrew, mostly words of
religion: *haham* (rabbi), *kal* (synagogue). From Greek: *meldar* (to read, to study). From
French, many through the schools of the Alliance Israélite Universelle from the nineteenth
century on: *abazur* (lampshade), *fusil* (rifle).

![A chart with three rows of word pairs, Judeo-Spanish on the left and modern Spanish on the right: fijo and hijo, muestro and nuestro, kaza and casa. Below them, four boxes show loanwords by source: Turkish (araba, musafir), Hebrew (haham, kal), Greek (meldar), French (abazur, fusil).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## *Judeoespañol* or *ladino*?

The names are themselves a debate. *El judeoespañol* (Judeo-Spanish) is the scholarly term in
Spanish. *El ladino* (Ladino) is the common name in Israel and in English, but many scholars and,
reportedly, many native speakers keep *ladino* for something narrower: the word-for-word
translation language of Hebrew and Aramaic sacred texts, a calque that followed Hebrew word
order. Speakers have also called their language *judezmo* or simply *espanyol*. In Spanish,
*ladino* has other senses too (in Central America, a person of non-Indigenous culture), so
*judeoespañol* is the safer choice in a formal text.

It was written in Hebrew letters: the printed Rashi script and the cursive *solitreo*. Today most
writers use the Latin alphabet with a phonetic spelling (*kaza*), a style associated with the
Israeli magazine *Aki Yerushalayim*.

## Vitality today

The language is endangered. Wikipedia's infobox gives about 51,000 native speakers (2018, citing
Ethnologue), and other estimates range much higher or lower; most fluent speakers are elderly,
and few children learn it. The Autoridad Nasionala del Ladino was founded in Jerusalem in 1997,
and the Akademia Nasionala del Ladino, whose constitution dates from 2018 and which was publicly
launched in Jerusalem in December 2020, was announced in 2018 as a future 24th member of ASALE and is
usually described as affiliated with it; ASALE's own statements in 2025 still spoke of 23
academies, so it is not counted as a full member. The RAE named eight Ladino specialists as
corresponding members in 2015.

Part of the culture's fame is its ballads: *romances* brought from medieval Spain, sung for
centuries, often by women, and collected by twentieth-century scholars. Here they are described,
not quoted.

### Example 1: reading three words against modern Spanish

Read *fijo*, *muestro* and *kaza* with three questions:

1. **Which sounds differ?** *Fijo* has *f* where Spanish has *h*; *muestro* has *m* for *n*;
   *kaza* has *k* and *z* where Spanish writes *c* and *s*.
2. **Is it an old form, a change or a spelling?** *Fijo* keeps an older form (medieval Spanish
   wrote *fijo* too); *muestro* is a change, also heard in some rural dialects; *kaza* is spelling.
   Judeo-Spanish keeps a *z* sound between vowels, which modern Spanish lost.
3. **What is the modern word?** *hijo, nuestro, casa*.

The method works for any sourced word: look for an old Spanish form first, a sound change
second, a loanword third.

## Text: a family's language

An article for a Mexican magazine. The family and the journalist are invented; the historical
background is general.

> **La lengua de la abuela Rebeca**
>
> Cuando yo era niña, mi abuela Rebeca me llamaba con palabras que no encontraba en ningún
> diccionario. Decía *kaza* donde mis amigas decían "casa", y a las visitas las llamaba
> *musafires*. Durante años pensé que era una forma de hablar de su pueblo. Tardé mucho en
> entender que esas palabras eran de otro tiempo y de otro lugar: eran judeoespañol.
>
> La familia de mi abuela llegó a la Ciudad de México en los años veinte, desde Esmirna, la
> ciudad turca que hoy se llama Izmir. Como otras familias sefardíes del antiguo Imperio otomano,
> buscaba trabajo y tranquilidad lejos de las guerras. Traía muy poco equipaje y una lengua que sus
> antepasados habían llevado de la península ibérica más de cuatro siglos antes, después del
> edicto de expulsión de 1492.
>
> En México, esa lengua sonaba extrañamente familiar. Los vecinos de la colonia entendían casi
> todo, aunque se reían de algunas palabras. El bisabuelo, que vendía telas, descubrió pronto que
> le convenía hablar como los clientes. Mi abuela, en cambio, guardó el judeoespañol para la
> cocina, las fiestas y las conversaciones con sus hermanas. En la calle hablaba el español de
> México; en casa, el de Esmirna. Los lingüistas tienen un nombre para esa división: diglosia.
>
> Mi madre ya creció con otra lengua dominante. Entendía a la abuela, pero le contestaba en
> español mexicano, y yo ni siquiera entendía. La historia de mi familia es la de muchas otras:
> en tres generaciones, el judeoespañol pasó de ser la lengua de todos los días a ser un recuerdo.
> Los especialistas calculan que hoy lo hablan pocas decenas de miles de personas en el mundo, en
> su mayoría mayores, aunque las cifras varían mucho según la fuente.
>
> Hace unos años decidí aprender lo que había perdido. Encontré cursos en línea, grupos de
> conversación y una sorprendente comunidad de jóvenes en Israel, Turquía, Francia y Estados Unidos
> que estudian la lengua de sus abuelos. Aprendí que en Israel funcionan una Autoridad y una
> Academia dedicadas a ella, y que algunos prefieren llamarla *ladino*, aunque muchos estudiosos
> reservan ese nombre para la lengua de las traducciones religiosas. Aprendí también a reconocer
> las capas de su historia: palabras que el español abandonó hace siglos, como *fijo* por "hijo";
> préstamos del turco, como el *musafir* de mi abuela; voces hebreas para la vida religiosa y
> francesas que llegaron con las escuelas del siglo XIX.
>
> Una lingüista con la que hablé me quitó otra idea equivocada. "El judeoespañol no es el
> castellano de 1492 conservado en una vitrina", me explicó. "Guardó rasgos que el español de la
> península perdió, pero también cambió por su cuenta durante cinco siglos, en contacto con el
> turco, el griego, el hebreo y el francés. Es una variedad con su propia historia, como la de
> México o la de Buenos Aires". Desde entonces, cuando alguien me dice que mi abuela hablaba
> "como en el Quijote", le contesto que no: hablaba como en Esmirna.
>
> Lo más difícil no fue el vocabulario, sino la confianza. Al principio me daba vergüenza
> equivocarme frente a los pocos hablantes que conocí. Una señora de Estambul, de más de ochenta
> años, me corrigió con paciencia durante una videollamada y al final me dijo, en su lengua, que
> le daba gusto oír a alguien joven hablarla. Esa tarde entendí que no estaba aprendiendo un
> idioma muerto, sino uno que espera que alguien lo siga usando.
>
> No sé si mis hijos hablarán judeoespañol. Sé que conocerán su historia: la de una aljama
> medieval, una judería que ya no existe, un edicto, un barco, una ciudad turca y un barrio de la
> Ciudad de México. Y sé que, cuando lean una palabra como *kaza*, sabrán que no está mal
> escrita, sino que viene de lejos.
>
> Los romances que cantaba mi abuela los guardo en una grabación vieja. No los entiendo todos.
> Pero cada vez que la escucho, la casa vuelve a llamarse *kaza*.

**Summary.** (1) The writer's grandmother used words like *kaza* and *musafires* that she later
learned were Judeo-Spanish. (2) The family came to Mexico City from Izmir in the 1920s, like other
Sephardic families of the former Ottoman Empire, carrying a language taken from Iberia after 1492.
(3) Neighbors understood almost everything; the great-grandfather adapted to his customers,
while the grandmother kept Judeo-Spanish for home and family, a situation linguists call
diglossia. (4) The writer's mother understood but answered in Mexican Spanish, and the writer
didn't understand at all: three generations took the language from daily use to memory, and
specialists estimate only a few tens of thousands of speakers, mostly elderly, with figures that
vary. (5) The writer took online courses, found young learners in several countries, and learned
about the Israeli institutions, the *ladino* debate and the layers of old forms, Turkish, Hebrew
and French words. (6) A linguist told her that Judeo-Spanish isn't the Spanish of 1492
preserved under glass but a variety with five centuries of its own history. (7) Her hardest step
was confidence, until an elderly speaker in Istanbul encouraged her. (8–9) Her children will know the history, and her grandmother's ballads survive on
an old recording.

**Glosses.** *Otra lengua dominante* = a different dominant language (*la lengua dominante* was
an honors word of C1 20h1); *le convenía* = it suited him, it was in his interest; *las capas* = the layers; *me
daba vergüenza* = I was embarrassed; *le daba gusto* = it pleased her; *viene de lejos* = it comes
from far away (and from long ago).

### Example 2: summarizing the article

A model summary in Spanish for a class handout (89 words), keeping the article's hedges:

> La autora cuenta cómo su familia sefardí, llegada de Esmirna a la Ciudad de México en los años
> veinte, perdió el judeoespañol en tres generaciones: la abuela lo reservaba para la casa, la
> madre lo entendía sin hablarlo y la autora no lo entendía. Explica que hoy lo hablan pocas
> decenas de miles de personas, aunque las cifras varían según la fuente, y que algunos lo llaman
> *ladino*. Decidió aprenderlo y descubrió una comunidad de jóvenes estudiantes. Concluye que no es
> una lengua muerta, sino una que necesita hablantes.

Notice what the summary keeps: the hedge on the numbers (*aunque las cifras varían*), the
attribution of the *ladino* name to "some" (*algunos*), and the writer's conclusion marked as hers
(*Concluye que*).

## Common mistakes

- **Calling Judeo-Spanish "medieval Spanish".** It keeps old forms but has five centuries of its
  own history and borrowings.
- **Using *ladino* without comment in a formal text.** Say *judeoespañol*, or note the debate.
- **Inventing Judeo-Spanish.** Spelling Spanish with *k* doesn't make it Judeo-Spanish; quote only
  forms from a source.
- **Stating speaker numbers as facts.** Give the source and say that estimates vary.
- **Confusing *la aljama* and *la judería*.** The first is the community; the second, the quarter.

## Key points

- After the edict of March 31, 1492, Jews who didn't convert left Spain; their diaspora reached
  the Ottoman Empire and North Africa.
- Judeo-Spanish keeps older forms (*fijo, favlar*), shows its own changes (*muestro*), and
  borrowed from Turkish, Hebrew, Greek, French and, in Haketia, Arabic.
- *Ladino* is a common name, but many scholars reserve it for the calque language of sacred
  translations.
- The language is endangered; institutions in Israel work to keep it alive.
- Recognize its forms; don't imitate them.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Guinea Ecuatorial y Filipinas: Spanish in Africa and Asia
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 counted three ASALE academies outside Spain and the Spanish-speaking Americas: the
United States, Equatorial Guinea and the Philippines. Lesson 20 covered the first. This lesson
covers the other two, where Spanish has very different lives: an official language and a **lingua
franca** in Central Africa, and in Asia a historical language, a source of loanwords and the base
of a **[[creole]]**. It also crosses the Pacific on the route that linked New Spain, Mexico's colonial
predecessor, with Manila. *La hispanofonía* (the Spanish-speaking world) is wider than most maps
show.

## Equatorial Guinea

Equatorial Guinea, on the island of Bioko and the mainland region of Río Muni, was a Spanish
colony until its independence on October 12, 1968. It is the only African country with Spanish
as an official language. Spanish is *cooficial* (co-official) there with French and Portuguese:
the constitutional texts compiled by Université Laval's language-planning site show Portuguese
added by a 2010 constitutional law, and French had been added earlier (sources differ on the
exact year, usually placing it in the late 1990s).

Spanish is the language of school, government and the press, but few *ecuatoguineanos*
(Equatorial Guineans) grow up with it alone. The largest group speaks Fang; Bubi is the
traditional language of Bioko; and smaller languages include an English-based creole and a
Portuguese-based one on the island of Annobón. So Spanish works as a *lengua franca*: a shared
language between speakers of different first languages. Studies describe features of Guinean
Spanish that come from contact with these languages, especially in pronunciation and intonation.
The Academia Ecuatoguineana de la Lengua Española was founded in 2013 and joined ASALE in 2016.

## The Philippines

Spanish arrived in 1565 with Miguel López de Legazpi's expedition, which sailed from New Spain,
and Manila was founded as the colonial capital in 1571. The *archipiélago* (archipelago) of more
than 7,000 islands was governed from Mexico City until Mexico's independence, and Spanish rule
ended in 1898, when the islands passed to the United States. Spanish was never the language of
most Filipinos: it was the language of government, the Church and an educated minority, and
English displaced it in the twentieth century.

Today the 1987 Constitution makes Filipino and English the official languages and says Spanish and
Arabic shall be promoted on a voluntary and optional basis. The Academia Filipina de la Lengua
Española, founded in 1924, is one of the 23 ASALE academies. What remains is *un remanente* (a
remnant): older speakers, Spanish surnames and place names, and thousands of words in the
Philippine languages. *El tagalo* (Tagalog), the base of Filipino, took *kutsara* (*cuchara*),
*bintana* (*ventana*), *sapatos* (*zapatos*), *silya* (*silla*), *relos* (*reloj*) and the greeting
*kumusta* (from *¿cómo está?*). Some came from Mexico: *kamote* (*camote*), *kamatis*
(tomato), *atole* and *petate* are Nahuatl words that reached Tagalog through Mexican Spanish
(examples from Wikipedia's list of Tagalog loanwords, read November 17, 2026).

## Chavacano: a Spanish-based creole

A **[[creole]]** (*la lengua criolla*) is a language that forms when speakers of different languages
build a shared one, usually from the vocabulary of one language and the grammar of others, and
children then learn it as their first language. *El chabacano* (Chavacano, as it is usually
spelled in English) is a group of Spanish-based creoles in the Philippines: in Zamboanga and
Cotabato on Mindanao, on the island of Basilan, and in Cavite and Ternate on Manila Bay. A page by
Ian Mackenzie (Newcastle University), drawing on Antonio Quilis (1996), gives about 1.2 million
speakers; that figure is old, so treat it as an estimate.

Its words are mostly Spanish; its grammar is Philippine. Verbs don't change for person or tense:
small markers before the verb do the work, *ta* for the present, *ya* for the past and *di* or
*ay* for the future. The plural marker *mana*, from Tagalog *mga*, goes before the noun, and
several pronouns come from Philippine languages (*kamó*, "you all"; *silá*, "they").

The Mexican reader can enjoy a pun here. In Mexico *el chabacano* is an apricot, and in general
Spanish the adjective *chabacano* means "tacky, vulgar". The creole's name is usually explained as
that adjective, first used dismissively by speakers of standard Spanish.

### Example 1: Chavacano and Spanish word by word

Mackenzie's page gives this sentence, from Quilis: *Ya mirá yo cun José*, "I saw José".

| Chavacano | Spanish source | Its job | Standard Spanish |
|---|---|---|---|
| *ya* | *ya* (already) | past marker | the ending of *vi* |
| *mirá* | *mirar* | the verb, unchanged | *vi* (*ver*) |
| *yo* | *yo* | subject, after the verb | *yo* (usually dropped) |
| *cun* | *con* | marks a person as object | *a* |
| *José* | *José* | | *José* |

Standard Spanish: *Vi a José.* Three steps work for any sourced sentence: find each word's Spanish
source; ask what job it does in the creole (often not its Spanish job: *ya* "already" became a
tense marker); then rebuild the Spanish sentence. Two more examples from the same page: *Mario ya
dormí na casa* (Mario slept in the house: *na* is "in"), and *el mana casa* (the houses).

![A chart. Five boxes give the Chavacano words Ya, mirá, yo, cun and José, each with its role written below in Spanish: past marker, verb (mirar), subject, object marker (con), name. Arrows lead ya, mirá and yo to the Spanish word Vi, cun to a, and José to José. A line at the bottom reads: Ya mirá yo cun José = Vi a José (I saw José).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The Manila galleon

From 1565 to 1815 the Manila galleon (*el galeón de Manila*, also *la nao de China*) crossed the
Pacific between Acapulco and Manila, usually once or twice a year. *El galeón* (galleon) carried
silver from New Spain westward and brought back silk, porcelain and spices from Asia, which were
carried overland to Veracruz and on to Spain. The return route, found by Andrés de Urdaneta in
1565, swung north on the winds and currents of the North Pacific before turning south along the
coast of California. People, foods and words traveled both ways.

![A schematic map of the Pacific. A route runs west from Acapulco across the Pacific to Manila, passing near Guam. A second route returns from Manila northeast across the North Pacific, reaches the coast of California and runs south to Acapulco. Labels give the dates 1565 to 1815.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: Spanish on the other side of the sea

A feature for a Mexican magazine (invented reporter and speakers; the facts are those above).

> **El español del otro lado del mar**
>
> En Acapulco casi nadie lo recuerda, pero durante dos siglos y medio la bahía fue el extremo
> americano de una ruta que llegaba hasta Asia. De aquí salía el galeón de Manila cargado de plata;
> aquí volvía, meses después, con sedas y porcelanas que cruzaban el país en mulas hasta Veracruz.
> Con la mercancía viajaban marineros, soldados, frailes y palabras. Por eso, cuando un filipino
> dice *kamote* o pide *atole*, está usando, sin saberlo, palabras que salieron de México.
>
> Hoy el español es oficial en un solo país de Asia y África, y ese país no está en Asia. En Malabo,
> la capital de Guinea Ecuatorial, el español es la lengua de la escuela, de los tribunales y de
> los periódicos. "En casa hablamos fang", me explica una maestra de secundaria. "Pero con mis
> alumnos bubis, con los vecinos de Annobón o con un funcionario, el español es lo que tenemos en
> común". Los lingüistas llaman a eso lengua franca. Ella lo llama, simplemente, "la lengua de
> todos".
>
> El español de Guinea no suena como el de México ni como el de Madrid. Tiene su propia entonación
> y algunas palabras locales, y los ecuatoguineanos defienden que es tan legítimo como cualquier
> otro. En 2013 fundaron su propia academia, que tres años después entró en la Asociación de
> Academias. Para muchos, ese ingreso fue un reconocimiento: la hispanofonía también es africana.
>
> En Filipinas la historia es otra. Allí el español fue durante siglos la lengua del gobierno y de
> una minoría culta, pero nunca la de la mayoría. Cuando las islas pasaron a Estados Unidos, en
> 1898, el inglés lo fue desplazando, y la Constitución de 1987 dejó como oficiales el filipino y
> el inglés. Lo que queda es un remanente: apellidos como Santos o Reyes, nombres de calles,
> algunos abuelos que todavía lo hablan y miles de palabras en el tagalo de todos los días. Un
> taxista de Manila no habla español, pero cuenta en voz alta el cambio con números que a un
> mexicano le resultan curiosamente familiares.
>
> Y luego está Zamboanga, en la isla de Mindanao. Allí, en la radio, en el mercado y en la calle,
> se oye una lengua que un hispanohablante entiende a medias: el chabacano. Las palabras son
> españolas; la gramática, filipina. En el mercado, una vendedora regatea en chabacano con un
> cliente y, cuando nota mi acento, cambia al inglés sin pestañear. Un locutor local me explica que el verbo no cambia: delante
> se pone una partícula que dice si la acción ya pasó, está pasando o va a pasar. "Para ustedes
> suena a español mal hablado", dice con humor. "Para nosotros es nuestra lengua materna, la que
> aprendimos de nuestras madres". Tiene razón: el chabacano es una lengua criolla, con sus propias
> reglas, y no un español defectuoso.
>
> Al locutor le divierte que en México el chabacano sea una fruta. "Lo sé, lo sé", se ríe. "Y que
> en el diccionario quiera decir de mal gusto. Nuestros abuelos le dieron la vuelta al insulto y
> lo convirtieron en nombre".
>
> El archipiélago tiene más de siete mil islas y decenas de lenguas, y el chabacano es solo una de
> ellas. Sus hablantes no saben bien cuántos son; las cifras disponibles son antiguas. Pero en las
> escuelas de Zamboanga se ha enseñado, se escribe en la prensa local y se canta en las fiestas.
>
> Desde un muelle de Zamboanga, mirando al este, el Pacífico parece no tener fin. Del otro lado,
> a miles de kilómetros, está Acapulco. Entre las dos orillas no queda ningún galeón, pero quedan
> el camote, el atole y una lengua que convirtió al español en algo nuevo.

**Summary.** (1) Acapulco was the American end of the Manila galleon route for two and a half
centuries, and Mexican words such as *kamote* and *atole* reached the Philippines with it. (2)
Spanish is official in only one country of Asia and Africa, Equatorial Guinea, where a teacher who
speaks Fang at home calls Spanish "everyone's language", a lingua franca. (3) Guinean Spanish has
its own sound and words; its academy (2013) joined ASALE three years later. (4) In the Philippines
Spanish was the language of government and an elite; English displaced it after 1898, and what
remains are surnames, street names, older speakers, loanwords and number words. (5) In Zamboanga a
radio announcer explains that Chavacano verbs don't change and that it is a creole, a mother
tongue, not bad Spanish. (6) He jokes about the name. (7) Figures are old, but Chavacano has been taught
in schools and is written. (8) Across the Pacific, the galleon's traces remain.

**Glosses.** *El extremo americano* = the American end; *en mulas* = by mule; *lo fue
desplazando* = gradually displaced it; *a medias* = halfway, partly; *le dieron la vuelta al
insulto* = they turned the insult around; *el muelle* = the pier.

### Example 2: summarizing the article

A model summary in Spanish (76 words) for a newsletter on Spanish around the world:

> El reportaje recorre el español fuera de América y España. Recuerda que el galeón de Manila unió
> Acapulco con Asia y llevó palabras mexicanas a Filipinas. Explica que en Guinea Ecuatorial el
> español es oficial y sirve de lengua franca entre hablantes de fang, bubi y otras lenguas. En
> Filipinas, en cambio, solo queda un remanente, salvo en Zamboanga, donde se habla el chabacano,
> una lengua criolla de base española cuyas cifras de hablantes son antiguas.

The summary keeps the article's caution about the numbers (*cuyas cifras … son antiguas*) and
adds no claim the article doesn't make.

## Pronunciation

- *ecuatoguineano*: e-cua-to-gui-ne-A-no, seven syllables; the *u* in *gui* is silent.
- *archipiélago*: ar-chi-PIÉ-la-go; *el tagalo*: ta-GA-lo.
- *Zamboanga*: zam-bo-AN-ga, four syllables.
- *cooficial*: co-o-fi-CIAL, the two *o*'s pronounced separately.

## Common mistakes

- **"Spanish is official in the Philippines."** It isn't, under the 1987 Constitution; it is
  promoted on a voluntary basis.
- **Calling Chavacano broken Spanish.** It is a creole with its own grammar and native speakers.
- **Forgetting Africa.** Equatorial Guinea has Spanish as an official language and an ASALE
  academy.
- **Confusing a lingua franca with a mother tongue.** In Equatorial Guinea, Spanish is the shared
  language for many people whose first language is Fang or Bubi.
- **Inventing Chavacano.** Quote only sourced examples.

## Key points

- Equatorial Guinea (independent in 1968) has Spanish, French and Portuguese as co-official
  languages; Spanish is its lingua franca, and its academy joined ASALE in 2016.
- In the Philippines, Spain ruled from 1565 to 1898; today Filipino and English are official, and
  Spanish survives in a remnant of speakers, names and Tagalog loanwords.
- Chavacano is a Spanish-based creole: Spanish words, Philippine grammar, tense markers *ta, ya,
  di*.
- The Manila galleon linked Acapulco and Manila from 1565 to 1815 and carried words both ways.

lessons.title: Con base en varias fuentes: writing from several sources (EMIE task 1)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 19 taught you to summarize one text, and C1 23 to write from one talk. At C2 you combine three
sources: two experts heard on the radio and two written texts, turned into one new text for a
stated reader. That is **[[mediation]]** in its fullest written form, and the product is a
**[[synthesis]]**: one text organized by points, not three summaries in a row. The theme is tourism on
Mexico's Caribbean coast.

## The task, as far as the sources tell us

| What | As the sources describe it |
|---|---|
| The test | *Expresión, mediación e interacción escritas*: three tasks in 150 minutes (Instituto Cervantes) |
| Task 1 input | a radio excerpt in which two experts talk, plus two informational texts on the same topic (the 2024 sample exam, as described in a 2024 study) |
| Task 1 output | 400–450 words in a genre and for a reader set by the instructions, summarizing and comparing the sources (same source) |
| Instructions | name the text type more precisely than the old format did (preparation sites) |
| Not settled here | how many times you hear the recording; how the text is marked: check the official guide |

How you split the 150 minutes is your decision. This course suggests about 70 minutes for task 1,
notes included, and 40 for each of the others: a suggestion, not an exam rule.

## The synthesis grid

Before writing, build a grid: sources across the top, points down the side. In each cell note the
source's position and its hedges, with a symbol for agreement, difference, addition or silence.

![A synthesis grid with three columns, radio, text A and text B, and five rows of points: capacidad de carga, derrama económica, renta vacacional, cruceros and medidas. Each cell holds a short note and a symbol: = for agreement, ≠ for difference, + for an addition, a dash for silence. A key under the grid explains the four symbols, and a margin note says to keep each source's hedges.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each row becomes a paragraph in which you confront the sources (*confrontar*: to compare texts
or versions; close to B1's *contrastar*). The language of comparison:

| Spanish | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *coincidir en* | to agree on | *Ambas fuentes coinciden en que falta información.* — Both sources agree that information is lacking. |
| *discrepar de* (B1) | to disagree with | *La carta discrepa del informe oficial.* — The letter disagrees with the official report. |
| *coincidente* | matching | *un diagnóstico coincidente* — a matching diagnosis |
| *la convergencia* (lesson 20) / *la divergencia* | convergence / divergence | *La divergencia más clara está en las medidas.* — The clearest divergence is in the measures. |
| *contraponer* | to set against | *El texto contrapone dos modelos de turismo.* — The text sets two models of tourism against each other. |
| *aunar* | to combine | *La propuesta aúna conservación y empleo.* — The proposal combines conservation and jobs. |
| *el contrapunto* | counterpoint | *La carta ofrece un contrapunto a la nota.* — The letter offers a counterpoint to the news item. |

*Contraponer* goes like *poner* (*contrapongo, contrapuse, contrapondré, contrapuesto*; command
*contrapón*). *Aunar* writes an accent where the stem is stressed: *aúno, aúnas, aúna, aunamos,
aúnan*; subjunctive *aúne*.

## Attribution and hedges

In a synthesis every claim belongs to someone, and **[[attribution]]** tells the reader to whom. The
reporting verb is part of the claim, so choose its strength to match the source:

| Strength | Reporting verbs and frames |
|---|---|
| certain | *afirma, asegura, confirma, constata* |
| argued | *sostiene, defiende, argumenta* |
| tentative | *plantea, sugiere, estima que podría, no descarta que* + subjunctive |
| warning | *advierte, alerta sobre* |
| concession, qualification | *reconoce, admite, matiza* |
| frames | *según…, a juicio de…, para…, en palabras de… (short quotation)* |

Keep each hedge and add none. If the economist says *podría haber ya una sobreoferta*, you write
*estima que podría existir una sobreoferta*, never *afirma que hay*; if a letter states something
flatly, report it as the letter's claim (*según la carta…*) instead of softening it. Quote only a
short phrase whose wording matters. The RAE's *Ortografía* recommends angle quotes (« ») in print;
Mexican publishing commonly uses " ", and either is fine here. Keep your own view apart, in the
genre's register: a report prefers *cabe señalar* to *yo creo*.

## The sources

The background is real: Quintana Roo collected 92,782 tonnes of sargassum in 2025 and about
138,000 by the end of September 2026, according to the state's environment department (*Por
Esto!*, October 1, 2026). The sources below, their towns and their figures are invented.

### Source 1: the radio excerpt

Also in the listening questions.

```dialogue
# Costa adentro
Conductora: Bienvenidos a Costa adentro. Hoy hablamos de un tema que en el Caribe mexicano ya no es nuevo: la masificación turística. Me acompañan la bióloga Itzel Canché y el economista Rodrigo Saldaña. Itzel, ¿cuánta gente aguanta una playa?
Canché: Depende de la playa. Lo que llamamos capacidad de carga no es un número mágico: incluye el arrecife, el agua dulce, la basura, el drenaje. En algunos tramos del litoral creemos que ya se rebasó, pero los datos son incompletos y conviene ser prudentes.
Conductora: Rodrigo, desde la economía, ¿la saturación es un problema?
Saldaña: Lo es, aunque no para todos por igual. La derrama económica del turismo sostiene a miles de familias; eso nadie lo discute. El problema es la estacionalidad: cuando llega el sargazo, la ocupación hotelera puede bajar en algunas zonas, y los empleos son los primeros en resentirlo.
Canché: Y ojo: el sargazo no lo causa el turismo. Es un fenómeno del Atlántico que todavía estamos estudiando.
Saldaña: De acuerdo. Lo que sí depende de nosotros es cómo crecemos. La renta vacacional, por ejemplo, ha multiplicado la oferta de cuartos sin pasar por los mismos permisos que un hotel. Podría haber ya una sobreoferta en ciertos destinos turísticos, aunque no tengo cifras definitivas.
Canché: Ahí coincidimos. Sin ordenamiento territorial, cada nuevo desarrollo suma presión sobre el agua y el manglar.
Conductora: ¿Una moratoria, entonces?
Saldaña: Yo no iría tan lejos. Preferiría reglas claras para todos.
Canché: Yo sí la consideraría en las zonas más frágiles, al menos mientras se mide bien la huella ecológica.
```

Summary: carrying capacity is several limits, and some stretches have probably passed it, though
data are incomplete (biologist); tourism income matters, seasonality is the problem, and rentals may
have created an oversupply, without firm figures (economist); tourism doesn't cause sargassum; both
want land-use planning; he prefers rules, she would consider a moratorium in fragile zones.
Glosses: *aguantar* (to bear); *el tramo* (stretch); *resentirlo* (to feel the effect).

### Source 2: a news item

> *Crecen las rentas vacacionales y los alquileres de los trabajadores*
>
> En los últimos cinco años, el número de viviendas anunciadas en plataformas de renta vacacional
> en Puerto Alegre se triplicó, de acuerdo con un estudio de la asociación local de hoteles. En el
> mismo periodo, el alquiler mensual promedio de un departamento de dos recámaras pasó de 7500 a
> 12 000 pesos, según datos de una inmobiliaria.
>
> Para la asociación, ambos fenómenos están relacionados: "Cada casa que se renta por noche es una
> casa menos para quien trabaja aquí", declaró su presidenta. Una investigadora de la universidad
> estatal matizó esa lectura: reconoció que la presión existe, pero advirtió que también influyen la
> llegada de nuevos residentes y la falta de vivienda social, por lo que "no hay evidencia
> concluyente" de que las plataformas sean la causa principal.
>
> El ayuntamiento prepara cambios al uso de suelo para limitar la renta vacacional en las colonias
> habitacionales. Organizaciones vecinales hablan ya de gentrificación turística y de la
> turistificación de sus barrios.

Summary: rental listings tripled and average rent rose from 7,500 to 12,000 pesos; the hotel
association links the two; a researcher names other causes and finds no conclusive evidence; the
council plans land-use changes. Glosses: *la inmobiliaria* (real-estate agency); *el ayuntamiento*
(town council). *La turistificación* (mass tourism's effect on a neighborhood) is recent: Fundéu
BBVA called it a valid neologism in 2018 (updated 2023); check the DLE before assuming an entry.

### Source 3: an open letter

> *Carta abierta a las autoridades municipales*
>
> Las cooperativas de pescadores y guías de Punta Arena nos dirigimos a ustedes ante el proyecto de
> un nuevo muelle para cruceros. El turismo de cruceros trae miles de visitantes en pocas horas,
> pero deja poco en la comunidad: la mayoría compra en las tiendas del propio puerto y regresa al
> barco antes de comer. Mientras tanto, el arrecife recibe más lanchas que nunca, y nadie ha medido
> todavía cuántas puede soportar.
>
> No nos oponemos al turismo; vivimos de él desde hace dos generaciones. Sabemos
> también que el puerto necesita empleo, y estamos dispuestos a colaborar con cualquier proyecto que
> lo genere sin dañar la bahía. Pedimos una moratoria a la
> construcción de nuevos muelles hasta que un estudio independiente determine la capacidad de carga
> de nuestra bahía, y pedimos que en ese estudio participen quienes conocen el mar todos los días.
> Un muelle se construye en meses; un arrecife tarda siglos en formarse.

Summary: cruise passengers spend little locally and the reef gets more boats than ever; the
cooperatives support tourism and jobs but ask for a moratorium on new piers until an independent study, with
local people, sets the bay's carrying capacity. Gloss: *la lancha* (small boat).

## The model: a report from the three sources

*Consigna* (original): you advise the tourism committee of Puerto Alegre's town council. In 400–450
words, report what the three sources say about tourism's effects and the measures discussed,
compare them, and assess them, for council members who aren't specialists. The model has 441 words.

> *Informe para la Comisión de Turismo: presión turística en el litoral*
>
> *Objeto*
>
> Este informe resume y compara tres fuentes recientes sobre los efectos del turismo en nuestro
> litoral: una entrevista radiofónica con la bióloga Itzel Canché y el economista Rodrigo Saldaña,
> una nota periodística sobre la renta vacacional y una carta abierta de las cooperativas de Punta
> Arena.
>
> *Diagnóstico*
>
> Las tres fuentes coinciden en que la presión turística es real, pero la describen desde ángulos
> distintos. Para Canché, la capacidad de carga no es una cifra única, sino un conjunto de límites
> (el arrecife, el agua, los residuos); cree que en algunos tramos ya se rebasó, aunque advierte que
> los datos son incompletos. Saldaña, por su parte, reconoce que la derrama económica sostiene a
> miles de familias y sitúa el problema en la estacionalidad: con la llegada del sargazo, la
> ocupación hotelera puede bajar en algunas zonas. Ambos especialistas aclaran que el sargazo no lo causa el turismo.
>
> La nota y la carta aportan dos casos concretos. Según la nota, los anuncios de renta vacacional se
> triplicaron en cinco años mientras el alquiler promedio subía de 7500 a 12 000 pesos. La
> asociación de hoteles atribuye el alza a las plataformas; una investigadora, en cambio, señala
> otras causas, como la llegada de nuevos residentes y la falta de vivienda social, y sostiene que "no hay evidencia concluyente". La carta, por último, afirma que el
> turismo de cruceros deja poco en la comunidad y que el arrecife recibe más lanchas que nunca.
>
> *Medidas en discusión*
>
> Es aquí donde las fuentes divergen. Saldaña, que considera posible una sobreoferta de cuartos,
> prefiere reglas claras para todos antes que una moratoria. Canché, en cambio,
> contempla una moratoria en las zonas más frágiles mientras se mide la huella ecológica, postura
> próxima a la de las cooperativas, que piden suspender nuevos muelles hasta contar con un estudio
> independiente. Los dos especialistas coinciden, además, en reclamar un ordenamiento territorial,
> y la nota informa que el ayuntamiento ya prepara cambios al uso de suelo.
>
> *Valoración*
>
> A juicio de quien firma, las fuentes permiten distinguir dos problemas que suelen confundirse:
> el volumen de visitantes y la forma en que se reparten sus beneficios. Cabe señalar, sin
> embargo, que ninguna aporta cifras sobre el agua o los residuos, precisamente los límites que
> menciona la bióloga, ni sobre lo que gasta cada visitante de crucero. Por ello, antes de decidir sobre una moratoria, convendría encargar el
