> estudio de capacidad de carga que piden las cooperativas y abrirlo a la participación de la
> comunidad. Una medida así aunaría las dos preocupaciones que recorren las tres fuentes: proteger
> el litoral y proteger el empleo.

Summary. *Objeto* names the sources. *Diagnóstico*: shared ground from different angles; the
biologist's and the economist's hedges kept (*cree que, advierte que… incompletos; puede bajar en algunas zonas*); the news item's figures, its two
readings and a three-word quotation; the letter's claim reported as the letter's (*afirma*).
*Medidas*: where the sources diverge, the planning both experts call for, and the council's plan reported in the news item. *Valoración*: the writer's
view, impersonal and apart (*a juicio de quien firma*: in the view of the undersigned), naming a
gap and recommending the study. Notice that the economist never "warns of" an oversupply: he only
thinks one possible.

```assignment
writing: es6-m6-w21-sintesis
```

## The coast in pictures

![A Caribbean coast scene: hotels and a palm tree on the left, a sandy beach sloping down to the sea with clumps of brown seaweed on the sand, a long pier running out toward a cruise ship on the right, and, under the clear water, a coral reef with fish. Four parts are labeled: el crucero, el muelle, el sargazo, el arrecife.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *aunar*, two syllables: ow-NAHR; but *aúno*, three, the accent splitting *a-ú*: ah-OO-noh.
- *la masificación*, five: mah-see-fee-kah-SYOHN; *la turistificación*, six:
  too-rees-tee-fee-kah-SYOHN.
- *la estacionalidad*, six: ehs-tah-syoh-nah-lee-DAHD.

## Common mistakes

- Three summaries in a row: organize by points and compare inside each paragraph.
- Changing a source's strength: *podría haber* becomes *hay*, or a flat claim gains a *quizá*.
- Judging a source while reporting it (*Saldaña tiene razón…*): save it for the assessment.
- Quoting long stretches instead of rephrasing.
- *auno, aunan* without the accent: *aúno, aúnan*.

## Key points

- Task 1 of the sample exam: a radio excerpt and two texts into 400–450 words, set genre, set reader.
- Grid first (sources × points), then one paragraph per point.
- Attribute every claim with a verb of the right strength; keep each hedge, add none.
- Keep your assessment separate, in the genre's register.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: De las notas al texto: rewriting and post-editing (EMIE task 2)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 combined several sources into one text. This lesson works on a single text at the
drafting desk: turning someone's notes into finished prose, repairing a weak draft, and fixing a
machine translation. All three are **[[reformulation]]**: saying the same content again, in the form
the reader needs. The setting is a Mexican museum preparing an exhibition on cacao, where a
*redactor* (copywriter; B2's *el editor* is the person who edits) writes the texts on the walls.

## Task 2, as far as the sources tell us

| What | As the sources describe it |
|---|---|
| 2024 sample exam | turn a list of notes into a 200–250-word text in a set genre and role (as described in a 2024 study) |
| The notes | shorter than in the old format, about 100 words (preparation sites) |
| Old format (before 2024) | correct and restructure a 150–250-word draft: errors, punctuation, precise vocabulary; sometimes a machine-translated text |
| Not settled here | whether the 2024 task still includes correcting a draft: check the official guide |

Because the exact form isn't confirmed, this lesson practices both shapes. The editing skills are
the same, and you will need them for your own drafts in every task.

## From notes to prose

*Los apuntes* (jotted notes) are *esquemáticos* (sketchy): no verbs, abbreviations, arrows, items
in any order. To turn them into a text, you expand each item into full clauses, order the
ideas for the reader, connect them, and set the register. You must also *explicitar* (spell
out) what the notes leave implicit, and leave out what the reader doesn't need, such as the
note-writer's reminders to themselves.

The exhibition designer (*el museógrafo, la museógrafa*) left these notes for the wall text
(*la cédula*, the museum label) of room 2:

| *Apuntes* | What they mean |
|---|---|
| *Sala 2 · "El cacao: bebida y moneda" · cédula temática 200–250 pal. · públ. general (adolesc. incl.)* | room 2, the title, a theme label of 200–250 words, for the general public, teenagers included |
| *cacao = semilla de árbol trop. · tierras bajas cálidas y húmedas (Tabasco, Soconusco)* | cacao is the seed of a tropical tree that grows in hot, humid lowlands |
| *consumo muy antiguo → residuos en vasijas · NO fechas exactas (debate)* | very old use, shown by residues in vessels; give no exact dates |
| *bebida: espuma = lo más apreciado · se vertía de un recipiente a otro* | the foam was prized; the drink was poured from one vessel into another |
| *moneda: semillas en mercados · tributo a Tenochtitlan* | the seeds served as money in markets and were paid as tribute |
| *vitrina 3: vaso trípode maya, jícara* | display case 3: a Maya three-legged vessel and a gourd cup |
| *cerrar: invitar a ver la vitrina · evitar "chocolate = náhuatl" (origen discutido)* | end by inviting visitors to the case; don't claim the word *chocolate* is Nahuatl, since its origin is disputed |

The text the *redactora* wrote (231 words):

> *El cacao: bebida y moneda*
>
> El cacao es la semilla de un árbol tropical que crece en las tierras bajas, cálidas y húmedas, del
> sureste de México y de Centroamérica, como las de Tabasco y el Soconusco, en Chiapas. Los pueblos
> mesoamericanos empezaron a aprovecharlo hace miles de años: los análisis de residuos en vasijas
> antiguas así lo demuestran, aunque los especialistas todavía discuten cuándo y dónde empezó su
> consumo.
>
> Lejos de ser una golosina, el cacao se tomaba como bebida, a menudo mezclado con agua, maíz o
> chile. Lo más apreciado era la espuma: para obtenerla, la bebida se vertía desde cierta altura de
> un recipiente a otro, una y otra vez.
>
> Sus semillas tuvieron además un valor muy distinto: servían como medio de intercambio en los
> mercados, y algunas regiones las entregaban como tributo a Tenochtitlan. Pocas monedas, en la
> historia, han podido también beberse.
>
> En la vitrina 3 se exhiben un vaso trípode maya, de un tipo que pudo servir para bebidas como esta,
> y una jícara, recipiente hecho con la cáscara seca de un fruto, que todavía hoy se usa en muchos
> lugares de México. Observe la forma del vaso: ¿por qué cree que tiene tres soportes?
>
> La palabra *cacao* llegó al español desde el náhuatl; el origen de la palabra *chocolate*, en cambio, sigue siendo
> motivo de debate. Esa historia la contamos en la sala siguiente.

Summary: what cacao is and where it grows; its ancient use, with the dating debate kept; the drink
and its prized foam; the seeds as money and tribute; the objects in case 3, with a question to the
visitor; the words *cacao* and *chocolate*. Glosses: *la golosina* (sweet, candy); *la jícara*
(gourd cup); *la cáscara* (shell, rind); *el soporte* (support, leg).

What the rewriting did: every note became a full clause; the warnings (*NO fechas exactas*,
*evitar…*) became careful wording (*todavía discuten, sigue siendo motivo de debate*) instead of
disappearing; connectors (*lejos de, además, en cambio*) link the paragraphs; one direct question
in *usted* involves the reader. A theme label is a short text for a standing reader, so it needs
*legibilidad* (readability): short paragraphs, no jargon, and one idea each.

```assignment
writing: es6-m6-w22-notas
```

## Repairing a draft

A *versión preliminar* (draft version; A2's *el borrador*) for room 3 came back with problems. The
errors in this draft are deliberate, planted for practice: don't copy its forms. Read it and spot
what you'd change before you look at the table.

> *El cacao después de la Conquista*
>
> Después de 1521 el cacao, que había sido una bebida de élites, se convirtió en un producto
> comercial muy importante. Los españoles al principio no les gustó su sabor amargo, pero
> eventualmente lo adoptaron añadiéndole azúcar, canela y otras especias. La nueva bebida adolecía
> de la espuma de la original, pero ganó seguidores en los conventos y en las casas ricas. Las
> semillas de cacao siguió circulando como moneda en algunos mercados durante la época colonial.
>
> El comercio con Europa, consistía de embarques que salían de Veracruz hacia Sevilla. En base a los
> documentos de la época se sabe de que el consumo creció en el siglo XVII y el chocolate se volvió
> súper popular, la gente lo tomaba diario. En la vitrina 4 se ven una chocolatera de cobre y un
> molinillo de madera, la chocolatera servía para calentar la bebida, el molinillo para hacer
> espuma. Esto dió origen a una costumbre que todavía existe: hoy, en Oaxaca y en
> Chiapas, muchas familias siguen preparando chocolate con agua y lo baten con molinillo hasta que la
> espuma cubre la taza.

Summary: after 1521 cacao became an important trade good; the Spanish first disliked its bitterness,
then added sugar and spices; the new drink spread in convents and rich houses; the seeds stayed in
use as money; trade ran from Veracruz to Seville; drinking grew in the seventeenth century; case 4
shows a copper pot and a wooden whisk, still used in Oaxaca and Chiapas to froth chocolate made
with water. Glosses: *adolecer de* (lesson 03: to suffer from a defect);
*el embarque* (shipment); *la chocolatera* (chocolate pot); *el molinillo* (wooden whisk).

| Draft | Problem | Better |
|---|---|---|
| *Los españoles al principio no les gustó* | *gustar* needs *a* + the person | *A los españoles, al principio, no les gustó* |
| *eventualmente lo adoptaron* | calque of English "eventually"; *eventualmente* means "possibly, now and then" | *con el tiempo lo adoptaron* |
| *adolecía de la espuma* | *adolecer de* is "to suffer from (a defect)", not "to lack" (lesson 03) | *carecía de la espuma* |
| *Las semillas… siguió* | agreement | *siguieron* |
| *El comercio con Europa, consistía de* | comma between subject and verb; *consistir en* | *El comercio con Europa consistía en* |
| *En base a… se sabe de que* | the DPD advises against *en base a* and prefers *sobre la base de*; *con base en* isn't faulted (lesson 08); dequeísmo (C1 03) | *Los documentos de la época muestran que* |
| *súper popular, la gente lo tomaba diario* | colloquial for a museum; a comma joining two sentences | *se volvió muy popular y se tomaba a diario* |
| *una chocolatera… de madera, la chocolatera servía* | comma splice; repetition | *…de madera: la primera servía para calentar la bebida, y el segundo, para hacer espuma.* |
| *Esto dió origen* | monosyllables take no accent; vague *esto* | *Así nació una costumbre que todavía existe.* |

The picture shows the same paragraph before and after.

![Two panels side by side. On the left, a draft paragraph marked in red: a crossed-out comma between subject and verb, a circled word eventualmente, an insertion mark adding a before los españoles, de struck out and replaced with en after consistía, and the accent on dió struck through. On the right, the clean final version of the same paragraph, with the changes highlighted in green.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Correcting is *pulir* (to polish) and *depurar* (to purge of errors); moving paragraphs around is
*reestructurar*; cutting a long text without losing ideas is *condensar*. No *corrector automático*
(spell-checker) catches *eventualmente* or *adolecer de*: both are real words, used in the wrong
sense.

Once the *versión final* (final version) is approved, someone has to *maquetar* it (lay it out) for
the panel. *La maquetación* is part of the *museografía* (exhibition design): the type size that
lets the *lector meta* (target reader) read from a few steps away in the *sala de exposición*
(exhibition hall), the line length, and whether paragraphs open with a *sangría* (indentation) or,
as on many panels, are separated by a blank line.

## Post-editing a machine translation

**[[Post-editing]]** (*la posedición*; to post-edit, *poseditar*) is correcting a *traducción automática*
(machine translation) so it reads as if written in Spanish. The RAE's guidance prefers the prefix *pos-* to *post-*
except before *s* (*posguerra, posoperatorio*; DPD, *pos-*: check), which gives *posedición*;
*postedición* also appears in translation studies. A label for case 4, written in English:

> This copper chocolate pot was used to heat the drink. Its long handle kept the hand away from the
> fire. The wooden whisk, known as a molinillo, was spun between the palms to raise the foam. Both
> objects belonged to a convent kitchen in Puebla in the eighteenth century. Please do not touch
> the display case.

The machine's version, then the post-edited one (both translate the English above):

> Esta olla de chocolate de cobre fue usada para calentar la bebida. Su largo mango mantenía la mano
> lejos del fuego. El batidor de madera, conocido como molinillo, era girado entre las palmas para
> levantar la espuma. Ambos objetos pertenecieron a una cocina de convento en Puebla en el siglo
> dieciocho. Por favor no toque el caso de exhibición.

> Esta chocolatera de cobre servía para calentar la bebida; su mango largo mantenía la mano lejos
> del fuego. El molinillo de madera se hacía girar entre las palmas para levantar espuma. Ambos
> objetos pertenecieron a la cocina de un convento de Puebla en el siglo XVIII. Favor de no tocar la
> vitrina.

What changed: the right term (*chocolatera*, *vitrina*: *caso de exhibición* translates "case"
word for word); the passive *fue usada, era girado* replaced by what Spanish prefers here (*servía
para, se hacía girar*); centuries in Roman numerals; and the polite notice Mexican signs use
(*Favor de no tocar*). In a *ficha técnica* (data sheet) or a *pieza de museo*'s label, check every
term against the museum's own records: a machine doesn't know the collection.

## In the exhibition hall

![A museum exhibition hall: a glass display case on a pedestal holding a three-legged vessel and a gourd cup, a large text panel on the wall beside it, and a small card with technical details at the foot of one object. Four parts are labeled: la vitrina, la pieza de museo, la cédula, la ficha técnica.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *la posedición*, four syllables: poh-seh-dee-SYOHN (no *t*).
- *la museografía*, six: moo-seh-oh-grah-FEE-ah; *el museógrafo*, five: moo-seh-OH-grah-foh.
- *reestructurar*, five: rreh-ehs-trook-too-RAHR (both *e*'s are heard).

## Common mistakes

- Copying the notes' order. Reorder for the reader: what they need first.
- Dropping the notes' warnings instead of turning them into careful wording.
- Trusting the spell-checker: false friends and misused words are spelled correctly.
- Post-editing word by word: change the structure when Spanish needs it (*servía para*, not *fue
  usada para*).
- Mixing *tú* and *usted* in one text: a museum chooses one and keeps it.

## Key points

- Task 2 of the 2024 sample exam: notes into a 200–250-word text; correcting a draft is the old
  format's shape, practiced here too.
- From notes: expand, order, connect, set the register; spell out what's implicit.
- Repairing a draft: agreement, government, punctuation, confusables, register, cohesion.
- Post-editing: terms, structure, conventions of the genre; check every term.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Una pirámide que se invierte: texts from data and oral mediation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

C1 20 taught you to report what a graph shows. At C2 you interpret the data, give possible causes
with the right caution, and explain them to readers or listeners who didn't ask for numbers. The
DELE C2 asks for this twice: a written text from a chart (writing task 3) and a spoken
presentation from several texts and a chart (speaking task 1). The theme is the aging of
Mexico's population and what it means for pensions.

## The two tasks, as far as the sources tell us

| Task | As the sources describe it |
|---|---|
| Writing, task 3 | a 200–250-word text in a set genre explaining data from tables and charts (the 2024 sample exam, as described in a 2024 study) |
| Speaking, task 1 | 30 minutes to prepare, a choice between two sets of materials (texts and charts), then a 5–6-minute presentation; at C2 the materials include several texts; notes may be consulted but not read aloud, and the examiner signals when five minutes have passed (Instituto Cervantes examiner-training material, 2023, for the 2024 version) |
| Speaking, task 1 | the points to cover are set out more clearly than before, and you must give an opinion (preparation sites) |

## Explaining data at C2

Describing (*pasó del 14 % al 24 %*) is C1. At C2 you add three layers: what the figures mean for
the reader, what might explain them, and what they can't show.

| Layer | Language |
|---|---|
| interpret | *esto significa que…; dicho de otro modo…; por cada diez personas en edad de trabajar habría…* |
| explain, cautiously | *se explica en parte por…; obedece, entre otros factores, a…; cabe atribuirlo a…* |
| set limits | *los datos no permiten afirmar que…; una correlación no prueba una causa* |
| project | *de mantenerse la tendencia…; según las proyecciones…; se trata de una proyección, no de un pronóstico* |
| extrapolate with care | *sería arriesgado extrapolar estos resultados a…* |

Three words to keep apart. *La media* (the statistical mean) and B2's *el promedio* both add up the
values and divide: *el promedio* is the everyday word, *la media* the statistical one. *La mediana*
(the median) is the middle value once the values are ordered. When a few very high values pull the
mean up, the median describes the typical case better: if the mean pension in a group is 6800
pesos and the median 4200, half the group gets 4200 or less. *El percentil* (percentile) generalizes
the idea: the 90th percentile is the value below which 90% of cases fall.

Two more: *la cohorte* (cohort) is a group born in the same years and followed over time, and *el
horizonte* of a projection is its time frame (*con un horizonte a 2050*). A projection says what
would happen if assumptions held, so its verbs are conditional or hedged: *pasaría, podría llegar
a*, never a flat future.

Two ratios recur in these texts. *La tasa de dependencia* (dependency ratio) counts dependents,
children and older people, per 100 people of working age; *la fecundidad* (fertility) is usually
measured as the average number of children per woman. Pension studies add *cálculos actuariales* (actuarial
calculations), which estimate, from life tables, how long a pension will have to be paid.

This course writes percentages as Mexican publications do, with a decimal point, and with the
RAE's space before the sign: *el 14.7 %*.

## The data and the texts

The picture is fictional data for an imaginary country, made for this lesson.

![Two population pyramids side by side, labeled datos ficticios. Each has six age groups, from 0–14 at the bottom to 75 and over at the top, men on the left and women on the right, in percent of the total population. In 2025 the pyramid is wide at the base, 22.5% aged 0–14, and narrow at the top, 14.2% aged 60 or over. In the 2050 projection the base has shrunk to 15.6% and the upper groups have grown to 23.8%, so the shape looks more like a column.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The two texts below are original; their figures are real and dated, their experts invented.

> *México ya no es un país joven*
>
> Durante décadas, la pirámide de población de México tuvo una base ancha y una cúspide estrecha.
> Esa imagen está cambiando. Según la Encuesta Intercensal 2025 del INEGI, en el país viven unos
> 19.2 millones de personas de 60 años o más, el 14.7 % de la población, y la edad mediana llegó a
> 32 años, frente a 29 en 2020. Es una proporción cercana a la que el Consejo Nacional de Población
> (CONAPO) esperaba para 2030.
>
> Para la demógrafa Laura Ibarra, el bono demográfico, ese periodo en que la población en edad de
> trabajar crece más que la que depende de ella, "no se ha cerrado, pero ya no durará mucho". Ibarra
> insiste en que la longevidad es un logro, no un problema: lo que le preocupa es que el
> envejecimiento avance más rápido que la capacidad de los sistemas de salud y de seguridad social
> para adaptarse. "Otros países envejecieron siendo ricos; nosotros vamos a envejecer antes",
> resume.

Summary: Mexico's pyramid is changing: 19.2 million people aged 60 or over (14.7%) and a median age
of 32 against 29 in 2020 (INEGI, 2025), close to what CONAPO projected for 2030. A demographer
says the demographic dividend hasn't closed but won't last, that longevity is an achievement, and
that her worry is the speed of aging. Gloss: *la cúspide* (apex).

> *¿Alcanzará la pensión?*
>
> Quienes empezaron a cotizar en el IMSS a partir de 1997 no se jubilarán con el antiguo sistema de
> reparto, en el que las cotizaciones de los trabajadores activos pagaban las pensiones de los
> jubilados, sino con cuentas individuales que administran las afores. La reforma de 2020 buscó
> mejorar las pensiones de esa generación: la cuota que pagan los patrones por cesantía y vejez sube
> de forma gradual y, en los salarios más altos, pasará del 3.15 % al 11.875 % del salario base en
> 2030; además, las semanas de cotización exigidas bajaron a 750 en 2021, cifra que aumenta 25 semanas por año hasta llegar a 1000 en 2031.
>
> Aun así, los especialistas consultados estiman que la tasa de reemplazo, la parte del último
> salario que representa la pensión, podría quedarse baja para quienes coticen pocos años o ganen
> poco, y recomiendan el ahorro voluntario. A ello se suma una pensión no contributiva que el
> Gobierno federal paga a las personas de 65 años o más.

Summary: since 1997 new IMSS workers retire with individual accounts managed by the *afores*, not
the old pay-as-you-go system; the 2020 reform gradually raises employers' old-age contribution (for the highest
salaries, from 3.15% to 11.875% of base salary by 2030) and set the required weeks at 750 in 2021, rising by 25 a year to 1,000 in 2031.
Experts think the replacement rate could stay low for some and recommend voluntary savings; there
is also a non-contributory pension from age 65. Glosses: *cotizar* (C1: here, to pay social
security contributions); *el patrón* (employer; the term Mexican labor law uses).

## The model: an article from the chart (task 3 shape)

*Consigna* (original): your high school's magazine asks for a short article (200–250 words) that
explains the pyramids to students aged 16 to 18. The model has 218 words.

> *¿Qué le pasa a la pirámide?*
>
> Una pirámide de población muestra cuántas personas hay en cada grupo de edad. En el país
> imaginario de nuestra gráfica, la de 2025 todavía tiene una base ancha: el 22.5 % de sus
> habitantes tiene menos de 15 años. La de 2050, en cambio, es una proyección, y se parece más a una
> columna que a una pirámide.
>
> ¿Qué cambia? Sobre todo, la parte de arriba. Las personas de 60 años o más pasarían del 14.2 % al
> 23.8 % de la población, mientras que los menores de 15 bajarían al 15.6 %. Dicho de otro modo: en
> 2025 hay unas 22 personas mayores por cada 100 en edad de trabajar; en 2050 habría unas 39.
>
> Este cambio suele explicarse por dos tendencias que actúan a la vez: nacen menos niños y la
> esperanza de vida es mayor. Ahora bien, la gráfica no muestra causas, solo cantidades, y una
> proyección depende de supuestos que pueden no cumplirse.
>
> ¿Por qué debería importarles a ustedes? Porque en 2050 rondarán los 40 años y formarán
> parte de la población económicamente activa que sostendrá, con su trabajo y sus cotizaciones,
> buena parte de la seguridad social. Entender hoy la forma de la pirámide es una manera de
> prepararse para ese relevo generacional, que no será igual al de sus padres.

Summary: what a pyramid shows; the 2025 shape and the 2050 projection; the key change, given as
percentages and then as a ratio the reader can picture; two usual explanations, with the limit
that the chart shows no causes and a projection rests on assumptions; why it matters to the
reader. Gloss: *el supuesto* (assumption).

```assignment
writing: es6-m6-w23-datos
```

## From the page to the room: the presentation

In speaking task 1 you mediate orally: you present several texts and a chart to someone who
hasn't read them. The plan sheet below is a way to use the 30 minutes: note the structure and key
words, never full sentences, because you may look at your notes but not read them aloud.

![A one-page presentation plan with seven boxes from top to bottom: introducción (tema y materiales), texto 1 (idea central y enfoque), texto 2 (idea central y enfoque), gráfico (lo que muestra y lo que no), comparación (coincidencias y diferencias), opinión (con razones) and cierre. A timeline along the right edge marks minute 0, minute 1, minute 4, minute 5 with the examiner's signal, and minute 6.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A model presentation from the two texts and the chart (a transcript of about two and a half
minutes, shorter than the exam's 5–6; also in the listening questions):

> Los materiales que elegí tratan del envejecimiento de la población y de sus consecuencias para
> las pensiones. Son dos textos breves, uno de carácter demográfico y otro económico, y una gráfica
> con dos pirámides de población. Voy a presentarlos en ese orden, luego los voy a relacionar y, al
> final, daré mi opinión.
>
> El primer texto parte de datos del INEGI: en México hay unos 19 millones de personas de 60 años o
> más, casi el 15 % de la población, y la edad mediana ya es de 32 años. Lo interesante es el
> enfoque de la demógrafa que cita: para ella, vivir más es un logro, y lo que le preocupa no es el
> envejecimiento en sí, sino su velocidad.
>
> El segundo texto pasa de la demografía a la economía. Explica que quienes empezaron a cotizar
> después de 1997 tendrán una pensión basada en su cuenta individual, y resume la reforma de 2020:
> más aportaciones de los patrones y menos semanas exigidas, aunque la cifra va subiendo hasta 2031.
> Los especialistas que cita estiman que, aun así, la tasa de reemplazo podría ser baja para
> algunos trabajadores.
>
> En cuanto a la gráfica, conviene aclarar que los datos son ficticios. Muestra cómo, en un país
> imaginario, la proporción de mayores de 60 pasaría de un 14 % a casi un 24 % entre 2025 y 2050,
> mientras se reduce la base.
>
> Si los comparo, los tres materiales coinciden en la dirección del cambio, pero cada uno mira un
> aspecto distinto: el primero, la sociedad; el segundo, el dinero; la gráfica, la forma general.
> Ninguno, por cierto, habla de quién cuidará a las personas mayores.
>
> Y esa es precisamente mi opinión: creo que el debate suele reducirse a las pensiones, cuando el
> cuidado, la salud y la vivienda importan tanto como el monto que cada quien reciba. Una pensión
> suficiente es necesaria, pero no basta para envejecer bien. En resumen, los materiales muestran
> un cambio que ya empezó, y la pregunta es si nos va a encontrar preparados.

Summary: the speaker names the materials and the plan; presents text 1 (the INEGI figures, the
demographer's view on speed); text 2 (individual accounts, the 2020 reform, the experts' hedged
concern); the chart, flagged as fictional; a comparison (same direction, three angles) and a gap
no source covers (care); a reasoned opinion and a closing line. Glosses: *el monto* (amount);
*cada quien* (Mexico: each person).

Signposting carries the listener: *voy a presentarlos en ese orden; en cuanto a la gráfica; si los
comparo; y esa es precisamente mi opinión; en resumen*. Notice that the speaker rounds the figures
for the ear (*casi el 15 %*), keeps the experts' hedges (*estiman que… podría*), and keeps her
opinion for the end.

## Pronunciation

- *la longevidad*, four syllables: lohn-heh-vee-DAHD (*g* before *e* like a strong English *h*).
- *actuarial*, three: ahk-twah-RYAHL.
- *la cohorte*, three: koh-OHR-teh (the *h* is silent).
- *extrapolar*, four: ehks-trah-poh-LAHR.

## Common mistakes

- Listing every figure. Choose the two or three that tell the story and say what they mean.
- Reading a cause into a chart: the chart shows how much, not why.
- A flat future for a projection: *en 2050 habrá* → *según la proyección, en 2050 habría*.
- *La media* when you mean the median: *la mediana*.
- In the presentation, reading your notes aloud, or leaving no time for your opinion.

## Key points

- Writing task 3 of the 2024 sample exam: 200–250 words explaining data in a set genre.
- Interpret, explain with caution, set limits, project with hedges.
- *La mediana* isn't *la media* (or B2's everyday *el promedio*): don't swap them in a statistical text.
- Speaking task 1: several texts and a chart; plan the structure, signpost, compare, give an
  opinion, close.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELE C2 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson describes what C2 means and how the Instituto Cervantes' DELE C2 tests it,
in its format since May 2024. Then it reviews the course in one chart that points back to lessons
01–23. Lessons 21–23 practiced the writing tasks and the oral presentation; the honors lessons
24h1 and 24h2 practice test 1 and the speaking test.

## What C2 means

The Council of Europe's *Common European Framework of Reference* (CEFR) groups C1 and C2 as the
*usuario competente* (proficient user), and the Spanish version of its scale names C2 *Maestría*,
the *nivel de maestría* (mastery level). In this course's words, its descriptors say that a C2
user:

- understands with ease almost everything heard or read, live or broadcast, in any form;
- summarizes and rebuilds arguments from different spoken and written sources into one coherent
  account;
- speaks and writes spontaneously, fluently and precisely, telling apart fine shades of meaning,
  and can rephrase an idea in several ways to get a shade exactly right;
- writes clear, smoothly flowing, complex texts in a style that suits the reader;
- keeps consistent grammatical control even while attention is elsewhere, and uses idioms and
  colloquial language aware of what they connote;
- mediates naturally: explains data, relays how a text presents its facts and arguments, and takes
  different roles as the people involved need.

Three things C2 isn't. It isn't *casi nativo* (near-native): the 2001 framework (section 3.6)
says that C2, though it has been called "Mastery", isn't meant to imply native or near-native
competence. It isn't error-free: a C2 text can contain a slip, and an *irreprochable* (flawless)
text bought by saying less isn't the goal. And it isn't showing off: the descriptors reward *la idoneidad* (suitability; C1's *la
adecuación*), *la pertinencia* (relevance) and *la concisión* as much as *la riqueza léxica*
(lexical richness). A better model than the native speaker is *el hablante culto* (educated
speaker) of any country, whose *versatilidad* (versatility) lets them move between registers
without effort.

## The DELE C2 since May 2024

The DELE C2 changed in May 2024: the 2014 guide, the 2018 specifications and older model papers
describe the previous exam. A DELE C2 certifies that you can understand nearly everything you hear
or read and express yourself spontaneously, fluently and precisely, with nuance, in academic and
professional settings (the Instituto Cervantes' DELE C2 page).

![A diagram of the DELE C2 with three boxes. Test 1, language use, reading and listening comprehension: 105 minutes, 52 items, seven tasks as preparation sites describe them, 33.33 points. Test 2, written expression, mediation and interaction: 150 minutes, three tasks of 400–450, 200–250 and 200–250 words in the 2024 sample exam, 33.33 points. Test 3, oral expression, mediation and interaction: 20 minutes plus 30 to prepare, three tasks, 33.34 points. Tests 2 and 3 are marked as the ones with mediation. A note at the bottom says the pass rule is published in the official guide and that preparation sites describe it as passing each test in the same session.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Test | Time | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. *Uso de la lengua, comprensión de lectura y auditiva* | 105 min | 52 items; as preparation sites describe it, seven tasks: a specialized or literary text with gaps testing fine differences of vocabulary; fragments to put back into a long text; short academic texts (abstracts, reviews) matched to statements; a lecture or talk; spontaneous broadcast excerpts, with ideas matched to speakers; a long debate or interview; and, new in 2024, short monologues matched to their communicative intention (24h1) |
| 2. *Expresión, mediación e interacción escritas* | 150 min | three texts: from a radio excerpt and two texts (400–450 words, lesson 21), from notes (200–250, lesson 22), from data (200–250, lesson 23), in the sample exam the Instituto Cervantes published (as described in a 2024 study) |
| 3. *Expresión, mediación e interacción orales* | 20 min + 30 to prepare | task 1, a 5–6-minute presentation from several texts and charts (lesson 23); task 2, a 5–6-minute interview on its topic; task 3, a conversation in which you choose between two news *titulares* (A2's *el titular*, headline) and negotiate your choice (24h2) |

The texts and recordings come from different varieties of Spanish: listen beyond Mexico (module 5).
The official page says test 3 may be held on the day before or after the main date.

## Scoring, passing and the scales

The three tests are worth 33.33, 33.33 and 33.34 points, 100 in all. The pass rule is published
in the Instituto Cervantes' exam guide; as preparation sites describe it, you must pass each of
the three tests in the same session, and one can't make up for another. Check it in the guide,
with dates and fees, which change.

The Instituto Cervantes says the 2024 version renewed the rating scales for writing and speaking
and added, for each task, a category of **[[task fulfilment]]** (*el cumplimiento de la tarea*): did
you do what this task asked, for this reader? For the speaking test, its examiner-training
material (2023, for the 2024 version) describes two kinds of mark. The interviewer gives a
**[[holistic scale]]** mark, one overall judgment of the three tasks; the rater, who listens, uses an
**[[analytic scale]]**, marking each task in separate categories (fluency, accuracy, range, and the
task's own mediation, interview or interaction category with task fulfilment). Each category has
four *bandas* (B2's *la banda*, here a score band), and the upper two pass. The 2024 guide may
describe this differently, and the written scales weren't available to this course: check both.

## A letter from someone who passed

An invented letter from a Canadian translator in Guadalajara to a friend starting her preparation
(317 words).

> Querida Anne:
>
> Me preguntas cómo me preparé para el C2. Te cuento lo que me funcionó, con la advertencia de que
> cada quien llega por un camino distinto.
>
> Lo primero fue dejar de perseguir palabras raras. Durante meses creí que la riqueza léxica
> consistía en coleccionar sinónimos; luego entendí que lo que se evalúa es la exactitud: elegir el
> término inequívoco, el que no deja dudas al lector. Una frase matizada vale más que tres
> adjetivos brillantes.
>
> Lo segundo fue escuchar mucho y de todas partes: podcasts argentinos, noticieros colombianos, una
> serie española. Al principio titubeaba con cada acento; al cabo de unas semanas, el titubeo se
> volvió curiosidad. Nadie te pide que imites esas variedades, pero sí que las entiendas.
>
> Lo tercero, escribir con fuentes. Cada domingo elegía un tema, leía dos artículos, escuchaba una
> entrevista y escribía una síntesis de cuatrocientas palabras. Después la dejaba descansar y la
> corregía en voz alta. La reformulación es un músculo: al principio cuesta encontrar otra manera de
> decir lo mismo; con práctica, aparecen cinco.
>
> Para la expresión oral me grabé muchas veces. Me fijaba menos en la dicción, que nunca será la de
> un hablante nativo, que en la claridad expositiva: si alguien que no ha leído los textos puede
> seguirme. La desenvoltura llega cuando dejas de tener miedo al silencio.
>
> Ahora, lo que no me funcionó: los modelos de examen anteriores a 2024. El formato cambió, y
> preparé durante semanas una tarea que ya no existe. Revisa siempre la fecha de cada material y
> consulta la guía oficial.
>
> Y una última cosa. El registro culto no es un disfraz: es saber cuándo una conversación pide
> *ahorita* y cuándo pide *a la brevedad*. Esa es, para mí, la competencia pragmática y
> sociolingüística de la que hablan los descriptores. Nadie espera que tu español sea intachable;
> esperan que sea tuyo, preciso y adecuado.
>
> Un abrazo y mucho ánimo,
>
> Claire

Summary: she stopped collecting rare words and aimed at the exact, unambiguous term; she listened to
many varieties until her hesitation became curiosity; she wrote a weekly synthesis from two articles
and an interview and corrected it aloud; she recorded herself, aiming at clarity rather than a
native accent; she warns against pre-2024 model papers; and she describes the educated register
as knowing what each situation calls for. Glosses: *cada quien* (Mexico: each person); *al cabo de*
(after); *el disfraz* (costume, disguise); *a la brevedad* (formal: as soon as possible).

## Strategies, test by test

- Test 1 (24h1): read for the gist first, then the items; eliminate options by collocation and
  register; in the monologue task, listen for tone and intention, not just words.
- Test 2 (21–23): plan to the instructions (genre, reader, purpose); grid your sources; keep every
  hedge; count your words; leave time to reread.
- Test 3 (23, 24h2): in the 30 minutes, note structure, not sentences; signpost; give an opinion
  with reasons; in the conversation, concede, redirect and keep the floor with poise.

## The course in one chart

| If you need to… | Lessons |
|---|---|
| choose the exact word, its connotation and collocations | 01, 10 |
| shift register on purpose | 02 |
| avoid confusable words and misused senses | 03 |
| use learned words and Latin phrases | 04 |
| use tenses for style; conjecture with the future and conditional | 05 |
| express conditions without *si*, and counterfactuals | 06 |
| build long sentences with relatives and *el cual* | 07 |
| use formal prepositional phrases and the right preposition | 08 |
| use and recognize figures of speech | 09 |
| write a review; describe style | 10 |
| analyze narrative point of view | 11 |
| read framing and implicature | 12 |
| read and explain legal, medical, financial and technical texts | 13–16 |
| write for readers across the Spanish-speaking world | 17 |
| understand Spain's and other countries' Spanish | 18–19 |
| follow the debates about usage | 20 |
| write from several sources; from notes; from data | 21–23 |

## What comes after C2

C2 is the top of the CEFR, but not the end of learning. The reading list has classics, podcasts and
reference works: the RAE and ASALE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* for doubtful usage,
corpora such as the Corpus del Español to see how words are really used and where, and FundéuRAE's
daily recommendations on new words. Read widely across countries, and keep writing for real
readers.

## Pronunciation

- *la idoneidad*, four syllables: ee-doh-nay-DAHD (*ei* as in "nay").
- *la desenvoltura*, five: deh-sehn-vohl-TOO-rah.
- *titubear*, four: tee-too-beh-AHR; *titubeo*, four: tee-too-BEH-oh.

## Common mistakes

- Preparing with pre-2024 models: the tasks and timings have changed.
- Treating C2 as "sounding native": the target is precision and fit, not an accent.
- Showing off vocabulary at the expense of *la pertinencia*: the rarest word is often the wrong one.
- Relying on remembered rules for passing, dates or fees: check the official guide each time.

## Key points

- C2 (*Maestría*): ease in understanding, precision and fine shades of meaning, smooth texts for
  the reader, mediation from several sources.
- The DELE C2 since May 2024: three tests of about 33 points each; 105, 150 and 20 (+30) minutes;
  mediation in tests 2 and 3.
- Task fulfilment is marked for each task; speaking uses a holistic and an analytic mark.
- The pass rule, the scales, dates and fees are in the official guide: check them there.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: DELE C2 test 1 in practice: language use, reading and listening
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 24 described the DELE C2's first test, *Uso de la lengua, comprensión de lectura y
auditiva*: 105 minutes and 52 items. This lesson practices it task by task with original material:
a long reading text, short items of each kind (here and in the questions), and listening questions
spoken by the course voice. It also names the moves that make multiple choice manageable at C2:
reading for the gist and for detail, eliminating options, and spotting traps.

## The seven tasks

As preparation sites describe it, the 2024 test kept the old format's reading tasks and first
listening task, cut the next listening task from 15 items to 7, and added a seventh task. The
descriptions of the unchanged tasks come from the old specification; check all of it, and the item
counts, in the 2024 guide.

| Task | Input (as described) | What it tests | A strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a complex specialized or literary text with gaps, three options each | fine differences of meaning and style between near-synonyms | try each option in the whole phrase: collocation, register, government |
| 2 | a long text (travel writing, a blog, an article, a story) with gaps and more fragments than gaps | text structure and cohesion | look at the connectors and pronouns on both sides of each gap |
| 3 | short academic texts (abstracts, reviews, records) and statements to match | locating precise claims | underline what each statement asserts; find its exact match, not its topic |
| 4 | a lecture or talk; choose the ideas it contains from a longer list | gist and main ideas | before listening, group the options by topic |
| 5 | spontaneous broadcast excerpts with two or three speakers; match ideas to speakers | who thinks what | note each speaker's position in a column |
| 6 | a long debate, meeting or interview, three-option questions | detail and attitude | read the questions first; they follow the recording's order |
| 7 | short monologues matched to their communicative intention (new in 2024) | tone, idioms, colloquial language | ask what the speaker is doing, not what they say |

The old specification said each recording is heard twice; whether that still holds is
unconfirmed. The texts and recordings come from different varieties of Spanish, and the device
voice that reads this course's listening questions can't reproduce them: hear real speakers too
(the reading list's podcasts help).

![A strategy chart for test 1 with three columns. Reading: first comprensión global (skim for the topic and the text's purpose), then the items, then comprensión detallada around each gap or claim, then descarte (cross out options by collocation, register and logic). Listening: before, read the options and group them; first hearing, gist and attitude; second hearing, check details. Throughout: the trap of an option that repeats words from the text with another meaning, and the speaker's intent (complaining, warning, joking).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Two kinds of reading

### Gist and detail

*La comprensión global* (gist comprehension) asks what the text is about and
what it is for; *la comprensión detallada* (detailed comprehension) asks exactly what one sentence
says. Do them in that order: a first, fast reading for the topic and the writer's purpose, then the
items, then a close reading only where each item points.

### Eliminating

*El descarte* (elimination of options) is often faster than looking for the right
answer. An option goes if it doesn't collocate (*poner de manifiesto*, never *hacer de
manifiesto*), if its register clashes with the text, if it changes the government (*incidir en*,
not *incidir a*), or if it's true but not what the text says.

### Traps

Every multiple-choice item has *enunciados distractores* (distractor statements; C1's
*el distractor*). The most common *trampa* (trap) repeats words from the text with a different
meaning or attributes a claim to the wrong person. A *pregunta capciosa* (trick question), built to
deceive, isn't the same thing, and good exams avoid them: the wrong options are wrong for a
reason you can name. If an option would make the text say a *contrasentido* (a contradiction in
terms, nonsense), it goes first.

## Worked example 1: a gapped text

An original paragraph with three gaps, in the style of task 1:

> El estudio (1) ___ de manifiesto que la contaminación lumínica altera los ciclos de las aves
> migratorias. Sus autores, no obstante, (2) ___ que la muestra era reducida e invitan (3) ___ la
> cautela al interpretar los resultados.

(1) *pone / da / hace*; (2) *reconocen / delatan / presumen*; (3) *a / en / de*.

The study shows that light pollution disrupts the cycles of migratory birds. Its authors, however,
admit that the sample was small and call for caution in interpreting the results.

- (1) *poner de manifiesto* is a fixed phrase; *dar* and *hacer* don't combine with it. Collocation
  decides.
- (2) Authors who admit a limitation *reconocen*. *Delatar* is to inform on someone; *presumir* is
  to boast, or to presume, which changes the meaning. Register and sense decide.
- (3) *invitar a* + noun or infinitive. Government decides.

## The reading text

An original essay (679 words), the kind of text that tasks 1 and 2 build on. The questions use
it for a fragment task.

> *Elogio de la fila*
>
> Pocas instituciones son tan antiguas, tan universales y tan poco pensadas por quienes las
> practican como la fila. Nadie la inventó y nadie la decreta, pero todos sabemos lo que exige:
> llegar, preguntar quién es el último y colocarse detrás. En la tortillería, en el banco o frente
> a la taquilla de un estadio, la fila convierte a un grupo de desconocidos en una pequeña comunidad
> con reglas que nadie ha escrito y que casi todos respetan.
>
> Lo asombroso no es que haya filas, sino que funcionen. Una fila no tiene policía ni reglamento; su
> única fuerza es la mirada de los demás. Basta que alguien intente colarse para que la comunidad,
> hasta entonces silenciosa, se manifieste: primero con un carraspeo, luego con un comentario en voz
> alta, finalmente con una protesta abierta. El que se cuela no rompe una norma legal, sino algo más
> delicado: la confianza en que el tiempo de cada uno vale lo mismo.
>
> Porque eso es, en el fondo, una fila: una declaración de igualdad. Frente a la ventanilla, el
> empresario y la estudiante esperan lo mismo, y el orden de llegada pesa más que el apellido o la
> cuenta bancaria. No es casual que desconfiemos de quienes "se saltan la fila", ni que la expresión
> se haya extendido a la política, a la salud o a la vivienda, siempre que alguien obtiene antes lo
> que otros esperan.
>
> Claro que la igualdad de la fila tiene sus matices. Hay filas preferentes para personas mayores,
> embarazadas o con discapacidad, y casi nadie las discute: la igualdad, en este caso, consiste en
> reconocer que no todos esperan en las mismas condiciones. Más polémicas son las filas que se
> compran: el acceso rápido en los aeropuertos, el boleto que permite entrar antes a un museo. Ahí la
> fila deja de ser un espacio común y se convierte en un servicio con precio.
>
> A principios del siglo XX, un ingeniero danés, Agner Krarup Erlang, empezó a calcular cuánto
> tenían que esperar las llamadas en una central telefónica. De aquellos cálculos nació la llamada
> teoría de colas, que hoy ayuda a bancos, hospitales y aeropuertos a decidir cuántas ventanillas
> abrir. La matemática de la espera, sin embargo, poco dice de cómo se vive. Cualquiera sabe que diez
> minutos en una fila que avanza se sienten más cortos que cinco en una que no se mueve, y que la
> espera incierta cansa más que la larga.
>
> Por eso muchas instituciones han sustituido la fila visible por el número de turno o la cita en
> línea. La medida es eficaz: nadie tiene que permanecer de pie, y el cuerpo queda libre para
> sentarse, leer o mirar el teléfono. Pero algo se pierde. En la fila de antes se conversaba, se
> prestaba una pluma, se comentaba el clima o la lentitud del trámite. La pantalla que anuncia los
> turnos ordena mejor, pero no reúne a nadie.
>
> No se trata de idealizar la espera. Las filas interminables para obtener un documento o una
> consulta médica son, con frecuencia, el síntoma de un servicio insuficiente, y nadie debería tener
> que perder una mañana entera para ejercer un derecho. Pero conviene distinguir entre la fila como
> fracaso administrativo y la fila como forma de convivencia. La primera hay que reducirla; la
> segunda, quizá, merece cierta gratitud.
>
> Tampoco hay que olvidar que las filas cambian de un país a otro. En algunos lugares se forman con
> una disciplina casi militar; en otros, la fila es más bien una nube de personas que saben, sin
> embargo, perfectamente quién llegó antes. Lo que parece desorden a un extranjero puede ser un
> orden distinto, sostenido por la memoria y no por la línea recta.
>
> La próxima vez que alguien pregunte "¿quién es el último?", vale la pena escuchar la pregunta con
> atención. Detrás de esa fórmula cotidiana hay un acuerdo extraordinario: personas que no se
> conocen y que probablemente no volverán a verse aceptan, sin que nadie las obligue, que llegar
> primero da derecho a ser atendido primero. Pocas leyes se cumplen con tanta naturalidad.

Summary by paragraph. (1) The line is an old, universal, unwritten institution that turns strangers
into a small community. (2) It works without police: only others' eyes; cutting in breaks trust that
everyone's time is equal. (3) A line declares equality, which is why "jumping the line" became a
metaphor for privilege. (4) Priority lines for older, pregnant or disabled people are accepted;
paid fast-track lines turn the line into a service. (5) Erlang's early-twentieth-century work on
telephone calls began queueing theory, but the math says little about how waiting feels:
uncertainty tires more than length. (6) Ticket numbers and online appointments are efficient but
end the line's sociability. (7) Endless lines often mean poor service; the essay separates the line
as administrative failure from the line as coexistence. (8) Lines differ by country: apparent
disorder can be another order, kept by memory. (9) "Who's last?" hides an extraordinary voluntary
agreement.

Glosses: *el elogio* (praise; lesson 09); *colarse* (to cut in line); *el carraspeo* (throat-clearing); *saltarse la fila* (to jump
the line); *la teoría de colas* (queueing theory; Spain usually says *la cola* for a line, Mexico mostly
*la fila*, though *la cola* is heard there too); *permanecer de pie* (to remain standing).

Read the essay once for its thesis (a line is an unwritten agreement of equality, worth
distinguishing from bad service) before you try the fragment questions: in task 2, knowing where
the argument turns (*Claro que…, Pero algo se pierde, No se trata de…*) tells you which fragment
can go where.

## Listening: who is speaking, and why

In the listening tasks, ask two questions of every speaker. Who is *el emisor* (the addresser, the
person sending the message; B1's *el remitente* is the sender of a letter) and who is *el receptor*
(the receiver)? And what is the *intencionalidad* (the speaker's intent; C1's *la intención
comunicativa*): to complain, warn, reassure, apologize, boast, persuade? Task 7, as preparation
sites describe it, turns on the second question: what a speaker means can be the opposite of what
the words say.

## Worked example 2: an intention in a colloquial monologue

An original monologue (Mexican, informal):

> ¿Sabes qué? Ya ni me digas nada. Llevo tres semanas esperando que me devuelvas el taladro, y hoy
> que lo necesito resulta que se lo prestaste a tu cuñado. No, no, no te estoy reclamando, ¿eh?
> Nomás digo que la próxima vez, antes de prestar lo ajeno, igual y me preguntas. ¿Va?

You know what? Don't even tell me. I've been waiting three weeks for you to give my drill back, and
today, when I need it, it turns out you lent it to your brother-in-law. No, no, I'm not
complaining, OK? I'm just saying that next time, before you lend what isn't yours, maybe you could
ask me. Deal?

Options: (a) to thank someone for a favor; (b) to reproach someone, ironically; (c) to ask to
borrow something; (d) to make clear that she isn't annoyed.

The answer is (b). The trap is (d): she says *no te estoy reclamando* (I'm not complaining), but
the denial is ironic; everything around it (*ya ni me digas nada*, three weeks, *lo ajeno*) is a
reproach. (a) and (c) pick up words (*prestar*) without the intent. Glosses: *nomás* (Mexico: just);
*igual y* (Mexico, informal: maybe); *¿Va?* (Mexico, informal: OK? deal?).

## Common mistakes

- Choosing the option that repeats the text's words: that's the classic trap.
- Answering from general knowledge: the item asks what this text says.
- Reading every word before looking at the items, then running out of time.
- In task 7, taking an ironic denial at face value.
- Spending too long on one hard item: mark it, move on, and come back.

## Key points

- Test 1 (105 minutes, 52 items): seven tasks as preparation sites describe them, from a gapped
  text to short monologues matched to intentions.
- Read for the gist, then the items, then in detail where they point.
- Eliminate options by collocation, register, government and logic.
- Distractor statements are wrong for a reason you can name; find it.
- Ask who is speaking to whom, and with what intent.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: DELE C2 speaking in practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 built a short presentation from two texts and a chart. This lesson takes the whole
speaking test, *Expresión, mediación e interacción orales*, task by task, with a full-length model
presentation, interview questions, and a model of the third task's negotiation. It also practices
what C2 conversation demands: holding the floor, conceding without giving in, steering back, and
answering a direct challenge with *aplomo* (composure).

## The three tasks and their timing

What follows comes from the Instituto Cervantes' examiner-training material (2023, for the 2024
version), plus one point from preparation sites; the 2024 guide may differ, so check it.

| Task | Preparation | Length | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Presentation | 30 minutes, with a choice between two sets of materials (several texts and charts) | 5–6 minutes | you present the materials from your notes (you may consult them, not read them); the interviewer signals at five minutes; preparation sites add that the points to cover are set out clearly and you must give an opinion |
| 2. Interview | none of its own (it continues task 1's topic) | 5–6 minutes | questions on task 1's topic in three parts: extending it, relating it to you, and the materials you didn't choose |
| 3. Conversation | about a minute to read the instructions | not stated (the test is 20 minutes in all) | you choose one of two news headlines, then negotiate and discuss your choice with the interviewer |

![A timing bar for the speaking test. Before it, a 30-minute block labeled preparación (tarea 1). Then the 20-minute test: tarea 1, presentación, 5 to 6 minutes, with a small flag at minute 5 labeled aviso; tarea 2, entrevista, 5 to 6 minutes; tarea 3, conversación y negociación, the remaining minutes, with a one-minute block at its start labeled leer instrucciones. A note says the length of task 3 isn't stated in the sources.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The material also describes how the test is marked, in general terms: the interviewer gives one
overall mark for the three tasks (a holistic scale, lesson 24), and a second examiner marks each
task in separate categories: fluency, accuracy, range, and the task's own category (mediation,
interview or interaction) with task fulfilment. That tells you what to show in each task: in the
first, that you relay and compare the materials; in the second, that you develop your answers;
in the third, that you interact and negotiate.

## Worked example 1: a full task 1 presentation

The materials (original; the chart's data are fictional):

| Material | What it says |
|---|---|
| Text 1, a column by an urban agronomist | Rooftop gardens cool buildings, produce a modest amount of food and, above all, bring neighbors together; she warns that not every roof bears the weight and that water and upkeep cost money. |
| Text 2, a news report | A fictional city funds vegetable gardens on school roofs; a parents' association supports it, an architect doubts the inspections are thorough enough. |
| Chart, a fictional survey | Residents who would join a rooftop garden: 41% of those aged 18–29, 35% of those 30–49, 22% of those 50 and over; the number of respondents and the city aren't given. |

The presentation (622 words, about five and a half minutes spoken; summary below):

> Buenas tardes. Elegí los materiales sobre los huertos en las azoteas, porque tocan algo que se
> discute poco: qué hacer con el espacio que tenemos encima de la cabeza. Son dos textos y una
> gráfica. Primero voy a presentar cada uno, después los voy a relacionar y, para terminar, les
> daré mi opinión.
>
> El primer texto es una columna de una agrónoma especializada en agricultura urbana. Su postura es
> favorable, pero no ingenua. Por un lado, enumera las ventajas de un huerto en la azotea: el
> edificio se calienta menos en verano, se producen algunos alimentos y, sobre todo, los vecinos
> tienen un motivo para encontrarse. Por otro, advierte que no todas las azoteas resisten el peso de
> la tierra y del agua, y que el riego y el mantenimiento tienen un costo que casi nunca se calcula
> al principio. Me pareció interesante que no presente los huertos como una solución al problema de
> los alimentos, sino como un proyecto social. De hecho, ella
> misma reconoce que la cantidad de comida que se obtiene es modesta, y que el beneficio principal
> es otro: que personas que viven en el mismo edificio, y que a veces ni se saludan, compartan una
> tarea.
>
> El segundo texto es una nota periodística sobre una ciudad que financia huertos en las azoteas
> de sus escuelas. Recoge dos voces. Una asociación de madres y padres de familia apoya el programa
> porque, según dice, los niños aprenden de dónde viene lo que comen. Un arquitecto, en cambio,
> duda de que las revisiones de la estructura sean suficientemente rigurosas, y pide que cada
> escuela tenga un estudio previo. Es decir, el segundo texto convierte en un caso concreto la
> advertencia que hacía la agrónoma.
>
> En cuanto a la gráfica, muestra los resultados de una encuesta, con datos ficticios, sobre quién
> participaría en un huerto en la azotea de su edificio. El interés baja con la edad: un 41 % de
> las personas de 18 a 29 años, un 35 % de las de 30 a 49, y solo un 22 % de las mayores de 50. La
> gráfica no explica por qué; podríamos pensar en el esfuerzo físico, o en que los jóvenes viven
> más a menudo en edificios con azotea común, pero eso ya sería interpretación mía. Tampoco
> sabemos cuántas personas respondieron ni en qué ciudad, así que conviene tomar las cifras como una
> tendencia y no como un resultado definitivo.
>
> Si relaciono los tres materiales, veo una coincidencia y una tensión. La coincidencia: todos
> presentan el huerto como algo más que producción de alimentos; es un espacio de encuentro y de
> aprendizaje. La tensión está entre el entusiasmo y la seguridad: la agrónoma y el arquitecto
> coinciden en que el peso y el agua no son detalles técnicos, sino la condición para que el
> proyecto funcione. Y la gráfica añade una pregunta que los textos no se hacen: si los más
> interesados son los jóvenes, ¿quién cuidará el huerto cuando se muden?
>
> Mi opinión es que los huertos en las azoteas valen la pena, pero solo si se planean como
> proyectos de largo plazo. Me convence la idea de empezar por las escuelas, porque ahí hay una
> comunidad estable y un motivo educativo claro. Ahora bien, le daría la razón al arquitecto:
> antes de subir un solo saco de tierra, hace falta un estudio de la estructura. Y añadiría algo que
> ninguno de los materiales menciona: el huerto necesita a alguien responsable, con tiempo
> reconocido, porque los proyectos que dependen solo de la buena voluntad suelen durar una
> temporada.
>
> En resumen, los textos coinciden en el valor del huerto, discrepan en el grado de cautela, y la
> gráfica nos recuerda que un proyecto comunitario depende de quién se queda. Muchas gracias.

Summary. The opening names the choice, the materials and the plan. Paragraphs 2 and 3 present each
text with its angle and its hedges (*advierte, según dice, duda de que*). Paragraph 4 reads the
chart, flags the data as fictional, and labels a possible explanation as the speaker's own
interpretation. Paragraph 5 compares: one point of agreement, one tension, one question the texts
don't ask. Paragraph 6 gives a reasoned opinion with a concession (*ahora bien, le daría la razón
al arquitecto*) and an addition. The close summarizes in one sentence. Glosses: *la azotea* (flat
roof); *el riego* (watering); *el saco* (sack).

## Task 2: the interview

The interviewer's questions extend the topic, relate it to you, and ask about the materials you
didn't choose. Develop each answer: an opinion, a reason, an example, a nuance.

| Question | In English |
|---|---|
| *¿Cree que este tipo de proyectos funcionaría en su ciudad?* | Do you think this kind of project would work in your city? |
| *¿Ha participado alguna vez en un proyecto vecinal? ¿Cómo le fue?* | Have you ever taken part in a neighborhood project? How did it go? |
| *¿Por qué no eligió los otros materiales?* | Why didn't you choose the other materials? |
| *Si usted fuera alcalde, ¿qué haría primero?* | If you were mayor, what would you do first? |

## Holding the floor, conceding, steering back

C2 interaction is a *tira y afloja* (a give-and-take): you concede what is reasonable, defend what
matters, and keep the conversation on the task. A concession (*la concesión*) isn't defeat: it
makes your *argumentación* (argumentation) credible. A *contraejemplo* (counterexample) answers a
generalization; *contraargumentar* (to counter-argue) answers a reason with a reason. When the
interviewer pushes with an *interpelación* (a direct challenge), answer it, then *reconducir* (steer
back) to your point. And a *silencio incómodo* (awkward silence) is better filled with a
rephrasing than with *este… este…*.

| Move | Formulas | In English |
|---|---|---|
| holding the floor | *Déjeme terminar la idea…; Si me permite, añado algo…* | Let me finish the thought…; If I may, I'll add something… |
| conceding | *En eso le doy la razón; Es cierto que…, pero…* | On that you're right; It's true that…, but… |
| counter-arguing | *Ese argumento tiene un punto débil:…; Precisamente por eso…* | That argument has a weak point:…; That's exactly why… |
| counterexample | *Pensemos, por ejemplo, en…* | Let's think, for example, of… |
| steering back | *Volviendo a lo que decíamos…; Pero lo que se discute aquí es…* | Getting back to what we were saying…; But what's at issue here is… |
| buying time | *Es una buena pregunta; déjeme pensarlo un segundo.* | That's a good question; let me think about it for a second. |
| taking a stand | *Lo tengo claro:…; Sin rodeos, yo elegiría…* | My mind is made up:…; To put it plainly, I'd choose… |

*La toma de postura* (taking a stand) is what task 1 asks at the end and task 3 asks from the start.

## Worked example 2: a task 3 conversation

Two original headlines: *Una ciudad apaga sus anuncios luminosos a medianoche* (A city switches
off its illuminated billboards at midnight) and *Una universidad sustituye los exámenes finales por
proyectos* (A university replaces final exams with projects). The candidate chooses the second.

```dialogue
# Tarea 3
Entrevistadora: ¿Cuál de las dos noticias eligió?
Candidato: La de la universidad. Me parece que plantea una pregunta de fondo: qué queremos medir cuando evaluamos.
Entrevistadora: Pero un proyecto se puede copiar o encargar a otra persona. Un examen, al menos, garantiza que el alumno lo hizo solo.
Candidato: En eso le doy la razón: el riesgo existe. Pero un examen también tiene sus trampas, y nadie propone eliminarlo por eso. Además, un proyecto bien diseñado incluye entregas parciales y una defensa oral, y ahí es muy difícil fingir.
Entrevistadora: ¿Y los alumnos que se ponen nerviosos al hablar en público? ¿No es injusto para ellos?
Candidato: Es un buen contraejemplo. Aunque, si lo pensamos bien, también hay alumnos a los que los exámenes les provocan pánico, y no por eso dejamos de examinarlos. Quizá la solución sea combinar: un proyecto con una parte escrita y una breve exposición.
Entrevistadora: Entonces ya no defiende sustituir los exámenes, sino mezclarlos.
Candidato: Matizo mi postura, sí. Pero volviendo a la noticia: lo valioso es que obliga a preguntarse para qué sirve la evaluación. Si solo sirve para poner una nota, el examen basta; si sirve para aprender, el proyecto ofrece más.
Entrevistadora: ¿Lo aplicaría en todas las carreras?
Candidato: Es una buena pregunta; déjeme pensarlo un segundo. No en todas por igual. En Medicina, por ejemplo, hay conocimientos que hay que comprobar uno por uno. Ahí yo mantendría los exámenes y añadiría proyectos.
```

Summary: the candidate chooses the university headline and states why; he concedes the cheating
risk but counter-argues (exams have their own tricks; partial deadlines and an oral defense); he
answers a counterexample about nervous students with a parallel case and a compromise; challenged
on changing his position, he names the change (*matizo mi postura*) and steers back to the
headline's real question; asked about all degree programs, he buys time and limits his claim. His
register stays *usted* throughout. Glosses: *de fondo* (fundamental); *fingir* (to fake it); *la
carrera* (degree program).

## Common mistakes

- Treating task 3 as a debate to win: the task is to interact and negotiate, and conceding is part
  of it.
- Reading notes aloud in task 1, or memorizing an opening that doesn't fit the materials.
- Short answers in task 2 (*Sí, creo que sí*): develop each one.
- Changing your position without saying so; *matizo mi postura* keeps you credible.
- Switching from *usted* to *tú* halfway: follow the interviewer's lead and keep it.

## Key points

- Task 1: 30 minutes to prepare; a 5–6-minute presentation from several texts and charts, with an
  opinion; consult notes, don't read them.
- Task 2: a 5–6-minute interview that extends the topic, relates it to you and asks about the other
  materials.
- Task 3: choose a headline, negotiate and discuss; concede, counter-argue, steer back.
- The marks look at fluency, accuracy, range and each task's own job, task fulfilment included.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Interpretar sin cabina: liaison interpreting and mediation in person
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 21–23 practiced mediation on paper and in a presentation. This lesson moves it into a room
with two people who don't share a language. The CEFR's C2 mediation descriptor speaks of mediating
effectively and naturally, taking on different roles as the people involved need: that is the
interpreter's everyday work. You won't become a professional interpreter in one lesson, and the
professional points below are general guidance, hedged; but a C2 user is often asked to interpret
informally, and should know what doing it well involves.

## Three ways to interpret

| Spanish | English | How it works | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| *la interpretación de enlace* | liaison interpreting | short turns, both ways, the interpreter sitting with the two parties | a doctor's office, a business meeting, a police station, a school |
| *la interpretación consecutiva* | consecutive interpreting | the speaker talks for a few minutes; the interpreter takes notes and then renders the whole passage | a speech, a press conference, a witness statement |
| *la interpretación simultánea* | simultaneous interpreting | the interpreter speaks almost at the same time as the speaker, usually from a soundproof *cabina* (booth; A2's *la caseta* is a toll booth) | international conferences |

**[[Liaison interpreting]]** (also called dialogue or community interpreting) is the one an advanced
learner is most likely to be asked for. **[[Consecutive interpreting]]** is its longer-turn relative;
both depend on memory and notes, and neither needs a booth: hence this lesson's title, *sin
cabina*.

## The ethics of the job

*La deontología* (professional ethics) of interpreting is set out in the codes of professional
associations and of the courts and health services that hire interpreters; the details vary by
country and setting, so read the code that applies to you. Most share these principles:

| Principle | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| accuracy | render everything, with the same meaning, tone and register; no *omisión* (omission) and no additions, including your own hedges or explanations |
| impartiality | no side-taking, no advice, no personal opinion; the interpreter is an *intermediario* (intermediary) for the message, not a party to it |
| *la confidencialidad* | what you hear stays in the room |
| transparency | if you must step out of the role (to ask for clarification, to correct a mistake, to point out a possible cultural misunderstanding), say so to both parties |
| first person | *trasladar* (to convey) the speaker's words as they said them: "I twisted my ankle" becomes *me torcí el tobillo*, not *dice que se torció el tobillo* |
| preparation | before an *encargo* (assignment), learn the setting's terms and the names involved |
| knowing your limits | decline an assignment you can't do well |

Many health and legal services advise against using family members, and especially children, as
interpreters: a relative may soften bad news, add their own view, or be put in a painful position,
and confidentiality is harder to keep. Where professional interpreters exist, that guidance is
worth following; check what the institution provides.

## Notes for consecutive turns

Consecutive notes record ideas and links, not words. C1 19 introduced the common symbols; an
interpreter's page adds a vertical layout, one idea per block, and a line between blocks.

![An interpreter's notepad page with three blocks separated by horizontal lines. Block one: ayer, then an arrow down to "excurs." and "tobillo" with a twisted-arrow symbol, then "hinch." and a plus sign before "dolor al apoyar". Block two: a check mark before "dedos", a cross before "tronido" (no cracking sound), and "¿creo?" circled to keep the speaker's hedge. Block three: "ALERG. ibuprof." underlined twice, with an arrow to "ronchas". A margin on the left marks who spoke: P for paciente.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two habits matter most. Note hedges as carefully as facts (the circled *¿creo?* above), because
dropping one changes the message. And make warnings and numbers impossible to miss (the allergy above is
underlined twice): an allergy or a dose is the last thing to reconstruct from memory.

## Worked example 1: a doctor and a patient

A clinic in Oaxaca. Megan, a Canadian tourist who speaks English, has hurt her ankle; Dr. Ruiz
speaks Spanish; Julián, a professional interpreter, has been sent by Megan's insurer. An original
transcript (614 words in both languages), with comments after it. The English lines translate the
Spanish ones and vice versa.

> Julián (to the doctor): Buenos días, doctora. Soy Julián Mena, intérprete de inglés. Voy a
> interpretar todo lo que se diga, en primera persona, y todo lo que escuche es confidencial. Si
> necesito aclarar algo, se lo diré a las dos.
>
> Julián (to the patient): Good morning. I'm Julián Mena, the interpreter. I'll interpret
> everything that is said, in the first person, and everything I hear is confidential. If I need to
> clarify something, I'll tell you both.
>
> Doctora: Buenos días. ¿Qué le pasó?
>
> Julián: Good morning. What happened to you?
>
> Megan: I was hiking near Hierve el Agua yesterday and I twisted my ankle on the way down. It's
> swollen, and it really hurts when I put weight on it.
>
> Julián: Ayer estaba haciendo senderismo cerca de Hierve el Agua y me torcí el tobillo al
> bajar. Está hinchado, y me duele mucho cuando apoyo el pie.
>
> Doctora: ¿Escuchó algún tronido cuando se cayó? ¿Puede mover los dedos?
>
> Julián: Did you hear a cracking sound when you fell? Can you move your toes?
>
> Megan: Yes, I can move them. I don't think I heard anything. Oh, and I'm allergic to
> ibuprofen. It gives me hives.
>
> Julián: Sí, puedo moverlos. Creo que no escuché nada. Ah, y soy alérgica al ibuprofeno: me
> salen ronchas.
>
> Doctora: Qué bueno que lo menciona. ¿Toma algún medicamento?
>
> Julián: I'm glad you mentioned it. Are you taking any medication?
>
> Megan: Just vitamins, and an antihistamine when I travel. I can't remember the name.
>
> Julián: Solo vitaminas, y un antibiótico cuando viajo… Perdón, corrección del intérprete: la
> paciente dijo "antihistamínico", no "antibiótico". Solo vitaminas, y un antihistamínico cuando
> viajo. No recuerdo el nombre.
>
> Julián (to the patient): A correction from the interpreter: I named the wrong medicine in
> Spanish at first, and I've corrected it.
>
> Doctora: Del uno al diez, ¿cuánto le duele?
>
> Julián: On a scale of one to ten, how much does it hurt?
>
> Megan: Maybe a seven. Eight when I walk.
>
> Julián: Como un siete. Ocho cuando camino.
>
> Doctora: Le voy a pedir una radiografía para descartar una fractura. Mientras tanto, reposo,
> hielo y el pie en alto.
>
> Julián: I'm going to order an X-ray to rule out a fracture. In the meantime, rest, ice, and
> keep your foot raised.
>
> Megan: Can you ask her if I'll be able to fly on Saturday? And is this going to be expensive?
> My insurance is a bit complicated.
>
> Julián: ¿Podré volar el sábado? Y ¿esto me va a salir caro? Mi seguro es un poco complicado.
>
> Doctora: Eso depende de la radiografía. Sobre el costo, en recepción le explican; yo no sé
> qué cubre su seguro.
>
> Julián: That depends on the X-ray. About the cost, they'll explain at reception; I don't know
> what your insurance covers.
>
> Megan (to Julián): Honestly, Julián, what would you do? Is she a good doctor?
>
> Julián (to the patient): You're asking for my personal opinion. As the interpreter I can't
> give one, but I'll interpret any question you'd like to ask the doctor.
>
> Julián (to the doctor): La paciente me pidió mi opinión personal sobre usted. Le expliqué que,
> como intérprete, no puedo dársela, y que con gusto interpreto cualquier pregunta que quiera
> hacerle.
>
> Doctora: Con mucho gusto le contesto lo que quiera. Llevo quince años en urgencias, por si le
> sirve de algo.
>
> Julián: I'll gladly answer anything you'd like to ask. I've worked in emergency medicine for
> fifteen years, if that's any help.
>
> Megan: OK. Thank you. Sorry, I'm just nervous.
>
> Julián: Está bien. Gracias. Perdón, es que estoy nerviosa.
>
> Doctora: Es normal. La enfermera la va a acompañar a rayos X.
>
> Julián: That's normal. The nurse will take you to X-ray.

Comments:

1. The opening. Julián tells both parties, each in their language, how he will work. A short
   introduction like this is common practice in liaison interpreting and prevents later surprises.
2. First person. *Me torcí el tobillo*, not *dice que se torció*. Each party talks to the other,
   not to the interpreter.
3. Hedges kept. *I don't think I heard anything* becomes *creo que no escuché nada*. A firmer
   *no escuché nada* would tell the doctor more than the patient said.
4. The allergy. Unprompted information, and the most important line of the session: rendered at
   once, in full, with the symptom.
5. A correction, made openly. Julián misspoke (*antibiótico*), noticed, and corrected himself
   in both languages. An uncorrected slip in a medical history is far worse than a brief
   interruption. *Maybe a seven* keeps its hedge too: *como un siete*.
6. *Can you ask her if…* Megan addresses Julián, but the question is for the doctor; he
   renders the question itself (*¿Podré volar…?*), as is usual practice.
7. Out of role, transparently. Asked for an opinion, Julián declines and then tells the doctor
   what happened. Nothing is said in the room that one party doesn't understand.
8. Register. The doctor's *usted* and the patient's informal English both come through:
   *Sorry, I'm just nervous* stays plain (*Perdón, es que estoy nerviosa*), neither more formal nor
   more emotional.

Glosses: *el tronido* (Mexico: cracking sound, pop); *las ronchas* (hives, welts); *descartar* (to
rule out); *rayos X* (X-ray department).

## Worked example 2: a word that needs asking about

A meeting in Monterrey between a parts supplier and a buyer from Texas. The supplier says:

> Proveedor: No se preocupe: el pedido se lo mandamos ahorita.

*Ahorita* (A1's word) can mean "right now", "in a little while" or, depending on the context, "later
on", and in a contract it matters which. The interpreter could guess, and either guess would add
a meaning the speaker didn't commit to. The transparent move is to ask:

> Intérprete (to both): Disculpen, como intérprete pido una aclaración: ¿"ahorita" quiere decir
> hoy mismo o en los próximos días? / Excuse me, as the interpreter I'm asking for clarification:
> does "ahorita" mean today or in the next few days?
>
> Proveedor: En esta semana, a más tardar el viernes.
>
> Intérprete: This week, by Friday at the latest.

Summary: the supplier promises to send the order *ahorita*; the interpreter, in both languages,
says she is stepping out of her role to ask what it means; the supplier answers "this week, by
Friday at the latest", and she renders that. Gloss: *a más tardar* (at the latest).

## Common mistakes

- Reporting instead of interpreting (*She says that…*): use the first person.
- Tidying up: dropping a hesitation, a hedge or a rude remark, or adding a polite one.
- Answering a question meant for the other party, or giving advice.
- Having a side conversation that one party can't follow.
- Guessing at an ambiguous word instead of asking, openly, in both languages.

## Key points

- Liaison interpreting works in short turns, both ways; consecutive in longer turns from notes;
  simultaneous from a booth, almost at the same time.
