- Accuracy, impartiality, confidentiality and transparency: render everything, take no side, keep
  it private, and step out of the role openly when you must.
- Speak in the first person; keep each speaker's hedges and register.
- In medical and legal settings, a professional is usually better than a relative.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El Lazarillo y la picaresca: from Tormes to the Periquillo
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors module reads four turning points of literature in Spanish, from 1554 to the 1950s,
with the tools of the whole course: 05's tenses, 07's long periods, 09's figures and 11's narrative
terms. Every work is retold in this course's own words, never quoted. This lesson follows a short
anonymous book that invented a genre, then the genre's Mexican heir, and ends with an original "new
picaresque" chapter set in today's Mexico City.

## A book without an author

*La vida de Lazarillo de Tormes y de sus fortunas y adversidades* survives in four editions dated
1554, printed in Burgos, Medina del Campo, Alcalá de Henares and Antwerp; an earlier one may have
been lost. In 1992 a copy of the Medina edition turned up walled inside a house in Barcarrota
(Badajoz). Nobody knows who wrote it: fray Juan de Ortega, Diego Hurtado de Mendoza and Alfonso de
Valdés are among many names proposed, and *el anonimato* (anonymity) is part of its legend. The
Inquisition banned it, a version with its anticlerical passages cut circulated instead, and in
Spain the full text was printed again only in the nineteenth century.

## The frame: a letter

The book is an *epístola*, a letter. An adult Lázaro writes to an unnamed person of rank, *Vuestra
Merced* (the ancestor of *usted*, C1 90), who has asked him to explain a certain *caso*. He answers
by telling his whole life. Two Lázaros share the text: the boy who lives the events and the man who
tells them and hides what suits him. In lesson 11's terms, the adult narrates, and much is
focalized through the boy.

## Three masters, retold

![A simplified map of central Spain, not to scale. A dotted route runs east and south from Salamanca, on the river Tormes, through Almorox, Escalona, Torrijos and Maqueda, to Toledo on the river Tajo, where the route ends.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The towns on the map are the ones the book names along the way. The retellings are mine:

*Nacido junto al río Tormes, Lázaro sirve de lazarillo a un ciego que, el primer día, le estrella
la cabeza contra un toro de piedra para enseñarle a desconfiar. En Maqueda, un clérigo avaro guarda
el pan bajo llave; Lázaro roba migajas con una copia de la llave hasta que el amo lo descubre. En
Toledo, un escudero elegante que no tiene ni para comer prefiere pasar hambre antes que perder la
apariencia de su honra, y Lázaro termina pidiendo limosna para los dos.*

Born by the river Tormes, Lázaro serves as guide to a blind man who, on the first day, smashes his
head against a stone bull to teach him distrust. In Maqueda, a stingy cleric keeps the bread under
lock and key; Lázaro steals crumbs with a copy of the key until his master finds him out. In
Toledo, an elegant squire who hasn't enough to eat would rather go hungry than lose the appearance
of his honor, and Lázaro ends up begging for them both.

Glosses: *las migajas* (crumbs), *la honra* (honor as reputation; lesson 12h1, an honors lesson).
C1's *el escudero* is here not a knight's attendant but a penniless *hidalgo* (C1), the lowest rank
of nobility. Then, briefly, a friar, a seller of papal indulgences, a chaplain, a constable; at
last Lázaro becomes Toledo's town crier, and the archpriest of San Salvador, whose wine he cries,
marries him to his own servant. People gossip about the three of
them; Lázaro insists he has never been better off. Most critics read that gossip as the *caso*.

## Hunger, honor and irony

Hunger drives the plot, and honor is its counterweight: the squire starves to protect an
appearance, and the grown Lázaro protects his by not hearing the rumors. The satire, above all of
the clergy, works through irony: the narrator tells a success story, and the reader sees a man
who sold his dignity for bread. The book means most in that gap.

## The picaresque after the Lazarillo

The **[[picaresque novel]]** (*la novela picaresca*) is the genre the Lazarillo started: the
first-person life of a *pícaro*, a rogue of low birth, who serves master after master and tells it
as an adult, in loosely linked episodes that satirize society. He wants to *medrar*, to climb, by
*astucia* (cunning) and *desvergüenza* (shamelessness). The Lazarillo never uses the word *pícaro*;
the label stuck with Mateo Alemán's *Guzmán de Alfarache* (Part I, Madrid, 1599; Part II, Lisbon,
1604), a best seller that mixes adventures and sermons. Alemán later sailed to New Spain (1608) and
is believed to have died there. In Francisco de Quevedo's *El Buscón* (1626), the genre turns darker
and dazzles with wordplay. With these three, *la picaresca* had its classics.

## The Mexican heir: El Periquillo Sarniento

José Joaquín Fernández de Lizardi (Mexico City, 1776–1827) wrote as *El Pensador Mexicano*, his
newspaper's name (1812). *El Periquillo Sarniento* began to appear in 1816, under the viceroyalty;
censorship held back its final volume until 1831. Pedro Sarmiento, nicknamed Periquillo, tells his
children his life so they won't repeat it: lazy student, failed novice, gambler, prisoner, fake
doctor, until he reforms. Long Enlightenment lessons on education and work interrupt the story. It
is often called the first Latin American novel, a title that depends on how you define "novel".

## Reading strategy: read the frame

Before judging a first-person narrative, ask: who writes, to whom, and why now? What does the
narrator want me to believe? Mark the sentences where he praises himself or explains away a fact:
that's where the irony sits.

### Example 1: modernizing a sixteenth-century sentence

This is my own imitation of the period's prose, not a line from the book:

*Y como el panadero viese que yo le servía con diligencia, díjome que, si en su casa estuviere un
año, me daría oficio; mas yo, que ya conocía amos, determiné de no fiarme dél.*

Causal *como* then took the subjunctive (*viese*; today *vio*); a pronoun could follow the verb
(*díjome* → *me dijo*); the future subjunctive (*estuviere*, recognition only) becomes a past
indicative in reported speech; *mas* is *pero*, *determinar de* is *decidir*, *dél* is *de él*:

*Y como el panadero vio que yo lo servía con diligencia, me dijo que, si me quedaba un año en su
casa, me daría un oficio; pero yo, que ya conocía a los amos, decidí no fiarme de él.*

And since the baker saw that I served him diligently, he told me that if I stayed a year in his
house, he'd give me a trade; but I, who already knew what masters were like, decided not to trust
him.

## The text: a new picaresque

This chapter is original. Its title imitates the book's title formula, and Lalo, like Lázaro,
writes to someone who asked for an explanation.

> #### Vida de Lalo de Tlalpan, y de sus amos y fortunas
>
> Licenciada:
>
> Me pide usted que le cuente por escrito el asunto que tanto se comenta en los pasillos de la
> alcaldía. Lo haré, pero desde el principio, porque nadie entiende a un hombre si no sabe de dónde
> salió.
>
> Nací en Tlalpan, en un cuarto de azotea cuyo techo de lámina cantaba con cada aguacero. Mi madre
> vendía tamales afuera de una estación del Tren Ligero; de mi padre sé lo que ella cuenta, que
> cambia según el día. Cuando cumplí doce años, me explicó que en la casa ya no cabía más hambre que
> la suya y me dejó encargado con don Chema, un franelero de la colonia del Valle.
>
> Don Chema tenía más astucia que dientes. El primer día me pidió que pegara la oreja a un
> parquímetro para oír las monedas, y cuando obedecí, me empujó la cabeza contra el metal.
>
> —En la calle, mijo, el que se confía, paga —me dijo, muerto de risa.
>
> Con él aprendí a apartar lugares con cubetas y a cobrar por cuidar lo que nadie amenazaba. Me
> pagaba con refrescos tibios y consejos fríos. Un día de lluvia le grité que la grúa se estaba
> llevando su coche; mientras él corría detrás, yo me subí al Metrobús en sentido contrario.
>
> Mi segundo amo fue Bruno, un *influencer* de comida que cada domingo se filmaba regalando tortas a
> los mendigos de la Alameda. En su departamento, sin embargo, el refrigerador tenía cerradura
> electrónica y él contaba los yogures cada mañana. Aprendí la clave mirando su reflejo en la
> ventana, y cada noche me comía una rebanada de jamón, nunca dos. Bruno culpó al gato de la vecina.
> No me descubrió ninguna cámara: me delató el propio refrigerador, que a las tres de la mañana le
> mandó al celular un aviso de puerta abierta. Me despidió en una transmisión en vivo que tuvo más
> vistas que todas sus tortas juntas.
>
> Creí que por fin iba a medrar cuando me contrató el licenciado Ulises Arriaga, consultor, de traje
> impecable y tarjeta con domicilio en Polanco. El domicilio resultó ser un departamento vacío, sin
> más muebles que un espejo. El licenciado no tenía ni para el metro, pero jamás lo habría tomado:
> alguien podía verlo. Juraba que acababa de comer en un restaurante francés mientras yo compraba
> tacos de canasta con mis propinas, y él se los comía de pie, con la dignidad de quien firma un
> contrato. Un mes después, el licenciado desaparecía sin pagar la renta y me dejaba como única
> herencia una corbata de seda. Así aprendí que la apariencia viste mucho y alimenta poco.
>
> No la canso con los que siguieron: un vendedor de cursos de abundancia, un diputado suplente, un
> tianguista de celulares de origen dudoso. De todos aprendí que la desvergüenza abre más puertas
> que el talento.
>
> Hoy soy vocero de la alcaldía gracias al licenciado Germán Bermúdez, director de Comunicación
> Social, hombre generoso como pocos. Él me presentó a su asistente, Yesenia, con quien me casé hace
> un año, y fue nuestro padrino de boda. Sé lo que dicen: que Yesenia se queda en la oficina hasta
> muy tarde, que el licenciado le regala perfumes. Yo no hago caso de chismes. Quien vive de dar
> noticias sabe cuántas son falsas. Además, el licenciado me juró por su madre que no hay nada, y
> Yesenia por la suya, y con dos madres de por medio, ¿quién soy yo para dudar?
>
> Así que, licenciada, puede escribir en su informe que no hay asunto alguno. Nunca he comido tan
> bien ni he dormido tan tranquilo. Que hablen los demás: yo, por primera vez en mi vida, tengo
> quincena segura.

In brief: Lalo writes to an official who has asked about a rumor at the borough office. He starts
with his birth in a rooftop room in Tlalpan, where his mother sells tamales. Left at twelve with don
Chema, a street parking attendant whose first lesson is a blow, he learns his tricks and escapes by
fooling him. Bruno, a food influencer, feeds beggars on camera but locks his own fridge, until the
smart fridge betrays Lalo's nightly ham. A consultant with a Polanco address and no money lives on
appearances, fed by Lalo's tacos, and vanishes owing rent. Now Lalo is the borough's spokesman,
married to his boss's assistant; he refuses to hear the gossip about them and tells the official
there is no "matter" at all.

Glosses: *el cuarto de azotea* (rooftop room), *dejar encargado con* (to leave in someone's care,
Mexico), *el franelero* (informal parking attendant who waves a cloth, Mexico City), *muerto de
risa* (laughing his head off), *el tianguista* (market stall holder),
*por su madre* (on his mother's life), *la quincena* (the paycheck, paid twice a month).

### Example 2: the irony of the last paragraphs

Lalo was asked about "the matter". He answers with three arguments: he ignores gossip, both people
swore, and he eats well. The third gives him away: it isn't evidence but a reason not to look, and
there the narrator and the reader part ways, as at the end of the Lazarillo. Note too the narrative
imperfect (lesson 05) in *Un mes después, el licenciado desaparecía*: it frames the moment like a
news report.

## Pronunciation

*Pícaro* stresses its first syllable: PEE-ka-ro. *Picaresca* is pee-ka-RES-ka, *epístola*
e-PEES-to-la. In *desvergüenza* the diaeresis makes the *u* sound: des-ber-GWEN-sa.

## Common mistakes

- *El ama*, not *la ama*: the feminine of *el amo* starts with a stressed *a*, so it takes *el* in
  the singular, *las amas* in the plural.
- *Medrar* isn't a neutral "improve": it means to climb or prosper, often with a hint of
  opportunism. For plain progress, *salir adelante* (C1) or *progresar*.
- *El lazarillo*, lowercase, is a blind person's guide; the book is *el Lazarillo*.

## Key points

- *Lazarillo de Tormes*: four editions dated 1554, author unknown, a letter to *Vuestra Merced*
  about a *caso*.
- The blind man, the cleric and the squire; a town crier's dubious marriage at the end.
- The picaresque novel: a rogue's life across masters, with social satire; *Guzmán de Alfarache*
  (1599, 1604), *El Buscón* (1626).
- *El Periquillo Sarniento* (1816–1831), often called the first Latin American novel.
- Read the frame: the irony lies between what the narrator says and what the reader sees.

lessons.title: Galdós y Clarín: the realist novel
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 90's pícaro told his own life. The nineteenth-century novel turns the camera around: a
narrator observes a whole society, and its great subject is *la burguesía*, the bourgeoisie. This
lesson presents Spain's two major realists, a Mexican heir, an original realist chapter set in 1890,
and the module's graded task, a literary commentary.

## Before realism: costumbrismo

**[[Costumbrismo]]** (*el costumbrismo*) painted local types and customs in short sketches, the
*artículos* or *cuadros de costumbres*: Mariano José de Larra and Ramón de Mesonero Romanos in
1830s Madrid, Guillermo Prieto (as "Fidel") in Mexico. The realists inherited its eye for detail,
and added plot and psychology.

## Realism and naturalism

**[[Realism]]** (*el realismo*) set out to show contemporary life as it is: ordinary people, money,
marriage, religion, politics, in a recognizable city. Many novels first reached readers as a
*folletín*, a serial printed in installments in newspapers. **[[Naturalism]]** (*el naturalismo*),
led in France by Émile Zola, went further: a novel as an experiment, with characters shaped by
heredity and environment. Emilia Pardo Bazán's *La cuestión palpitante* (1883), essays first
printed in a newspaper, introduced the debate in Spain and caused a scandal; Spanish naturalism
stayed milder than Zola's.

## Benito Pérez Galdós

Galdós (Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, 1843 – Madrid, 1920) made Madrid his subject. His *Episodios
nacionales*, 46 novels in five series (1873–1912), tell the century's history through invented
lives. *Doña Perfecta* (1876) is a *novela de tesis*, a novel that argues a thesis, here against
intolerance in a provincial town. In *Fortunata y Jacinta* (1886–1887), Juanito Santa Cruz, heir of
a rich merchant family, is married to Jacinta, who can't have children, while his lover Fortunata, a
working-class woman, bears him a son and, dying, leaves the boy to Jacinta.

## Leopoldo Alas, Clarín

Leopoldo Alas (Zamora, 1852 – Oviedo, 1901), a law professor in Oviedo, signed his feared reviews
as Clarín. *La Regenta* (two volumes, Barcelona, 1884 and 1885) takes place in Vetusta, a
provincial capital usually read as Oviedo. Ana Ozores, married to a much older retired judge, is
torn between Fermín de Pas, an ambitious *canónigo* who is her confessor, and Álvaro Mesía, the
local seducer. The *adulterio* ends in a duel that kills her husband, and Vetusta, its *beatas*
and its casino, turns its back on her. Both writers lean on **[[free indirect style]]** (lesson 11):
the narrator's voice takes on a character's thoughts, with no *pensó que*.

## Mexican realism

Federico Gamboa (Mexico City, 1864–1939) is the main Mexican naturalist. *Santa* (1903) follows a
young woman from Chimalistac who, seduced and abandoned, ends up in a brothel in the capital; its
1932 film version is often called Mexico's first sound feature. Emilio Rabasa's *La bola* (1887)
satirizes local politics.

## Reading strategy: who is speaking this sentence?

Realist narrators move in and out of their characters. For each sentence, ask whose words they
are: the narrator's (judging from above), a character's spoken words, or a character's thoughts in
the narrator's voice. Exclamations, questions and colloquial words in a third-person passage
usually mark the third.

### Example 1: three ways to report a thought

Take *¡Qué fácil era todo en París!* from the chapter below. As direct thought: *Clemencia pensó:
"¡Qué fácil es todo en París!"* As indirect thought: *Clemencia pensó que todo era muy fácil en
París.* The chapter's version is free indirect style: the narrator's imperfect, but Clemencia's
exclamation and her point of view. "How easy everything was in Paris!"

## The text: a realist chapter

This chapter is original; Pétrea is an invented city whose name, like Clarín's Vetusta, describes
it ("stony").

![A character map of the chapter. Inside the Requena house are don Anselmo and Clemencia, joined by a line marked "esposos", and Remedios, Anselmo's sister, linked to him by a line marked "hermanos". To one side the canon Leandro Ibarra is linked to Clemencia ("su confesor"), and Remedios is linked to him by a line marked "le cuenta todo" (she tells him everything). Outside, in the street, the engineer from Mexico City is linked to Clemencia by a dotted line ("un saludo"). Above, the pharmacy's tertulia is linked to don Anselmo ("habla del tren").](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> #### Capítulo III. La tarde en Pétrea
>
> A las tres de la tarde, Pétrea bostezaba con la conciencia tranquila de las ciudades que
> no esperan nada. El sol caía a plomo sobre la plaza de Armas, sobre los cuatro fresnos que el
> Ayuntamiento regaba los jueves y sobre las torres de la catedral, cuyas campanas habían marcado
> durante tres siglos las horas de rezar, de comer y de murmurar. Solo en la botica de don
> Prisciliano Ortega había vida: allí se reunía la tertulia de los notables, que se llamaban a sí
> mismos "la gente decente" y que, a falta de ateneo, discutían de filosofía entre el bicarbonato y
> el láudano.
>
> Aquel martes de 1890 el tema era el ferrocarril. La vía llegaría en junio, y con ella, decía don
> Anselmo Requena, dueño del almacén de telas La Perla de Lyon, llegarían el progreso, el orden y
> los figurines de París con solo dos semanas de retraso. Don Anselmo era un burgués de cincuenta y
> cinco años, liberal en el casino y católico en su casa, que admiraba la ciencia siempre que no le
> cambiara las costumbres.
>
> —Dicen que el ingeniero que mandaron de México es un muchacho —comentó el boticario—, y que lee
> a Zola.
>
> —Que lea lo que quiera —respondió don Anselmo—, mientras los rieles lleguen derechos.
>
> Mientras tanto, en el balcón de la casa Requena, Clemencia leía el folletín de *El Eco de
> Pétrea*. La condesa de la novela acababa de huir con un capitán de húsares, y Clemencia, con el
> periódico sobre las rodillas, miró la calle vacía. ¡Qué fácil era todo en París! Allí las mujeres
> huían, lloraban y morían de amor en el último capítulo. En Pétrea, en cambio, nadie se moría de
> nada que no fuera el tifo o la edad. Tenía veintiocho años, un marido que le hablaba de algodones
> y una cuñada que olía a cera de iglesia. ¿Eso era la vida? ¿Eso iba a ser, hasta el final, su
> vida?
>
> Entonces pasó él. Clemencia supo quién era antes de verle la cara, porque en Pétrea nadie
> caminaba tan deprisa. El ingeniero levantó el sombrero y siguió su camino sin detenerse. No había
> sido nada, un saludo de cortesía. Y sin embargo, ¿por qué le temblaban las manos? Dobló el
> periódico con cuidado, como quien esconde una carta.
>
> Remedios, que bordaba detrás de la persiana, no vio el saludo; lo adivinó, que en una beata es lo
> mismo. A las seis, antes del rosario, ya se lo había contado al canónigo Ibarra en la sacristía,
> con tantos detalles que el ingeniero, en su relato, había llegado a detenerse bajo el balcón.
>
> Don Leandro Ibarra era un hombre de cuarenta años, alto y pálido, a quien todo Pétrea veía ya con
> la mitra de obispo. Confesaba a Clemencia desde que ella se casó y conocía sus aburrimientos
> mejor que el marido. Esa misma noche visitó la casa Requena, aceptó una taza de chocolate y, como
> quien no quiere la cosa, habló de las lecturas peligrosas.
>
> —Los folletines franceses, hija mía, son veneno con azúcar. Le traeré a usted la vida de santa
> Teresa.
>
> Clemencia bajó los ojos y prometió leerla. El canónigo se fue satisfecho, y don Anselmo, que no
> había entendido nada, lo acompañó hasta la puerta hablando del ferrocarril.
>
> Esa noche, Clemencia guardó la vida de santa Teresa en el ropero y el folletín debajo de la
> almohada. Ella aún no sabía lo que sentía. Pétrea, en cambio, ya lo sabía todo, y al día siguiente
> lo comentaría en la botica, en la sacristía y en el mercado, como se comentan en provincia las
> cosas que todavía no han pasado.

In brief: at siesta time in 1890, the provincial city of Pétrea yawns; only the notables'
tertulia in the pharmacy is awake, discussing the railway due in June. Don Anselmo, a cloth
merchant, liberal in public and Catholic at home, welcomes progress as long as nothing changes,
and shrugs off the news that the young engineer reads Zola. On her balcony his wife Clemencia, 28,
reads a French serial and wonders whether her dull life is all there is. The engineer passes and
raises his hat; her hands tremble. Her sister-in-law Remedios guesses the rest and tells the canon
Ibarra, Clemencia's confessor, who visits that night and warns her against serials. Clemencia
promises to read a saint's life instead, but hides the serial under her pillow. The city already
"knows" what she doesn't.

Glosses: *a plomo* (straight down, of the sun), *la botica* (old-style pharmacy), *el láudano*
(laudanum), *los figurines* (fashion plates), *México* (Mexico City, in period usage), *los
húsares* (hussars), *como quien no quiere la cosa* (casually, as if in passing), *la mitra* (a
bishop's miter).

### Example 2: a model literary commentary

A *comentario de texto* (lesson 10) situates a passage, states its theme, analyzes how it works and
judges it. This model (416 words by the course's count) covers only the chapter's first part, up to
the dialogue in the pharmacy:

> *El fragmento abre el capítulo III de una novela realista ambientada en Pétrea, una ciudad
> provinciana de México, en 1890. Antes de presentar a la protagonista, el narrador describe la
> ciudad a la hora de la siesta y la tertulia de notables que, en la botica, discute la llegada del
> ferrocarril.*
>
> *El tema central es el contraste entre una ciudad inmóvil y un progreso que llega de fuera. Desde
> la primera frase, Pétrea bosteza como una persona: la prosopopeya convierte a la ciudad en un
> personaje colectivo, satisfecho de no esperar nada. Las campanas, que marcan "las horas de rezar,
> de comer y de murmurar", resumen la vida provinciana en una gradación irónica: la última hora, la
> del chisme, desmiente la solemnidad de las otras dos.*
>
> *En cuanto a la técnica, el narrador es omnisciente y no renuncia a juzgar. Su ironía es de raíz
> costumbrista: los notables que se llaman a sí mismos "la gente decente" discuten de filosofía
> "entre el bicarbonato y el láudano", y la enumeración rebaja sus pretensiones al nivel de la
> farmacia. El retrato de don Anselmo funciona del mismo modo. Es "liberal en el casino y católico
> en su casa", una antítesis que define al burgués de la época mejor que cualquier explicación, y
> su fe en el progreso tiene un límite preciso, puesto que admiraba la ciencia "siempre que no le
> cambiara las costumbres".*
>
> *Cabe destacar, además, el breve diálogo final. El boticario menciona que el ingeniero lee a
> Zola, el maestro del naturalismo, y don Anselmo responde que le da igual mientras los rieles
> lleguen derechos. El lector atento percibe una amenaza que el personaje no ve: con el tren no
> llegarán solo mercancías, sino ideas, y quizá un forastero capaz de alterar el orden de su propia
> casa. El diálogo funciona, así, como una discreta anticipación del conflicto.*
>
> *Desde el punto de vista del estilo, el fragmento alterna períodos largos, en los que los
> relativos acumulan información, con réplicas breves y secas. Esa alternancia reproduce el ritmo
> de la ciudad: la lentitud de la descripción y, de pronto, la chispa de una frase.*
>
> *En conclusión, el pasaje cumple las funciones de una apertura realista: sitúa la acción, crea un
> ambiente y anuncia un conflicto. A mi juicio, su mayor acierto es que la crítica social nunca se
> formula de manera explícita. Nace de los detalles, de un adjetivo o de una enumeración, y obliga
> al lector a sacar sus propias conclusiones, como habrían querido Galdós y Clarín.*

In brief, paragraph by paragraph: (1) it situates the passage; (2) it states the theme, a still
city facing progress, shown by personification and the bells' ironic gradation; (3) it analyzes
the omniscient narrator's costumbrista irony and the antithesis that defines don Anselmo; (4) it
reads the closing dialogue as a hint of the coming conflict; (5) it describes the style's rhythm;
(6) it concludes and judges: the criticism lives in details, never stated outright.

Borrow *en cuanto a* (as for), *cabe destacar* (it is worth stressing), *desde el punto de vista
de* (from the point of view of) and *a mi juicio* (in my view).

### Your turn

Write a commentary of 400–450 words for readers of a literary magazine on the chapter's second
part, from *Mientras tanto, en el balcón* to the end. The length is that of the DELE C2's first
writing task; the exam itself sets no literary commentary. Checklist: situate the passage in one or two sentences; state its theme; analyze
at least two techniques (free indirect style, irony, the narrator's distance, a figure from lesson
09); support each point with a short phrase from the text; organize it in paragraphs with
connectors; end with a reasoned judgment.

```assignment
writing: es6-h1-w91-comentario
```

## Pronunciation

*Galdós* stresses its last syllable (gal-DOS); *Clarín*, cla-REEN. *Canónigo* is ca-NO-ni-go,
four syllables; *folletín*, fo-ye-TEEN, with Mexican yeísmo.

## Common mistakes

- *Costumbrismo* is not "costume": it comes from *las costumbres* (customs).
- *Naturalismo* in literature isn't nature writing; it is Zola's method of heredity and
  environment.
- *La beata* in a novel is usually ironic: not simply devout, but showily and intrusively so.

## Key points

- Costumbrismo sketched types; realism observed a whole society; naturalism added heredity and
  environment (Zola; Pardo Bazán's *La cuestión palpitante*, 1883).
- Galdós: *Episodios nacionales*, *Doña Perfecta* (1876), *Fortunata y Jacinta* (1886–1887).
- Clarín: *La Regenta* (1884–1885), Vetusta, a canon and a seducer.
- Gamboa's *Santa* (1903), Mexico's best-known naturalist novel.
- A commentary situates, states the theme, analyzes techniques with evidence and judges.

lessons.title: Lorca y la Generación del 27
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 90 and 91 read novels. This one turns to a group of poets and dramatists, often called
Spain's most brilliant since the Golden Age, and to Federico García Lorca, its best-known member. No
poet is quoted here: their work is described, and the images you'll practice decoding are original.
The reading strategy is lesson 09 applied to literature: decode the image.

## The Generation of '27

The **[[Generation of '27]]** (*la Generación del 27*) takes its name from December 1927, when several
young poets met at the Ateneo of Seville to mark the three-hundredth anniversary of Luis de
Góngora's death. They admired Góngora's difficult Baroque metaphors and, at the same time, popular
song and the avant-garde (C1's *la vanguardia*). The usual list includes Pedro Salinas, Jorge
Guillén, Gerardo Diego, Vicente Aleixandre (Nobel Prize, 1977), Dámaso Alonso, Rafael Alberti,
Luis Cernuda, Emilio Prados, Manuel Altolaguirre and Lorca. Women artists and writers around them,
such as the painter Maruja Mallo and the poet Concha Méndez, were long left out of that list;
recent books and documentaries have brought them back.

## Federico García Lorca

![A vertical timeline of Lorca's life and works, one row per year: 1898, born in Fuente Vaqueros (Granada); 1922, the cante jondo contest in Granada with Falla; 1928, Romancero gitano; 1929–1930, a trip to New York and Cuba; 1932, La Barraca tours the villages; 1933, premiere of Bodas de sangre; 1934, premiere of Yerma; 1936, in August, shot near Granada; 1940, Poeta en Nueva York is published; 1945, premiere of La casa de Bernarda Alba in Buenos Aires.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Lorca was born on June 5, 1898, in Fuente Vaqueros, near Granada. In Madrid he lived at the
Residencia de Estudiantes, where his friends included Salvador Dalí and Luis Buñuel. In 1922 he
helped Manuel de Falla organize a contest of *cante jondo* in Granada. His *Romancero gitano*
(1928), a *romancero* of eighteen ballads (one ballad is *un romance*, a word lesson 08h1, an honors
lesson, teaches in its older sense of early Spanish) set in an
Andalusia of Roma people, moon and civil guards, made him famous. A stay in New York (1929–1930) and
Cuba produced *Poeta en Nueva York*, published only in 1940. Under the Second Republic he directed
La Barraca, a student *teatro ambulante* that took Golden Age plays to villages from 1932. In
1933–1934 he spent months in Buenos Aires, where he gave a lecture on *duende*.

In July 1936 the Civil War began. In August, Lorca was arrested in Granada and shot (*el
fusilamiento*) by Nationalist forces in the hills between Víznar and Alfacar; the date usually given
is August 18. His *paradero* is still unknown: searches since 2009 have not found his remains (as of
2026). Poets across the Spanish-speaking world wrote *elegías* for him.

## The rural tragedies

Three plays retold in a line each. *Bodas de sangre* (premiered 1933): on her wedding day a bride
runs away with her former love, and the groom's pursuit ends with both men dead. *Yerma* (1934): a
woman longs for a child in a loveless marriage, and the longing ends in violence. *La casa de
Bernarda Alba* (finished in June 1936, premiered in Buenos Aires on March 8, 1945, by Margarita
Xirgu's company): a widow imposes years of mourning on her five daughters; the youngest's secret
love ends in her death, and the mother imposes her own version of it on the house.

## Duende and cante jondo

*El cante jondo* is the oldest, most solemn layer of *el flamenco*. In his lecture, Lorca called
*duende* the dark force that makes a performance shiver: it rises from inside the performer and
is bound up with the nearness of death, unlike the inspiration a muse brings from outside. In ordinary Spanish a *duende* is an elf
or goblin, and *tener duende* means to have that indefinable charm.

## Surrealism

**[[Surrealism]]** (*el surrealismo*) took its program from André Breton's first manifesto (Paris,
1924): images from dreams and the unconscious, free of logic. Its Spanish faces were Dalí and
Buñuel (the film *Un chien andalou*, 1929). Critics often call Lorca's New York poems
*surrealistas*, though how far they fit the movement is debated.

## Exile in Mexico

After 1939 Mexico took in thousands of Spanish Republican exiles. Emilio Prados lived there from
1939 and died in Mexico City in 1962; Luis Cernuda settled there in 1952 and died there in 1963;
Manuel Altolaguirre and Concha Méndez arrived in the 1940s. Several of them printed books in
Mexico, as Altolaguirre had in Madrid.

## The greguería

Ramón Gómez de la Serna (Madrid, 1888 – Buenos Aires, 1963) invented *la greguería*, a one-line
joke built on a metaphor; he summed it up as humor plus metaphor. These three are my own, written
for this lesson about things he never saw:

- *El código QR es un crucigrama que solo resuelven los teléfonos.* A QR code is a crossword only
  phones can solve.
- *La contraseña del wifi es el apellido secreto de cada casa.* The Wi-Fi password is every
  house's secret surname.
- *La luz amarilla del semáforo es un "tal vez" que nadie respeta.* The yellow light is a "maybe"
  that nobody respects.

## Reading strategy: decode the image

When a sentence makes no literal sense, find the two things it joins, ask what they share, and say
it plainly; then ask what the image adds that the plain sentence loses.

### Example 1: decoding an original image

*El tren dormía en la estación con un solo ojo abierto* (mine). Two things are joined: a train and a
sleeping animal (personification, which lesson 09 calls prosopopoeia). What they share: stillness
and one light on, the headlamp. Plainly: the train stood still at night with its headlamp lit. What
the image adds: a sense of watchfulness, as if the train could wake at any moment.

### Example 2: building a greguería

Pick an everyday object (an umbrella). List what it does (it opens when it rains, it's forgotten
when the sun comes out). Find something else that behaves like that (a fair-weather friend, in
reverse). Compress: *El paraguas es el amigo que solo nos busca cuando llueve* (mine). The umbrella
is the friend who only looks for us when it rains. Keep it to one sentence: a greguería that needs
explaining has failed.

## The text: a reportage from 1932

This reportage is invented; the troupe and the village don't exist, though student troupes such as
La Barraca did tour Spain's villages at the time. It is written in general Spanish, as a journalist
of the period might have, with a few words of rural Castile.

> #### Teatro en la era: una noche con La Carreta Azul
>
> Valdecebros, julio de 1932. El camión llegó al pueblo a las siete de la tarde, cubierto de polvo
> y de muchachos. Eran catorce estudiantes de Madrid, chicos y chicas, con un baúl de trajes, dos
> faroles de petróleo y un telón azul que ellos mismos habían pintado. Se llaman La Carreta Azul y
> recorren Castilla con un propósito que su director, Tomás Arenal, estudiante de Filosofía y
> Letras, explica sin modestia:
>
> —Queremos devolverle al pueblo un teatro que era suyo. Cervantes y Calderón no escribían para las
> academias.
>
> Valdecebros tiene doscientos vecinos, una iglesia románica, ninguna escuela digna de ese nombre
> y, hasta esta noche, ninguna experiencia del teatro. El alcalde, un labrador republicano, les
> prestó la era. El cura, en cambio, los miró desde la puerta de la iglesia con la desconfianza que
> en estos días despierta todo lo que llega de la capital.
>
> Montar el escenario les llevó una hora. Los mozos ayudaron a clavar las tablas; las mozas, al
> principio, solo miraban, y después cosieron el dobladillo del telón, que se había roto en el
> camino. Cuando se puso el sol, el chofer acercó el camión y encendió los faros. Aquella fue toda
> la iluminación: dos faros, dos faroles y una luna que, según el tío Basilio, el pastor más viejo
> del pueblo, "también quería ver".
>
> La función empezó con un entremés de Cervantes, *El retablo de las maravillas*, en el que dos
> pícaros anuncian un espectáculo que solo pueden ver los de sangre limpia y, como nadie quiere
> pasar por impuro, todo el público finge ver lo que no existe. Los vecinos tardaron unos minutos
> en entender la broma, y cuando la entendieron se rieron tanto que los actores tuvieron que
> esperar. Una mujer gritó, señalando al alcalde, que él sí estaba viendo toros invisibles. El
> alcalde, buen perdedor, se puso de pie y saludó.
>
> Después vino un auto sacramental de Calderón. Aquí el silencio fue absoluto. Los versos, que en
> la ciudad suenan a museo, sonaron en la era como algo dicho por primera vez. Rosario, una niña de
> nueve años que nunca había salido del pueblo, no apartó los ojos del actor que hacía de Mundo.
> Al terminar, le pregunté qué le había gustado más.
>
> —Que hablaban como en la iglesia —me dijo—, pero se les entendía.
>
> No hubo aplausos al principio. Hubo un silencio largo, el de quien no sabe si está permitido
> aplaudir, y luego un estruendo que hizo ladrar a todos los perros del pueblo. El tío Basilio se
> acercó a Tomás Arenal con la boina en la mano.
>
> —¿Y cuándo vuelven ustedes?
>
> Tomás no supo qué contestar. La Carreta Azul tiene programados veintitrés pueblos hasta
> septiembre y ningún dinero para el invierno. Prometió volver "el año que viene", y el viejo
> asintió como asienten los que han oído muchas promesas.
>
> A medianoche, mientras desmontaban el escenario, las mozas trajeron pan, queso y vino. Nadie
> quería irse a dormir. Una de las actrices enseñó a las niñas a hacer una reverencia, y los mozos
> intentaron, entre risas, recitar los versos que recordaban. El cura, me dijeron, había visto
> la función entera desde la puerta de la iglesia, sin acercarse, y no se había movido hasta el
> final.
>
> Salimos al amanecer. Desde el camión, Valdecebros parecía otra vez un pueblo cualquiera, pardo y
> callado entre los trigales. Pero en la era quedaba un rectángulo de tierra pisada donde, por una
> noche, doscientas personas habían visto lo que no existe y lo habían creído. Eso, me dijo Tomás
> mientras se dormía con la cabeza sobre el baúl, es exactamente el teatro.

In brief: a journalist joins La Carreta Azul, fourteen Madrid students touring Castile, in the
village of Valdecebros in July 1932. The republican mayor lends them the threshing floor; the
priest watches with distrust. Lit by the truck's headlights, they perform a Cervantes interlude
about tricksters whose show only the "pure-blooded" can see, and the villagers roar with laughter.
A Calderón sacramental play brings total silence; a nine-year-old says the actors spoke like in
church but could be understood. After a long, uncertain silence comes thunderous applause. An old
shepherd asks when they'll return, and the director, with no money for winter, promises next year.
The village shares bread and wine; the priest, it turns out, watched the whole play. Leaving at
dawn, the director says that a village believing in what doesn't exist is exactly what theater is.

Glosses: *la era* (threshing floor), *los mozos, las mozas* (the village's young men and women),
*el dobladillo* (hem), *el tío Basilio* (old Basilio: *tío* as a rural title for an older man in
Spain), *de sangre limpia* (of "pure blood", a Golden Age obsession), *la boina* (beret), *pardo*
(brownish gray).

## Pronunciation

*Lorca* is LOR-ca, with one tap of the tongue for the *r*. *Jondo* begins with the rasped *j*:
HON-do. *Greguería* is gre-ge-REE-a, four syllables, the *u* silent. *Fusilamiento* is
fu-see-la-MYEN-to.

## Common mistakes

- *La Generación del 27* is capitalized; *el surrealismo* and *el flamenco* are not.
- *El fusilamiento* is an execution by firing squad, not any shooting (*el tiroteo*).
- *El paradero* is someone's whereabouts; in Mexico it can also be a bus stop, so let context
  decide.

## Key points

- The Generation of '27: Seville, December 1927, the Góngora tercentenary; tradition plus
  avant-garde.
- Lorca (1898–1936): *Romancero gitano* (1928), *Poeta en Nueva York* (published 1940), *Bodas de
  sangre* (1933), *Yerma* (1934), *La casa de Bernarda Alba* (premiered 1945).
- Killed in August 1936; his remains have not been found.
- Duende, cante jondo, surrealism; the greguería of Gómez de la Serna.
- Decode an image: find the two things joined, what they share, and what the image adds.

lessons.title: Borges y lo fantástico: from Buenos Aires to Arreola and Amparo Dávila
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The realists of lesson 91 wanted fiction to look like life. The writers here do the opposite: they
let something impossible break into an ordinary world, and make the reader doubt. This last lesson
of the module defines the fantastic, presents Jorge Luis Borges and the Río de la Plata circle,
then two Mexican masters, and ends with an original fantastic story set in Mexico City.

## What "the fantastic" means

In *Introduction à la littérature fantastique* (1970), Tzvetan Todorov defined **[[the fantastic]]**
(*lo fantástico*) as a hesitation: it lasts while the reader, and often a character, can't decide
whether a strange event has a natural explanation or a supernatural one. If the story finally
explains it, we're in the uncanny; if it accepts new laws of nature, in the marvelous. Not every
critic follows Todorov, but his test is useful. It also separates *el relato fantástico* from
magical realism (B1 12h1 and C1 93, both honors lessons): there, the impossible is told calmly, as
normal, and nobody hesitates. In the fantastic, the *irrupción* of the impossible is
*inquietante*, unsettling.

## Jorge Luis Borges

Borges (Buenos Aires, August 24, 1899 – Geneva, June 14, 1986) spent his teens in Geneva and
Spain, then returned to Buenos Aires and wrote poems and essays before his famous stories. *Historia
universal de la infamia* (1935) was followed by *Ficciones* (1944) and *El Aleph* (1949). From 1955
to 1973 he directed Argentina's National Library while losing his sight. He shared the Cervantes
Prize in 1979 with Gerardo Diego, a poet of lesson 92's generation, and never received the Nobel.

His themes recur like objects in a dream: the *laberinto*, the mirror, the library, the
*enciclopedia*, the *infinito*, the double. Retold in a sentence each:

- In "La biblioteca de Babel", people live inside an endless library of identical rooms that holds
  every possible book, almost all of them nonsense.
- In "Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote", a French writer sets out to write, not copy, some
  chapters of Cervantes's novel word for word, and the narrator reads the identical words as a
  different work.
- In "El Aleph", the narrator sees, from a basement in Buenos Aires, a tiny sphere that shows the
  whole universe at once.
- In "Las ruinas circulares", a man dreams a son into being, then discovers that he too is
  being dreamed.

Borges also wrote reviews of books that don't exist: the review is real, the book *apócrifo*. His
stories mix *metafísica* and detective plots, and they question what a *ficción* is. Many use
**[[mise en abyme]]** (*la puesta en abismo*): a work that contains a smaller image of itself, like the
dreamer dreamed by another.

![A drawing titled "Un laberinto dentro de sí mismo": a square labyrinth of dark walls. In its center there is a framed picture of the same labyrinth, and in the center of that picture an even smaller copy, ending in a dark dot. The caption says that the same labyrinth appears in the center, smaller each time.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The Río de la Plata circle

Around Victoria Ocampo's magazine *Sur* (founded 1931), Borges, Adolfo Bioy Casares and Silvina
Ocampo compiled an *Antología de la literatura fantástica* (1940). In Bioy's *La invención de
Morel* (1940), with a prologue by Borges, a fugitive on an island falls in love with a woman who
turns out to be an image endlessly replayed by a machine. Silvina Ocampo (1903–1993) wrote cruel,
strange stories of children and households, collected in books such as *La furia* (1959).

## The Mexican fantastic

Juan José Arreola (Zapotlán el Grande, Jalisco, 1918 – Guadalajara, 2001) wrote very short, ironic
pieces. *Confabulario* (1952) includes "El guardagujas", in which a traveler waiting for a train
learns from a switchman that the railway system is absurd beyond belief; his sketches of animals
became his own *bestiario*. Amparo Dávila (Pinos, Zacatecas, 1928 – 2020), once Alfonso Reyes's
secretary, published *Tiempo destrozado* (1959), *Música concreta* (1964) and *Árboles
petrificados* (1977, Xavier Villaurrutia Prize). In one of her best-known stories, "El huésped", a
husband brings a nameless creature into the house, and his wife lives in terror of it. Her
fantastic grows out of fear inside the home, and of *la otredad*, the otherness of what we can't
name (a key word in Octavio Paz's essays).

## Reading strategy: find the irruption

Mark the sentence where the impossible first appears. Then list every explanation the story
allows (fatigue, a joke, a dream, the supernatural) and notice which ones the ending leaves open.
If more than one survives, you're reading the fantastic.

### Example 1: conjecture as hesitation

Lesson 05's future and conditional of conjecture are the fantastic's natural grammar. In the story
below, Inés thinks: *Habrá sido el cansancio* (it must have been fatigue) and *Sería algún colega
con ganas de bromear* (it was probably some colleague in the mood for a joke). Each conjecture
offers a natural explanation, and the hedge tells us she doesn't quite believe it. Compare the
certain *Fue el cansancio*: with it, the hesitation, and the fantastic, would end.

### Example 2: spotting the mise en abyme

In the story, an encyclopedia entry describes the woman who is reading it, and later her reading
of that very description. The entry contains the scene that contains the entry: that's the mise
en abyme. The last paragraph widens it to you, the reader, which is a Borgesian move.

## The text: a fantastic story

This story is original. It nods to Borges's apocryphal entries and Arreola's bestiaries without
following any story of theirs.

> #### Entrada sin autor
>
> Inés Arteaga trabajaba de noche. A las once encendía la computadora en una oficina de Coyoacán y
> revisaba, hasta el amanecer, las entradas que los colaboradores de la *Enciclopedia Abierta del
> Español* habían escrito durante el día. Le gustaba esa vigilia: el edificio vacío, el zumbido
> del refrigerador, las palabras quietas en la pantalla, esperando que alguien les quitara una
> coma.
>
> La noche del 12 de marzo, el sistema le asignó una entrada nueva en la sección de bestiario. Se
> titulaba "Quietzal" y no tenía autor. Inés la leyó con la sonrisa de quien descubre una broma: el
> quietzal, decía el texto, es un ave diminuta que no habita los bosques sino los textos poco
> leídos, y se alimenta de erratas. Hace su nido en las notas al pie. Nadie lo ha visto, porque
> desaparece en cuanto alguien lo busca.
>
> Era una entrada apócrifa, sin duda, pero estaba bien escrita, y Inés pensó en dejarla un rato
> antes de borrarla. Siguió leyendo. El último párrafo decía que el quietzal tiene un solo
> depredador conocido: cierta correctora de Coyoacán que, a las 3:07 de la madrugada, con un suéter
> azul y una taza de café ya frío, lee su propia descripción en una pantalla.
>
> Inés miró el reloj de la computadora. Eran las 3:07. Llevaba puesto el suéter azul, y el café,
> desde luego, estaba frío.
>
> Se rio en voz alta, para que la oyera el edificio. Sería algún colega con ganas de bromear, alguno
> de los muchachos del turno de la tarde que sabían de su suéter y de su café. Revisó el historial
> de cambios: la entrada se había creado a las 3:06. El campo del autor estaba vacío. Borró la
> entrada, escribió en la bitácora "contenido apócrifo, eliminado" y se fue a casa cuando ya
> clareaba.
>
> La noche siguiente, a las tres, el sistema volvió a asignarle "Quietzal". La entrada era la misma,
> pero tenía un párrafo más: la correctora, decía, intentó destruir la descripción, sin saber que el
> quietzal se alimenta también de lo que se borra. Desde entonces, añadía, el ave es un poco más
> grande.
>
> Inés no se rio esta vez. Habrá sido el cansancio, se dijo; llevaba tres meses durmiendo de día y
> tal vez había escrito ella misma la entrada, medio dormida, y luego lo había olvidado. Revisó de
> nuevo el historial. El autor de la última versión tenía nombre ahora: era su propio usuario. La
> hora de la edición era exactamente la hora en que ella la estaba leyendo.
>
> Durante una semana no dijo nada. Cada noche la entrada crecía. Describía su escritorio, la
> mancha de humedad del techo, el temblor de sus manos al abrirla. Inés empezó a buscar en sus
> propios textos el rastro de un ave diminuta y a encontrar, en cada página que corregía, una
> errata que no estaba ahí un segundo antes. Ya no sabía si el quietzal la perseguía o si ella,
> desde algún rincón de sí misma que no conocía, lo estaba inventando. Esa otredad le daba más miedo
> que cualquier fantasma.
>
> El viernes llamó a su jefe, el doctor Mendiola, y le pidió que viera la entrada con sus propios
> ojos. El doctor llegó a las tres de la mañana, en pijama debajo del abrigo, y se sentó a su lado.
> Inés abrió la sección de bestiario. No había ninguna entrada titulada "Quietzal". Tampoco en el
> historial. Mendiola le puso una mano en el hombro y le recomendó unos días de descanso.
>
> Inés se tomó dos semanas. Durmió de noche, caminó por los Viveros, no encendió la computadora.
> Cuando volvió al trabajo, el primer texto que el sistema le asignó era una entrada nueva, sin
> autor, en la sección de ficción. Se titulaba "Entrada sin autor". Contaba la historia de una
> correctora de Coyoacán y de un ave que se alimenta de erratas, y terminaba con un párrafo que Inés
> leyó dos veces: en algún lugar, decía, alguien está leyendo ahora mismo esta historia, y no
> conviene que levante la vista de la página, porque el quietzal, que es infinito, ya ha aprendido a
> esconderse también en sus libros.

In brief: Inés, a night copy editor at an online encyclopedia in Coyoacán, finds an anonymous entry
in its bestiary section about the "quietzal", a tiny bird that lives in little-read texts and
feeds on typos. Its last paragraph describes her, at that very minute, reading it. She blames a
prankish colleague and deletes it. The next night it is back, with a paragraph about her deleting
it; now the edit history names her own user as the author, at the moment she is reading. She
wonders whether fatigue made her write it half asleep. Each night the entry grows and describes her
more closely. When her boss comes to see it, it has vanished, and he sends her to rest. When she
returns, a new anonymous entry tells her whole story, under this story's title, and warns that
someone is reading it now and had better not look up from the page.

Glosses: *quitarle una coma* (to remove a comma from it), *la errata* (typo, B2), *las notas al
pie* (footnotes), *el depredador* (predator), *la bitácora* (log), *clarear* (to grow light, at
dawn), *los Viveros* (the Viveros de Coyoacán, a tree nursery and park).

## Pronunciation

*Borges* is BOR-hes, with the rasped Spanish *g* before *e*. *Apócrifo* is a-PO-kree-fo,
*metafísica* me-ta-FEE-see-ka, *laberinto* la-be-REEN-to. *Irrupción* has a strong trilled *rr*:
ee-rroop-SYON.

## Common mistakes

- *Lo fantástico* (the genre of hesitation) is not *la fantasía* (fantasy with dragons and
  invented worlds).
- *Apócrifo* means falsely attributed or invented, not "apocalyptic".
- Not every strange story is magical realism: ask whether anyone, character or reader, hesitates.
- *El infinito* is the noun (*el miedo al infinito*); *infinito* also works as an adjective
  (*un ave infinita*).

## Key points

- Todorov (1970): the fantastic lasts while the reader hesitates between a natural and a
  supernatural explanation.
- Borges (1899–1986): *Ficciones* (1944), *El Aleph* (1949); labyrinths, libraries, infinity,
  apocryphal books, mise en abyme.
- Bioy Casares's *La invención de Morel* (1940); the 1940 anthology with Silvina Ocampo.
- The Mexican fantastic: Arreola's *Confabulario* (1952), Amparo Dávila's *Tiempo destrozado*
  (1959).
- Read the fantastic by finding the irruption and the explanations the ending leaves open.

sections.name: Precisión y matiz (precision, register and the learned word)
Estilo, retórica y lengua literaria (style, rhetoric and literary language)
Un idioma, muchas normas (Spanish across the world)
Mediación y el DELE C2 (mediation and the C2 exam)
Honors: Del Lazarillo a Borges (classics across the Spanish-speaking world)

questions.stem: What do we know for certain about the publication of Lazarillo de Tormes?
choices: Four editions dated 1554 survive, and the author is unknown.
Mateo Alemán published it in Madrid in 1599.
It first appeared in Mexico City in 1816.
Francisco de Quevedo signed the first edition in 1626.
questions.explanation: Four editions dated 1554 survive (Burgos, Medina del Campo, Alcalá de Henares and Antwerp), and nobody knows who wrote it. 1599 is Alemán's Guzmán de Alfarache, 1816 Lizardi's Periquillo and 1626 Quevedo's Buscón.

questions.stem: How is the Lazarillo framed?
choices: As a chronicle written by a historian about a famous rogue.
As a play performed in a Toledo square.
As a letter in which the adult Lázaro answers a person of rank who has asked him about a certain "caso".
As a diary the boy keeps while serving his masters.
questions.explanation: The book is an epístola to an unnamed Vuestra Merced who wants an explanation of a "caso"; the adult Lázaro answers by telling his whole life. It isn't a chronicle, a play or a diary written as events happen.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this simplified map of Lázaro's road. (Almorox and Torrijos are labeled for you.)

image.alt: A simplified, partly unlabeled map of central Spain. A dotted route with arrows runs from a large dot on a river in the west, to Almorox, to a dot below it, to Torrijos, back west to another dot, and on to a large dot in the southeast near a second river. Five places are numbered: 1 the large dot in the west, 2 the river beside it, 3 the dot between Almorox and Torrijos, 4 the dot reached after Torrijos, and 5 the large dot where the route ends.

questions.explanation: Lázaro is born by the Tormes, near Salamanca, in the west; the route goes through Almorox and Escalona, then Torrijos and Maqueda, where he serves the stingy cleric, and ends in Toledo, where he meets the squire and finally becomes town crier. Seville and Alcalá de Henares aren't on his road (Alcalá is only one of the cities where an edition was printed).

questions.stem: Put these moments of Lázaro's life in the order in which the book tells them.
choices: He serves as a blind man's guide.
He steals bread from a stingy cleric in Maqueda.
He begs to feed a penniless squire in Toledo.
He becomes town crier and marries the archpriest's servant.
questions.explanation: The blind man comes first, then the cleric of Maqueda, then the squire in Toledo; after several briefer masters, the book ends with Lázaro as town crier, married to the archpriest of San Salvador's servant.

questions.stem: Why do most critics read the end of the Lazarillo as ironic?
choices: Because Lázaro admits that he has lied in every chapter.
Because Lázaro insists he has never been better off, and the reader sees the dishonor he refuses to see.
Because the archpriest punishes Lázaro in the last chapter.
Because the narrator suddenly switches to the third person.
questions.explanation: Lázaro insists he has never been better off, while the town gossips about his wife and the archpriest; the reader sees a man who sold his dignity for bread. He never admits to lying, the archpriest doesn't punish him, and the narration stays in the first person.

questions.stem: Which of these are features of the picaresque novel as the lesson defines it? Select all that apply.
choices: A first-person life of a rogue of low birth
Service to one master after another
Satire of the society the rogue crosses
A knight-errant who fights giants for a lady
An omniscient narrator who knows every character's mind
questions.explanation: The picaresque novel is the rogue's own life story, told as an adult, across a series of masters, satirizing society. The knight-errant belongs to the chivalric romance that Don Quijote parodies, and the pícaro tells his story in the first person, not as an omniscient narrator.

questions.stem: Which statement about Mateo Alemán is accurate?
choices: He wrote the Lazarillo and signed it with a pen name.
He founded the newspaper El Pensador Mexicano.
He wrote El Buscón, the darkest picaresque novel.
He wrote Guzmán de Alfarache (1599, 1604) and later sailed to New Spain.
questions.explanation: Alemán's Guzmán de Alfarache fixed the label pícaro; he sailed to New Spain in 1608. The Lazarillo is anonymous, El Pensador Mexicano was Lizardi's newspaper, and El Buscón is Quevedo's.

questions.stem: Which statement about El Periquillo Sarniento is accurate?
choices: It began to appear in 1816, and censorship held back its last volume until 1831.
It was written by Mateo Alemán after he settled in Mexico.
It is the first novel ever written in Spanish.
Its narrator is a squire who starves to keep up appearances.
questions.explanation: Lizardi's novel began to appear in 1816, under the viceroyalty, and its final volume came out in 1831. It is often called the first Latin American novel (not the first in Spanish: the Lazarillo is centuries older). The starving squire is the Lazarillo's third master; Periquillo is a student, gambler and fake doctor who tells his children his life.

questions.stem: Modernize the end of the lesson's imitation, "determiné de no fiarme dél": "decidí no fiarme ___".
questions.explanation: Dél is the old contraction of de + él; modern Spanish writes the two words separately (de él), unlike del (de + el, the article). Determinar de + infinitive has become decidir + infinitive.

questions.stem: Build the sentence from Lalo's story in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I was born in a rooftop room whose tin roof sang with every downpour.
questions.explanation: Cuyo (whose) agrees with the thing possessed (techo, masculine singular) and links the room to its roof. The fronted order (En un cuarto de azotea cuyo techo… nací) is also accepted. Que su techo is the nonstandard replacement for cuyo that lesson 07 describes: common in speech, but careful writing uses cuyo.

questions.stem: "Creí que por fin iba a medrar cuando me contrató el licenciado." What does medrar mean here?
choices: to get ahead socially, with a hint of opportunism
questions.explanation: Medrar is to climb or prosper, often with an opportunistic tone: exactly the pícaro's goal. It doesn't mean to calm down, be fooled or move.

questions.stem: In Lalo's story, how is he caught stealing ham at Bruno's apartment?
choices: The smart fridge sends Bruno a door-open alert at three in the morning.
The neighbor's cat leads Bruno to the kitchen.
questions.explanation: No camera catches him: the fridge itself sends an alert to Bruno's phone, a modern echo of the whistling key that betrays the boy in Maqueda. Bruno had blamed the neighbor's cat; the cleaning lady doesn't appear in the story.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: La astucia is the pícaro's cunning and la desvergüenza his shamelessness; el anonimato is the state of the Lazarillo's author; an epístola is a (formal or literary) letter; el lazarillo, from the book's title, is a blind person's guide. Beggar is el mendigo, which isn't on the left.

questions.stem: What did naturalism add to realism?
choices: Characters shaped by heredity and environment, with the novel treated as an experiment
A return to knights, giants and enchanters
Plots set only in the distant past
questions.explanation: Naturalism, led by Zola, treated the novel as an experiment and its characters as products of heredity and environment. It kept prose and contemporary settings.

questions.stem: What was Emilia Pardo Bazán's La cuestión palpitante (1883)?
choices: A novel about adultery in Oviedo
A collection of essays, first printed in a newspaper, that brought the debate on naturalism to Spain
A sketch of Madrid customs from the 1830s
A serial novel printed in Mexico City
questions.explanation: Her essays introduced Zola's naturalism to Spanish readers and caused a scandal. The Oviedo novel is Clarín's La Regenta; the 1830s sketches are costumbrismo.

questions.stem: Match each work to its author.
questions.explanation: Galdós wrote Fortunata y Jacinta (1886–1887), Clarín La Regenta (1884–1885), Gamboa Santa (1903), Pardo Bazán La cuestión palpitante (1883) and Rabasa La bola (1887). Mateo Alemán wrote the picaresque Guzmán de Alfarache (lesson 90).

questions.stem: What is Vetusta in La Regenta?
choices: A real village near Zamora where Clarín was born
The name of Ana Ozores's family estate
An invented provincial capital that readers usually identify with Oviedo
A newspaper that printed the novel as a serial
questions.explanation: Vetusta ("ancient") is invented, but its cathedral, casino and society are usually read as Oviedo's, where Clarín taught. Clarín was born in Zamora, a city.

questions.stem: Which passage is in free indirect style?
choices: Clemencia se preguntó si aquello era la vida.
Yo me pregunto si esto es la vida.
¿Eso era la vida? Tenía veintiocho años y un marido que le hablaba de algodones.
questions.explanation: Free indirect style keeps the narrator's third person and past tense (era, tenía) but takes on the character's own question, with no verb of thinking. The first is direct thought, the second indirect thought (se preguntó si), and the third is a first-person narrator.

questions.stem: Clemencia thinks, in direct thought: "¡Qué fácil es todo en París!" Write the verb as the chapter does, in free indirect style: "¡Qué fácil ___ todo en París!"
questions.explanation: Free indirect style moves the thought into the narrator's past: es becomes the imperfect era, while the exclamation stays Clemencia's.

questions.stem: Which details from the chapter carry the narrator's irony? Select all that apply.
choices: The notables discuss philosophy "entre el bicarbonato y el láudano".
Don Anselmo is "liberal en el casino y católico en su casa".
Remedios guessed the greeting, "que en una beata es lo mismo".
questions.explanation: The first three undercut the characters: philosophy among the pharmacy jars, an antithesis that exposes a double life, and a jab at the busybody's imagination. The railway's arrival date is plain information.

questions.stem: What does the canon recommend when he visits the Requena house?
choices: That Clemencia travel to Mexico City for a rest
That she read a life of Saint Teresa instead of French serials
That don Anselmo invest in the railway
That Remedios stop gossiping in the sacristy
questions.explanation: He calls French serials "poison with sugar" and promises to bring her a life of Saint Teresa. Clemencia promises to read it, then hides the serial under her pillow.

questions.stem: What does the chapter's last sentence suggest?
choices: That Clemencia has already decided to leave her husband
That the engineer has written Clemencia a letter
That the canon will report Clemencia to the bishop
That the city gossips about things before they even happen
questions.explanation: Clemencia doesn't yet know what she feels, but Pétrea "already knows everything" and will talk about it, as provincial towns talk about things that haven't happened yet. Nothing has been decided or written.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a literary commentary in the order the lesson's model follows.
choices: Situate the passage in the work
Analyze the techniques, with evidence from the text
questions.explanation: The model situates the passage, states its theme, analyzes the narrator's irony, the dialogue and the style with short phrases from the text, and ends with its judgment (A mi juicio…).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Don Anselmo admired science, provided it didn't change his habits.
questions.explanation: Siempre que meaning "provided that" takes the subjunctive, here the imperfect subjunctive after a past verb (cambiara; cambiase is also correct). The condition can follow or open the sentence, sit between the subject and the verb as an aside (Don Anselmo, siempre que…, admiraba la ciencia), and the subject can follow the verb in literary prose (admiraba la ciencia don Anselmo). The indicative cambia doesn't fit: with the indicative, siempre que means "whenever".

questions.stem: In the model commentary, what does "Cabe destacar, además, el breve diálogo final" do?
choices: It adds another point worth stressing.
questions.explanation: Cabe destacar (it is worth stressing) with además adds a new point of analysis. The conclusion opens with En conclusión, the summary comes in the first paragraph, and nothing is contradicted.

questions.stem: What does the word costumbrismo come from?
questions.explanation: Costumbrismo portrays local customs, las costumbres. It has nothing to do with costumes (los disfraces, el vestuario) or with cost; costumbre is feminine.

questions.stem: Why is the Generation of '27 called that?
choices: Because its members were all born in 1927
After a December 1927 tribute in Seville for the three-hundredth anniversary of Góngora's death
Because Lorca published Romancero gitano in 1927
After a 1927 law that created La Barraca
questions.explanation: The poets met at the Ateneo of Seville in December 1927 to honor Góngora, who died in 1627. They were born around 1900; Romancero gitano is from 1928, and La Barraca dates from the Second Republic.

questions.stem: Fill in the missing works on this timeline of Lorca's life.

image.alt: A vertical timeline of Lorca's life from 1898 to 1945. Some rows are filled in: 1898, born in Fuente Vaqueros; 1922, the cante jondo contest; 1929–1930, the trip to New York and Cuba; 1932, La Barraca on tour; 1936, shot near Granada in August. Five rows are empty boxes, numbered 1 to 5: 1928, 1933, 1934, 1940 and 1945.

choices: Se publica Poeta en Nueva York
Estreno de La casa de Bernarda Alba
questions.explanation: Romancero gitano came out in 1928; Bodas de sangre premiered in 1933 and Yerma in 1934; Poeta en Nueva York, written in 1929–1930, was published only in 1940; La casa de Bernarda Alba, finished in June 1936, premiered in Buenos Aires in 1945. Ficciones is Borges (1944) and La Regenta Clarín (1884–1885).

questions.stem: What is known about Lorca's remains, according to the lesson (as of 2026)?
choices: They were moved to a mausoleum in Granada in 1975.
They were found in 2009 and identified by DNA.
They rest in Buenos Aires, where his last play premiered.
They have not been found, despite searches since 2009.
questions.explanation: Searches near Víznar and Alfacar since 2009 have not found his remains; his whereabouts (su paradero) are still unknown. The other three are invented.

questions.stem: Where and when did La casa de Bernarda Alba premiere?
choices: In Buenos Aires, in 1945, after Lorca's death
In Madrid, in 1933, directed by Lorca
In Granada, in 1936, a month before the war
In New York, in 1930, in English
questions.explanation: Lorca finished the play in June 1936; Margarita Xirgu's company premiered it in Buenos Aires on March 8, 1945. 1933 in Madrid is Bodas de sangre.

questions.stem: Match each play to its plot, as the lesson retells it.
choices: A bride runs away with her former love on her wedding day.
A woman longs for a child in a loveless marriage.
A widow imposes years of mourning on her five daughters.
A squire starves to keep up appearances.
questions.explanation: These are Lorca's three rural tragedies (1933, 1934, finished 1936). The starving squire belongs to the Lazarillo (lesson 90).

questions.stem: How does Lorca's lecture describe duende?
choices: As the gift of a muse who whispers the right words
As a technique that any singer can learn in a few lessons
As a dark force that makes a performance shiver, rising from inside the performer and bound up with death
As the Andalusian name for the guitar's sixth string
questions.explanation: In his lecture (Buenos Aires, 1933) duende is a dark force from inside the performer, set against the muse's inspiration from outside; the lesson describes it, as here, without quoting. It isn't a technique or part of a guitar.

questions.stem: "Esa cantante tiene duende." What does tener duende mean in everyday Spanish?
choices: to be possessed by a goblin
to have an indefinable charm or magic
questions.explanation: In folklore a duende is an elf or goblin, but tener duende means to have that indefinable charm, especially in performance.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, which of these writers lived in exile in Mexico? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Prados (from 1939), Cernuda (from 1952) and Altolaguirre (from the 1940s) lived in Mexico; Prados and Cernuda died in Mexico City. Gómez de la Serna settled in Buenos Aires, where he died in 1963.

questions.stem: Complete with the word for "whereabouts": "Todavía se desconoce el ___ de sus restos."
questions.explanation: El paradero is a person's or thing's whereabouts. In Mexico it can also mean a bus stop, so context decides.

questions.stem: "El tren dormía en la estación con un solo ojo abierto." What is the train's "one open eye"?
choices: A passenger looking out of the window
questions.explanation: The image turns the train into a sleeping animal (prosopopoeia, lesson 09); what they share is stillness with one light on, the headlamp. The others don't fit "one eye" on the train itself.

questions.stem: Build the lesson's greguería in Spanish.
questions.prompt: A QR code is a crossword only phones can solve.
questions.explanation: Los teléfonos is the subject of the relative clause, placed after its verb, so the verb is plural: que solo resuelven los teléfonos. The singular resuelve doesn't agree with it.

questions.stem: What does Rosario, the nine-year-old, like most about the sacramental play?
choices: The costumes, which were the brightest she had seen
That the actors spoke like in church, but she could understand them
That her brother had a part in it
questions.explanation: She tells the reporter that they spoke like in church but could be understood. Nothing in the text mentions costumes, length or her brother.

questions.stem: In the Cervantes interlude the troupe performs, why does everyone pretend to see the show?
choices: Because the mayor has ordered them to applaud
Because the actors pay them to pretend
Because the tricksters say only people of "pure blood" can see it, and nobody wants to look impure
Because the lights have gone out
questions.explanation: In El retablo de las maravillas, two tricksters claim that only those of "clean blood" can see their show, so everyone pretends. The villagers laugh because they recognize the trick.

questions.stem: How does Todorov define the fantastic?
choices: As the hesitation between a natural and a supernatural explanation of a strange event
As any story with dragons, wizards and invented worlds
As a story that calmly tells impossible events as normal
As a realist novel set in the future
questions.explanation: For Todorov the fantastic lasts while the reader, and often a character, hesitates. Dragons and invented worlds are fantasy (la fantasía); telling the impossible calmly is magical realism.

questions.stem: What separates the fantastic from magical realism, in the lesson's terms?
choices: The fantastic always takes place in Argentina.
In magical realism the impossible is told as normal and nobody hesitates; in the fantastic its irruption is unsettling.
Magical realism never includes anything impossible.
The fantastic is written only in verse.
questions.explanation: Both include the impossible; the difference is the reaction. Magical realism accepts it calmly; the fantastic makes it inquietante and keeps us doubting. Neither is tied to one country or to verse.

questions.stem: Match each Borges story to its retelling.
choices: People live in an endless library that holds every possible book.
A writer sets out to write chapters of Cervantes's novel word for word.
From a basement, the narrator sees a tiny sphere that shows the whole universe.
A man dreams a son into being and finds he is dreamed too.
A fugitive falls in love with an image replayed by a machine.
questions.explanation: These are the four retellings in the lesson. The fugitive and the machine belong to Bioy Casares's La invención de Morel (1940).

questions.topic: The Río de la Plata circle
questions.stem: What happens in Bioy Casares's La invención de Morel (1940)?
choices: A detective solves a crime in a Buenos Aires library.
A boy serves a series of masters on an island.
A traveler learns from a switchman that the railway is absurd.
A fugitive on an island falls in love with a woman who turns out to be an image replayed by a machine.
questions.explanation: Borges wrote its prologue. The railway and the switchman are Arreola's "El guardagujas"; the boy with many masters is the picaresque.

questions.stem: Which statement about Amparo Dávila is accurate?
choices: She was born in Pinos, Zacatecas, in 1928, and published Tiempo destrozado in 1959.
She founded the magazine Sur with Victoria Ocampo.
She won the Cervantes Prize together with Borges.
questions.explanation: Dávila (1928–2020), once Alfonso Reyes's secretary, published Tiempo destrozado (1959), Música concreta (1964) and Árboles petrificados (1977, Xavier Villaurrutia Prize). Sur was Victoria Ocampo's; Confabulario is Arreola's; Borges shared the Cervantes Prize with Gerardo Diego in 1979.

questions.stem: What happens in Arreola's "El guardagujas" (Confabulario, 1952)?
choices: A woman lives in terror of a creature her husband brings home.
A traveler waiting for a train learns from a switchman that the railway system is absurd beyond belief.
A proofreader finds an encyclopedia entry about herself.
A man dreams a son into being.
questions.explanation: The creature in the house is Amparo Dávila's "El huésped"; the proofreader is the lesson's original story; the dreamer is Borges's "Las ruinas circulares".

questions.stem: Inés guesses, in direct thought, that it must have been fatigue. Complete with the future perfect of conjecture: "___ sido el cansancio", se dijo.
questions.explanation: The future perfect of conjecture (habrá sido) makes a guess about the recent past from the speaker's now (lesson 05). The certain fue would end the hesitation; habría sido places the guess relative to a past moment, as in reported thought (pensó que habría sido…).

questions.stem: Which of these are examples of mise en abyme? Select all that apply.
choices: A dreamer who discovers that he too is being dreamed
An encyclopedia entry that describes the woman reading it, as she reads it
A labyrinth with a smaller copy of itself at its center
A narrator who tells events out of chronological order
A creature that lives in a house and has no name
questions.explanation: Each of the first three contains a smaller image of itself. Telling events out of order is analepsis or prolepsis (lesson 11), and a nameless creature is a fantastic motif, not a mirror of the work.

questions.stem: What does this picture illustrate?

image.alt: A drawing titled "Un laberinto dentro de sí mismo": a square labyrinth whose center holds a framed copy of the same labyrinth, which holds an even smaller copy.

choices: A frame story with three narrators
The Generation of '27's tribute in Seville
Mise en abyme: the work contains a smaller image of itself, again and again
The hesitation that defines the fantastic
questions.explanation: The labyrinth holds a framed copy of itself, which holds another: a visual mise en abyme, one of Borges's favorite devices. It doesn't show narrators, a historical event or a reader's hesitation.

questions.stem: Where does the impossible first break into "Entrada sin autor"?
choices: When Inés finds the office empty at eleven
When the system assigns her a bestiary entry
When the entry's last paragraph describes her at 3:07, in her blue sweater, and the clock says 3:07
When her boss arrives in pajamas
questions.explanation: An entry about an invented bird is only a joke; the irruption comes when the text describes her, at that very minute, exactly as she is. Her boss's visit comes much later and finds nothing.

questions.stem: Put the events of "Entrada sin autor" in order.
choices: Inés finds an anonymous entry about the quietzal.
She deletes it as an apocryphal prank.
The entry returns with a paragraph about its deletion.
Her boss finds no trace of the entry.
After two weeks of rest, she finds an entry that tells her whole story.
questions.explanation: The story moves from a joke to an intrusion: the entry, its deletion, its return (now signed by her own user), the boss's visit, and the final entry that widens the mise en abyme to the reader.

questions.stem: Build the sentence from the story in Spanish.
tiles: Inés se rio en voz alta
accept: Inés se rio en voz alta
questions.prompt: Inés laughed out loud so that the building would hear her.
questions.explanation: Para que (so that) always takes the subjunctive; after a past verb, the imperfect subjunctive oyera (oyese is also correct). The purpose clause can also open the sentence (Para que la oyera el edificio, Inés se rio en voz alta), and the subject el edificio follows its verb, as often in Spanish. Se rio has no written accent (RAE 2010).

questions.stem: "La reseña hablaba de un libro apócrifo." What kind of book is it?
choices: A book about the end of the world
A book that is invented or falsely attributed
questions.explanation: Apócrifo means falsely attributed or invented: Borges wrote reviews of apocryphal books. It doesn't mean apocalyptic, rare or devotional.

questions.stem: A report says: "El proveedor adujo problemas de transporte." What does "adujo" tell you that "dijo" wouldn't?
choices: The supplier offered transport problems as a reason, and the writer may doubt it.
The supplier shouted about the transport problems.
The supplier denied that there were transport problems.
The supplier was interrupted while talking about transport.
questions.explanation: Aducir is to offer something as a reason, and it is often used of reasons the writer suspects are excuses. It says nothing about volume (that would be gritar), denial (negar) or being interrupted.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that fits best: "—¿Y usted quién se cree? —le ___, furioso, el cliente al mesero, sin siquiera saludar."
questions.explanation: Espetar is to say something blunt or rude, suddenly, to someone (espetarle algo a alguien): exactly a furious question fired without a greeting. Aducir offers a reason; apostillar adds a remark after someone else has spoken, which doesn't fit an opening line; balbucear (to stammer) clashes with furioso.

questions.stem: You want to describe your sister's figure with admiration. Which word does it best? "Mi hermana es muy ___."
questions.explanation: Esbelta (slender) adds admiration. Delgada is neutral, a plain fact; flaca is plain and informal and can sound critical (though in Mexico it is also an affectionate nickname); escuálida suggests an unhealthy thinness.

questions.stem: A coffee tasting note praises "una acidez brillante". What does it mean?
choices: The coffee has gone sour and should be thrown out.
The coffee has a shiny surface.
The coffee has a lively, pleasant acidity.
questions.explanation: In coffee tasting, la acidez is a virtue: a lively, fresh quality, here compared to citrus. In everyday speech tengo acidez means heartburn, but a tasting note uses the tasters' sense. Brillante describes the acidity, not the surface.

questions.stem: Complete with argüir in the preterite: "La abogada ___ que el contrato no era válido."
questions.explanation: Arguyó. The ü appears only before i (argüir, argüimos, argüí); before y it disappears: arguyo, arguyó, arguyeron, arguyendo.
