Code-switching: moving between languages (Te llamo después, I'm driving). Calque: word-for-word translation (llamar para atrás for devolver la llamada).
el préstamo léxico (loanword: el tianguis), el sustrato (earlier language left traces), la convergencia (languages growing alike)
When transmission between generations stops: grandparents monolingual in one language, grandchildren in another. Assimilation speeds it; language loyalty slows it.
Two languages or varieties with separate roles (school vs home). Ferguson, 1959. Classic example: Spanish and Guarani in Paraguay.
acuñar (to coin), caer en desuso (to fall out of use), el desuso; másteres / másters both accepted (DPD 2nd ed., 2024)
Academies set spelling; governments choose official languages (Mexico's 2003 Ley General de Derechos Lingüísticos de los Pueblos Indígenas); schools choose what is taught.
Generic masculine (los estudiantes), doubling (los estudiantes y las estudiantes), neutral wording (el alumnado): all standard. Forms in -e: not accepted by the RAE.
RAE: the generic masculine is inclusive (Bosque report, 2012; report on the Constitution, 2020). Many public guides (INMUJERES in Mexico): doubling and neutral wording. Report each with its source.
March 31, 1492: the edict signed in Granada ordered Jews to convert or leave. Conversos stayed; the Sephardim left in a diaspora.
The Ottoman Empire (Thessaloniki, Istanbul, Izmir, Sarajevo) and North Africa (Tetuán, Tangier: Haketia)
The self-governing Jewish (or Muslim) community / the Jewish quarter of a town
Sephardic, from Sefarad (the Hebrew name for Iberia). Plural sefardíes (also sefardís).
fijo (hijo), favlar (hablar): the old f-; baxo with an sh sound (bajo); muestro (nuestro)
Turkish: araba, musafir; Hebrew: haham, kal; Greek: meldar; French: abazur, fusil; Arabic: in Haketia
Ladino is common in Israel and English; many scholars reserve it for the calque language of sacred translations. In a formal Spanish text, write judeoespañol.
Rashi script (print), solitreo (cursive), today mostly Latin letters with phonetic spelling (kaza), as in Aki Yerushalayim.
Endangered; estimates vary (about 51,000 native speakers in Ethnologue, 2018). Autoridad Nasionala del Ladino (1997), Akademia Nasionala del Ladino (affiliated with ASALE).
Independent October 12, 1968; Spanish co-official with French and Portuguese; Spanish is the lingua franca among Fang, Bubi and others; academy 2013, ASALE 2016.
Legazpi 1565, Manila 1571, governed from New Spain until 1821, Spanish rule until 1898. 1987 Constitution: Filipino and English official; Spanish and Arabic promoted voluntarily.
kutsara (cuchara), bintana (ventana), sapatos (zapatos), kumusta (¿cómo está?); via Mexico: kamote, kamatis, atole, petate
A Spanish-based creole (Zamboanga, Cavite, Ternate): Spanish words, Philippine grammar. Markers ta (present), ya (past), di/ay (future); plural mana. Ya mirá yo cun José = Vi a José.
Chavacano (the creole); in Mexico, an apricot; as an adjective, tacky. The creole's name is usually traced to the adjective.
1565–1815, Acapulco ↔ Manila: silver west, silk and porcelain east; the return route (Urdaneta, 1565) swung north and down the coast of California.
Creole: a new language with native speakers built from several (Chavacano). Lingua franca: a shared language between speakers of different first languages (Spanish in Equatorial Guinea).
One text from several sources, organized by points: build a grid (sources × points), then write one paragraph per point, comparing the sources inside it. 400–450 words in the 2024 sample exam.
to agree on / to disagree with: Ambas fuentes coinciden en que… ; La carta discrepa del informe.
convergence / divergence between sources: La divergencia más clara está en las medidas.
to set against, contrast (like poner): contrapongo, contrapuse, contrapondré, contrapuesto; command contrapón.
to combine, join: aúno, aúnas, aúna, aunamos, aúnan; subjunctive aúne; aunar esfuerzos = to join forces.
to compare texts or versions side by side; close to B1's contrastar.
certain: afirma, asegura; argued: sostiene, defiende; tentative: plantea, sugiere, estima que podría; warning: advierte; concession: reconoce, admite; qualification: matiza.
Report a source with its own strength: podría haber una sobreoferta → estima que podría existir una sobreoferta, never afirma que hay. Add no hedge the source didn't use.
Only a short phrase whose wording matters, in quotation marks; otherwise rephrase and attribute.

cards.front: Your own view in a report
cards.back: Keep it apart, in the genre's register: a juicio de quien firma, cabe señalar que…; not yo creo.
carrying capacity: how much use a place can bear without damage.
the money an activity brings into a place (usual in Mexican news).

cards.front: el uso de suelo / el ordenamiento territorial
cards.back: land use (zoning) / land-use planning: usual Mexican terms; cambio de uso de suelo = rezoning.
mass tourism's effect on a neighborhood; Fundéu BBVA called it a valid neologism (2018, updated 2023).
pier, dock; also a metal spring.
Notes (about 100 words, per preparation sites) into a 200–250-word text in a set genre and role. The old format corrected a draft instead; practice both.

cards.front: From notes to prose: four moves
cards.back: Expand (full clauses), order (for the reader), connect (connectors), set the register; spell out what the notes leave implicit.
to spell out, make explicit; not A1's deletrear (to spell letter by letter).
polish / purge of errors / restructure / condense a text.
museum label or wall text (cédula temática, cédula de objeto); not B2's la cédula profesional.
data sheet: material, date, provenance of a museum piece; also a product's specifications.
el redactor writes the texts (copywriter, staff writer); B2's el editor edits or publishes them.
post-editing a machine translation; RAE guidance prefers pos- to post- (except before s); postedición is also seen.
possibly, now and then; not English "eventually" (con el tiempo, finalmente).
to suffer from (a defect), not "to lack" (carecer de).
terms (chocolatera, vitrina), structure (servía para, not fue usada para), centuries in Roman numerals, sign conventions (Favor de no tocar), tú / usted kept consistent.
target reader; meta is invariable: los lectores meta.
paragraph indentation; also bloodletting and the wine drink.
A 200–250-word text in a set genre explaining data from tables and charts.

cards.front: Explaining data at C2: four layers
cards.back: interpret (dicho de otro modo…), explain cautiously (se explica en parte por…), set limits (los datos no permiten afirmar…), project with hedges (según la proyección, habría…).

cards.front: la media / la mediana / el promedio
cards.back: mean (statistical) / median (middle value) / B2's everyday average. When a few high values pull the mean up, the median shows the typical case.
percentile: the 90th percentile is the value below which 90% of cases fall.
a group born in the same years and followed over time.
A projection says what would happen if its assumptions hold: use the conditional or a hedge (pasaría, podría llegar a).
dependents (children and older people) per 100 people of working age.
demographic dividend: the period when the working-age population grows faster than the dependent population.

cards.front: el sistema de reparto / la cuenta individual
cards.back: pay-as-you-go system (today's contributions pay today's pensions) / individual account (each worker's own savings, managed in Mexico by an afore).
replacement rate: the share of the last salary that the pension replaces.
About 19.2 million people aged 60 or over (14.7% of the population); median age 32, against 29 in 2020 (as reported in September 2026).

Employers' old-age (cesantía y vejez) contribution rises gradually, for the highest salaries from 3.15% to 11.875% of base salary by 2030; the weeks of contributions required were 750 in 2021, rising by 25 a year to 1,000 in 2031 (CONSAR's summary and El Financiero, as reported).

30 minutes to prepare; a choice between two sets of materials (several texts and charts at C2); a 5–6-minute presentation; consult notes, don't read them; signal at five minutes (examiner-training material, 2023).
introduction (topic, materials) → text 1 → text 2 → chart → comparison → opinion with reasons → closing sentence.
Understands with ease virtually everything heard or read, and expresses themselves spontaneously, very fluently and precisely, telling apart finer shades of meaning.
The Spanish version of the CEFR groups C1 and C2 as usuario competente and names C2 Maestría.
Test 1 (language use, reading, listening): 105 min, 52 items. Test 2 (EMIE): 150 min, 3 tasks. Test 3 (EMIO): 20 min + 30 to prepare, 3 tasks. About 33.33 points each, 100 in all.
Published in the Instituto Cervantes' exam guide; preparation sites describe it as passing each test in the same session. Check the guide.
The interviewer gives a holistic mark for the three tasks; the rater marks each task analytically (fluency, accuracy, range, the task's own category with task fulfilment), in four bands.
B2's la banda in its exam sense: a score band on a rating scale.

cards.front: la idoneidad / la pertinencia / la concisión
cards.back: suitability / relevance / concision: what C2 rewards as much as lexical richness.
Short monologues matched to their communicative intention (as preparation sites describe it): listen for what the speaker is doing, not just the words.
gist comprehension / detailed comprehension: read for the gist first, then the items, then in detail where they point.
elimination of options: by collocation, register, government and logic; por descarte = by elimination.
a trap / a distractor statement: the classic trap repeats words from the text with another meaning.
Déjeme terminar la idea…; Si me permite, añado algo…
En eso le doy la razón; Es cierto que…, pero…; Ese argumento tiene un punto débil:…
Volviendo a lo que decíamos…; Pero lo que se discute aquí es…
to steer back; like conducir: reconduzco, reconduje, recondujeron; subjunctive reconduzca.
liaison (short turns, both ways), consecutive (longer turns from notes), simultaneous (almost at the same time, from a booth).
accuracy (no omissions, no additions), impartiality, confidentiality, transparency when stepping out of the role; speak in the first person.
"I twisted my ankle" → Me torcí el tobillo, not Dice que se torció el tobillo.
Don't guess: ask for clarification openly, in both languages, as the interpreter.
to convey (into another language); also to move or transfer someone or something.
interpreting booth; A2's la caseta is a toll booth.

glossary.definition: A genre born in Spain with the anonymous Lazarillo de Tormes (1554): the first-person life of a rogue (pícaro) of low birth, who serves one master after another and tells his story as an adult, in loosely linked episodes that satirize society. Guzmán de Alfarache (1599, 1604) and El Buscón (1626) fixed its rules; El Periquillo Sarniento (1816) is its best-known Mexican heir.

The nineteenth-century movement that set out to show contemporary life as it is: ordinary people, money, marriage, religion and politics in a recognizable place, seen by an observant narrator. In Spain its masters are Galdós and Clarín.

A movement led in France by Émile Zola that treated the novel as an experiment: characters are shaped by heredity and environment. Emilia Pardo Bazán brought the debate to Spain (La cuestión palpitante, 1883); Federico Gamboa's Santa (1903) is the best-known Mexican example.

Writing (and painting) that portrays the types, customs and speech of a place in short sketches, popular from the 1830s (Larra and Mesonero Romanos in Madrid, Guillermo Prieto in Mexico). Realism inherited its eye for detail.

The group of Spanish poets named after the December 1927 tribute in Seville for the three-hundredth anniversary of Góngora's death: among them Salinas, Guillén, Diego, Aleixandre, Alonso, Alberti, Cernuda, Prados, Altolaguirre and García Lorca. They joined tradition (Góngora, popular song) and the avant-garde.

The avant-garde movement launched by André Breton's manifesto (Paris, 1924) that sought images in dreams and the unconscious, free of logic. In Spain its best-known figures are Dalí and Buñuel; Lorca's New York poems are often linked to it, though how closely is debated.

In Tzvetan Todorov's definition (1970), a story in which the reader, and often a character, hesitates between a natural and a supernatural explanation of a strange event. If the story explains it, it becomes the uncanny; if it accepts new laws, the marvelous. Unlike magical realism, the fantastic makes the impossible unsettling.
A work that contains a smaller image of itself: a story inside a story that mirrors it, a picture inside the same picture, a dreamer who is dreamed. Borges uses it often.

A word that shares most of its meaning with another but not all of it. Near-synonyms can differ in denotation, connotation, register, collocation, region, intensity and evaluation: delgado, esbelto, flaco and escuálido describe the same body with different attitudes. Test a choice by putting each candidate in the same sentence.
What a word refers to, its literal content, apart from any attitude it carries: el aroma denotes a pleasant smell, el sabor a taste.

The attitude, feeling or associations a word carries beyond its denotation: esbelto praises, escuálido worries or scorns, though both describe a thin body. A word with a negative connotation is pejorative (peyorativo).

A habitual combination of words that native speakers prefer over equally logical alternatives: esgrimir un argumento, aducir razones, infligir una derrota, infringir una norma. A corpus shows a word's collocations in its concordance lines.

A move from one register into another inside the same text. By accident it is a slip (a colloquialism in an insurance claim); on purpose it is a device that creates humor or irony through incongruity (an official word such as el siniestro dropped into family talk).

The special vocabulary of a trade or group (el argot de los médicos), or the slang of the street; close to la jerga. Caló first means the Romani variety of the Spanish Gitanos (its usual sense in Spain); in Mexico it is widely used for street slang. Learned for recognition at C2, not imitated.

A word so similar in form to another that writers confuse them, though their meanings differ: infligir (to inflict) and infringir (to break a rule), absolver and absorber, proveer and prever, perjuicio and prejuicio, expiar and espiar, actitud and aptitud.

An error of meaning: a word used with a sense it doesn't have, such as adolecer de (to suffer from a defect) for carecer de (to lack), or detentar (to hold unlawfully) for ostentar (to hold a title). Compare solecism, an error of syntax.
An error of syntax: of agreement, government or word order, such as Hubieron quejas for Hubo quejas. Compare impropriety, an error of meaning.

A word borrowed from written Latin or Greek and only lightly adapted, after the language had formed: clamar, íntegro, estricto, delicado. Learned words keep Latin consonant clusters, vowels and often stress, and usually sound more formal than their inherited twins.
A word that came down from spoken Latin through centuries of speech and changed with it: llamar, entero, estrecho, delgado. Compare learned word.
A pair of words from the same Latin word, one inherited and one learned: llamar / clamar (clamare), entero / íntegro (integrum), estrecho / estricto (strictum), delgado / delicado (delicatum).

A word, phrase or construction taken from Latin. Unadapted Latin phrases (a priori, de facto, grosso modo, in situ, motu proprio, statu quo, per capita) are written, per the RAE's Ortografía (2010), in italics and without accents.

The form under which a dictionary files an entry: the infinitive for verbs, the masculine singular for nouns and adjectives (canté and cantaríamos are found at cantar). Grouping forms under their headword is lemmatizing (lematizar).

An abbreviation in a dictionary entry that limits a sense: by place (Méx., Am., Esp.), by register (coloq., vulg.), by attitude (despect.), by time (desus., obsolete) or by field (Der., law). Read the labels before the definition.

A large, searchable collection of real texts (el corpus, plural los corpus), used to see how often a word is used, in which countries and with which words. Examples: the RAE's CORPES XXI (texts from 2001 on) and the Corpus del Español.

In corpus work, a list of every occurrence of a word, one per line, with the word in the center and its context on both sides (keyword in context). Reading down the column after the word shows its collocations. In grammar, la concordancia means agreement instead.

A place name (el topónimo); toponymy (la toponimia) studies them. Mexican toponyms often come from Nahuatl (Chapultepec, Mazatlán), add a saint (San Juan Teotihuacan) or honor a person (Hidalgo); many in Spain come from Arabic (Guadalajara, Alcalá).

The name for the people of a place (el gentilicio): tapatío (Guadalajara), regiomontano (Monterrey), capitalino (Mexico City). Spanish writes demonyms in lower case, and some have registers: chilango and regio are colloquial.
The name a language gives to a foreign place, different from the local one: Londres for London, Pekín for Beijing (much of the press now also writes Beijing). Spanish keeps the established exonyms.

How a verb presents an event in time: as a whole, finished (perfective: the preterite, murió) or from inside, ongoing or as background (imperfective: the imperfect, moría). Spanish marks it in the past tenses.

The imperfect used for a single, completed past event, usually pinned down by a time phrase, for a slowed-down or closing effect in news and fiction: Dos horas después, la policía detenía al sospechoso. A preterite (detuvo) is the plain choice and is never wrong.
The present tense used for past events to bring them close: En 1969 Bernal publica su novela. Neutral in biographies and timelines; in fiction a switch into it puts the reader inside a scene.

The future (simple or perfect) used for a guess: Serán las once (It must be about eleven); Habrá salido (He must have left). The conditional does the same for a past moment: Tendría setenta años; Habría sido el chofer.

The conditional used in the press for unconfirmed information: El sospechoso habría huido (The suspect has reportedly fled). Frequent; FundéuRAE and newspaper style guides advise attributing the claim to a source instead.

Hube + participle after apenas, en cuanto, cuando, no bien, for an event just before another: Apenas hubo terminado, se fue (No sooner had he finished than he left). Literary only; read it, don't produce it.

A statement about what would be or would have been if something that didn't happen had happened: Si no hubiera llegado la imprenta, hoy leeríamos menos. A mixed counterfactual pairs a past condition with a present result.
The condition half of a conditional sentence: si llueve in Si llueve, se suspende el partido; or a structure without si, such as de haberlo sabido.
The result half of a conditional sentence: se suspende el partido in Si llueve, se suspende el partido.

A protasis expressed without si: de + infinitive (De seguir así…), de + compound infinitive (De haberlo sabido…), a gerund (Saliendo ahora…), a set participle (Bien mirado…), con + infinitive, a poco que, de no ser por, como + subjunctive.

A subjunctive tense (fuere, hubiere, tuviere) ordinary in Old Spanish, now found in old laws and fixed phrases: sea como fuere (be that as it may), sea cual fuere (whatever it may be). Read others as present subjunctives.
A relative clause, without commas, that picks out which ones you mean: Los vecinos que protestaron recibieron respuesta (only those who protested).

A relative clause, between commas, that adds information about all the antecedent: Los vecinos, que protestaron, recibieron respuesta (all of them protested). After a noun, quien without a preposition appears only in this kind.
In grammar and rhetoric, a long sentence whose clauses form one unit of sense: a main clause with subordinate clauses and asides, held together by commas, dashes and semicolons.

An aside that interrupts a sentence and could be lifted out without breaking it, set off by commas, dashes or parentheses depending on how strongly it interrupts: La arcilla —según los geólogos— se compacta.
A fixed group of words, usually ending in a preposition, that works as one preposition: a la luz de, en virtud de, sin perjuicio de. Its parts can't be changed (a la luz de, not en la luz de).
The preposition or construction a verb or adjective requires: consistir en, incidir en, redundar en, abogar por, propender a, carecer de.

The Castilian of the Middle Ages, conventionally up to about the end of the fifteenth century, with spellings for sounds since lost (f-, ç, ss, x) and forms such as the future subjunctive and -ades endings.
The study of old handwriting: letter shapes, abbreviations (a tilde for a missing n, q with a mark for que) and how to date and read a hand.
The matching of forms: a verb agrees with the head of its subject in person and number, and articles and adjectives agree with their noun in gender and number.
Agreement by meaning rather than grammatical form: La gente llegó tarde y se quejaron. Accepted for a collective in a later clause; avoided within the collective's own clause.
A noun with one grammatical gender for beings of either sex: la persona, la víctima, el personaje, la jirafa. Agreement follows the noun: La víctima, un hombre de 40 años, fue trasladada.
A noun singular in form that names a group: la gente, el público, el comité. It takes a singular verb in its own clause: La gente llegó tarde.

A deliberate pattern of meaning, order or sound that makes words stand out: tropes such as metaphor and metonymy, figures of order such as chiasmus and hyperbaton, of linking such as polysyndeton, of sound such as alliteration. One strong figure per paragraph carries weight; a figure in every sentence reads as bombastic (ampuloso).
A figure that uses a word in a sense that isn't its own: metaphor (by resemblance), metonymy (by closeness) and synecdoche (part and whole).

A trope that names a thing by something closely linked to it: the author for the work (leí a Rulfo), the building for the institution (Palacio Nacional anunció), the container for its contents (se tomó dos tazas).
A trope that names the whole by a part or a part by the whole: seis bocas que alimentar (six people), México ganó (the national team). Many manuals treat it as a kind of metonymy.
Two words with clashing meanings joined in one phrase: una calma impaciente, un silencio que grita. A whole statement that seems to contradict itself is a paradox.
A statement that seems to contradict itself but holds a truth: para encontrar tu voz, primero hay que callar. Compare oxymoron, which joins two clashing words in one phrase.
Two elements repeated in reverse order, A B / B A: no cambié mi pueblo; mi pueblo me cambió. A favorite figure for a closing line.

One word, usually a verb, serves several phrases and is understood in the rest: Él pidió café; ella, té. When the shared word takes two senses (Mi abuela contaba historias; mi madre, el dinero; perdió el miedo y el autobús), English also calls it syllepsis.
Repeating a conjunction where it isn't needed (y… y… y…), for a slow, cumulative effect: escribí en cocinas y en camiones y en salas de espera.
Leaving out conjunctions between items, for speed and urgency: llegó, firmó, se fue.
A word order a reader feels as unusual, mainly in verse or solemn prose: de la ciudad las luces se apagaban. Ordinary Spanish fronting (ayer llegó mi hermana) is not hyperbaton.
A series that rises (or falls) step by step: una libreta, un cuento, una novela, una vida. Not the climax of a plot (el clímax).
Repeating a sound, usually a consonant, in nearby words: la lluvia lenta y limpia.
Giving human traits or a voice to things, animals or ideas: las palabras me esperaban en la mesa; la ciudad bosteza.
Turning away from the audience to address someone absent or dead, or something that can't answer: Y a ti, abuela… Not el apóstrofo, the punctuation mark.
Deliberate exaggeration that no one takes literally: te esperé una eternidad. Not la hipérbola, the curve in geometry.
In rhetoric, repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive phrases or sentences: por los que leen, por los que escriben, por los que esperan.
Opposed ideas set side by side in parallel form: llegamos con dudas y nos vamos con planes.
A question asked for effect, not for an answer: ¿Quién no ha dudado alguna vez? It works when the audience can only answer one way.
An adjective that states a quality the noun already has, usually placed before it, for emphasis or literary tone: la blanca nieve. One adds color; several in a row make prose overdone (recargada).
The study of how form creates meaning in a text: word choice, order, rhythm, figures and register.

A structured analysis of a text in four steps: theme (what it is about), structure (its parts), form (register, syntax, figures, vocabulary) and assessment (what the form does for the content, and how well).

The voice that tells a story, never simply the author: omniscient (knows every mind), witness (narrador testigo, first person beside the main character), protagonist (tells his or her own story), or second person (tú).
The point of view from which events are perceived, which may differ from the voice that tells them: zero (omniscient), internal (through one character) or external (only what a camera would record).

A character's thoughts given in the narrator's voice without a verb of thinking. Spanish marks it with the imperfect and conditional (llegaría), the character's deixis with past tenses (mañana, ahora) and questions or exclamations with no pensó: El camión llegaría mañana. ¿Y si Julián no venía?
A character's thoughts given directly, usually in the present and the first person, often without full syntax or punctuation: the nearest point to the character's mind.
A jump back in time within a narrative; in Spanish la analepsis, plural las analepsis.
A jump forward in time, often announcing an outcome: Años más tarde, vendería la casa. In Spanish la prolepsis, plural las prolepsis.
A story that contains another story, such as a conversation in which someone tells a tale.
Fiction that talks about its own writing or draws attention to its own invention.
A text's dialogue with other texts, through allusion, quotation, parody or rewriting.
Many voices in one work with none in charge; its typical form is the ensemble novel (la novela coral).
The word choices that decide how an issue is seen before any argument is made: ajuste or aumento, reforma or recorte, actualización tarifaria or tarifazo.

What a sentence takes for granted: seguiremos mejorando assumes the service has been improving; ya no habrá cortes admits there were cuts. Carried by verbs like seguir, volver a, dejar de and by definite descriptions.

What a sentence suggests without saying it, inferred because a speaker is assumed to be relevant and informative: algunos cumplieron implies that others didn't. Unlike a presupposition, it can be denied.
A method for reading public texts by asking who acts (and who is hidden or blamed), what is assumed, what is implied and what is left out, then judging the frame.

The great period of Spanish literature and art, roughly from the early sixteenth century to the late seventeenth (its end is often placed at Calderón's death in 1681): Cervantes, Lope, Góngora, Quevedo, Calderón, and in New Spain Sor Juana and Ruiz de Alarcón.

The formula of Golden Age theater associated with Lope de Vega (Arte nuevo de hacer comedias, 1609): three acts called jornadas, tragic and comic mixed, many meters, and plots of love, honor (la honra) and intrigue (el enredo).
A one-act religious allegory with abstract figures as characters, performed for the feast of Corpus Christi; Calderón was its master. Autos were banned in 1765.

The Hispanic literary movement of about 1880 to 1915 (Martí, Gutiérrez Nájera, Darío, Silva, Nervo), which renewed verse and prose through musicality, exoticism, synesthesia and new meters. Not English modernism, which is later and closer to the vanguardias.

In Spanish, a fourteen-syllable line split into two halves of seven, revived by the modernistas. French counts its alexandrine as twelve syllables because the two languages count line endings differently.
Verse with no fixed meter or rhyme; the modernistas pointed toward it, and the avant-gardes made it common.

The language of a profession or field (law, medicine, finance, technology): everyday grammar plus terms whose meaning the field fixes, fixed formulas, and genre conventions such as the parts of a ruling or a patent claim. Spanish: el lenguaje de especialidad.

A word or phrase whose meaning a field fixes precisely, often by law or standard: el fallo (the deciding part of a ruling), la jurisprudencia (binding case law), el estado de la técnica (prior art). An everyday word can be a term in one field (la suspensión, a stay in an amparo).

In Mexico, a federal lawsuit in which a person (el quejoso) asks the federal courts to protect constitutional rights against an act of authority (el acto reclamado). Historians usually trace it to Yucatán's 1841 constitution and the 1847 Acta de Reformas; today articles 103 and 107 of the Constitution and the Ley de Amparo govern it. The court can grant a stay (la suspensión) and, in the end, grant or deny the amparo, or dismiss the case (sobreseer).

Court decisions that bind other courts. Spanish la jurisprudencia (a false friend: English jurisprudence usually means legal theory). In Mexico a court's criterion is published as a tesis, which binds only under the conditions the Ley de Amparo sets; those rules have changed with reforms, so check the current text.

A fixed expression a legal genre requires or expects, recognized as a whole: el suscrito (the undersigned), en lo sucesivo (hereinafter), por lo expuesto y fundado, se resuelve; in deeds, ante mí and doy fe. Used in legal documents, not in ordinary prose or in plain explanations.

The set of documents a health service keeps on each patient: identification, history (anamnesis), physical examination, studies, diagnosis, plan and progress notes. In Mexico, el expediente clínico, regulated by NOM-004-SSA3-2012; in Spain, la historia clínica.

What a central bank says about its likely future decisions (Hacia delante, la Junta evaluará…). Markets read its exact wording, so its hedges (se prevé, podría, no se descarta, de materializarse) must be reported at their own strength.

The part of a patent that defines exactly what is protected (la reivindicación). Each claim is one sentence: a preamble, the transition que comprende (comprising), the elements, and the characterizing part introduced by caracterizado porque. Dependent claims narrow an earlier one (La válvula de conformidad con la reivindicación 1…).

Everything made public anywhere before a patent application's filing date (el estado de la técnica). An invention is new only if the prior art doesn't contain it, and involves an inventive step only if it wouldn't be obvious to a skilled person in the field.

The leaflet inside a medicine's box: in Mexico el instructivo (also el inserto), in Spain el prospecto. It has fixed sections (formula, indications, contraindications, precautions, adverse reactions, interactions, dosage and route, overdose, legends) and gives instructions with the usted imperative and the impersonal se (consérvese).

A document drafted and authorized by a notary in his or her protocol (la escritura pública), which the law treats as proof. In Mexico it usually runs: proemio, comparecencia, antecedentes, cláusulas, generales y certificaciones, autorización.

The idea that a language has several centers of prestige, each setting the standard for its own country. Spanish is pluricentric: the educated usage of Mexico, Colombia, Argentina or Spain is a standard in its own right, and the 23 ASALE academies describe these standards together in panhispanic works (the DLE, the Nueva gramática, the DPD).

The form of a language that a country's educated speakers use in formal speech and writing (in Spanish, la norma culta). Spanish has several standard varieties with one shared spelling; Mexico's is the model of this course.

A word or use typical of one region (el regionalismo); a localism (el localismo) belongs to a single city or area. Spanish names them by place: mexicanismo, americanismo, peninsularismo (Spain), chilenismo, argentinismo, colombianismo. The DLE marks many with a country label (Méx., Esp., Am.).

A line on a dialect map that marks where one feature (a word, a sound, a form) gives way to another: the line between carro and coche, for example. Isoglosses for different features rarely coincide and rarely follow national borders.

The use of le as a direct object, mainly for a person: A Juan le vi (Mexico: lo vi). Frequent in central and northern Spain and described in Paraguay and Andean Ecuador; the RAE accepts it for one male person but not for women or things. This course writes lo.
The use of la as an indirect object for a woman: La dije que viniera for Le dije que viniera. Heard in central Spain; not accepted by the norm.
The use of lo as an indirect object: Lo di un regalo for Le di un regalo. Rarer than laísmo, found in parts of central Spain, stigmatized and not accepted by the norm.

Using vos as the familiar "you" for one person, with its own verb forms: vos hablás, vos sos, ¡vení! (Río de la Plata, Central America and other areas). In Chile, informal speech often keeps the pronoun tú with voseo endings (¿cómo estái?), which is called verbal voseo.
Using tú as the familiar "you" for one person, as in Mexico, Peru, the Caribbean and Spain.
Using usted even with family and close friends, as many speakers do in parts of Colombia and Costa Rica: Mi amor, ¿usted ya comió?

A subject pronoun said or written although the verb ending already shows the person: yo creo que yo voy. Spanish usually drops such pronouns; Caribbean Spanish uses them much more, which goes with questions like ¿Qué tú quieres?

Moving between two languages within one conversation or sentence, as bilinguals do: Te llamo después, I'm driving. Research describes it as a skilled practice with its own patterns, not as a sign of weak Spanish. Different from a calque, a phrase translated word for word.

Someone who grew up hearing a language at home (their heritage language) but was schooled mainly in another, like many Spanish speakers in the United States. Heritage speakers often speak with native ease and write less confidently.
The situation in which two or more languages are used by the same people. It leaves loanwords (préstamos léxicos), substrate traces and, over time, convergence between the languages.

An earlier language whose speakers shifted to another and left traces in it: Nahuatl in Mexican Spanish, Quechua in Andean Spanish. Loanwords are the clearest trace; how much grammar a substrate leaves is often debated.

A community's move from one language to another over generations, which happens when parents stop passing the first language to their children (intergenerational transmission). Among immigrant families it often takes three generations.

A situation in which two languages or varieties have separate social roles, one for school, law and writing and the other for home. The term was made famous by Charles Ferguson in 1959; Spanish and Guarani in Paraguay are the usual Spanish-speaking example.

Wording meant to make women and, for some, nonbinary people visible: gender doubling (los estudiantes y las estudiantes), collective or neutral words (el alumnado) and, outside the norm, forms in -e (les estudiantes). The RAE and many public guides disagree about it; describe each position with its source.

The use of masculine forms for mixed groups or unspecified people: los estudiantes for a mixed class. The RAE's grammar treats it as inclusive; many guides recommend doubling or neutral wording instead. All three options are standard.

The Spanish of the Sephardic Jews, carried from Spain after 1492 to the Ottoman Empire and North Africa (where it is called Haketia). It keeps older forms (fijo for hijo), has its own changes and borrowed from Turkish, Hebrew, Greek, French and Arabic. Often called Ladino, a name many scholars reserve for the calque language of sacred translations. Endangered today.

A language formed when speakers of different languages build a shared one, usually with vocabulary from one language and grammar shaped by others, and then learned by children as their first language. Chavacano in the Philippines is a Spanish-based creole.
A language used for communication between people whose first languages differ, as Spanish is in Equatorial Guinea between speakers of Fang, Bubi and other languages.

Passing on what someone else said or wrote to a person who needs it, in the form and language they need: summarizing, explaining, comparing sources, interpreting. The CEFR Companion Volume (2020) describes it in detail, and the DELE C2 includes it in its writing and speaking tests.
A text that combines several sources into one account organized by points, comparing what each source says, rather than summarizing them one after another.
Saying who holds each claim in a text built from sources (según…, sostiene que…, a juicio de…), with a reporting verb whose strength matches the source.
Saying the same content again in another form: expanding notes into prose, restructuring a draft, or rephrasing an idea so it fits the reader, the genre or a finer shade of meaning.
Correcting a machine translation so that it reads as if written in the target language: terms, structure, register and the conventions of the genre.

Whether a text or a spoken performance does what the task asked, for the stated reader or listener and in the stated genre. The Instituto Cervantes added a task-fulfilment category for each task in the 2024 DELE C1 and C2.
A rating scale that gives one overall judgment of a performance, rather than separate marks for separate features.
A rating scale that marks separate features of a performance (such as fluency, accuracy, range and task fulfilment) one by one.
Interpreting in short turns, in both directions, between two parties who sit together: a doctor and a patient, a buyer and a supplier.
Interpreting after the speaker has finished a passage of a few minutes, usually from notes, rather than at the same time (simultaneous interpreting).

references.title: Mediation, rewriting, texts from data and the DELE C2 at a glance
references.body:
## Writing from several sources

1. Read the instructions for **purpose, genre and reader**: they decide the register.
2. Make a grid: sources across the top, the points down the side; mark where they agree
   (*coinciden*), differ (*discrepan*) or add something.
3. Plan: an opening that states the issue for this reader; one paragraph per point, comparing
   sources; your assessment, kept apart from the sources; a close that fits the genre.
4. Attribute every claim, keep each source's hedges, add none, and quote no more than a short
   phrase.

| Move | Phrases |
|---|---|
| attributing | *según la especialista…, a juicio de…, como sostiene…, en palabras de… (short quotation)* |
| agreeing sources | *ambas fuentes coinciden en que…; el artículo confirma lo que plantea la entrevista* |
| differing sources | *mientras que…, …; frente a esta postura, …; las cifras contradicen…* |
| adding | *a ello se suma…; el segundo texto aporta un dato que…* |
| keeping a hedge | *la autora estima que podría…* (not *la autora asegura que…*) |
| your view | *a mi juicio…; cabe preguntarse si…; lo que ninguna de las fuentes aborda es…* |

## From notes or a draft to a finished text

| Step | Check |
|---|---|
| expand | full sentences, subjects and verbs; abbreviations written out |
| connect | connectors of cause, contrast and addition; one main idea per paragraph |
| correct | agreement, prepositions (*consistir en*), confusable words (*infligir / infringir*), accents |
| punctuate | commas around parentheticals, semicolons between long items, no comma between subject and verb |
| register | the reader's register throughout; no word from the wrong register |
| post-edit a machine translation | calques, false friends, word order, *usted / tú* consistency, terms checked |

## Writing about data

| Purpose | Phrases |
|---|---|
| describing | *la cifra se duplicó; pasó del 12 % al 19 %; tres de cada diez* |
| comparing | *muy por encima de la media; la mediana es más baja que la media, lo que indica…* |
| interpreting | *esto se explica en parte por…; cabe atribuirlo a…* |
| caveats | *los datos no permiten afirmar que…; se trata de una proyección, no de un pronóstico* |
| projecting | *de mantenerse la tendencia, …; las proyecciones apuntan a que…* |

## Presenting several texts orally

Open with the topic and the materials (*Los textos que he elegido abordan…*); present each with
its angle; compare them; give your opinion with reasons; close with a summary or a question.
Signpost: *en primer lugar…, por otra parte…, en cuanto al gráfico…, para concluir…*.

## The DELE C2 at a glance (since May 2024)

| Test | Time | Tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Language use, reading and listening comprehension | 105 min | reading and listening tasks, 52 items (seven tasks, as preparation sites describe them) |
| 2. Written expression, mediation and interaction | 150 min | three texts: from several sources (400–450 words), from notes (200–250), from data (200–250), as in the sample exam the Instituto Cervantes published |
| 3. Oral expression, mediation and interaction | 20 min, plus 30 min to prepare | presentation from several texts (5–6 min), interview (5–6 min), conversation and negotiation on a headline |

Each test is worth a third of the 100 points. The pass rule, the scoring scales and dates are in
the Instituto Cervantes' official guide and on its exam site: check them there, because they
change.

references.title: Precision and register at C2: near-synonyms, confusables and learned words
references.body:
## Choosing among near-synonyms

Near-synonyms differ in connotation, register, collocation, region and intensity. Test a word by
putting it in the sentence: does it change what we learn about the speaker or the thing?

| Field | Neutral | More precise (and what it adds) |
|---|---|---|
| saying | *decir, afirmar, comentar* | *aducir* (offers a reason: *adujo falta de tiempo*), *esgrimir* (wields an argument), *argüir* (contends, formal), *apostillar* (adds a pointed remark), *espetar* (blurts out, rudely) |
| manner of speaking | *murmurar, hablar bajo* | *mascullar* (between the teeth, annoyed), *balbucear* (stammering, unsure), *farfullar* (fast and unclear), *refunfuñar* (grumbling) |
| thin | *delgado* (neutral) | *esbelto* (elegant, positive), *flaco* (plain, often informal), *escuálido* (unhealthily thin, negative) |
| stubborn | *terco* (negative) | *tenaz* (positive: keeps going), *perseverante* (positive, effort over time) |
| taste | *sabroso, fuerte* | *afrutado, ahumado, terroso, astringente, aterciopelado, untuoso* |

*Peyorativo* marks a word that judges negatively: *un politicastro* is a pejorative *político*.

## Register markers

| Register | Typical markers | Example (one event) |
|---|---|---|
| administrative / legal | impersonal and passive forms, nouns for actions, set formulas | *Se levantó el acta correspondiente al siniestro.* — The official record of the incident was drawn up. |
| press | the narrative imperfect, attribution, nominal headlines | *Un choque en Insurgentes provocaba ayer largas filas.* — A crash on Insurgentes caused long lines yesterday. |
| neutral | full sentences, plain words | *Ayer chocaron dos carros en Insurgentes.* — Two cars crashed on Insurgentes yesterday. |
| colloquial | ellipsis, fillers, intensifiers | *¿Supiste? Chocaron dos carros en Insurgentes, bien feo.* — Did you hear? Two cars crashed on Insurgentes, really bad. |

A deliberate shift (an official word in a chat, a slang word in a formal text) creates humor or
irony: *incongruencia* used on purpose. Used by accident, it reads as a slip.

## Confusable pairs (paronyms)

| Word | Means | Not to be confused with |
|---|---|---|
| *infligir* | to inflict (*infligir un daño*) | *infringir*, to break (*infringir una norma*) |
| *absolver* | to acquit, to absolve | *absorber*, to absorb |
| *proveer* | to supply | *prever*, to foresee |
| *el perjuicio* | harm, detriment | *el prejuicio*, prejudice |
| *expiar* | to atone for | *espiar*, to spy |
| *la actitud* | attitude | *la aptitud*, aptitude |

**Senses where careful writing and frequent use differ** (check the DLE and the DPD for each
before you mark anything wrong):

| Word | Careful-writing sense | Frequent extension |
|---|---|---|
| *adolecer de* | to suffer from a defect: *El informe adolece de imprecisiones.* | used for "to lack" (*adolece de recursos*) |
| *detentar* | to hold unlawfully | used for *ostentar* (to hold a title lawfully) |
| *sendos* | one each: *Llegaron con sendos regalos* (each with one gift) | used for "both" or "big" |
| *álgido* | very cold; critical, culminating | the culminating sense is now common |
| *lívido* | bruised; very pale | — |
| *bizarro* | gallant, brave | "bizarre", from English |

## Learned words and Latin phrases

Spanish often has two words from one Latin root: an **inherited** word that changed in speech and
a **learned** word borrowed later from writing (*llamar / clamar*, *entero / íntegro*, *estrecho /
estricto*). Learned words keep Latin or Greek spellings and stress (*el espécimen, la metástasis*)
and fill formal and scientific registers.

| Phrase | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *a priori* | beforehand, before evidence | *Rechazó la idea a priori.* |
| *de facto* | in fact (whatever the law says) | *un monopolio de facto* |
| *grosso modo* | roughly | not *a grosso modo* |
| *in situ* | on site | *Lo examinaron in situ.* |
| *motu proprio* | of one's own accord | not *de motu propio* |
| *sui generis* | one of a kind | *un estilo sui generis* |
| *el statu quo* | the status quo | not *el status quo* |
| *per capita* | per person | the DPD (2005) wrote *per cápita*; follow the RAE's current form |
| *sine qua non* | indispensable | *condición sine qua non* |

In print, Latin phrases are usually set in italics, like other unadapted foreign expressions.

references.title: Specialized Spanish: law, medicine, finance and technology
references.body:
## What specialized texts share

| Feature | Example | Why |
|---|---|---|
| impersonal and passive forms | *Se concede el amparo. Se observa edema.* | the institution, not a person, speaks |
| nouns for actions | *la interposición del recurso, la administración del fármaco* | compact, formal |
| long periods with relatives | *…, en virtud del cual…, mismo que…* | many conditions in one sentence |
| fixed formulas | *por lo expuesto y fundado; caracterizado porque* | genre conventions |
| terms of Greek or Latin origin | *etiología, comorbilidad, usufructo* | precision across languages |
| hedged statements | *compatible con, se prevé que, podría* | claims limited to the evidence |

*Mismo que* as a relative (*el documento, mismo que se anexa*) is frequent in Mexican
administrative writing; style guides advise against it (check the DPD before saying more).

## Law (Mexico)

| Part of a ruling | What it contains |
|---|---|
| heading and *resultandos* | who the parties are and what happened in the case |
| *considerandos* | the court's reasoning, with the legal grounds |
| *puntos resolutivos* | the decision: *PRIMERO. Se concede el amparo…* |

Formulas: *el suscrito* (the undersigned), *en lo sucesivo* (hereinafter), *en términos de* (under),
*por lo expuesto y fundado* (for the reasons and on the grounds stated), *se resuelve* (it is
resolved). In older statutes, the future subjunctive: *el que causare…* (whoever causes…). Check the
current terms of the Ley de Amparo before naming the parties.

## Medicine

| Section of a clinical record | Typical language |
|---|---|
| *anamnesis* (history) | *Paciente femenina de 58 años que acude por dolor torácico. Refiere… Niega…* |
| *exploración física* | *TA 150/95 mmHg. Ruidos cardiacos rítmicos.* |
| *cuadro clínico, diagnóstico diferencial* | *Cuadro compatible con…; a descartar…* |
| *nota de evolución, epicrisis* | *Evoluciona favorablemente. Se da de alta.* |

Roots: *-itis* (inflammation), *-algia* (pain), *-emia* (in the blood), *hiper- / hipo-* (above /
below normal), *-ectomía* (removal). To the patient: *usted*, plain words, one idea per sentence,
and a check that the person understood.

## Finance and central banks

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *la Junta de Gobierno decidió por unanimidad mantener…* | the board decided unanimously to hold… |
| *incrementar (reducir) en 25 puntos base* | raise (cut) by a quarter of a percentage point |
| *el balance de riesgos se mantiene sesgado al alza* | risks remain tilted upward |
| *en caso de materializarse* | should it materialize |
| *el activo / el pasivo / el patrimonio* | assets / liabilities / equity |
| *la liquidez / la solvencia* | short-term / long-term ability to pay |

Report a statement with its hedges: *prevé* stays *prevé*, not *asegura*.

## Patents and technical reports

| Part | Language |
|---|---|
| title and abstract | *Válvula ahorradora de agua para grifería doméstica* |
| prior art | *En el estado de la técnica se conocen dispositivos que…* |
| claims | one sentence each: *1. Una válvula que comprende un cuerpo…, caracterizada porque…* |
| dependent claims | *2. La válvula de la reivindicación 1, en donde…* |
| technical report | passive and impersonal forms, units and tolerances: *Se midió un caudal de 6 L/min ± 0.2.* |

The RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) accepts both the decimal point and the decimal comma: Mexico uses
the point (*0.2*), Spain the comma (*0,2*). Follow the convention of the text you are writing.

references.title: Style: figures of speech, narrative technique, reviews and reading between the lines
references.body:
## Figures of speech

All examples are original.

| Figure | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| hyperbole (*la hipérbole*) | exaggerates | *Te lo he dicho mil veces.* — I've told you a thousand times. |
| anaphora (*la anáfora*) | repeats the start of phrases | *Por los que leen, por los que escriben, por los que esperan.* |
| antithesis (*la antítesis*) | sets opposites side by side | *Tan cerca del éxito, tan lejos de la calma.* |
| rhetorical question | asks without wanting an answer | *¿Quién no ha dudado alguna vez?* |
| metonymy (*la metonimia*) | names a thing by something near it | *Leí a Galdós* (his books). *La Corona decidió* (the monarchy). |
| synecdoche (*la sinécdoque*) | a part for the whole, or the whole for a part | *Hay cuatro bocas que alimentar.* — There are four mouths to feed. |
| oxymoron (*el oxímoron*) | joins contradictory words | *un silencio ensordecedor* — a deafening silence |
| paradox (*la paradoja*) | an apparent contradiction with a truth inside | *Cuanto más sé, menos sé.* |
| chiasmus (*el quiasmo*) | reverses the order in the second half | *Vivir para escribir, escribir para vivir.* |
| zeugma (*el zeugma*) | one word serves several phrases | *Perdió la cartera y la paciencia.* — He lost his wallet and his patience. |
| polysyndeton (*el polisíndeton*) | repeats the conjunction | *y llovía, y llovía, y nadie se movía* |
| asyndeton (*el asíndeton*) | drops the conjunctions | *Llegó, miró, se fue.* |
| hyperbaton (*el hipérbaton*) | inverts the normal order | *De la ciudad las luces se apagaban.* |
| gradation (*la gradación*) | builds step by step | *Lo pensó, lo dijo, lo gritó.* |
| alliteration (*la aliteración*) | repeats sounds | *el susurro suave del sereno* |
| prosopopoeia (*la prosopopeya*) | gives human traits to things | *La ciudad despierta y bosteza.* |
| apostrophe (*el apóstrofe*) | addresses someone absent or something | *¡Oh, maestros que ya no están!* |

A speech opens with an *exordio* (it wins the audience) and closes with a *peroración* (it moves
and sums up). One or two figures per paragraph carry weight; a figure in every sentence reads
as *ampuloso*.

## Narrative technique

| Term | Spanish | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| omniscient narrator | *el narrador omnisciente* | knows every mind and moves freely in time |
| witness narrator | *el narrador testigo* | first person, beside the main character |
| focalization | *la focalización* | whose eyes the scene is seen through |
| free indirect style | *el estilo indirecto libre* | a character's thoughts in the narrator's voice, often in the imperfect and conditional, with no *pensó que*: *Mañana hablaría con él. ¿Y si no la escuchaba?* |
| interior monologue | *el monólogo interior* | a character's thoughts directly, in the present, often without full syntax |
| analepsis / prolepsis | *la analepsis, la prolepsis* | a jump back (flashback) / forward (flash-forward) |
| *in medias res* | *in medias res* | the story starts in the middle of the action |
| frame story | *el relato marco* | a story that contains another story |
| metafiction | *la metaficción* | a text that talks about its own writing |
| intertextuality | *la intertextualidad* | a text that echoes another |
| polyphony | *la polifonía* | many voices, none dominant |

## The review and the textual commentary

A review: what the work is (genre, author, context) → what it attempts → how well it does it, with
evidence → comparison → verdict for the reader.

| Praise | Mixed | Criticism |
|---|---|---|
| *magistral, logrado, encomiable, loable, una prosa depurada, pulcro, sobrio* | *desigual, con altibajos, irregular* | *fallido, manido, trillado, efectista, recargado, ampuloso, soporífero, anodino* |

Adjective position: an epithet before the noun stresses a quality already expected (*la blanca
nieve*); some adjectives change meaning with position: *un pobre hombre* (pitiable) / *un hombre
pobre* (poor); *un gran escritor* (great) / *un escritor grande* (big); *cierto rumor* (a certain
rumor) / *un rumor cierto* (a true rumor).

A textual commentary (*comentario de texto*): topic → structure (parts and how they connect) →
form (register, syntax, figures, vocabulary) → assessment (what the form does for the content).

## Reading between the lines

| Ask | Look for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Who acts? | agentless passives, nominalizations | *Se tomó la decisión de ajustar las tarifas.* (who decided?) |
| What is assumed? | presuppositions | *Seguiremos mejorando el servicio* (assumes it has improved) |
| What is implied? | implicatures | *Algunos funcionarios cumplieron* (implies others didn't) |
| How is it framed? | word choice | *ajuste* vs *aumento*; *reordenamiento* vs *recorte* |
| How precise is it? | vague quantifiers | *hasta un 30 %* (perhaps much less) |

A neutral rewrite names the agent, states the figure exactly and removes loaded words.

references.title: Relatives, long sentences, prepositional phrases and agreement
references.body:
## Relatives in formal writing

| Relative | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *que* | the default, without a preposition | *El acuífero que abastece a la ciudad se agota.* — The aquifer that supplies the city is running out. |
| *el que, la que* | after a preposition | *el pozo del que sacan agua* — the well they draw water from |
| *el cual, la cual* | after a preposition, especially a long one, or far from the antecedent | *la norma conforme a la cual se otorgan los permisos* — the rule under which permits are granted |
| *quien, quienes* | people, after a preposition or in a nonrestrictive clause | *los vecinos, quienes presentaron la queja,* — the residents, who filed the complaint, |
| *lo que, lo cual* | a whole clause | *El suelo cede, lo cual agrieta los muros.* — The ground gives way, which cracks the walls. |
| *cuyo, cuya* | possession, agreeing with the thing possessed | *una colonia cuyas calles se hunden* — a neighborhood whose streets are sinking |
| *donde, en el que, en que* | place (*donde* also loosely for "in which") | *la zona donde (en la que) se bombea más* — the area where most is pumped |

*Que su* for *cuyo* (*una colonia que sus calles se hunden*) is frequent in speech and avoided in
careful writing.

**Restrictive or nonrestrictive?** The commas change the meaning:
- *Los vecinos que protestaron recibieron respuesta.* — Only the residents who protested got an
  answer.
- *Los vecinos, que protestaron, recibieron respuesta.* — The residents (all of them) protested
  and got an answer.

## The long sentence (the period)

1. Find the main clause: subject, verb, object.
2. Bracket each parenthetical (*el inciso*): between commas, dashes or parentheses.
3. Link each relative to its antecedent; prefer *el cual* when the antecedent is far away.
4. Split the sentence when a reader must hold more than one open clause, or when two
   parentheticals sit side by side.

A semicolon separates parts that already contain commas: *El primer pozo, perforado en 1950,
se secó; el segundo, más profundo, todavía funciona.* — The first well, drilled in 1950, dried
up; the second, deeper one still works.

## Formal prepositional phrases

| Phrase | Plain equivalent | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *merced a* | *gracias a* | *merced a la ayuda recibida* |
| *a tenor de* | *según, de acuerdo con* | *a tenor de lo dispuesto en el reglamento* |
| *de cara a* | *pensando en* | *de cara a la próxima temporada* |
| *en pos de* | *en busca de, detrás de* | *en pos de un clima templado* |
| *en virtud de* | *por, debido a* | *en virtud del acuerdo firmado* |
| *a efectos de* | *para* | *a efectos de este informe* |
| *en detrimento de* | *perjudicando a* | *en detrimento del bosque* |
| *a expensas de* | *a costa de* | *a expensas de los vecinos* |
| *en lo tocante a* | *en cuanto a* | *en lo tocante a la tala* |
| *a instancias de* | *a petición de* | *a instancias de la comunidad* |
| *al amparo de* | *protegido por* | *al amparo de la ley* |
| *a la zaga (de)* | *detrás (de)* | *ir a la zaga de otros países* |
| *so pretexto de* | *con la excusa de* | *so pretexto de limpiar el terreno* |
| *en vísperas de* | *justo antes de* | *en vísperas de la migración* |
| *a la luz de* | *considerando* | *a la luz de los nuevos datos* |
| *a falta de* | *sin* | *a falta de datos fiables* |
| *sin perjuicio de* | *sin afectar* | *sin perjuicio de otras sanciones* |

**Contested phrases.** *En base a* is very frequent, in Mexico too, but norm guides prefer *con
base en* or *sobre la base de*; *a nivel de* is best kept for real levels (*a nivel del mar*);
*desde el punto de vista* is the usual form (not *bajo el punto de vista*). Check the DPD's
current entries before marking any of these wrong.

**Government** (the preposition a verb takes): *consistir en, incidir en, redundar en* (*redunda
en beneficio de todos*), *abogar por, propender a*.

## Hard cases of agreement

| Case | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *la mayoría de* + plural noun | *La mayoría de los vecinos votó / votaron.* | both occur |
| *ser* with a plural predicate | *Lo que necesito son vacaciones.* | the verb agrees with the plural |
| *uno de los que* | *Es uno de los que más sabe / saben.* | both occur |
| passive *se* | *Se venden casas.* | *se vende casas* is nonstandard |
| ambiguous nouns | *el mar / la mar; el azúcar / la azúcar* | both genders, with differences of use |
| epicene nouns | *la persona, la víctima, el bebé* | one gender for both sexes |

references.title: Tenses as style, conditions without si, and older forms
references.body:
## Tenses used for an effect

| Use | Form | Example | Production? |
|---|---|---|---|
| historical present | present for past events | *En 1539 llega a la ciudad la primera imprenta.* — In 1539 the first printing press arrives in the city. | yes |
| narrative imperfect | imperfect for a single, completed past event, often with a time phrase | *Dos horas después, la policía detenía al sospechoso.* — Two hours later the police arrested the suspect. | allowed in narrative writing; never required |
| oneiric and playful imperfect | imperfect for a dream or a game | *Yo era el detective y tú eras el ladrón.* — I'd be the detective and you'd be the thief. | recognition |
| future of conjecture | future (simple or perfect) for a guess about the present or the past | *Serán las diez. Habrá salido ya.* — It must be ten. She must have left already. | yes |
| conditional of conjecture | conditional (simple or perfect) for a guess about the past | *Tendría veinte años. Habría sido el chofer.* — He must have been twenty. It must have been the driver. | yes |
| concessive future | future to grant a point before *pero* | *Será muy listo, pero no sabe escuchar.* — He may be very smart, but he can't listen. | yes |
| future of command | future for a solemn order | *No matarás.* — Thou shalt not kill. | recognition |
| conditional of rumor | conditional for an unconfirmed report | *El sospechoso habría huido a otro estado.* — The suspect has reportedly fled to another state. | recognition; many style guides advise against it in news |
| pretérito anterior | *hube* + participle after *apenas, en cuanto, cuando* | *Apenas hubo terminado, se fue.* — No sooner had he finished than he left. | recognition (literary) |
| literary *-ra* | *-ra* for a past (often pluperfect) | *el que fuera presidente* — the man who was (had been) president | recognition; accepted |

## Conditions without *si*

| Structure | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *de* + infinitive | *De seguir así, no llegamos.* — If we go on like this, we won't make it. | present or future condition |
| *de* + compound infinitive | *De haberlo sabido, te habría llamado.* — Had I known, I'd have called you. | past, contrary to fact |
| *de* + infinitive + subject | *De haber ganado ellos, todo sería distinto.* — Had they won, everything would be different. | subject after the infinitive |
| gerund | *Saliendo ahora, llegamos a tiempo.* — If we leave now, we'll be on time. | the context gives the condition |
| participle | *Bien mirado, no es tan grave.* — Looked at closely, it isn't so serious. | set phrases above all |
| *con* + infinitive | *Con avisar bastaba.* — Letting us know would have been enough. | "just by…" |
| *a poco que* + subjunctive | *A poco que estudies, apruebas.* — If you study even a little, you'll pass. | |
| *de no ser por* | *De no ser por ella, nos habríamos perdido.* — If it weren't for her, we'd have got lost. | + noun or *que* + subjunctive |
| *como* + subjunctive | *Como no llegues a las ocho, nos vamos.* — If you're not here by eight, we're leaving. | a warning or threat, usually |

Earlier connectors still work: *a menos que, salvo que, siempre y cuando, en el supuesto de que,
con tal de que, en caso de que* (+ subjunctive).

**In the result of a past condition** both *habría* and *hubiera* are standard: *Si lo hubiera
sabido, habría (hubiera) venido.* *Hubiese* also occurs; it is accepted, never required.

**Mixed times:** *Si no hubiera llegado la imprenta, hoy leeríamos menos.* — If the printing press
hadn't arrived, we would read less today (past condition, present result).

**Future subjunctive** (recognition, except two fixed phrases): *sea como fuere* (be that as it
may), *sea cual fuere el resultado* (whatever the result may be). In old laws: *el que causare un
daño…* (whoever causes damage…).

## Older forms you will read (recognition)

| Form | Old text | Modern Spanish |
|---|---|---|
| *f-* for later *h-* | *fazer, fijo* | *hacer, hijo* |
| *ç, ss, x* | *plaça, passar, dixo* | *plaza, pasar, dijo* |
| second person plural in *-ades, -edes* | *cantades* | *cantáis* |
| *vos* as a polite singular | *vos sois* | *usted es* |
| future subjunctive | *si vinieres* | *si vienes* |
| *maguer* | *maguer que* | *aunque* |
| *asaz* | *asaz difícil* | *muy difícil* |

The old examples above are invented illustrations of the spellings, not quotations.

references.title: Spanish across the world: norms, grammar and words by region
references.body:
## One language, several standards

Spanish is **pluricentric**: each country has an educated norm (*norma culta*), and the
academies of the Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española (ASALE) describe them together.
A word can be general, or marked for a country or region (*Méx., Esp., Am., Ant.*) in the DLE.
For readers in several countries, prefer general words and explain a local one once.

| Mexico | Spain | Often understood everywhere |
|---|---|---|
| *el carro* | *el coche* | *el auto, el automóvil* |
| *la computadora* | *el ordenador* | *la computadora* is the wider choice in the Americas |
| *el celular* | *el móvil* | *el teléfono* |
| *el departamento* | *el piso* | *el apartamento* |
| *ustedes* (all registers) | *vosotros* (familiar), *ustedes* (formal) | *ustedes* |

## Grammar features you will read and hear (recognition)

| Feature | Where (simplified) | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *vosotros* and its verb forms | Spain (most of it) | *¿Vosotros venís mañana?* — Are you all coming tomorrow? |
| leísmo of person | much of Spain; parts of the Americas | *A Juan le vi ayer.* (Mexico: *lo vi*) |
| laísmo, loísmo | parts of central Spain | *La dije que viniera* (for *le dije*): not standard |
| perfect for today's events | most of Spain | *Esta mañana he salido temprano.* (Mexico: *salí*) |
| *a por* | Spain | *Voy a por pan.* — I'm going to get bread. (Mexico: *voy por pan*) |
| non-inverted questions with a pronoun | the Caribbean | *¿Qué tú quieres?* (*¿Qué quieres tú?*) |
| infinitive with a subject | the Caribbean and elsewhere, informal | *para yo entenderlo* (*para que yo lo entienda*) |
| *más nada, más nunca* | the Caribbean, Venezuela, the Canary Islands | *No dijo más nada.* (*nada más*) |
| *dice* as "they say, reportedly" | the Andes | *Mañana llueve, dice.* |
| double possessive | the Andes | *su casa de Juan* (*la casa de Juan*) |
| voseo | Río de la Plata, Central America, other areas | *vos tenés, vos sabés* |
| verbal voseo with *tú* | Chile, informal | *¿Tú estái cansado?* |
| *ustedeo* (usted with intimates) | parts of Colombia, Costa Rica and elsewhere | *Mi amor, ¿usted ya comió?* |

Describe these as features of a place and a register, never as errors, except where the norm
says otherwise (laísmo and loísmo are not accepted; the RAE accepts *le* for a masculine singular
person as a direct object). For Mexican and international writing, use *lo / la*, *ustedes* and
the standard question order.

## Words by region (recognition)

| Spain | Chile | Río de la Plata | Venezuela and the Caribbean | the Andes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *currar, el curro* (work) | *al tiro* (right away) | *el bondi* (bus) | *el chamo* (kid) | *la chompa* (sweater) |
| *flipar* (be amazed) | *cachar* (get it) | B1's *el laburo* (job) | *el pana* (buddy) | *el choclo* (corn) |
| *molar* (be cool) | *fome* (boring) | B2's *che* (hey) | *la vaina* (thing) | |
| *el chaval* (kid) | *pololear* (go steady) | | | |
| *majo* (nice) | | | | |

## Contact and change

- **Substrate:** words and features from languages spoken before Spanish (Nahuatl in Mexico,
  Quechua in the Andes, Guarani in Paraguay).
- **Code-switching:** moving between Spanish and English in one conversation, common among
  bilinguals in the United States; it follows patterns and is not a sign of weak Spanish.
- **Calques:** *llamar para atrás* (to call back), *aplicar para un trabajo* (to apply for a job).
- **Change in progress:** new words (*tuitear*), new plurals for loanwords (*másteres* and
  *másters*, both accepted in the DPD's second edition, as reported in 2024), and debated uses
  (inclusive language: the RAE keeps the generic masculine in its own guidance; many public
  bodies recommend doubling or neutral wording). Describe positions with their dates; don't
  judge them.

language.name: Spanish
language.vocabSource: Estimate including Spanish A1 to C1's 4,092 words, core and honors, plus this course's 622 core words (no official DELE C2 word list; CEFR vocabulary-size research gives about 4,500-5,000 words at C2, measured for English learners within the 5,000 most frequent words, so the test can't show more); see RESEARCH.md

vocab.example: El Día de Muertos es el 1 y el 2 de noviembre.
vocab.exampleEn: The Day of the Dead is on 1 and 2 November.
vocab.note: Mexico usually says Día de Muertos; Día de los Muertos is common elsewhere.

vocab.example: Todos los años ponemos una ofrenda en la sala.
vocab.exampleEn: Every year we set up an ofrenda in the living room.

vocab.example: Hay dos velas en la ofrenda.
vocab.exampleEn: There are two candles on the ofrenda.

vocab.example: Compramos flores en el mercado.
vocab.exampleEn: We bought flowers at the market.

vocab.example: Las flores de cempasúchil son de color naranja.
vocab.exampleEn: Mexican marigolds are orange.
vocab.note: Often in the phrase la flor de cempasúchil. From Nahuatl.

vocab.example: Mi hermano escribe su nombre en una calavera de azúcar.
vocab.exampleEn: My brother writes his name on a sugar skull.
vocab.note: una calavera de azúcar = a sugar skull

vocab.example: Mañana vamos a comprar pan de muerto.
vocab.exampleEn: Tomorrow we're going to buy Day of the Dead bread.

vocab.example: El papel picado tiene muchos colores.
vocab.exampleEn: The papel picado is in lots of colours.

vocab.example: Las posadas son del 16 al 24 de diciembre.
vocab.exampleEn: The posadas are from 16 to 24 December.
vocab.note: pedir posada = to ask for a place to stay

vocab.example: ¡Feliz Navidad!
vocab.exampleEn: Merry Christmas!

vocab.example: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo!
vocab.exampleEn: Happy New Year!

vocab.example: En Semana Santa mucha gente viaja a la playa.
vocab.exampleEn: At Easter lots of people travel to the beach.

vocab.example: El 16 de septiembre es día festivo en México.
vocab.exampleEn: 16 September is a public holiday in Mexico.

vocab.example: ¿Cómo celebran la Navidad en tu país?
vocab.exampleEn: How do people celebrate Christmas in your country?

forms.present: recuerdo, recuerdas, recuerda, recordamos, recordáis, recuerdan
forms.subjunctive: recuerde, recuerdes, recuerde, recordemos, recordéis, recuerden

vocab.example: Recuerdo mucho a mi abuelo.
vocab.exampleEn: I often think of my grandfather.
vocab.note: o → ue: recuerdo, recordamos.

forms.present: muero, mueres, muere, morimos, morís, mueren
forms.preterite: morí, moriste, murió, morimos, moristeis, murieron
forms.subjunctive: muera, mueras, muera, muramos, muráis, mueran

vocab.example: Mi abuelo murió el año pasado.
vocab.exampleEn: My grandfather died last year.
vocab.note: o → ue in the present, o → u in the preterite (murió). Participle: muerto.

vocab.example: Emma escribe en su diario todas las noches.
vocab.exampleEn: Emma writes in her diary every night.

vocab.example: Coyoacán es un barrio muy bonito.
vocab.exampleEn: Coyoacán is a very pretty neighbourhood.

vocab.example: En el zócalo de mi pueblo hay una iglesia.
vocab.exampleEn: There's a church on the main square of my town.
vocab.note: el Zócalo, with a capital, is Mexico City's main square (Plaza de la Constitución).

vocab.example: La catedral está en el lado norte del Zócalo.
vocab.exampleEn: The cathedral is on the north side of the Zócalo.

vocab.example: En el palacio hay murales de Diego Rivera.
vocab.exampleEn: In the palace there are murals by Diego Rivera.

vocab.example: El castillo está en un cerro.
vocab.exampleEn: The castle is on a hill.

vocab.example: El Bosque de Chapultepec es un parque enorme.
vocab.exampleEn: Chapultepec Park (the Bosque de Chapultepec) is a huge park.

vocab.example: Los murales cuentan la historia de México.
vocab.exampleEn: The murals tell the history of Mexico.

vocab.example: Estamos en el siglo XXI.
vocab.exampleEn: We're in the twenty-first century.
vocab.note: Written with Roman numerals, read as numbers: el siglo XXI = el siglo veintiuno.

vocab.example: Soy estudiante de intercambio en México.
vocab.exampleEn: I'm an exchange student in Mexico.

vocab.example: El Templo Mayor es una pirámide antigua.
vocab.exampleEn: The Templo Mayor is an ancient pyramid.
vocab.note: After the noun: ancient, very old. Before the noun: former (mi antiguo jefe = my former boss).

vocab.example: ¡El Zócalo es enorme!
vocab.exampleEn: The Zócalo is huge!

vocab.example: ¿Dónde queda el museo? — Queda cerca del parque.
vocab.exampleEn: Where's the museum? — It's near the park.
vocab.note: For places that don't move. Not quedarse (to stay).

forms.present: recomiendo, recomiendas, recomienda, recomendamos, recomendáis, recomiendan
forms.subjunctive: recomiende, recomiendes, recomiende, recomendemos, recomendéis, recomienden

vocab.example: Te recomiendo el Museo de Antropología.
vocab.exampleEn: I recommend the Museum of Anthropology (to you).
vocab.note: e → ie: recomiendo, recomendamos.

vocab.example: Mi abuela sabe muchas leyendas.
vocab.exampleEn: My grandmother knows lots of legends.

vocab.example: Popocatépetl era un guerrero valiente.
vocab.exampleEn: Popocatépetl was a brave warrior.
vocab.note: feminine: la guerrera

vocab.example: La princesa esperó muchos meses.
vocab.exampleEn: The princess waited many months.
vocab.note: prince: el príncipe

vocab.example: Los dioses mayas crean el mundo.
vocab.exampleEn: The Maya gods create the world.
vocab.note: feminine: la diosa. With a capital, Dios = God.

vocab.example: El rey tiene una hija.
vocab.exampleEn: The king has a daughter.
vocab.note: queen: la reina. los Reyes Magos = the Three Kings.

vocab.example: Popocatépetl ganó la guerra.
vocab.exampleEn: Popocatépetl won the war.

vocab.example: Su corazón estaba muy triste.
vocab.exampleEn: Her heart was very sad.

vocab.example: El colibrí es un pájaro muy pequeño.
vocab.exampleEn: The hummingbird is a very small bird.

vocab.example: Un colibrí vuela cerca de la ventana.
vocab.exampleEn: A hummingbird is flying near the window.
vocab.note: The plural colibrís is also correct.

vocab.example: La princesa también es muy valiente.
vocab.exampleEn: The princess is very brave too.

vocab.example: La princesa se enamoró de un guerrero.
vocab.exampleEn: The princess fell in love with a warrior.
vocab.note: enamorarse de alguien (of, with: de, not con). estar enamorado = to be in love.

vocab.example: ¡Eso es mentira!
vocab.exampleEn: That's a lie!

forms.present: vuelo, vuelas, vuela, volamos, voláis, vuelan
forms.subjunctive: vuele, vueles, vuele, volemos, voléis, vuelen

vocab.example: Los colibríes vuelan muy rápido.
vocab.exampleEn: Hummingbirds fly very fast.
vocab.note: o → ue: vuela, volamos.

vocab.example: Los dos volcanes van a estar juntos para siempre.
vocab.exampleEn: The two volcanoes are going to be together forever.

vocab.example: Había una vez un rey y una princesa.
vocab.exampleEn: Once upon a time there was a king and a princess.

vocab.example: En mi ciudad hay muchos letreros bilingües.
vocab.exampleEn: In my city there are lots of bilingual signs.

vocab.example: El letrero dice "Salida".
vocab.exampleEn: The sign says "Exit".
vocab.note: Spain usually says el cartel.

vocab.example: Prohibido fumar.
vocab.exampleEn: No smoking.

vocab.example: ¡Peligro! No pasar.
vocab.exampleEn: Danger! Keep out.

vocab.example: Hay un estacionamiento enfrente del parque.
vocab.exampleEn: There's a parking lot opposite the park.
vocab.note: Spain: el aparcamiento.

vocab.example: Empuje la puerta, por favor.
vocab.exampleEn: Push the door, please.

vocab.example: Para salir, jale la puerta.
vocab.exampleEn: To get out, pull the door.
vocab.note: Mexico and much of Latin America; Spain says tirar (Tire = Pull).

vocab.example: Mi hermana está embarazada.
vocab.exampleEn: My sister is pregnant.
vocab.note: False friend: NOT embarrassed (that is avergonzado, or in Mexico me da pena).

vocab.example: La fiesta fue un éxito.
vocab.exampleEn: The party was a success.
vocab.note: False friend: an exit is la salida.

vocab.example: Olvidé mi carpeta en la escuela.
vocab.exampleEn: I forgot my folder at school.
vocab.note: False friend: a carpet is la alfombra.

vocab.example: Compré una novela en la librería.
vocab.exampleEn: I bought a novel at the bookshop.
vocab.note: False friend: a library is la biblioteca.

vocab.example: Estudio en la biblioteca de la universidad.
vocab.exampleEn: I study in the university library.

vocab.example: ¿Cuál es tu dirección actual?
vocab.exampleEn: What's your current address?
vocab.note: False friend: "actual" (real) is real or verdadero; "actually" is en realidad.

forms.preterite: realicé, realizaste, realizó, realizamos, realizasteis, realizaron

vocab.example: La escuela realiza un examen cada mes.
vocab.exampleEn: The school holds an exam every month.
vocab.note: False friend: to realize is darse cuenta. z → c before e: realicé, realice.

vocab.example: Me di cuenta de mi error.
vocab.exampleEn: I realized my mistake.
vocab.note: darse cuenta de algo; dar is irregular: me doy cuenta, me di cuenta.

vocab.example: ¡Hola, Daniel!
vocab.exampleEn: Hi, Daniel!

vocab.example: Adiós, gracias.
vocab.exampleEn: Goodbye, thank you.

vocab.example: Hasta luego, Ana.
vocab.exampleEn: See you later, Ana.

vocab.example: Buenas noches. ¡Hasta mañana!
vocab.exampleEn: Good night. See you tomorrow!

vocab.example: Buenos días, ¿puede repetir, por favor?
vocab.exampleEn: Good morning, can you repeat, please?

vocab.example: Buenas tardes. Disculpe…
vocab.exampleEn: Good afternoon. Excuse me…

meanings: good night (or good evening after dark)
vocab.example: Buenas noches y hasta mañana.
vocab.exampleEn: Good night and see you tomorrow.
vocab.note: Used to greet after dark and to say goodbye at night.

vocab.example: Sí, gracias.
vocab.exampleEn: Yes, thank you.
vocab.note: With an accent. Without it, si means 'if'.

vocab.example: No, gracias. No escribo mucho.
vocab.exampleEn: No, thank you. I don't write much.
vocab.note: Before a verb it means 'not': No hablo inglés.

vocab.example: Otra vez, por favor.
vocab.exampleEn: Again, please.

vocab.example: Gracias, señora.
vocab.exampleEn: Thank you, madam.

vocab.example: ¡Muchas gracias! – De nada.
vocab.exampleEn: Thank you very much! – You're welcome.

vocab.example: Gracias. – De nada.
vocab.exampleEn: Thanks. – You're welcome.

vocab.example: ¡Perdón! ¿Puede repetir?
vocab.exampleEn: Sorry! Can you repeat?

vocab.example: Disculpe, ¿cómo se escribe su nombre?
vocab.exampleEn: Excuse me, how is your name spelled?
vocab.note: Formal (usted). To a friend: disculpa.

meanings: excuse me (to get past or leave)
vocab.example: Con permiso, gracias.
vocab.exampleEn: Excuse me, thank you.

vocab.example: ¿Puede repetir, por favor? Más despacio.
vocab.exampleEn: Can you repeat, please? More slowly.

vocab.example: Más despacio, por favor.
vocab.exampleEn: More slowly, please.

vocab.example: Otra vez, por favor: ¿cómo se escribe?
vocab.exampleEn: Again, please: how is it spelled?

vocab.example: ¿Cómo se escribe tu apellido?
vocab.exampleEn: How is your surname spelled?

vocab.example: ¿Puede deletrear el apellido, por favor?
vocab.exampleEn: Can you spell the surname, please?

vocab.example: ¿Cómo se escribe? – Se escribe con hache.
vocab.exampleEn: How is it spelled? – It's spelled with an h.
vocab.note: Irregular participle: escrito.
