vocab.exampleEn: Judeo-Spanish keeps words that Spanish lost centuries ago.

vocab.note: Also an adjective. Many scholars keep ladino for the word-for-word translation language of Hebrew sacred texts; in Central America a ladino is a person of non-Indigenous culture.
vocab.example: En Israel muchos llaman ladino al judeoespañol.
vocab.exampleEn: In Israel many people call Judeo-Spanish Ladino.

vocab.note: Plural sefardíes (sefardís is also used); also a noun (los sefardíes). From Sefarad, the Hebrew name for the Iberian Peninsula.
vocab.example: Su familia es sefardí y llegó de Turquía.
vocab.exampleEn: Her family is Sephardic and came from Turkey.

vocab.example: La diáspora sefardí llegó al Imperio otomano y al norte de África.
vocab.exampleEn: The Sephardic diaspora reached the Ottoman Empire and North Africa.

vocab.example: La expulsión de 1492 separó a los sefardíes de la península.
vocab.exampleEn: The expulsion of 1492 separated the Sephardim from the peninsula.

vocab.example: La aljama tenía sus propias autoridades.
vocab.exampleEn: The aljama had its own authorities.

vocab.example: Paseamos por la antigua judería de Toledo.
vocab.exampleEn: We walked through the old Jewish quarter of Toledo.

vocab.note: la conversa
vocab.example: Muchos conversos vivieron bajo la sospecha de la Inquisición.
vocab.exampleEn: Many converts lived under the Inquisition's suspicion.

vocab.note: The Judeo-Spanish of northern Morocco, rich in Arabic words. Spellings vary (haquitía, jaquetía, haquetía); the DLE's form was not checked.
vocab.example: Su abuela de Tetuán hablaba haquitía.
vocab.exampleEn: Her grandmother from Tetuán spoke Haketia.

vocab.example: El edicto se firmó en Granada el 31 de marzo de 1492.
vocab.exampleEn: The edict was signed in Granada on March 31, 1492.

vocab.note: Also a noun (los ecuatoguineanos).
vocab.example: La literatura ecuatoguineana se escribe sobre todo en español.
vocab.exampleEn: Equatorial Guinean literature is written mostly in Spanish.

vocab.note: As an adjective, chabacano means tacky, vulgar; the creole's name is usually explained from that adjective.
vocab.example: En Zamboanga se habla chabacano.
vocab.exampleEn: Chavacano is spoken in Zamboanga.

vocab.example: El chabacano es una lengua criolla de base española.
vocab.exampleEn: Chavacano is a Spanish-based creole language.

vocab.example: En Guinea Ecuatorial el español funciona como lengua franca.
vocab.exampleEn: In Equatorial Guinea Spanish works as a lingua franca.

vocab.note: Same form for both genders.
vocab.example: El guaraní es cooficial con el español en Paraguay.
vocab.exampleEn: Guarani is co-official with Spanish in Paraguay.

vocab.example: El galeón de Manila llegaba a Acapulco cargado de seda.
vocab.exampleEn: The Manila galleon reached Acapulco loaded with silk.

vocab.note: The base of Filipino, one of the Philippines' official languages.
vocab.example: En tagalo, la palabra para cuchara viene del español.
vocab.exampleEn: In Tagalog, the word for spoon comes from Spanish.

vocab.note: The DLE's entry was not checked; the word is common in academic and press use.
vocab.example: La hispanofonía también incluye a Guinea Ecuatorial.
vocab.exampleEn: The Spanish-speaking world also includes Equatorial Guinea.

vocab.example: El archipiélago filipino tiene más de siete mil islas.
vocab.exampleEn: The Philippine archipelago has more than seven thousand islands.

vocab.note: C1's el vestigio (trace) is close.
vocab.example: En Manila queda un remanente de hablantes de español.
vocab.exampleEn: A remnant of Spanish speakers remains in Manila.

vocab.note: la masificación turística = tourist overcrowding, mass tourism.
vocab.example: La masificación turística preocupa a los vecinos del centro.
vocab.exampleEn: Tourist overcrowding worries the people who live downtown.

vocab.example: En Semana Santa, la saturación de las playas es evidente.
vocab.exampleEn: At Easter, the overcrowding of the beaches is obvious.

vocab.note: In ecology and tourism, how much use a place can bear without damage; for a vehicle or a structure, its load capacity.
vocab.example: Nadie ha calculado la capacidad de carga de esta bahía.
vocab.exampleEn: Nobody has calculated the carrying capacity of this bay.

vocab.note: Usual in Mexico (rentar, la renta); Spain usually says el alquiler vacacional.
vocab.example: Rentamos el departamento en una plataforma de renta vacacional.
vocab.exampleEn: We rented the apartment on a vacation-rental platform.

vocab.note: A floating brown seaweed that in recent years has reached the beaches of Mexico's Caribbean coast in large amounts.
vocab.example: Este año el sargazo llegó a las playas antes de lo previsto.
vocab.exampleEn: This year the sargassum reached the beaches earlier than expected.

vocab.note: Usual in Mexican news for the money an event or activity brings into a place (check the DEM). In Spain la derrama is more often a one-off levy shared among the owners of a building.
vocab.example: El festival dejó una derrama económica de varios millones de pesos.
vocab.exampleEn: The festival brought in several million pesos of spending.

vocab.example: Cancún es uno de los destinos turísticos más visitados del país.
vocab.exampleEn: Cancún is one of the most visited tourist destinations in the country.

vocab.example: La estacionalidad hace que muchos empleos duren solo unos meses.
vocab.exampleEn: Seasonality means that many jobs last only a few months.

vocab.example: Viajar en avión aumenta mucho la huella ecológica de unas vacaciones.
vocab.exampleEn: Flying greatly increases the ecological footprint of a vacation.

vocab.note: B1's discrepar (to disagree); its opposite is la convergencia.
vocab.example: La principal divergencia entre las fuentes está en las medidas.
vocab.exampleEn: The main divergence between the sources is in the measures.

forms.present: aúno, aúnas, aúna, aunamos, aunáis, aúnan
forms.subjunctive: aúne, aúnes, aúne, aunemos, aunéis, aúnen

vocab.note: A written accent on the ú where the stem is stressed: aúno, aúnas, aúna, aunamos, aúnan; subjunctive aúne; command aúna. aunar esfuerzos = to join forces.
vocab.example: Las dos asociaciones aunaron esfuerzos para limpiar la playa.
vocab.exampleEn: The two associations joined forces to clean the beach.

vocab.note: B1's contrastar (to check against other sources) is close; confrontar also means to confront or face someone.
vocab.example: Antes de escribir, confronté las dos versiones del informe.
vocab.exampleEn: Before writing, I compared the two versions of the report.

vocab.note: Also the musical term.
vocab.example: Su testimonio sirve de contrapunto a las cifras oficiales.
vocab.exampleEn: Her testimony serves as a counterpoint to the official figures.

vocab.note: Same form for both genders; plural coincidentes. B1's coincidir (to agree, to coincide).
vocab.example: Las dos encuestas dieron resultados coincidentes.
vocab.exampleEn: The two surveys gave matching results.

forms.present: contrapongo, contrapones, contrapone, contraponemos, contraponéis, contraponen
forms.preterite: contrapuse, contrapusiste, contrapuso, contrapusimos, contrapusisteis, contrapusieron
forms.subjunctive: contraponga, contrapongas, contraponga, contrapongamos, contrapongáis, contrapongan

vocab.note: Like poner: contrapongo, contrapuse, contrapondré, contrapuesto; command contrapón.
vocab.example: El autor contrapone el turismo de cruceros al de estancias largas.
vocab.exampleEn: The author sets cruise tourism against long-stay tourism.

vocab.example: Más de cien científicos firmaron la carta abierta.
vocab.exampleEn: More than a hundred scientists signed the open letter.

vocab.example: La ocupación hotelera bajó durante los meses de sargazo.
vocab.exampleEn: Hotel occupancy fell during the sargassum months.

vocab.note: A recent coinage for mass tourism's effect on a neighborhood's shops and social life; Fundéu BBVA called it a valid neologism (2018, updated 2023). Check the DLE for an entry.
vocab.example: Los vecinos denuncian la turistificación del barrio.
vocab.exampleEn: Residents are protesting against the touristification of the neighborhood.

vocab.example: La gentrificación turística ha expulsado a muchas familias del centro.
vocab.exampleEn: Tourist gentrification has pushed many families out of the center.

vocab.example: El ayuntamiento aprobó una moratoria de dos años para nuevos hoteles.
vocab.exampleEn: The town council approved a two-year moratorium on new hotels.

vocab.note: Usual in Mexico for planning what may be built where (check); Spain often says la ordenación del territorio.
vocab.example: Sin ordenamiento territorial, la costa se llena de construcciones.
vocab.exampleEn: Without land-use planning, the coast fills up with buildings.

vocab.note: Usual in Mexico (cambio de uso de suelo = rezoning; check); Spain usually says el uso del suelo.
vocab.example: La empresa pidió un cambio de uso de suelo para construir un hotel.
vocab.exampleEn: The company applied for rezoning to build a hotel.

vocab.note: A2's la costa is the everyday word; el litoral is more technical. Also an adjective: la zona litoral.
vocab.example: El litoral de Quintana Roo mide cientos de kilómetros.
vocab.exampleEn: Quintana Roo's coastline is hundreds of kilometers long.

vocab.note: Also a metal spring.
vocab.example: El crucero atracó en el muelle a las ocho de la mañana.
vocab.exampleEn: The cruise ship docked at the pier at eight in the morning.

vocab.example: El turismo de cruceros trae miles de visitantes en pocas horas.
vocab.exampleEn: Cruise tourism brings thousands of visitors in a few hours.

vocab.example: En temporada baja hay una sobreoferta de cuartos.
vocab.exampleEn: In the low season there is an oversupply of rooms.

vocab.note: In Mexican museums, the text panel or label for a room or an object (cédula temática, cédula de objeto; INAH's Gaceta de Museos writes of cédulas de objetos). B2's la cédula profesional is a professional license.
vocab.example: La cédula explica de dónde viene la pieza.
vocab.exampleEn: The label explains where the piece comes from.

vocab.example: La ficha técnica indica el material, la fecha y la procedencia.
vocab.exampleEn: The data sheet gives the material, the date and the provenance.

vocab.note: la museógrafa.
vocab.example: El museógrafo decidió el orden de las vitrinas.
vocab.exampleEn: The exhibition designer decided the order of the display cases.

vocab.example: La museografía de la sala guía al visitante sin que lo note.
vocab.exampleEn: The room's exhibition design guides visitors without their noticing.

vocab.note: Also a shop window; Mexico also says el aparador.
vocab.example: No toque la vitrina, por favor.
vocab.exampleEn: Please don't touch the display case.

vocab.example: Antes de entregar el texto, hay que pulirlo.
vocab.exampleEn: Before handing in the text, you have to polish it.

vocab.note: Of a text, to remove errors and padding; of water, to purify; of software, to debug.
vocab.example: Depuramos la lista antes de enviarla.
vocab.exampleEn: We cleaned up the list before sending it.

vocab.note: Both e's are written and pronounced: re-es-.
vocab.example: Reestructuré el informe para que la conclusión fuera al principio.
vocab.exampleEn: I restructured the report so that the conclusion came first.

vocab.example: Condensa los tres párrafos en uno solo.
vocab.exampleEn: Condense the three paragraphs into one.

vocab.note: la redactora. Writes the texts; B2's el editor edits or publishes them. In a newspaper, el redactor is a staff writer, and el redactor jefe the editor in chief.
vocab.example: La redactora escribió todas las cédulas de la exposición.
vocab.exampleEn: The copywriter (a woman) wrote all the labels for the exhibition.

vocab.example: La traducción automática confundió "case" con "caso".
vocab.exampleEn: The machine translation mistook "case" for "caso".

vocab.note: Correcting a machine translation. The RAE's guidance prefers pos- to post- except before s (DPD, pos-: check); la postedición is also used.
vocab.example: La posedición de este folleto llevó una tarde.
vocab.exampleEn: Post-editing this leaflet took an afternoon.

vocab.note: Same spelling question as la posedición: posteditar is also seen.
vocab.example: Hay que poseditar la traducción antes de publicarla.
vocab.exampleEn: The translation has to be post-edited before it is published.

vocab.example: Sus apuntes son demasiado esquemáticos para entenderlos sin ella.
vocab.exampleEn: Her notes are too sketchy to understand without her.

vocab.note: To make explicit what a text leaves implied; not A1's deletrear (to spell out letter by letter).
vocab.example: Conviene explicitar quién es el lector meta.
vocab.exampleEn: It's worth spelling out who the target reader is.

vocab.note: Also bloodletting, literal and figurative (una sangría económica), and the wine drink.
vocab.example: Cada párrafo empieza con una sangría.
vocab.exampleEn: Each paragraph begins with an indent.

vocab.example: La maquetación del catálogo está casi lista.
vocab.exampleEn: The catalog's layout is almost ready.

vocab.example: Maquetaron el folleto en dos días.
vocab.exampleEn: They laid out the leaflet in two days.

vocab.note: A2's el borrador is the everyday word for a draft.
vocab.example: Te mando la versión preliminar para que la revises.
vocab.exampleEn: I'm sending you the draft version for you to check.

vocab.note: Usually plural: los apuntes (class notes, jottings). Also a quick sketch.
vocab.example: Me prestó sus apuntes de la clase.
vocab.exampleEn: She lent me her notes from the class.

vocab.example: La sala de exposición abre a las diez.
vocab.exampleEn: The exhibition hall opens at ten.

vocab.note: Also ironic, for something hopelessly old: mi computadora es una pieza de museo.
vocab.example: Esta jícara es una pieza de museo del siglo XVIII.
vocab.exampleEn: This gourd cup is an eighteenth-century museum piece.

vocab.example: Las frases cortas mejoran la legibilidad de una cédula.
vocab.exampleEn: Short sentences make a label easier to read.

vocab.note: meta stays invariable: los lectores meta, el público meta.
vocab.example: Antes de escribir, define a tu lector meta.
vocab.exampleEn: Before you write, define your target reader.

vocab.example: El corrector automático no detecta las palabras mal usadas.
vocab.exampleEn: The spell-checker doesn't catch misused words.

vocab.example: La versión final se imprimirá en la sala.
vocab.exampleEn: The final version will be printed in the hall.

vocab.example: La pirámide de población de México se está estrechando en la base.
vocab.exampleEn: Mexico's population pyramid is narrowing at the base.

vocab.note: The period when the working-age population grows faster than the population that depends on it.
vocab.example: El bono demográfico no durará para siempre.
vocab.exampleEn: The demographic dividend won't last forever.

vocab.note: Dependents (children and older people) per 100 people of working age.
vocab.example: La tasa de dependencia aumentará cuando envejezca la población.
vocab.exampleEn: The dependency ratio will rise as the population ages.

vocab.note: B2's la natalidad is the birth rate; la tasa global de fecundidad = total fertility rate.
vocab.example: La fecundidad ha bajado en casi todo el país.
vocab.exampleEn: Fertility has fallen in almost all of the country.

vocab.note: Also a guesthouse.
vocab.example: Mi abuela cobra su pensión el primer día del mes.
vocab.exampleEn: My grandmother collects her pension on the first of the month.

vocab.note: la jubilada; A2's jubilarse (to retire). Also an adjective: un maestro jubilado.
vocab.example: Los jubilados se reúnen en la plaza los jueves.
vocab.exampleEn: The retirees meet in the square on Thursdays.

vocab.note: Mexico: Administradora de Fondos para el Retiro, a firm that manages workers' individual retirement accounts. CONSAR and the press usually write Afore; the RAE's legal dictionary (DPEJ) has AFORE, marked Mexico; this course writes it in lower case as a common noun, and every form is accepted.
vocab.example: Puedes consultar el saldo de tu afore en línea.
vocab.exampleEn: You can check your retirement-fund balance online.

vocab.note: C1's cotizar; also a price quote and a share price.
vocab.example: Le faltan cien semanas de cotización para jubilarse.
vocab.exampleEn: She needs another hundred weeks of contributions to retire.

vocab.note: A projection is conditional on its assumptions, unlike A2's el pronóstico (forecast).
vocab.example: Según las proyecciones, la población dejará de crecer.
vocab.exampleEn: According to the projections, the population will stop growing.

vocab.example: Es una proyección con un horizonte a 2050.
vocab.exampleEn: It's a projection with a 2050 time horizon.

vocab.example: La cohorte nacida en los noventa entrará pronto en la madurez.
vocab.exampleEn: The cohort born in the nineties will soon reach middle age.

vocab.note: The middle value of an ordered series. Spain also calls a highway's central strip la mediana; Mexico says el camellón.
vocab.example: La mediana es más baja que la media, porque unos pocos ganan mucho.
vocab.exampleEn: The median is lower than the mean, because a few people earn a lot.

vocab.note: A1's medio (half); B2's el promedio is the everyday word for an average. las medias = stockings, tights.
vocab.example: La media de edad del grupo es de 34 años.
vocab.exampleEn: The group's mean age is 34.

vocab.example: Su ingreso está en el percentil 90.
vocab.exampleEn: Her income is in the 90th percentile.

vocab.example: Sería arriesgado extrapolar estos datos a todo el país.
vocab.exampleEn: It would be risky to extrapolate these data to the whole country.

vocab.example: La longevidad es un logro, no un problema.
vocab.exampleEn: Longevity is an achievement, not a problem.

vocab.example: En un sistema de reparto, los trabajadores activos pagan las pensiones actuales.
vocab.exampleEn: In a pay-as-you-go system, today's workers pay current pensions.

vocab.example: Cada trabajador ahorra en su propia cuenta individual.
vocab.exampleEn: Each worker saves in their own individual account.

vocab.note: The share of a worker's last salary that the pension replaces.
vocab.example: Una tasa de reemplazo del 40 % significa cobrar menos de la mitad del último salario.
vocab.exampleEn: A replacement rate of 40% means getting less than half of your last salary.

vocab.note: Same form for both genders; plural actuariales.
vocab.example: Los cálculos actuariales estiman cuánto tiempo se pagará cada pensión.
vocab.exampleEn: Actuarial calculations estimate how long each pension will be paid.

vocab.example: En muchos pueblos no hay relevo generacional en el campo.
vocab.exampleEn: In many villages there is no new generation to take over the farms.

vocab.example: La esperanza de vida ha aumentado en las últimas décadas.
vocab.exampleEn: Life expectancy has risen in recent decades.

vocab.note: PEA, the term INEGI uses for people who work or are looking for work (check INEGI's definition).
vocab.example: La población económicamente activa incluye a quienes buscan trabajo.
vocab.exampleEn: The labor force includes people who are looking for work.

vocab.example: La pensión no contributiva no depende de haber cotizado.
vocab.exampleEn: A non-contributory pension doesn't depend on having paid contributions.

vocab.example: Sin seguridad social, muchos trabajadores no tendrán pensión.
vocab.exampleEn: Without social security, many workers won't have a pension.

vocab.example: El ahorro voluntario puede mejorar la pensión.
vocab.exampleEn: Voluntary savings can improve the pension.

vocab.note: C1's la adecuación (appropriateness) is close.
vocab.example: Se evalúa la idoneidad del registro para el lector.
vocab.exampleEn: The suitability of the register for the reader is assessed.

vocab.example: Su versatilidad le permite pasar del registro coloquial al formal sin esfuerzo.
vocab.exampleEn: Her versatility lets her move from the colloquial to the formal register effortlessly.

vocab.example: La riqueza léxica no consiste en usar palabras raras.
vocab.exampleEn: Lexical richness doesn't mean using rare words.

vocab.example: El cumplimiento de la tarea se califica en cada parte del examen.
vocab.exampleEn: Task fulfillment is marked in each part of the exam.

vocab.note: B2's la soltura (ease in speaking) is close.
vocab.example: Habla en público con desenvoltura.
vocab.exampleEn: She speaks in public with poise.

vocab.example: Dudo de la pertinencia de ese ejemplo.
vocab.exampleEn: I doubt the relevance of that example.

vocab.example: La concisión es una virtud en una cédula de museo.
vocab.exampleEn: Concision is a virtue in a museum label.

vocab.example: Necesitamos un término inequívoco.
vocab.exampleEn: We need an unambiguous term.

vocab.note: Same form for both genders; plural irreprochables.
vocab.example: Su conducta fue irreprochable.
vocab.exampleEn: Her conduct was beyond reproach.

vocab.note: Same form for both genders; plural intachables.
vocab.example: Tiene una trayectoria intachable.
vocab.exampleEn: He has a spotless record.

vocab.note: Adjective phrase; feminine casi nativa. The CEFR doesn't define C2 as near-native.
vocab.example: Tiene un nivel casi nativo, aunque se le nota un ligero acento.
vocab.exampleEn: Her level is near-native, though she has a slight accent.

vocab.note: la usuaria competente. The Spanish version of the CEFR groups C1 and C2 as usuario competente.
vocab.example: El MCER agrupa los niveles C1 y C2 bajo el nombre de usuario competente.
vocab.exampleEn: The CEFR groups the C1 and C2 levels under the name proficient user.

vocab.example: Lo que se evalúa es la exactitud, no la cantidad de palabras.
vocab.exampleEn: What is assessed is accuracy, not the number of words.

vocab.note: B2's la vacilación (hesitation) is close.
vocab.example: Respondió sin titubeos.
vocab.exampleEn: She answered without hesitation.

vocab.note: Regular: titubeo, titubeé, titubeó.
vocab.example: Cuando le preguntaron la fecha, titubeó.
vocab.exampleEn: When they asked her the date, she faltered.

vocab.note: B1's matizar (to qualify a statement).
vocab.example: Dio una respuesta matizada.
vocab.exampleEn: She gave a nuanced answer.

vocab.example: La reformulación es una forma de comprobar que entendiste.
vocab.exampleEn: Rephrasing is a way of checking that you understood.

vocab.example: En una defensa de tesis se espera el registro culto.
vocab.exampleEn: At a thesis defense, the educated register is expected.

vocab.example: Su dicción es clara, aunque habla rápido.
vocab.exampleEn: Her diction is clear, though she speaks fast.

vocab.example: La competencia pragmática incluye saber cuándo ser indirecto.
vocab.exampleEn: Pragmatic competence includes knowing when to be indirect.

vocab.example: La competencia sociolingüística te dice si tutear o no.
vocab.exampleEn: Sociolinguistic competence tells you whether to use tú or not.

vocab.note: la hablante culta.
vocab.example: El modelo no es el hablante nativo, sino el hablante culto.
vocab.exampleEn: The model isn't the native speaker but the educated speaker.

vocab.example: En la presentación se valora la claridad expositiva.
vocab.exampleEn: Clarity of exposition is valued in the presentation.

vocab.note: The Spanish version of the CEFR names C2 Maestría (as a Universidad de Alicante summary of the levels gives it, read 2026-11-17).
vocab.example: El nivel de maestría es el más alto del marco.
vocab.exampleEn: The mastery level is the highest in the framework.

vocab.note: por descarte = by elimination.
vocab.example: Llegué a la respuesta por descarte.
vocab.exampleEn: I got to the answer by elimination.

vocab.note: C1's la intención comunicativa (communicative intent).
vocab.example: Lo difícil es captar la intencionalidad del hablante.
vocab.exampleEn: The hard part is grasping the speaker's intent.

vocab.note: Feminine la emisora, which also means a radio station. B1's el remitente is the sender of a letter.
vocab.example: El emisor elige las palabras pensando en su receptor.
vocab.exampleEn: The addresser chooses the words with the receiver in mind.

vocab.note: la receptora; also a radio receiver.
vocab.example: El receptor no siempre entiende lo que el emisor quiso decir.
vocab.exampleEn: The receiver doesn't always understand what the addresser meant.

vocab.note: hacer trampa = to cheat.
vocab.example: Esa opción es una trampa: repite una palabra del texto.
vocab.exampleEn: That option is a trap: it repeats a word from the text.

vocab.example: Un buen examen no hace preguntas capciosas.
vocab.exampleEn: A good exam doesn't ask trick questions.

vocab.example: Decir que una ley obliga a ser libre es un contrasentido.
vocab.exampleEn: To say that a law forces you to be free is a contradiction in terms.

vocab.example: La primera lectura es de comprensión global.
vocab.exampleEn: The first reading is for gist comprehension.

vocab.example: Las preguntas de detalle exigen una comprensión detallada.
vocab.exampleEn: Detail questions require detailed comprehension.

vocab.note: B1's el enunciado (instructions; statement); C1's el distractor (wrong option).
vocab.example: Cada pregunta tiene tres enunciados distractores.
vocab.exampleEn: Each question has three distractor statements.

vocab.example: Respondió a la crítica con aplomo.
vocab.exampleEn: He answered the criticism with composure.

forms.present: reconduzco, reconduces, reconduce, reconducimos, reconducís, reconducen
forms.preterite: reconduje, recondujiste, recondujo, recondujimos, recondujisteis, recondujeron
forms.subjunctive: reconduzca, reconduzcas, reconduzca, reconduzcamos, reconduzcáis, reconduzcan

vocab.note: Like conducir: reconduzco, reconduje, recondujeron; subjunctive reconduzca.
vocab.example: La moderadora recondujo el debate hacia el tema.
vocab.exampleEn: The moderator steered the debate back to the topic.

vocab.example: Tras un largo tira y afloja, llegaron a un acuerdo.
vocab.exampleEn: After a long give-and-take, they reached an agreement.

vocab.note: Written with aa (contra- + argumentar); regular -ar.
vocab.example: Si te interpelan, contraargumenta con datos.
vocab.exampleEn: If you're challenged, counter-argue with data.

vocab.note: In grammar, the concessive clause (aunque…); in business, a franchise or a license.
vocab.example: Hacer una concesión no es perder la discusión.
vocab.exampleEn: Making a concession isn't losing the argument.

vocab.example: Su argumentación era sólida, pero le faltaban ejemplos.
vocab.exampleEn: His argumentation was sound, but it lacked examples.

vocab.example: La tarea pide una toma de postura clara al final.
vocab.exampleEn: The task asks for a clear stand at the end.

vocab.example: Un solo contraejemplo basta para refutar una regla absoluta.
vocab.exampleEn: A single counterexample is enough to refute an absolute rule.

vocab.note: In parliaments, a formal questioning of a minister.
vocab.example: Contestó la interpelación sin perder la calma.
vocab.exampleEn: She answered the challenge without losing her temper.

vocab.example: Tras la pregunta hubo un silencio incómodo.
vocab.exampleEn: After the question there was an awkward silence.

vocab.example: En el hospital trabaja en interpretación de enlace.
vocab.exampleEn: At the hospital she does liaison interpreting.

vocab.example: En la rueda de prensa hubo interpretación consecutiva.
vocab.exampleEn: There was consecutive interpreting at the press conference.

vocab.example: La conferencia tendrá interpretación simultánea al inglés.
vocab.exampleEn: The conference will have simultaneous interpreting into English.

vocab.note: A2's la caseta is a toll booth; la cabina telefónica = phone booth; also an aircraft cabin or a truck's cab.
vocab.example: Las intérpretes se turnan cada media hora en la cabina.
vocab.exampleEn: The interpreters take turns in the booth every half hour.

vocab.example: La confidencialidad es parte del código de ética.
vocab.exampleEn: Confidentiality is part of the code of ethics.

vocab.example: Una omisión puede cambiar el sentido de lo que dijo el médico.
vocab.exampleEn: An omission can change the meaning of what the doctor said.

vocab.note: la intermediaria; in trade, a middleman.
vocab.example: El intérprete es un intermediario, no una parte.
vocab.exampleEn: The interpreter is an intermediary, not a party.

vocab.example: La deontología del intérprete prohíbe dar consejos.
vocab.exampleEn: The interpreter's professional ethics forbid giving advice.

vocab.note: por encargo = to order, on commission. A1's la tarea is a task or homework.
vocab.example: Antes de cada encargo, preparo un glosario.
vocab.exampleEn: Before each assignment, I prepare a glossary.

vocab.note: Also to move or transfer someone or something: lo trasladaron a otra oficina.
vocab.example: Hay que trasladar el tono, no solo las palabras.
vocab.exampleEn: You have to convey the tone, not just the words.

readingList.title: La Regenta
readingList.author: Leopoldo Alas, Clarín
readingList.note: Clarín's great novel of 1884–1885 about a provincial cathedral city, its clergy and its gossip, free because it is in the public domain. The page doesn't say which edition the ebook follows or whether it is the whole novel, so check the table of contents. It is long and dense; read it with honors lesson 91 and take a chapter at a time.

readingList.title: Fortunata y Jacinta
readingList.author: Benito Pérez Galdós
readingList.note: Galdós's novel of 1887, two women's lives in the Madrid of its time, free in the public domain. Spain's Spanish of the nineteenth century, with Madrid speech in the dialogue; the page doesn't say which edition it follows. Read it with honors lesson 91 and core lesson 18.

readingList.title: Spanish books on Project Gutenberg (most downloaded)
readingList.note: The current list of the most downloaded Spanish ebooks, all in the public domain. On the day this list was checked it included Rubén Darío's Azul… (honors lesson 12h2), Horacio Quiroga's stories, Ricardo Palma's Tradiciones peruanas, Sarmiento's Facundo and Guillermo Prieto's Viaje a los Estados Unidos; the ranking changes daily, so search for a title if it isn't shown.

readingList.title: Material de Lectura
readingList.note: UNAM's series of short literary booklets, published since 1977, with almost five hundred titles of poetry, stories, narrative and essays, and digital versions online since 2007 (figures from the linked UNAM Global article, February 2024). Each booklet is an author's selection with an introduction, which makes it a good way into the writers of lessons 11 and 93. The article links the series' site but doesn't say whether every booklet is free.

readingList.title: Voces desde El Colegio Nacional (podcast)
readingList.note: A free podcast made from talks and conversations by members of El Colegio Nacional about Mexican literature; the first season had 22 episodes, the first a talk by Juan Villoro on Martín Luis Guzmán (linked article, July 2024). Academic Spanish at natural speed, good listening for lessons 9, 11 and 23; search for it in your podcast app.

readingList.title: Un idioma sin fronteras (podcast)
readingList.note: A weekly program about the Spanish language, about half an hour an episode, from Spain's international public radio (the link is a podcast directory's page, which listed a new episode in October 2026). Peninsular Spanish on the topics of module 5: neologisms, Spanish in other countries, usage. Listen in a podcast app or on RTVE's site.

readingList.title: Diccionario panhispánico de dudas (second edition)
readingList.note: The academies' guide to doubtful usage, whose second edition was presented in November 2024 with about 370 new entries and many revised ones (the linked Excélsior article); the first edition has been free on the RAE's website. Check there which edition the site shows before you cite it. Use it with lessons 3, 8, 8h2 and 20.

readingList.title: Corpus del Español (web and dialects)
readingList.author: Mark Davies
readingList.note: A searchable collection of about two billion words of Spanish from web pages in twenty-one countries, collected in 2013–2014, according to the linked comparison page (which compares it with the RAE's CORPES XXI). Use it, as lesson 4h1 shows, to see how often a word or phrase is used and in which countries; the page doesn't say whether you need to register, so check the site's terms.

readingList.title: DELE C2 (exam page)
readingList.note: What the DELE C2 diploma certifies, its three tests and their times and points. The exam changed in May 2024 and this page's table for test 1 still shows the earlier version, so use lesson 24 and the Instituto Cervantes exam site for the current tasks. Dates, fees and registration change every year.

criteria.name: Task fulfilment
criteria.description: Does the text work as a literary commentary on the assigned passage, for the stated reader and at the set length?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Situates the passage precisely in a sentence or two, states its theme clearly, analyzes rather than retells, and ends with a judgment. It covers only the assigned part, in the writer's own words, within 400–450 words.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Has every part of a commentary, in a sensible order, but one part is thin (a vague theme, a summary a little too long). Stays on the assigned passage and within the length.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Retells much of the passage before analyzing it, or leaves out the theme or the judgment, or drifts into the first part already covered by the model. The length is noticeably off.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Mostly a plot summary or a personal reaction, with no clear commentary structure, or copies the lesson's model or long stretches of the passage.

criteria.name: Interpretation and critical appraisal
criteria.description: Does the commentary explain how the passage creates its meaning, with evidence?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Analyzes at least two techniques with insight (for example how free indirect style lets us hear Clemencia, or how the narrator's irony judges Pétrea), supports each with a short, well-chosen phrase, and connects them in a reading of its own. The judgment follows from the analysis.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Identifies and explains two techniques with evidence; the interpretation is sound, though the links between points or between analysis and judgment could be closer.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Names techniques correctly but explains their effect only in general terms (es muy expresivo), or gives evidence for one point only. The judgment is asserted more than argued.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Names no technique, or misidentifies them, and offers opinions without support from the text.

criteria.name: Precision and range
criteria.description: Is the vocabulary exact, varied and right for literary analysis?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Chooses the exact word throughout, including literary terms used correctly (estilo indirecto libre, narrador omnisciente, ironía, antítesis…), and conveys finer shades of meaning (sugiere, insinúa, desmiente, matiza) without repetition.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Uses a wide range with literary terms mostly correct; occasional repetition or a general word where a precise one was available.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Relies on a limited set of evaluative words (interesante, importante, bonito), or misuses a literary term in a way that blurs a point.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Vocabulary is too general or inaccurate to carry the analysis; terms are missing or wrong.

criteria.name: Coherence and cohesion
criteria.description: Does the commentary read as a smoothly flowing, well-organized text?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Each paragraph has one clear job, and the argument builds from situation to judgment. Connectors and references (este recurso, dicho contraste) are varied and invisible; the reader never has to reread to follow.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Well organized in paragraphs with varied connectors; one transition is abrupt or one paragraph mixes two points.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Paragraphing is uneven, or connectors are few and repetitive (además, también), so the line of argument is sometimes hard to follow.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Ideas follow each other without visible order or links; it reads as a list of remarks.

criteria.name: Accuracy and register
criteria.description: Is the Spanish accurate and the register consistently formal and literary-critical?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Keeps consistent control of complex grammar (long periods with relatives, mood after evaluation and concession, the present of commentary) in an appropriate, effective formal style; any slip is minor and rare.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Accurate and formal, with a few minor slips (an accent, an agreement) that never distract; the register stays consistent.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Errors in mood, agreement or tense appear more than occasionally, or the register slips into conversational phrases.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Frequent errors make sentences hard to follow, or the register is unsuitable for a commentary.

criteria.name: Task fulfilment for the reader
criteria.description: Does the text do what the reader needs: understand what happened and know what to do next?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every point the prompt asks for is there, in an order that suits this reader (what happened, what it means for her, what comes next); the reader could act on it without asking a single question.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: All the points are there and the reader can act on them; one is brief or comes in a less helpful place.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: One required point is missing or unclear (for example why the deductible applies, or what happens next), or the text follows the report's order rather than the reader's needs.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Several points are missing, or the text is written for a different reader (another insurer, a friend).

criteria.name: Facts kept, nothing added
criteria.description: Are the source's facts and hedges relayed accurately?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every fact of the report and the two added facts is kept exactly (date, time, place, injuries, damage, the driver who fled, the deductible, the appraisal); nothing is invented, inflated or softened.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: All facts are kept; one minor detail (the time, the side of the car) is approximate but not wrong.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: One fact is lost or changed (the motorcyclist's injury made worse or left out), or one small fact is added.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Several facts are lost or wrong, or the text adds claims the report doesn't make (who was at fault, amounts).

criteria.name: Precision and reformulation
criteria.description: Is the jargon explained in exact, plain words?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Each technical term is reformulated in plain Spanish that is still exact (the deductible as the part of the cost she pays, the appraisal as the expert's assessment at the workshop); the choice of words reflects fine shades of meaning (reassuring without promising).

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The terms are explained clearly and correctly; one explanation is a little vague or leans on another technical word.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Some jargon is copied from the report unexplained, or an explanation is imprecise enough to mislead (the deductible as a fine, or as optional).

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The report's wording and abbreviations are mostly copied, or the explanations are wrong.

criteria.name: Register and tone
criteria.description: Is one register chosen for this reader and held throughout?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Usted with matching pronouns and possessives throughout; a tone that is respectful, warm and professional at once, with no colloquial slips and no stiff formulas the reader would find cold.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The register is right and consistent; one phrase is a little stiff or a little casual for the reader.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: The register wavers: a tú form, a colloquialism, or a passage that slips back into the report's style.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The register doesn't suit the reader (the report's jargon throughout, or chatty and colloquial).

criteria.name: Coherence and accuracy
criteria.description: Does the text flow, and is the language under control?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The text reads smoothly, with connectors and reference that make each step follow from the last; grammar, agreement, accents and punctuation are under consistent control.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The text flows well; there are one or two slips that a careful reread would catch and that never affect meaning.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Some jumps between ideas or repeated connectors; several errors of agreement, accents or punctuation, none of which blocks meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The order is hard to follow, or errors are frequent enough to distract the reader or blur the meaning.

criteria.name: Task and reader
criteria.description: Does the review do what the task asks, for the publication it names?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Names its publication and writes for its readers throughout; has a ficha, a description that gives nothing away, an assessment, a comparison and a verdict that says for whom; stays within 200–250 words.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Covers every part of the task for the named readers; one part (the comparison or the verdict) is brief, or the length is slightly outside the range.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: One required part is missing (no comparison, no verdict, no ficha) or the review gives away the ending; the reader is only loosely kept in mind.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Retells the work or gives a personal reaction instead of a review, or names no publication and writes for no one in particular.

criteria.name: Judgment and evidence
criteria.description: Is the assessment balanced, and is every judgment earned?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every judgment rests on a concrete, well-chosen piece of evidence described in the writer's own words; strengths and weaknesses are weighed so that the verdict follows from them; a concession makes the criticism more credible.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Gives at least two strengths and two weaknesses with evidence and one concession; one judgment is asserted rather than shown.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Judgments are mostly asserted (magistral, fallido) with little evidence, or the review is all praise or all criticism with no concession.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Gives opinions without reasons, or quotes the work at length in place of assessing it.

criteria.name: Precision and range
criteria.description: Does the vocabulary carry the exact weight the writer means?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Chooses evaluative words with their exact weight and register (loable for an intention, logrado for a result, manido or trillado for worn material, sobrio or recargado for style), uses adjective position on purpose, and softens criticism with precise, idiomatic means.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Uses a wide evaluative range accurately; one word is slightly off in weight or register, or one cliché slips in.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Relies on general words (bueno, interesante, aburrido) for most judgments, or uses several evaluative words with the wrong weight.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The vocabulary is too limited or too imprecise for the reader to know how good the writer thinks the work is.

criteria.name: Coherence and style
criteria.description: Does the review read as one smooth, well-organized text in an apt style?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Moves from describing to judging in clear paragraphs, with connectors that fit the logic and the register; the style is controlled, with at most one striking image and no stacked epithets.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Well organized and easy to follow; a transition is abrupt or one sentence is overloaded.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: The order of ideas wanders (verdict before description, judgments scattered), or the style swings between colloquial and pompous.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Reads as a list of remarks with no structure.

criteria.name: Grammatical control
criteria.description: Is the Spanish accurate, even in complex sentences?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Consistent control of complex sentences (concessions, relatives, the right mood after si bien and other connectors), agreement and spelling; any slip is rare and doesn't affect meaning.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Accurate throughout, with a few minor slips in agreement, accents or punctuation that a careful reread would catch.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Errors in mood, agreement or prepositions recur and sometimes make the reader stop.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Frequent errors make parts of the review hard to follow.

rubrics.title: Explaining a technical text to a lay reader

criteria.name: Task fulfilment for the reader
criteria.description: Does the text do what the brief asks, for the stated reader and publication?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every point the brief lists is covered in a sensible order; the title and opening tell a non-expert what the text is about and why it matters to them; the length is within the range.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: All the points are covered, with one handled briefly or slightly out of order; the opening serves the reader; the length is within or very close to the range.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: One point is missing or the text is written more for an expert than for the stated reader (unexplained terms, report structure copied); or the length is clearly outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Several points are missing, or the text doesn't address the stated reader at all, or it is far too short or long to do the job.

criteria.name: Relaying the source accurately
criteria.description: Are the source's facts, figures, hedges and limits passed on exactly, with nothing added?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every figure is right and attributed to the report; every hedge and limit keeps its strength (se estima stays an estimate; not extrapolable stays a limit); nothing is added: no new facts, prices, advice or praise.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The facts and figures are right and attributed; one hedge is slightly weakened or one minor detail is lost, without misleading the reader.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: A figure is wrong or unattributed, a key limit is missing (the water isn't drinkable; results come from one house), or the writer adds a claim the report doesn't make.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Several facts are wrong, hedges are turned into certainties, or the text mixes the writer's own claims with the report's so the reader can't tell which is which.

criteria.name: Precision and range
criteria.description: How exactly and flexibly does the writer choose words and reformulate?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Technical ideas are reformulated precisely in everyday Spanish (a first-flush diverter explained, not just named); word choice is exact and varied, with the finer shades a C2 reader expects; terms kept are defined once and used consistently.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Reformulation is clear and mostly precise; an occasional word is general where a more exact one exists, or one term is left undefined.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: The text often copies the report's terms or phrasing, or reformulations lose precision (a figure rounded misleadingly, a term explained wrongly).

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Little reformulation: long stretches repeat the source, or the vocabulary is too limited to explain the mechanism.

criteria.name: Coherence and cohesion
criteria.description: Does the text flow as a whole?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The text reads smoothly from problem to mechanism to results to limits; paragraphs have one job each; connectors and references are varied, precise and correctly punctuated.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Well organized and easy to follow, with an occasional abrupt step or a repeated connector.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: The order is mostly clear, but some paragraphs mix ideas or the links between them are thin or repetitive.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Hard to follow: ideas jump without links, or the text is a list of facts without paragraphs.

criteria.name: Accuracy and register
criteria.description: How controlled is the Spanish, and is the register right throughout?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Grammar, spelling, accents and punctuation are consistently controlled, even in complex sentences; the register suits a neighbors' newsletter from start to finish, neither bureaucratic nor too casual; numbers and units follow one convention.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Errors are rare and never affect meaning; one slip of register or one inconsistency in numbers or units.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Errors are noticeable (agreement, mood, accents) though meaning is clear, or the register shifts between the report's style and a chatty one.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Frequent errors make some sentences hard to understand, or the register is wrong for the reader throughout.

rubrics.title: Adapting a text for readers across the Spanish-speaking world (C2)

criteria.name: Task fulfilment for an international reader
criteria.description: Whether the adaptation keeps the source's information and purpose and works for readers in any Spanish-speaking country, within 200–250 words.

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Keeps every piece of information a visitor needs and the source's purpose, leaves out only what an international reader doesn't need, and stays within 200–250 words with a note.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Keeps the information and purpose; one minor detail is lost or one local item still needs a word of explanation; within the length.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Loses or changes one useful piece of information (a price, a time, a direction), or leaves several items that only a Mexican reader would follow, or misses the length or the note.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Drops or distorts several pieces of information, or rewrites the text for a different purpose, or gives no note.

criteria.name: Regional choices
criteria.description: How well each local word or reference is replaced, explained or kept, without swapping in another region's words.

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Chooses general words throughout (or gives two widespread options where none is general), explains a local item once where keeping it adds value, and never replaces a Mexicanism with a word from Spain or another single region.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Handles nearly all local items well; one choice is debatable (a word still mostly regional, or an explanation that could be shorter).

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Handles the obvious items (carro, camión, padrísimo) but misses several others, or swaps one or two in from another region (coche, ascensor) as if they were neutral.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Leaves most local items untouched, or turns the text into another region's Spanish.

criteria.name: Note on the changes
criteria.description: Whether the note explains the main changes accurately and gives reasons, as a reader or editor would need.

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Groups the changes by kind (vocabulary, slang, references, register) and gives a precise reason for each, in a sentence or two, with the exact word for the linguistic point (mexicanismo, de uso general, se entiende en toda la región).

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Explains the main changes with reasons; one kind of change is missing or one reason is vague.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Lists changes without reasons, or explains only one or two of them, or describes a change inaccurately.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The note is missing, or it doesn't match what the adaptation actually changed.

criteria.name: Coherence and register
criteria.description: Whether the adapted text reads as smooth, natural Spanish in a register that fits a museum's friendly visitor page.

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Reads as an original, smoothly flowing text, not a patched one: friendly and clear, with one consistent form of address and register, and well-chosen connectors.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Flows well; one sentence still shows the patching, or the register slips once.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Reads as the source with words swapped; register mixes friendly and stiff, or tú and usted.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Hard to follow, or the register is wrong for a visitor page throughout.

criteria.name: Accuracy and precision
criteria.description: Grammatical control, spelling and the exact word, at the level of a near-native writer.

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Consistent control of grammar and spelling, accents and punctuation included; every word is the precise one, with no calque or false friend.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Very few slips, none of which affects meaning; vocabulary is precise.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Several slips (agreement, accents, an anglicism such as "tips" kept without reason) or an imprecise word that blurs one point.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Frequent errors that make parts unclear or unreliable for a visitor.

criteria.name: Relaying the sources
criteria.description: Does the text report what each source says, accurately, with its strength and its hedges?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every relevant claim is there and attributed to the right source with a reporting verb of the right strength; every hedge is kept and none is added; facts, figures and positions are exact; at most a short phrase is quoted, and only where the wording matters.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The relevant claims are there and correctly attributed; one reporting verb is slightly too strong or too weak, or a minor point is left out, without misleading the reader.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: A hedge is lost or a claim is strengthened (a possibility reported as a fact), a figure is wrong, or a claim is attributed to the wrong source; or long stretches follow a source's wording.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Several claims are missing, distorted or unattributed, so the reader can't tell who said what.

criteria.name: Comparing and synthesizing
criteria.description: Is it one text organized by points, showing where the sources agree, differ and add?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The text is organized by points, not by sources; within each point it shows convergence, divergence and additions precisely (coinciden en, frente a, a ello se suma) and names what no source covers.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Mostly organized by points with clear comparisons; one passage summarizes a source on its own instead of comparing.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Largely three summaries in a row, with comparison only at the end, or agreements and differences stated vaguely.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No real comparison: the sources are summarized separately, or only one is used.

criteria.name: Task fulfilment, genre and reader
criteria.description: Does the text do what the instructions ask, in the genre and register they set, for the stated reader?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every part of the instructions is done, including a reasoned assessment kept apart from the sources; the genre's conventions (title, opening, closing) are used naturally; the reader gets the context they need; the length is within the range.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The task is done in the right genre and register, with one weaker part (a thin assessment, a missing convention); the length is within or very close to the range.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: A part of the task is missing (no assessment, or the writer's view mixed into the reporting), the register slips for this reader, or the length is clearly outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text doesn't match the genre, purpose or reader the instructions set, or is far too short or long.

criteria.name: Coherence and cohesion
criteria.description: Does the text flow smoothly as a whole?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Smoothly flowing: each paragraph has one function, transitions are varied and exact, references (la primera, dicha propuesta, esta última) are always clear, and punctuation supports the long sentences.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Clear and cohesive, with an occasional repeated connector or a reference the reader has to check twice.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: The line of the text is followable but connectors are few or mechanical, or some paragraphs mix points.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Hard to follow: ideas jump without links, or there are no real paragraphs.

criteria.name: Precision, range and accuracy
criteria.description: How exact, how wide and how controlled is the Spanish?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The exact word for each shade of meaning, a wide range of structures used naturally, consistent grammatical control; errors are rare slips that a careful reader barely notices; spelling and punctuation follow the norm.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Precise and varied, with a few minor errors (an accent, a preposition) that never affect meaning.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Generally accurate but with approximate words, some repetition, or errors in mood, agreement or government that a reader notices.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that make the reader stop.

criteria.name: Task fulfilment, genre and reader
criteria.description: Is it the text the notes describe, in the set genre and role, for the stated reader?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every relevant note is used, nothing that matters is invented, and the writer's private reminders are turned into the right message (or left out); the genre's conventions (subject line, greeting, closing) and one register are used throughout; the length is within the range.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: The task is done in the right genre and register, with one note underused or one minor convention missing; the length is within or very close to the range.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: A relevant note is missing, a private reminder is copied into the text, or the register shifts (tú and usted mixed); or the length is clearly outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text doesn't do what the notes and instructions ask, or the reader couldn't act on it.

criteria.name: From notes to prose
criteria.description: Are the notes turned into finished, explicit prose?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Every note becomes full, natural sentences; abbreviations and symbols are written out; what the notes leave implicit (why, for whom, what to do next) is spelled out; the order suits the reader, not the notes.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Fully written out and well ordered, with one item kept close to note form or one implicit point left unstated.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Some items remain list-like or follow the notes' order mechanically; some implicit information is missing.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Largely the notes with a few verbs added.

criteria.name: Coherence and cohesion
criteria.description: Does the text read as one piece?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Paragraphs with one function each; varied, exact connectors; no repetition the reader notices; punctuation supports the reading.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Cohesive and clear, with an occasional repeated connector or a slightly abrupt transition.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Followable, but items are listed with few links or with repetitive connectors.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Disconnected sentences or no paragraphing.

criteria.name: Precision, register and accuracy
criteria.description: How exact and how controlled is the Spanish, and is the register right for the reader?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Precise vocabulary for the setting, formulas of the genre used naturally, consistent control of grammar; errors are rare slips; spelling and punctuation follow the norm.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Precise and appropriate, with a few minor errors that never affect meaning.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Approximate words, a colloquial slip, or noticeable errors in agreement, government or punctuation.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that make the reader stop.

criteria.name: Selecting and interpreting data
criteria.description: Are the key figures chosen, compared and interpreted, with the right caution?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The figures that tell the story are chosen and compared accurately; their meaning is made clear for this reader (ratios, comparisons they can picture); possible causes are hedged; the text says what the data can't show.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Accurate selection and a sound interpretation, with one figure listed without comment or one caveat missing.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Figures are listed rather than interpreted, a key contrast is missed, or a cause is stated as fact.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The data are misread, or the text says little about them.

criteria.name: Task fulfilment, genre and reader
criteria.description: Does the text do what the instructions ask, in the genre and register they set, for the stated reader?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: The genre's conventions (title, opening that frames the data, close) are used naturally; the register suits the reader; every part of the instructions is done; the length is within the range.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Right genre and register, with one weaker part or one missing convention; the length is within or very close to the range.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Part of the task is missing, the register doesn't suit the reader, or the length is clearly outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text doesn't match the genre, purpose or reader the instructions set.

criteria.name: Coherence and cohesion
criteria.description: Does the text flow as an explanation rather than a list?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: A clear line from what the data show to what they mean; varied, exact links between figures and ideas; references always clear.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Clear and cohesive, with an occasional mechanical transition.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Mostly a sequence of figures with few links.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Hard to follow, or no structure.

criteria.name: Precision and accuracy
criteria.description: How exact and how controlled is the Spanish of numbers, comparison and hedging?

levels.label: Strong C2
levels.description: Exact language for quantities and comparison (la mitad, tres de cada diez, casi el triple), statistical terms used correctly (media, mediana, proporción), hedges varied and natural; errors are rare slips.

levels.label: C2
levels.description: Precise and varied, with a few minor errors that never affect meaning.

levels.label: Close to C2
levels.description: Repetitive data verbs, a misused statistical term, or noticeable errors.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that make the reader stop.

writing.title: Comentario de texto: un capítulo realista
writing.prompt:
Write a literary commentary (*comentario de texto*), in Spanish, on the **second part** of the original realist chapter in lesson 91, "Capítulo III. La tarde en Pétrea": from *Mientras tanto, en el balcón* to the end. The passage is repeated below. The lesson's model covers only the first part, so don't reuse its points.

1. Situate the passage in one or two sentences: where it falls in the chapter, the time and place, the characters.
2. State its theme.
3. Analyze how it works: at least two techniques, for example free indirect style, the narrator's irony and distance, a figure of speech (lesson 09), the contrast between characters or between Paris and Pétrea. Support each point with a short phrase from the passage.
4. End with a reasoned judgment of the passage.

Write 400–450 words, the length of the DELE C2's first writing task (the exam itself sets no literary commentary: this task practices critical appraisal at that length). Write for an educated reader of a literary magazine, in a formal register, in paragraphs, with varied connectors (*en cuanto a, cabe destacar, sin embargo, así, en conclusión*…). Quote only short phrases from the passage, and don't copy the lesson's model. Before you submit, reread with the checklist in the lesson and the rubric. If you study alone, rate your draft against the rubric; ask a teacher or a Spanish speaker for feedback when you can.

> Mientras tanto, en el balcón de la casa Requena, Clemencia leía el folletín de *El Eco de > Pétrea*. La condesa de la novela acababa de huir con un capitán de húsares, y Clemencia, con el > periódico sobre las rodillas, miró la calle vacía. ¡Qué fácil era todo en París! Allí las mujeres > huían, lloraban y morían de amor en el último capítulo. En Pétrea, en cambio, nadie se moría de > nada que no fuera el tifo o la edad. Tenía veintiocho años, un marido que le hablaba de algodones > y una cuñada que olía a cera de iglesia. ¿Eso era la vida? ¿Eso iba a ser, hasta el final, su > vida? > > Entonces pasó él. Clemencia supo quién era antes de verle la cara, porque en Pétrea nadie > caminaba tan deprisa. El ingeniero levantó el sombrero y siguió su camino sin detenerse. No había > sido nada, un saludo de cortesía. Y sin embargo, ¿por qué le temblaban las manos? Dobló el > periódico con cuidado, como quien esconde una carta. > > Remedios, que bordaba detrás de la persiana, no vio el saludo; lo adivinó, que en una beata es lo > mismo. A las seis, antes del rosario, ya se lo había contado al canónigo Ibarra en la sacristía, > con tantos detalles que el ingeniero, en su relato, había llegado a detenerse bajo el balcón. > > Don Leandro Ibarra era un hombre de cuarenta años, alto y pálido, a quien todo Pétrea veía ya con > la mitra de obispo. Confesaba a Clemencia desde que ella se casó y conocía sus aburrimientos > mejor que el marido. Esa misma noche visitó la casa Requena, aceptó una taza de chocolate y, como > quien no quiere la cosa, habló de las lecturas peligrosas. > > —Los folletines franceses, hija mía, son veneno con azúcar. Le traeré a usted la vida de santa > Teresa. > > Clemencia bajó los ojos y prometió leerla. El canónigo se fue satisfecho, y don Anselmo, que no > había entendido nada, lo acompañó hasta la puerta hablando del ferrocarril. > > Esa noche, Clemencia guardó la vida de santa Teresa en el ropero y el folletín debajo de la > almohada. Ella aún no sabía lo que sentía. Pétrea, en cambio, ya lo sabía todo, y al día siguiente > lo comentaría en la botica, en la sacristía y en el mercado, como se comentan en provincia las > cosas que todavía no han pasado.

writing.title: Rewrite for another reader: from claim report to a letter for the policyholder
A critical review for a named publication
writing.prompt:
Write a **critical review** in Spanish (200–250 words, the length of the DELE C2's shorter writing tasks) of a **book, play or exhibition that you know well**: something you have read or seen yourself, in any language, recent or not.

Write it for a **named publication** and its readers: choose one, real or invented, and say which at the top (for example, *la sección cultural de un diario de Guadalajara*, *una revista universitaria*, *el boletín de una biblioteca pública*). Pitch the register to those readers: neutral to formal, with room for one striking image.

Your review should:

1. Open with a *ficha*: title, author (or company, or curator), publisher or venue, year.
2. Present the work and describe what it attempts, **without giving away the ending**.
3. Assess it: at least **two strengths and two weaknesses**, each supported by a concrete piece of evidence (a scene, a character, a staging choice, a room of the exhibition), described in your own words. **Don't quote** the work: describe it.
4. Concede at least once (*si bien…, con todo…, no es…, pero sí…*) and soften at least one criticism (*se echa de menos…, se le podría reprochar…*).
5. Compare it with one other work (the author's earlier work, or something similar).
6. End with a verdict that says **for whom** the work is worth it, and why.

Use the evaluative vocabulary of lesson 10 with its exact weight (*loable* for an intention, *logrado* for a result; *manido* or *trillado* for worn material; *sobrio* or *recargado* for style), and at least one adjective whose position matters (*un viejo…, cierto…, un simple…*). Invent no facts about real people: if you're unsure of a date or a prize, leave it out.

Before you hand it in, reread it against the checklist in the lesson and rate it with the rubric. If you study alone, use the rubric to find your next step; ask a teacher or a Spanish speaker for feedback when you can.

writing.title: Explaining a technical report to lay readers
writing.prompt:
This task practices what lesson 16 taught: explaining a technical text from outside your own field to readers who aren't experts, without adding to it or losing anything from it. The input below is an original, invented test report.

**Your task.** The newsletter of a neighborhood association (*asociación de colonos*) in Guadalajara is preparing an issue on saving water. Its readers are homeowners and tenants, not engineers. Using only the report below, write an article that explains:

- what the system is and what problem it addresses;
- how it works, in plain words, defining or replacing any technical term you keep;
- what the test found, with the figures and their source;
- what the report itself says the results don't show, and what the water can't be used for.

Give your article a title. Write **200–250 words in Spanish**, in a register that suits neighbors you don't know personally. Keep every hedge and limit the report gives (*se estima, en las condiciones del ensayo, no son extrapolables*) at its own strength, and add no facts, figures, prices or recommendations of your own.

**The report** (invented):

> **Informe técnico IT-07/2026 (ficticio). Evaluación de un sistema de captación pluvial para vivienda unifamiliar** > > **Objeto.** Se evaluó el desempeño de un sistema de captación de agua de lluvia instalado en una vivienda con 90 m² de azotea en la zona metropolitana de Guadalajara, durante la temporada de lluvias de 2026 (de junio a septiembre). > > **Descripción.** El sistema consta de canaletas perimetrales, un separador de primeras lluvias, un filtro de malla de 0.5 mm, una cisterna de polietileno de cinco mil litros y una bomba que lleva el agua a un tinaco independiente. > > **Resultados.** Se captaron 41 m³ de agua en 74 días con lluvia, es decir, un promedio de unos 550 L por día de lluvia (± 15 %). Se estima que el volumen captado equivalió al 38 % del consumo total de la vivienda en el periodo (108 m³) y se destinó a usos que no requieren agua potable: sanitarios, lavado de ropa y riego. En las condiciones del ensayo, el separador de primeras lluvias redujo en un 60 % la turbidez del agua almacenada respecto de la misma instalación sin separador. > > **Limitaciones.** Los resultados corresponden a una sola vivienda y a una temporada con precipitación cercana al promedio histórico, por lo que no son extrapolables sin más a otras viviendas o zonas. El agua captada no es apta para consumo humano sin un tratamiento adicional de desinfección. El filtro requirió limpieza cada dos semanas durante la temporada.

Glosses: *la canaleta* = gutter; *el separador de primeras lluvias* = first-flush diverter, which discards the first, dirtiest water from the roof; *la cisterna* = underground or ground-level storage tank; *el tinaco* = rooftop water tank (Mexico); *la turbidez* = cloudiness of water; *apta para consumo humano* = safe to drink.

Before you hand in, go through the checklist in lesson 16 and count your words.

writing.title: Adaptation: a museum page for readers in every Spanish-speaking country
writing.prompt:
**Situation.** The Museo del Callejón in Puebla (an invented museum) wants an international version of its visitor page for travelers from every Spanish-speaking country, from Madrid to Buenos Aires. Adapt the page below for those readers, then add a short note headed *Nota sobre los cambios* that explains your main changes and why. Write **200–250 words in all** (adapted text and note together), in Spanish.

**How to work.** Follow lesson 17's method: find every local item (Mexicanisms, slang, anglicisms, local places, prices, times); for each one, use a general word, explain it once, or leave it out if the reader doesn't need it; don't replace Mexican words with Spain's or Argentina's; make references explicit (currency, 24-hour times); keep the information, the purpose and a friendly but clear register. In the note, group your changes by kind and give a reason for each kind. This is practice for the adaptation skill, not an exam task.

**The page** (invented, in Mexican Spanish):

> **Antes de tu visita**
>
> ¡Qué onda! Si ya te animaste a venir al Museo del Callejón, aquí van unos tips para que tu visita esté padrísima. > > **Horarios y boletos.** Abrimos de martes a domingo, de 10 a 6. El boleto cuesta 80 pesos; los domingos la entrada es libre para nacionales. Lo puedes comprar en la taquilla o en línea, con tarjeta o en efectivo. Si eres estudiante, trae tu credencial y te hacemos descuento. > > **Cómo llegar.** Desde el zócalo son unas cinco cuadras caminando. Si vienes en camión, bájate en la parada de la 5 Oriente. Si vienes en carro, aquí no hay estacionamiento, pero a una cuadra hay uno público que no está caro. > > **Durante la visita.** Las mochilas grandes se quedan en los lockers de la entrada. Puedes tomar fotos, pero sin flash. Si necesitas el baño, los sanitarios están junto al elevador, en planta baja. Si vienes con niños, pregunta por el recorrido infantil de los sábados. > > **Para terminar.** En el patio hay una cafetería donde venden aguas frescas, nieves y antojitos poblanos; te recomendamos las chalupas. Ahorita estamos remodelando la tienda, así que los recuerditos los vendemos en la taquilla. ¡No te vayas sin subir a la terraza: la vista de los volcanes está bien chida!

*Nacionales* = Mexican citizens; *la credencial* = (student) ID card; *el zócalo* = the main square of a Mexican city; *la 5 Oriente* = a street in Puebla's grid (5 Oriente Street); *las nieves* = sorbet-like ices; *las chalupas* = small fried tortillas with toppings, a Puebla specialty.

writing.title: Writing task 1 practice: an article from three sources
writing.prompt:
This task has the shape of DELE C2 writing task 1 as the 2024 sample exam is described: one radio excerpt with two experts and two written texts, synthesized for a stated reader. The sources below are **scaled down**: the exam's recording and texts are longer. In the exam you hear the recording and can't read it, so ask someone to read the radio excerpt aloud to you while you take notes (the official guide says how many times you hear it in the exam). On your own, read it once at normal speed, close it, and work from your notes.

**Your task.** The residents' association of the historic center of San Andrés (an invented city) publishes a monthly newsletter. Write an article for its readers, residents who don't specialize in the topic, that presents what the three sources say about night-time noise and the measures proposed, compares them, and ends with your own assessment. Give it a title. Write 400–450 words in Spanish. Attribute every claim, keep each source's hedges, add none, and quote no more than a short phrase.

**Source 1: a radio excerpt** (invented; all figures invented)

> **Conductor:** En el centro histórico de San Andrés, los vecinos se quejan del ruido nocturno desde hace años. Nos acompañan la ingeniera acústica Sofía Lara y el economista Daniel Ortega. Sofía, ¿de cuánto ruido hablamos? > > **Lara:** Las mediciones que hicimos en tres calles superan de noche los niveles que recomiendan las guías de salud, sobre todo los fines de semana. Pero ojo: medimos en pocos puntos y durante un solo mes, así que no lo generalizaría a todo el centro. > > **Ortega:** Nadie niega el problema. Lo que pido es que no se olvide que los bares y restaurantes dan trabajo a cientos de personas, muchas de ellas jóvenes. Un cierre a la una de la mañana podría reducir sus ingresos, aunque todavía no hay un estudio que lo cuantifique. > > **Lara:** Hay soluciones intermedias. Un buen aislamiento acústico reduce mucho el ruido que sale de los locales; el problema es el ruido de la calle: la gente que sale a fumar o a esperar un taxi. > > **Ortega:** En eso coincidimos. Yo apostaría por reglas claras para todos y por inspecciones, más que por horarios más cortos. > > **Lara:** Yo no descartaría ajustar los horarios en las calles más afectadas, al menos como prueba.

**Source 2: a news item** (invented)

> *El cabildo discutirá el horario de los bares del centro*
>
> El cabildo de San Andrés discutirá la próxima semana una propuesta para que los bares del centro histórico cierren a la una de la mañana de domingo a jueves y a las dos los fines de semana. La regidora que la presentó asegura que la medida "devolverá el descanso a los vecinos". La cámara local de restauranteros se opone y estima que el cambio afectaría a unos 300 empleos, aunque no ha explicado cómo llegó a esa cifra. Según el ayuntamiento, el año pasado se recibieron más de 900 quejas por ruido en el centro, el doble que hace cinco años.

**Source 3: an opinion column** (invented)

> *Cerrar antes no es la solución*
>
> Vivo en el centro y toco la guitarra en sus bares desde hace diez años. El ruido que de verdad no nos deja dormir no sale de los locales bien aislados, sino de la calle a la hora del cierre: si todos cierran a la misma hora, todos salimos a la vez. Por eso propongo horarios escalonados, apoyo económico para insonorizar los locales y más transporte nocturno, para que nadie tenga que esperar media hora en la banqueta. Cerrar antes solo cambiaría el ruido de hora.

Glosses: *el cabildo* (town council); *la regidora* (council member); *la cámara de restauranteros* (restaurant owners' association); *escalonado* (staggered); *insonorizar* (to soundproof); *la banqueta* (Mexico: sidewalk).

Before you hand in, check your article against lesson 21: a grid of sources and points, one paragraph per point, verbs of the right strength, your view kept apart, and the word count.

writing.title: Writing task 2 practice: an e-mail from notes
writing.prompt:
This task has the shape of DELE C2 writing task 2 as the 2024 sample exam is described: you turn a list of notes into a finished text in a set genre and role.

**Your task.** You coordinate the education department of the (invented) Museo del Sureste, which is showing the exhibition from lesson 22. Your director left you the notes below. Write the formal e-mail to the principals of the city's middle schools (*secundarias*) that the notes describe, in Spanish, 200–250 words, with a subject line. Use every relevant note, spell out what the notes leave implicit, leave out the director's reminders to you, and keep one register (*usted / ustedes*) throughout.

**The notes**

> - correo a directores de secundarias (zona centro)
> - expo "El cacao: bebida y moneda" · 3 salas · hasta el 30 de junio > - visitas guiadas gratis p/ grupos escolares · mar–vie, 9 a 13 h > - máx. 35 alumnos x grupo + 2 docentes > - taller 40 min: hacer espuma c/ molinillo (en el patio, NO comida en salas) > - reservar mín. 2 semanas antes → formulario en la web o por tel. (núm. en la firma, no repetir) > - guía didáctica PDF p/ docentes (antes de la visita) > - accesibilidad: rampas en todo el museo; cédulas en braille en sala 1 > - ¡no prometer transporte! (no tenemos presupuesto)

Glosses: *p/* (para); *x* (por); *c/* (con); *la prepa / la secundaria* (high school / middle school); *el docente* (teacher).

When you finish, compare your e-mail with the notes line by line: is every item there, in full sentences, in an order that suits a busy principal?

writing.title: Writing task 3 practice: an article from data
writing.prompt:
This task has the shape of DELE C2 writing task 3 as the 2024 sample exam is described: a text in a set genre that explains data from tables or charts.

**Your task.** A company in Guadalajara publishes a monthly newsletter for its employees. The human resources department asks you for a short article (200–250 words, in Spanish) that explains the results of the survey below to colleagues of all ages: what the data show, what they might mean, and what they don't show. Give it a title. Choose and interpret the key figures rather than listing them all, and keep your caution where the data can't prove a cause. The article informs; it doesn't sell any product.

**Survey of 1,000 employees of several companies (invented data)**

| Edad | Hace ahorro voluntario para el retiro |
|---|---|
| 18–29 años | 9 % |
| 30–44 años | 17 % |
